events.title: Anthropic in talks with neocloud Nscale over second multibillion-dollar deal, source tells CNBC
events.summary: Anthropic is in talks with U.K. neocloud Nscale for a second multibillion-dollar deal to lease computing capacity, a source told CNBC. The two companies previously inked a similar deal for a data center on the same site in the U.S. Publicly listed neoclouds have recently come under pressure, amid concerns over heavy debt. Anthropic is in talks with U.K. neocloud Nscale for a second multibillion-dollar deal to lease computing capacity at a site in the U.S., a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The agreement would cover a second 460-megawatt data center at the same West Virginia site as the first deal, the person said. The person asked not to be named because they were not authorized to discuss the talks. The deal could be worth around $45 billion, the person said. CNBC reported the first deal in August. Bloomberg first reported that Anthropic and Nscale were in talks over a second deal. Anthropic declined to comment. Nscale has been approached for comment. Nvidia -backed Nscale is one of several companies that have emerged in recent years to develop the infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence. The company builds or leases data centers and sells computing capacity to hyperscalers and AI labs. Rivals CoreWeave and Nebius have seen their shares drop 28% and 27%, respectively, in the past month, amid concerns over heavy borrowing. Nscale has faced its own challenges. On Sunday, U.K. newspaper The Telegraph reported that Microsoft had pulled out of a deal to anchor an Nscale data center just outside London, amid delays connecting to the country's power grid. An Nscale spokesperson told CNBC that it remained "committed" to the project and was "exploring alternative power sources for the site." "Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," the spokesperson added. The U.K.-based company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange in September. Anthropic said earlier this year that growing demand for its Claude AI models and products has caused "inevitable strain" on its infrastructure. Since then, it has announced a flurry of deals with infrastructure partners to try and increase its computing capacity, including major agreements with Advanced Micro Devices , Elon Musk's SpaceX , Google and Broadcom .

events.title: What options traders expect from SpaceX earnings after the bell
events.summary: Traders are expecting more gains for SpaceX stock after it reports earnings after the bell. Options market-makers are pricing about a 6% swing for SpaceX after the event, according to Cboe LiveVol data. While there are about as many open call contracts as puts on the stock, daily trading volume has leaned toward calls the past week, Barchart data shows. It's been a busy three months for SpaceX . The company delivered four astronauts to the International Space Station in record time, expanded its mobile network spectrum, is reportedly eyeing a $40 billion debt deal to buy Nvidia chips, and CEO Elon Musk said he plans to give shares to every kid in America next year. Traders think all that means more gains for the stock after it reports earnings after the bell Tuesday. Options market-makers are pricing about a 6% swing for SpaceX after the event, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's less than half the 13% it erased after its inaugural report in August, a selloff that turned out to be the low for the shares, which rallied 60% the following two months before reversing before dropping as much as 19% the past two weeks. Among the 1.1 million contracts traded Monday – 20% higher volume than the 30-day average – 665,000 were calls, with more bought than sold, according to Cboe LiveVol. Traders also bought more calls than puts, and sold more puts than they bought, the data show, decidedly bullish flow as the space giant heads into its second earnings. The most popular call contract for Friday expiry was the 170-strike, which needs about a 14% rally, according to SpotGamma data. There was also notable buying in the 190-strike call for month-end, a 40-cent contract that needs SpaceX to rally 29% to break even. For that to happen, SpaceX will have to rally through two more share lockup periods: a scheduled release two days after earnings, as well as another on October 26 that together will amount to over 1.6 billion eligible shares for sale. So far that hasn't been a problem for the stock, as releases on Sep. 9, 10, and 24 had no discernible effect on the share price. Implied volatility is much lower in SpaceX going into this report compared to last quarter, as reflected in the implied move. SpaceX traded with an IV of 62 on Monday, compared to above 110 before releasing second-quarter earnings, according to ThinkOrSwim.

events.title: Three months of PM Andy Burnham: Can he sustain the ‘hope vibe’?
events.summary: The UK’s new prime minister has made big promises and is a popular leader, but there is still talk of an early election. Andy Burnham’s UK foreign policy tested by Brexit, US ties and Iran war London, United Kingdom – There was a moment towards the end of Andy Burnham’s conference speech in Liverpool that, through silence, spoke volumes. The new prime minister and Labour leader fell quiet. list 1 of 4 UK PM Andy Burnham says it is ‘clear’ Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote list 2 of 4 UK PM Andy Burnham vows to renegotiate post-Brexit trade deal with EU list 3 of 4 UK PM Andy Burnham met Man City chairman during time as Manchester mayor list 4 of 4 UK police rule out probe into Palestine Action post by PM adviser’s wife For 20 seconds he stood, saying nothing. He hadn’t forgotten his words. He was gathering his emotions for a passage of the speech he hadn’t been able to make it through in rehearsals without crying. Burnham’s father had died just a couple of weeks before, and this was the section where he’d talk about it. As the audience realised what was coming they stood, applauding, and urging him on with shouts of “Come on, lad!’ and “Come on, Andy!” Thanking them, he composed himself and continued. Conference speeches are theatre, and contemporary British political standards require that a leader be relatable. But there’s little doubt that Andy Burnham handled this moment with an emotional register that struck many as genuine. His predecessor Keir Starmer sometimes came across as wooden, almost robotic and uncomfortable in front of cameras. Burnham, the seventh prime minister in 10 years, is more emotional. He talks big ideas and grand solutions and relishes the opportunity to communicate. In the vibes-denominated currency of modern political discourse, this matters. The polls speak for themselves. Politico’s Poll of Polls had the Labour Party retake top spot shortly after Burnham became PM – a position it has not relinquished since. At the end of September, Ipsos found Andy Burnham to be the only politician with a positive net favourability rating. YouGov’s polling also judges him the most popular politician in the UK at the moment. But to keep up, Burnham must deliver tangible change before the next general election. Unless he calls one early, that will be 2029. According to political analyst Sam Freedman, “So many in Westminster keep coming back to an early election, despite Burnham ruling it out … No one can quite figure out how Burnham keeps the hope vibe going for three more years with relatively little visible progress.” ‘Going back to what Labour was in the 50s’ In the Welsh town of Port Talbot, terraces of workers’ cottages cluster beside the UK’s largest steelworks. Like much of Wales, Port Talbot did vote Labour for a century – until elections for the Senedd Cymru or Welsh Parliament in May. Labour was beaten to an unprecedented third place behind Plaid Cymru’s nationalists, and the anti-immigration Reform UK. But that was before Burnham took over. Myles Lewis, who organises social walks for the town’s elderly, told Al Jazeera that Labour had not convinced people on immigration, and Starmer’s communication wasn’t good enough. “[But now], it’s kind of going back to what Labour was in the 50s and 60s, where they actually looked after the working-class people. I do believe Andy Burnham can get there because I think he has the interests of the working-class people.” In his first weeks in power, Burnham delivered a quick flurry of eye-catching, domestic, cost-of-living-focused policies. He capped bus fares, cut the value-added tax (VAT) on electricity bills, and cut business rates for pubs. He said that he would end street homelessness, reindustrialise the country, take services back into public control, and start the biggest build-out of social housing since World War II. The mayor of Greater Manchester for nine years, Burnham supports the devolution of powers from Westminster to the UK’s nations and regions. In July, he announced mayors could keep a share of business rates from April 2027 and of income tax from 2028. And his conference speech in September set out the contours of some big political battles to come, including a national social care service, free at the point of use, paid for by changing the UK pensions’ triple lock from 2030. It would arrive next parliament. Burnham also pitched a national commission on electoral reform, with a manifesto commitment to overhaul the voting system. And he delivered a blunt verdict on Brexit: that it “has done more harm than good”. He wouldn’t rule out an in-out referendum, or a pledge for the UK to rejoin the European Union, in Labour’s next manifesto, he said. On foreign affairs, there is less blue water between Burnham and his predecessors. When he travelled to Ukraine in August, the UK’s new prime minister came with a headline-grabbing gift – British know-how to build the long-range SCALP missile.

events.title: HPE Spaceborne Computer 4 to launch AI straight to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s FLIP rover
events.summary: Forget space datacenters. Before the end of the year, Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) will have AI running on the Moon. This isn’t some exec’s loony fantasy either. HPE has been building orbital compute platforms for the International Space Station (ISS) for years. Now, it’s sending its fourth-gen Spaceborne Computer to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s Flex Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP) lunar rover. Part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, the rover is set to be deployed near the Moon’s south pole by the Voyager Technologies Griffin-1 lander later this year. Assuming a safe landing on the surface, FLIP will serve as a test bed for a range of emerging technologies including HPE’s latest space-faring compute platform. Specifically, Spaceborne Computer 4, which for the sake of brevity we’ll just call SBC4, will carry out a number of AI and HPC-centric experiments during the rover’s year long mission on the lunar pole. What we know about SBC4 so far The actual silicon powering SBC4 is still a bit of a mystery. We’re told the reason for the secrecy largely comes down to the high-risk nature of the mission. If the hardware fails, HPE’s compute partner doesn’t want their name tied to it. No guts but for the glory, we suppose, though Kioxia doesn't seem too worried. What we do know is that it is equipped with a low-power central processing unit, a graphics processor, and will be equipped with a pair of mirrored Kioxia SSDs totaling 1 TB of capacity. That said, while it'll be among the most powerful computers on the Moon, it's still a pretty small system. The FLIP rover doesn't have an unlimited power or thermal budget. The rover's radiators can only dissipate so much heat. Measuring in at around 5x10 inches and about an inch thick, while not a particularly big system, it's still large enough to house any number of existing compute platforms. For all we know, it could be powered by Nvidia’s GB10, AMD’s Xilinx Versal AI, or the guts of an old smartphone. We won't know until the thing powers up. Less of a mystery is what SBC4 will be running and where. NASA plans to run a series of tuned LLM tests on the system, including a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to assist with searching and interpreting onboard documents. Additionally, the system will be tasked with running machine learning algorithms against camera and LiDAR data. However, without knowing how large these LLMs are, it’s hard to infer the nature of the underlying hardware. We’re told to expect more details about the chips powering SBC4 once it’s up and running. Alongside AI, SBC4 will also run several high performance computing (HPC) benchmarks designed to push the system to its limits. These benchmarks include high performance Linpack (HPL) and high performance conjugate gradient (HPCG), which means HPE and Astrolab will soon hold the distinction of the first Top500 submission made from a celestial body. Not only do HPE’s systems power some of the fastest supercomputers on Earth, but they could soon hold the number one spot on the Moon — not that that’s a particularly high bar. Beyond bragging rights, a workload like HPL could have other benefits like helping to keep the rover from icing over during the roughly 14-day-long night cycles the rover will repeatedly endure over the course of its mission. Hardening SBC4 for the Moon The Rover and by extension SBC4 will have to contend with extreme vibration stresses during launch and landing, wild temperature swings, not to mention cosmic rays and solar radiation since the Moon lacks the thick atmosphere and magnetic field that shields terrestrial compute. But, as it turns out, radiation might not be as big a problem as you’d think. According to Fernandez, SBC4 is largely assembled from off-the-shelf components, including the solid state drives. The compute platform is using standard Kioxia BG6 M.2 drives with the main line of protection being a software RAID 1. “It’s a silent mirror. The boot order is to try this and if something has happened to it, go here,” Mark Fernandez, HPE’s chief scientist of space tech and solutions, explained. “With our nine years' experience in the Space Station using drives, we’ve even convinced them we don’t need to do anything special for space.” However, this wasn’t always the thinking. As we reported at the time, early Spaceborne Computers suffered from high SSD failure rates. But as it turned out, so did the same drives deployed terrestrially. The cause of the failures wasn’t cosmic rays or energetic particles from the Sun, but rather bad capacitors, he explained. “I’ve had zero SSD failure since 2019.” While off-the-shelf electronics are surprisingly radiation resistant — at least within FLIP’s mission parameters — HPE has invested heavily in software based redundancy and recovery. Fernandez calls this “hardware hardening in software.” The idea being that the spare CPU cycles are used to continuously monitor and compare hardware metrics against a state table. If a parameter exceeds the specified threshold, SBC4 will take action to protect itself. “At a high level, I say, I like to be running at full speed. I can't do that. I'll run at a slower speed. If I can't do that, I'd like to be booted, but not running anything, and then maybe the server will recover. And worst case, I'd like to be powered down rather than get destroyed,” he explained. At the edge of the edge FLIP is primarily intended as a proof of concept vehicle, which is to say it’s a test bed for technologies that may eventually find their way to the Moon on other missions. The inclusion of SBC4 reflects the realities of operating at the far edge of Earth’s orbit. The latency between Earth and the Moon is nowhere near as bad as Mars's up to 44 minute round-trip communication time, but even 2.5 seconds makes real-time control from Houston, or in this case Astrolab’s mission control, which by the way is also powered by HPE's Greenlake Private Cloud stack, in Hawthorne, California a bit unwieldy. Further complicating matters is the bandwidth afforded the rover. When Artemis 2 traveled around the Moon earlier this year, astronauts weren’t able to send back high-res photographs in real time due to the lack of bandwidth. It was only after the mission was on its way back to Earth that they were able to establish a big enough pipe to transmit the full-res images. For this reason, SBC4 is designed to operate “at the edge of the edge,” Fernandez said. Given the bandwidth constraints, it’s far easier to process as much of the data and telemetry gathered by the rover’s array of cameras, lidars, and environmental sensors locally. “It’s important to ship back insight to Earth rather than all the raw data whenever possible. So having the edge compute capability to process the raw data locally, save on bandwidth back to Earth,” Astrolab CEO Jaret Matthews said. Matthews isn’t the only one to share this perspective. events.title: Google Cloud outage hits UK banks
events.summary: Online services for a number of U.K. banks in and around London are being disrupted by a Google Cloud outage LONDON -- Online services for a number of U.K. banks in and around London were disrupted by a Google Cloud outage Tuesday. The cloud outages began just after 2 a.m. eastern, or 6:08 a.m. GMT. The center of the outage is London, but the impact can extend outside of the U.K. if apps in other countries rely on London-based infrastructure. “Our engineering team continues to investigate the issue,” Google Cloud said early Tuesday. It said that it was starting to see a recovery of services. events.title: ServiceNow CFO: Overwork doesn’t make you a better leader
events.summary: Good morning. Being a CFO today can require the stamina of an elite athlete. Yet many corporate leaders fail to apply one of the most important lessons athletes learn: recovery is essential to sustained performance. Gina Mastantuono, president and CFO of ServiceNow , a Fortune 500 company, has spoken about the benefits of fitness for both personal health and leadership, pointed to a workplace culture in which senior employees still equate overwork with commitment. “There’s always been this idea that if you have to work 14-hour days and get four hours of sleep, that shows you’re working the hardest and deserve the most,” she said. “That is such a terrible example for the people around us.” Mastantuono spoke during a panel at the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit with Olympic champion Janet Evans, chief athlete officer for the LA28 organizing committee, and Alicia Hatch, Deloitte’s U.S. sports chief commercial officer and women’s sports leader. For Mastantuono, recovery isn’t a distraction from high performance; it’s a prerequisite for it. Just as the body needs rest to recover from exercise, professionals need time to recharge if they want to remain effective over the long term. Prioritizing recovery has helped her improve her work-life balance, listen more thoughtfully instead of reacting impulsively, and remain composed under pressure. Those benefits extend beyond the individual to the teams she leads. “When we do focus on taking care of ourselves, then we are much better bosses, much better colleagues, much better parents,” she said. But the lessons athletes bring to leadership extend beyond recovery. They also learn to make decisions under pressure, adapt to changing circumstances, and keep moving toward a goal despite uncertainty. “How many of you have ever made a high-stakes call with incomplete information and a lot of people watching?” Hatch asked the audience. “We face this every single day.” She continued, “94% of female C-suite executives played sports growing up. And there’s a reason for that.” Sports teaches us confidence, teamwork, resilience. “But it’s also an amazing simulator for making decisions under pressure, performing continuously, even with changing circumstances,” Hatch said. Evans offered a practical example of how an athlete’s mindset can translate into leadership. When LA28 chairman Casey Wasserman approached her in 2015 about joining the effort to bring the Olympics to Los Angeles, she knew the city faced a formidable competitor in Paris for the 2024 Games. Rather than abandon the goal when Paris emerged as the likely winner, the team shifted its focus to securing the 2028 Games. Evans said that experience reflected the qualities athletes bring to leadership: persistence, faith in a goal, and the ability to pivot when circumstances change. Pursuing ambitious goals, she suggested, requires a willingness to take risks, work through setbacks, and adapt along the way. That mindset may be particularly relevant as women’s sports gain commercial momentum. Deloitte projected earlier this year that global revenues from women’s sports would reach at least $3 billion in 2026, a 340% increase over four years. Soccer and basketball are expected to lead, each accounting for 35% of global women’s sports revenue. As women’s sports continue to grow, the leadership lessons associated with athletics are increasingly relevant beyond the playing field. For executives, that means not only developing the resilience to perform under pressure, but also recognizing when to step back and recover. You can watch the complete panel session here .  Sheryl   Estrada Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Data center stocks slide as Korea IPO plunges 30%, pressuring tech sentiment
events.summary: Elice Group has been compared to CoreWeave, the U.S. neocloud at the center of last week's sell-off. Concerns about overcapacity in computing power amid lackluster AI revenues are persisting. Data center stocks struggled Tuesday following a lackluster initial public offering overnight from a South Korean cloud company that has been compared to U.S. neocloud CoreWeave. The bearish sentiment spilled into U.S. tech equities. CoreWeave shares lost 4% just after market open Tuesday; Nebius shed about 4%. Iren was down about 6%. HSBC said in a Monday note that the troubles for the heavily levered CoreWeave are not going away. "Debt market woes and moderating LLM revenues are exacerbating structural concerns for neoclouds ," HSBC analyst Abhishek Shukla wrote. Shukla has a reduce rating on CoreWeave with a price target of $39, implying 36.5% downside. Elice's IPO was small, having raised just $150 million, according to Reuters . Its market cap also equates to roughly $1.3 billion. The company provides a range of AI-related services, including cloud computing equipment, training libraries and application interfaces for businesses. Despite its size, investors are likely looking at it as a a signal of investor sentiment toward the AI build-out. Trouble for neoclouds, which some investors see as the weakest link in the emerging AI value chain, started earlier this month with less-than-stellar revenues reported by the private AI algorithm companies and pressure from higher interest rates. Frontier model Anthropic showed a deceleration in quarterly revenues, with sales dropping from 140% growth in the second quarter to 45% in the third. OpenAI also disappointed, reporting revenue that was $20 billion shy of what analysts expected, analyst Stephanie Roth at Wolfe said in a Sunday note. Profitability concerns for AI algorithm companies were the focus of a report last week from advisory firm Gartner predicting that 80% of neoclouds could cease independent operations by 2030. "Our research indicates that enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures" between 2027 and 2030, Will Sommer, senior director analyst at Gartner, said. Gartner stood by its analysis in a Monday interview with CNBC. "At the moment, we have more compute capacity than we have demand, and we have a lot of the tokens and processing power being given away in freemium solutions," Gartner chief forecaster John Lovelock told CNBC. "Everyone in the AI race is running for a last-man standing position. Pretty much every market that Gartner is tracking in our AI race is likely to collapse down to a duopoly." Chip stocks are also feeling some pain on Tuesday. Micron is down close to 2% as of market open; AMD is down about 1.5%; and Nvidia is down about 1%.

events.title: General Motors beats Wall Street's Q3 earnings expectations, narrows full-year guidance
events.summary: General Motors beat Wall Street’s expectations on the top- and bottom-lines. The Detroit automaker raised its free cash flow expectations and narrowed its 2026 full-year guidance. GM also announced a new multiyear stock buyback of $20 billion, but didn’t give a specific timeframe for the repurchase. DETROIT — General Motors narrowed its 2026 earnings guidance and raised its free cash flow expectations after beating Wall Street's third-quarter expectations. The Detroit automaker also announced a new multiyear stock buyback of $20 billion after GM completed a $6 billion share repurchase program that was announced in January. GM did not disclose a specific time to complete the program. Despite the positive news, GM stock was off roughly 6% during early trading Tuesday as the company's outlook missed Wall Street's expectations. Wall Street analysts were mixed before the report on whether GM would raise its guidance Tuesday amid concerns of slowing sales and rising commodity costs. Analysts' expectations included a midpoint of $13.41 per share for the year compared with GM's new $13.25 per share midpoint, according to LSEG. Several analysts in investor notes Tuesday said GM's third-quarter results were solid, but raised concerns about whether higher costs and pressures on vehicle pricing would limit earnings growth next year. Here's how GM performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.70 adjusted vs. $3.63 expected Revenue: $50.02 billion vs. $48.7 billion expected GM's new guidance includes adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $14.5 billion and $15.5 billion, or $12.75 to $13.75 adjusted earnings per share, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of between $11.5 billion and $12.5 billion. That compares with its raised guidance from July that included adjusted EBIT of between $14 billion and $16 billion, or $12 to $14 adjusted EPS, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of $9.5 billion to $11.5 billion. "I think the market's been pretty consistent from what we've said all year," GM CFO Paul Jacobson told CNBC's Phil LeBeau . "Our fourth quarter's going to be down sequentially. ... I think the fact that we're able to hold our guidance in the face of that late inflationary pressure in the year is another sign of the GM team executing really well." GM on Tuesday said it expects commodity inflation costs to be around $2 billion, which was the high end of its previous guidance. That includes higher costs for logistics and dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, chips that are impacting multiple industries . While the inflationary costs were at the automaker's high end of guidance, GM said its gross tariff costs are expected to be at the low end of its expected $2.5 billion to $3.5 billion range. Warranty costs are expected to be at high end between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, GM said. Jacobson said vehicle pricing is relatively flat as inflationary costs continue to increase. He said the company would assess where consumers are in the coming year when deciding if it should pass costs along by raising prices more than normal. "GM is performing well, and we are working hard to continue our momentum despite growing inflationary pressures through strategic investments in new products and services, and through improved quality and operating efficiency," GM CEO Mary Barra said Tuesday in a letter to shareholders. The automaker also said the costs of its pullback in all-electric vehicles announced last year were "substantially completed," saying it has recorded $11.2 billion in such charges since the second half of last year, including paying $4.6 billion of $7.4 billion in cash through the third quarter. The company's net income attributed to stockholders was $3.3 billion during the third quarter, up roughly $2 billion from a year earlier. GM's North American operations continued to lead the automaker's results, accounting for $3.6 billion of its $4.1 billion in adjusted EBIT results during the third quarter. GM's 2025 third-quarter results included $48.59 billion in revenue, net income attributable to stockholders of $1.3 billion and earnings per share of $2.80 adjusted.

events.title: Apple shares aren't cheap. Here's how to get long for less
events.summary: Among Jim Cramer's many famous phrases, his one about Apple often stands out: Own it. Don't trade it. The saying speaks to the company's enduring ability to overcome any obstacle, whether it's concerns about new products or worries about the global economy. The tech giant recently topped $5 trillion for the first time and is closing in on Nvidia as the world's most valuable company. More gains could be ahead. Apple recently described the demand for the iPhone Duo, the long awaited foldable iPhone as "nothing short of extraordinary" after pre-orders opened last Friday. The demand was so great, that estimated delivery times pushed back to late January (so much for a stocking stuffer) within minutes of orders being accepted. Combine this with Homeview, the company's new smart hub, new MacBook Pro models and iPads with OLED displays and the Mac studio and associated chips released several weeks ago and the hardware landscape for the most successful consumer electronics company in history is starting to compete with the AI trade for investors' attention. The only problem is that the company already has a lot of good news baked into its valuation. Compounding this hardware momentum is the software catalyst. The deep integration of Apple Intelligence, including upgraded Siri AI and Visual Intelligence, means that Apple is becoming part of the AI story, with the benefit that, on a relative basis, they haven't had the enormous Capex that is concerning those investors who are concerned that the AI trade is getting frothy as many companies use all their organic cash flow (Amazon, Alphabet) or substantially more than their organic cash flow (Oracle). Apple's anticipated revenues for FY2027 exceeds $500 billion. Expected EBITDA exceeds $180 billion, but the company's capex is paltry relative to the other megacaps at only $13.5 billion in Capex. Result? $156 billion in anticipated free cash flow, and the company reported ~$62 billion in net cash when they reported results for the quarter ended June 27th. The primary headwind for AAPL is valuation. With a $5 trillion market capitalization, Apple is contending with the law of large numbers. Moving the needle at this scale requires monumental revenue beats that are increasingly difficult to engineer. This is particularly true as the stock is already priced quite richly. AAPL's trading at nearly 36 FY2027 EPS estimates of 9.59 well above the long-term average multiple. Apple options are priced above average too, and that may be the good news, because elevated short term premium can help finance the purchase of longer dated optionality. With Apple supported by an extraordinary string of recent product releases and massive free cash flow, but possibly suppressed by high valuations, this could be an excellent opportunity for a call spread risk reversal. The Short Legs: Sell December 310 puts and the December 375 calls Selling the shorter dated December 310-puts and December 375 calls offsets the cost of buying the longer dated February calls. Ideally, you want Apple shares to stay between the two, short strikes by December expiration and above $360 by February expiration. One note of caution. By selling that downside put will tie up some margin, you could be on the hook to buy the stock at the put's strike by expiration. If AAPL chops sideways as it digests its valuation, the short strangle expires worthless, lowering the cost basis of your long. events.title: Marco Rubio says ‘we’re about as close as you can be’ to an India trade deal after talks in Mumbai
events.summary: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio held talks with India’s foreign minister in Mumbai on Tuesday as the two countries seek to deepen energy cooperation and move closer to finalizing a trade deal. India and the United States seek to revive trade negotiations stalled for months by tensions over American tariffs and the Indian government’s purchases of Russian oil. “We’re very, very close. I would say we’re about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement,” Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday. “I think there’s a small number of items left to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly.” Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said that they discussed ways to strengthen bilateral ties in trade, energy, technology and defense, along with talks on regional developments. Jaishankar and Rubio also held a trilateral meeting with United Arab Emirates Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who also was visiting India. Rubio said that the three officials met to discuss “regional energy security and advance our shared economic priorities.” Washington imposed tariffs of up to 50% on most Indian goods in August 2025 after trade talks broke down. Under a framework agreed upon in February, the tariff rate was reduced to 18%, but the negotiations have since stalled. Earlier this month, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said that the talks had “plateaued.” Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, however, said last week that the first tranche of a trade deal was in its final stages. India says its final tariff rate should be similar to those of competing manufacturing countries such as Vietnam. India’s purchases of discounted Russian crude since the start of the war in Ukraine in February 2022 have strained ties with the United States at times. The Indian government has said that it would expand energy imports, including from the U.S., while diversifying suppliers to maintain market stability and keep prices affordable. Despite tensions, the two countries continue to deepen defense and technology ties, with Washington viewing India as a key counterweight to China in the Indo-Pacific. Rubio’s visit to India follows a trip to Uzbekistan this week to promote trade and ties with Central Asia . Rubio told reporters in the United States on Saturday before his departure that India had diversified its energy sources, but continued to buy substantial volumes of Russian oil, making an immediate shift to other suppliers difficult. “You’ve got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it’s hard to pivot from one day to the next,” he said. “But they’re also an important ally and partner of the United States.” Rubio is scheduled to visit a refinery in the city of Jamnagar in Gujarat state on Wednesday and meet with business leaders, according to the U.S. State Department. The Jamnagar facility, operated by Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries , is the world’s largest refining complex. In March, U.S. President Donald Trump announced that the company was investing $300 billion to set up an oil refinery in Brownsville, Texas. Rubio last visited India in May . ___ A previous version of this story was corrected to show that Rubio’s comments on India diversifying its energy portfolio were made on Saturday while he was still in the U.S., not on Sunday in Uzbekistan. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters ICO reprimands Ogi Networks and Data Cymru after ransomware breach exposes info of 3,300 people, mostly children Bullhorn sees red after cyberattack knocks recruitment platform offline 1 hour ago Whitehall shuts the front door on digital ID but leaves the back open 3 hours ago UK finance watchdog wants firms to report AI failures and close calls 4 hours ago Why cyber resilience is now a boardroom priority for UK public services 6 hours ago ICANN testing tech to let law enforcement access non-public WHOIS info 11 hours ago A test account protected by "Password1" helped an intruder steal personal data relating to 3,300 people, mostly children, in a ransomware attack that has drawn regulatory rebukes for two Welsh organizations. The Information Commission's Office (ICO) issued reprimands rather than fines to Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and the Local Government Data Unit – Wales, also known as Data Cymru. According to the ICO, altnet ONL provided server and connectivity infrastructure, licensing, and support to Data Cymru, which helps public bodies across Wales make effective use of data. On November 1, 2024, Data Cymru suffered a ransomware attack after a miscreant exploited a test account called Test2 to infiltrate its network and encrypt 182.7 GB of data housed in a file server and an internal database server. "Before deploying the ransomware, the threat actor exfiltrated 42 GB of data from a primary domain controller, a file server and an SQL server," the ICO said on Tuesday in its reprimand of ONL [PDF]. ONL told the ICO it created the test account on January 13, 2012, during its initial project for Data Cymru. "ONL confirmed that the creation of the 'Test2' account was likely intended to test user account access before migrating 'real' users to its services," the ICO said. "When it was created, the 'Test2' account was given the password of 'Password1'." The ICO cited Bitwarden's password strength tool, which rated "Password1" as "very weak" and estimated a cracking time of less than a second. "The local administrator accounts on the three impacted systems all had the same password. This meant that once one system had been breached, the local account hashes could be collected and used by the threat actor to authenticate access to other systems on the Data Cymru network," the regulator added. "ONL confirmed that it did not carry out any reviews of local administrator accounts following their initial deployment. This meant these accounts remained active, regardless of whether they were used, and continued to use the same default passwords set at the time of their creation in January 2012, as part of ONL's initial project with Data Cymru, for more than 12.5 years." The data watchdog reprimanded ONL under Article 32 of the UK GDPR because it failed to put in place "appropriate technical and organisational measures" to ensure processing systems and services were safe, and it didn't regularly assess or evaluate those measures. It found ONL had no auditing procedures to review user accounts within Data Cymru's Active Directory. The ICO's separate reprimand of Data Cymru [PDF] also detailed failures in its security arrangements. "Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors," said ICO head of investigations David Doodson. "This incident shows how a single weak password, attached to an account that was no longer needed, can leave the door open to a serious cyber-attack that can affect thousands. "The responsibility for these failures did not sit with one organisation alone. ONL created the test account whilst Data Cymru retained overall control of its network, including the ability to instruct ONL to create or remove accounts. Neither had put in place sufficiently clear and effective measures to ensure that old accounts were routinely identified and removed.

events.title: No, Alberta isn’t leaving Canada as voters overwhelmingly reject independence for oil-rich province
events.summary: Voters in Canada’s oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, with early referendum results Tuesday delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push for national unity amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats . With more than 1.5 million votes counted, 76% supported remaining in Canada , while close to 24% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta. The referendum wasn’t a direct vote on independence. Approval would have set Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada . “Albertans made a clear choice,” Carney said. “They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada.” Carney said that the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse , with Alberta at its center. Alberta’s separatists, however, saw a silver lining. “We don’t have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada. “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media. Smith, who called the referendum amid pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party, or UCP, despite opposing independence, said that she would address the province Tuesday evening about the results and Alberta’s future. “We are a solid country that’s united from coast to coast to coast,” Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters. Results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday. Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves , is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Canada’s federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but hasn’t traditionally translated into widespread support for independence. Despite the proposal’s apparent failure, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that won’t disappear. Carney earlier urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity. “Vote like Canada’s future depends on it, because it does,” he told a rally on Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up. Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said. Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular. At a separatist referendum night gathering at an Edmonton restaurant, the crowd fell quiet as results rolled in. “We’re not going anywhere,” said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project. “We’ve dominated the conversation in the last year. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.” Rath had said he would be thrilled if 30% of Albertans voted to begin the separation process. He wants Smith ousted as leader of her governing United Conservative Party and said the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party. Dustin Degenhardt, a Wainwright voter, said that Albertans have long been mistreated by Canada’s federal government. “Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony,” he said after voting Monday. “They want to take and take and take from us, and not return anything.” Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a “referendum on a referendum” rather than healthcare. With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, “It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united; instead we’re fighting among ourselves.” ___ Ty ONeil contributed to this report from Wainwright. events.title: UAE and France deepen defence ties with Rafale F5 fighter-jet deal
events.summary: Defence co-operation is among the areas covered by a series of agreements signed by the UAE and France as the two countries look to bolster ties amid geopolitical uncertainty triggered by the Iran war. They signed an intergovernmental agreement for co-operation on the Dassault Rafale F5 standard within the French and Emirati Rafale programmes during the visit of French President Emmanuel Macron to Abu Dhabi. The agreements also cover technical and financial specifications for industrial co-operation between the two countries on the future of combat aviation, as France and the UAE strengthen defence ties. Another agreement focuses on strategic autonomy in defence and reducing dependence on third countries as part of a strategic defence partnership between the two nations. The latest agreements come as the UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy, focuses on localising defence manufacturing through Edge Group , a defence conglomerate with more than 35 companies under its umbrella. The group has played a key role in countering Iranian drones directed at the UAE during the war. Mr Macron visited an Edge Group industrial site during his visit. Edge , set up in 2019, specialises in developing advanced technology for weapons systems, cyber protection and electronic warfare. The group maintains several industrial partnerships with French companies and recently signed a co-operation agreement with the French Defence Procurement Agency. Mr Macron's visit “reflects a shared commitment to strengthening industrial and technological co-operation and developing joint projects”, the Elysee Palace said in a statement. The French Defence Ministry also signed an agreement with the UAE to enhance interoperability between the two armed forces, strengthen industrial resilience and advance co-operation in future-orientated technology, including artificial intelligence and space. The latest agreements come as Abu Dhabi is preparing to host the International Defence Exhibition and Conference (Idex) in January, an event expected to attract hundreds of defence companies from across the globe to showcase their latest high-tech weapons. Mr Macron then headed to Bahrain, where French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and his Bahraini counterpart, Abdullatif Al Zayani, agreed to bolster co-operation on the “peaceful uses of nuclear energy”, the French government said. France and Bahrain signed a defence co-operation agreement in February during a visit to Paris by Bahrain's King Hamad bin Isa. The UAE and Bahrain were among the Gulf countries France helped protect with air defence and anti-drone assets during Iranian attacks this year. France has also co-operated closely with Bahrain at the UN Security Council to find a diplomatic solution to Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz . Energy, AI and advanced technology The UAE and France signed new deals in energy, AI and advanced technology as the two countries seek to strengthen investment and economic ties. The preliminary agreements were signed in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Mr Macron in Abu Dhabi. In AI and advanced technology, three agreements were signed with France's AI start-up AMI Labs to strengthen research and technological co-operation and explore new applications across several key sectors, according to the Abu Dhabi Media Office. The deals involve Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), Abu Dhabi's G42 and computing company Analog. MBZUAI will focus on strengthening co-operation with AMI Labs in AI research and development, while G42 aims to establish a framework for strategic co-operation in cloud computing infrastructure and AI models. Analog's deal with AMI Labs focuses on exploring opportunities to integrate AI models into robotics and physical AI applications, creating new avenues for developing intelligent systems and expanding their use in industrial and technology sectors. The UAE and France will also boost co-operation in the energy sector, with Adnoc Gas and Schneider Electric signing an initial pact to assess advanced technologies and identify opportunities to enhance operational efficiency and improve the performance of energy systems. Adnoc Refining and Technip Energies also signed two contracts covering a refining capacity enhancement project and a sustainable aviation fuel project. In his opening remarks at the UAE-France Business Dialogue at Qasr Al Watan in Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled underscored the importance of bilateral co-operation in ensuring reliable energy supplies and building resilient supply chains amid changes in the global economy. The UAE and France have strong economic ties, with more than 600 French businesses currently operating in the UAE and $4 billion worth of goods exported annually from France to the UAE, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs website. UAE investments are also growing in France. In 2021, UAE-based Gulf Islamic Investments made a $301 million investment in Altais Towers, while Abu Dhabi's Mubadala Investment Company signed an initial agreement with Bpifrance, committing to invest €1 billion ($1.12 billion) in the LAC1 Fund, a €10 billion fund managed by Bpifrance.

events.title: Kroger and Albertsons: the food fight every dealmaker should be watching
events.summary: When two large companies agree to merge, they typically promise to use “reasonable best efforts” to win regulatory approval. In plain English that means, “we’ll try.”   But when supermarket giant Kroger agreed to acquire Albertsons for $24.6 billion in 2022, a pledge to try was not enough. In a form of commitment that amounts to what the lawyers call “hell or high water,” Kroger agreed to take “any and all actions” necessary to win approval. That is a big burden, which was understandably interpreted by Albertsons as a clear signal that Kroger was committed to honoring its contract and was all in on the deal. Then the high water arrived. In December 2024, on the same day, a federal judge in Oregon granted the Federal Trade Commission’s request to block the merger and a state judge in Seattle did the same in a suit brought by Washington’s Attorney General. Albertsons terminated the deal and sued Kroger the next day. I can only assume the Albertsons team was dumbstruck to discover that, when the water rose, Kroger bailed. This week, the Delaware Court of Chancery began hearing from the formidable legal teams both grocery giants have fielded, and will ultimately have to decide whether Kroger did indeed do everything it could to honor its contract. Both sides’ pre-trial briefings show the roadmaps they will each follow over the course of the two-week trial to make their respective cases. Quite frankly, based on those detailed documents, it does not look good for team Kroger. If Albertsons succeeds, the resulting damage award Kroger must pay could prove to be significant. According to the plaintiff’s calculations, an award could be more than $8 billion – which is ironic considering Albertsons will argue that Kroger prioritized its financial return over its obligations. This is a case every dealmaker in America will be watching closely, both because of the money involved but also because the court might better define what the words “any and all actions” really mean. A review of what has been filed suggests that Kroger’s argument will be that it really, really, really tried. The company spent heavily pursuing approval and had every economic incentive to close, but the Biden administration’s skeptical regulators were just never satisfied that the company’s proposed plans would protect competition and consumers. You cannot bill us for the politically motivated actions of others, Kroger will say. The problem, says Albertsons, is that the contract is clear. Trying hard is not enough to fulfill what the contract requires. Even former Kroger CEO Rodney McMullen has conceded under oath that Kroger had agreed to do whatever the contract required. When attorneys transact a merger between two retail giants like Albertsons and Kroger, a standard strategy to address anticompetitive concerns is to spin off a new competitor. But the spin off must be truly able to compete. It is not just a matter of selling off a certain number of stores, a selection of private label products, manufacturing sites, and other assets. You must offload the right stores and the right assets to build a viable business that shoppers will consider. Albertsons will argue that Kroger did not even try. Instead of deciding what to sell off to create a new competitor, Kroger focused on what stores and assets it would never sell. In other words, the merged company would hold on to Kroger’s crown jewels, and any new firm would get the leftovers. As a result, the courts and the FTC both decided that the new competition would be inadequate.  Indeed, Kroger allegedly baked the resistance into the pay packages granted to its top leaders. Senior executives stood to collect bonuses worth as much as six times their base salaries if the merger closed while delivering Kroger’s targeted financial returns. That incentivized those bosses to resist selling more valuable stores or other assets, even if it cost them the deal. Then there are the departures the lawyers on both sides seem eager to avoid explaining. McMullen, who was Kroger’s Chairman and CEO through most of the approval fight, and his CFO Gary Millerchip left the company at crucial moments in the process. McMullen’s departure was blamed on unspecified personal behavior issues. Millerchip’s was tied to a lucrative new job at Costco. To this day, the actual reason for McMullen’s departure remains shrouded in secrecy. But all of this should not obscure what the Delaware court is being asked to decide. This is not, at its core, a referendum on McMullen’s character, Kroger’s corporate culture, the alleged avarice of its senior leaders, or even the company’s allegedly poor divestiture process. It is a contract case. Kroger made a specific, unusually demanding promise that it would take “any and all actions” necessary to get the merger approved. Albertsons says when the necessary actions became too expensive – when Kroger figured out it would have to sell stores and assets it wanted to keep – Kroger called it quits. That is the whole dispute. Kroger will say it spent a ton, had the smartest advisors, and did everything reasonable. In short, Kroger tried hard and was thwarted by the regulators. Albertsons’ reply will clearly be that trying hard was not what Kroger promised. The contract the company signed was to get the deal done, come hell or high water, and because of its failure, Kroger should be forced to pay for its weak efforts and a failed merger.   The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune . events.title: ‘A spark suddenly ignites’: Europe’s Gen Z takes to the streets as economies fail to deliver jobs, schools fail to deliver education
events.summary: Rising fuel costs, discontent with the state of schools, declining public services and a housing crisis are fueling an autumn of protests in Europe. Crowds have protested for weeks in major cities, with some demonstrations marked by arrests, looting, injuries and violence across France, Italy and Albania. In Spain and Portugal, tent camps have sprung up to protest unaffordable housing. Young Europeans are experiencing “a strong sense of uncertainty and a lack of control,” said María Silvestre, professor of sociology at the University of Deusto in Spain. “And when specific situations come together, a spark suddenly ignites that is capable of channeling that discontent and driving people into the streets.” Cities have turned into battlefields as top EU economies, including France, Italy and Spain, approach pivotal elections, while far-right parties have made electoral gains in Germany and could do so elsewhere. It also comes as Europe faces a critical moment in its support for Ukraine, with President Donald Trump making overtures to President Vladimir Putin even as Russia is blamed for increasingly frequent arson attacks, cyberattacks and other acts of sabotage in NATO countries. Right-wing politicians have seized on the chaos. While protests in France have appeared broad-based, Trump portrayed immigrants as responsible for the destruction , writing Monday on his Truth Social platform: “The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!” Many of the protests have been fueled by frustrated young people. Other actors, including black-clad, masked agitators, have fomented violence, but French authorities and police have not blamed immigrants. Here’s a look at what’s driving the unrest: Students say education resources are dwindling In France, which has a centuries-old tradition of popular protest, high schoolers have staged blockades and demonstrations for more than three weeks, demanding more resources for schools they describe as understaffed and dilapidated, especially in lower-income neighborhoods. The protests broadened as France’s CGT labor union and other activists joined in while students paused for a fall break. The movement now includes demands over rising living costs and public services. Despite hundreds of thousands of people marching peacefully, the weekend’s unrest led to 2,400 arrests and serious disturbances in parts of France, including looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux. In Limoges, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall and nearly destroyed the building. Some schools were set on fire. As students and rioters threw firebombs and law enforcement responded with tear gas , hundreds have been injured. French President Emmanuel Macron condemned Saturday’s violence , accusing far-left activists of trying to foment chaos by attacking buildings and police. “Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” Macron said Sunday in a rare televised address. In Spain, elementary and secondary schoolteachers began an indefinite strike in Madrid last week to demand better pay and working conditions. Discontented teachers staged similar walkouts elsewhere in Spain this year. Unaffordable housing stymies young people In Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol, tarpaulin tents have blanketed the square for weeks to protest rising housing costs , sparked by the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal , an 87-year-old woman who later died while hospitalized. Smaller protest camps followed in other Spanish cities. The public pressure led the ruling Socialist government to approve affordable housing measures, but they lacked support in Parliament, leading Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call for an early election in November. A general strike also was called for November — the first in 14 years. Similar housing protests have sprung up in Portugal’s largest cities, Lisbon and Porto, and in Barcelona, a focal point of Spain’s overtourism and housing challenges. Spain’s minimum wage is 1,221 euros ($1,370), while the average monthly rent for an 80-square-meter apartment is around 1,130 euros (about $1,270), according to an analysis by the business newspaper Expansión. “Most of my paycheck goes to the rent. My roommate struggles to make ends meet just like I do,” said Diana Manzanares, a 20-year-old waitress at the Madrid encampment. “This is my reality and the reality of most of us living in this city.” Untenable living costs as inflation rises in Italy “Italia in Piazza,” or Italy in the Streets, has galvanized thousands of demonstrators, voicing demands for better employment, healthcare, education, and access to housing, as well as higher wages. Inflation in Italy rose to 4.2% in September, surpassing the eurozone’s 3.8%, according to government data. The peaceful marches were followed by violent riots in Turin and Bologna, and in Italy’s finance and fashion capital of Milan, where masked rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire. Milan police said 271 people were arrested — most of them minors — and 14 security officers were injured during two days of unrest. Now a newly formed group calling itself the “Oct. 17 Movement” has announced what it describes as a “permanent mobilization” to demonstrate every Saturday at 3 p.m. in cities across Italy. Students in Albania join anti-corruption protests Anti-government protests have stretched over a week in Albania’s capital of Tirana, with clashes escalating after high school and university students joined the broad anti-government “Flamingo” movement calling for Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. Rama has condemned the protesters as “ideologized and radicalized” by antifa , an umbrella term for loosely organized far-left militants. President Trump has designated the movement a terrorist organization in the United States. Ending corruption is a major demand of the movement, which was named for the natural habitat of flamingos in an area where Rama’s government agreed to allow a major luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law. They also want protections for healthcare, education, and public pensions, according to its website. In Serbia , the university students leading mass anti-corruption protests for nearly two years are challenging an attempted return to power by the Balkan country’s former populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in parliamentary elections. The former authoritarian president is aiming to be named prime minister after the Oct. 25 vote. The youth-backed Students’ List party is believed to be running close to Vucic’s party, making the outcome uncertain and fueling fears of possible violence. events.title: SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Reliable Robotics has been working for nearly a decade to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft. Now, with a $115 million funding boost, the Mountain View, California-based startup has a longer runway as it pushes to get its autonomous flight system certified by the Federal Aviation Administration — a critical milestone that co-founder and CEO Robert Rose said the startup is inching toward. The financing is an extension of its Series D round and includes $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round, which now totals $275 million, has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark. Other investors include Gideon Strategic Partners, RockCreek, Geek Ventures, Gold Hill Capital, Sparkwave Capital and others. Reliable has raised $380 million to date. “We continue to make steady progress and deliver evidence to the FAA and every day, we inch closer and closer,” said Rose, a former director of flight software at SpaceX who has also had stints at Tesla and Google. Reliable co-founder and CTO Juerg Frefel is also a SpaceX veteran who spent nearly a decade there as an engineer. And in aviation — one of the most regulated industries in the world — moving toward certification of new technology is progress. Reliable Robotics is working to gain FAA certification on four fronts, all of which are linked to its goal of autonomous flight. Its first product, called continuous autopilot engagement, handles the engine startup, taxiing, takeoff, and landing for the pilot, who remains in the aircraft and interacts with the autonomous flight system through a touchscreen. Rose expects to receive certification for this critical first system in 18 to 24 months. The second certification, which Rose says is at least three years away, removes the pilot from the cockpit and moves them to a ground-control station. Reliable is also working toward certification of a collision-avoidance radar, which the company has developed in-house after failing to attract legacy suppliers to take on the project. Most conventional radar systems use an antenna that moves to scan the surrounding airspace. Reliable has developed a solid-state radar that has no moving parts and scans the sky at a longer range and at much higher resolution, according to Rose. It’s also easier to maintain because there are no moving parts and it costs less, he added. “This is of great interest to operators these days, given the collisions that we’ve had recently in commercial aviation,” he said, adding that the radar also works on the ground to prevent collisions with other aircraft or infrastructure. Rose expects the solid-state radar to be certified by the end of 2027. The final certification is for its airline, called Reliable Airlines, which will be the first airline certified to use the autonomous flying technology. The airline is based in Albuquerque and uses six Cessna Caravans — workhorses of the aviation industry — to fly cargo six days a week. (The FAA certifies equipment, but the agency also must certify the airline operations under a separate set of regulations.) While the certification process is lengthy, Nimble Partners founder John Burbank said the benefits will be broad and significant. “It’s a much bigger effort and much bigger opportunity than to just build one plane,” Burbank said, noting that Reliable is building a system that can be adopted by any airframe. “They had a really big vision nine years ago, and saw this as something needed and essential. Once they get the first one approved, then everyone will realize this is going to be the path for the industry, just as we’re seeing the path for the auto industry being autonomous.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: DeepSeek fires back at U.S.federal agency ban as ‘overstretching of the concept of national security’
events.summary: China hit back Tuesday at a U.S. ban on Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek’s products for federal civilian agencies, highlighting friction in the two AI powers’ heated technology race. The agencies should remove DeepSeek and its affiliated products, as well as third party products and services developed using DeepSeek, from their IT systems, the Department of Homeland Security said in a notice made public on Monday. The department’s order, dating back to late July, also blocks civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services. DeepSeek is one of China’s leading and best-known AI companies and its open-source models are widely available in countries including the United States . They are mostly free to use. The notice in the Federal Register alleges that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors.” It said concerns include that its servers are located in China and that Chinese authorities’ could potentially access private company infrastructure and sensitive U.S. data. In Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China will “will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies” when asked at a regular press conference about the U.S. ban. “China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security and the politicizing of science, technology, economic and trade issues,” she told reporters at a routine briefing. DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment. U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet in mid-November on the sidelines of the APEC, or Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, leaders’ summit in Shenzhen, China. AI is expected to be on the agenda. China and the U.S. have recently made progress in some collaboration on AI governance, including a U.S. proposal for setting up of a notification system on national security-related incidents, but the two countries are still at odds on many issues . U.S.-led restrictions still ban China from accessing some of the world’s most advanced AI chips and the machines that make them. Last week, Beijing rolled out new proposed plans to restrict exports of certain advanced AI models. The U.S. has also said Chinese AI startups including DeepSeek engaged in large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American AI models, claims that Beijing has dismissed. Earlier this year, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced it was barring imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots in a move seen as targeting China. events.title: No cancellation of planned FDI in UAE this year despite Iran war, Ministry of Investment says
events.summary: No planned foreign direct investment in the UAE has been cancelled this year, despite the uncertainties created by the US-Iran war, a senior government official has said. The overall stock of FDI in the UAE this year might be fractionally lower than the record levels achieved in 2025, as global investors assess the impact of conflict in the region. However, the Emirates remains firmly on course to achieve its 2031 FDI targets, Mohammad Abdulrahman Alhawi, Undersecretary of the UAE Ministry of Investment, told The National in an interview on Tuesday. “Everyone we've spoken to has said: 'We haven't cancelled our plans. We are just either waiting, or we're delaying a little bit, or we're decreasing the quantum a little bit but the country is capable of making up,'” Mr Alhawi said on the sidelines of the 10th HSBC Future Forum in Dubai. “Very understandable [that] people will wait and see how the conflict is resolved.” The good thing, Mr Alhawi said, is that even though the conflict been going on since late February, it has helped investors better understand the resilience of the UAE and the capabilities of its government in dealing with a crisis. “I think that's the message that our investors have received over time and I think, maybe not immediately but in the next few years, that will definitely be a positive thing, as more investment is coming,” he said. FDI into the UAE rose by about 6 per cent last year to a record $48.24 billion, the ninth highest total in the world, according to the UN Conference on Trade and Development ( Unctad ) data. The Emirates was also the top recipient of FDI in the Middle East, ahead of Saudi Arabia, which ranked 13th, Unctad said in its World Investment Conference 2026 report released in July. The UAE has maintained consistent FDI inflow momentum over the past few years and was expected to continue on the growth trajectory this year before the war-driven disruption to economy and trade. Like its peers in the six-member economic bloc of the Gulf Co-operation Council and its Arab neighbours, the UAE has faced a wave of missile and drone attacks, but Mr Alhawi said it remains “100 per cent” on target to the achieve the $65 billion annual FDI targets by 2031. “You'll have some years when it'll grow slightly less or slightly more,” he said. “But now that we've reached the $40 billion [plus] range, we expect to keep that for a couple more years before jumping to the next level, which is the $65 billion range, which is where we want to be.” While various governments at the emirate level are incentivising investors to boost FDI inflows, the UAE federal government is focused on investing in its own economy. Special attention is being paid to developing ports and related infrastructure on the East Coast, as well as improving and expanding rail connectivity, and oil and gas pipeline infrastructure. “Now, that investment does two things: one, it shows our confidence in our economy, and two, it shows that we're building different routes and paths for our main value proposition, which is being a logistical hub,” Mr Alhawi said. “We're investing in the right places, which means the investors that are already here can see the impact this will have and they will see it over the next year or so.” Partnerships with investors The UAE is more than capable of executing those projects on its own but it is seeking participation of foreign investors in these schemes to make them a part of the UAE growth story. Mr Alhawi said the Ministry of Investment is bringing capital together and is in talks with investors over joint ventures. Options for global investors to team up with the UAE sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices, are also open, he said. “We're super open,” Mr Alhawi said. “I mean, we can build infrastructure ourselves if we want to, but building it with partners makes it makes it more efficient, makes it better, makes it more long term. “We'd love to have partners wherever we can and we've seen actually quite an influx of people saying, ‘Oh, you're building infrastructure, so let's work with you’, which is great. A very positive sign.” Infrastructure pipeline Investment in infrastructure is among the central planks of the UAE’s economic diversification agenda and Mr Alhawi said the scale of investment required for East Coast projects is significant. HSBC estimates the UAE project finance pipeline is in excess of $190 billion in funding to build the planned the infrastructure projects. The UAE accounts for about 22 per cent of the broader Middle East, North Africa and Turkey region infrastructure project pipeline of $872 billion, data from HSBC's New Networks of Capital: Meant Infrastructure report indicates. “The ultimate risk is the government, and here we are talking about the large-scale projects [such as] the Al Maktoum [International] Airport ... the Dubai sewage system ... and what is happening in Fujairah [projects],” Mohamed Al Marzooqi, chief executive of HSBC UAE told The National . “So, these are the paymasters and I don't think we have even touched the surface, to be honest, when it comes to tapping into those financing solutions.” The easiest solution, he said, would be to tap the loan market and financial institutions in the country. They are all “hungry for quality assets 100 per cent here in the UAE”. HSBC, Mr Al Marzooqi said, is not only willing to leverage its own balance sheet, it can also help structure deals in many other ways for project owners and investors. Opportunity knocks The sheer size of the MENAT pipeline underpins the scale of the region’s medium and long-term investment potential despite geopolitical headwinds, HSBC said in the report released on Tuesday. Even with a “complex global and regional operating environment”, international businesses and institutional investors expect the region to remain and infrastructure investment destination and flows of capital will continue over the rest of the decade, the lender said. The HSBC-commissioned analysis of MEED data has identified the $872-billion pipeline of individual project packages within a wider $1.4 trillion planned and unawarded infrastructure pipeline. The value of planned but unawarded infrastructure projects and programmes increased by 54 per cent between January 2023 and January 2026, from $792 billion to $1.22 trillion,” data shows “Infrastructure planning activity has continued this year, with the pipeline increasing a further 15 per cent to $1.4tn between January and October 2026,” the HSBC report said.

events.title: U.S. crude oil tops $105, Brent crude at five-month highs amid Mideast tensions
events.summary: Oil prices climbed on Tuesday as investors continued to monitor simmering tensions in the Middle East and the U.S. front-month futures contract neared expiration. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November were up 2% to $105.75 per barrel by 9:02 a.m. ET, pulling back from a session high of $110.48. The November contract expires on Tuesday. WTI for December was 1.3% higher at $99.82 per barrel. Global benchmark Brent crude futures for December delivery were trading above $110 at the highest levels since May. Brent was last up 1% at $110.70. Developments in the Middle East remain in focus, with attacks on commercial ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz escalating in recent weeks. At least 18 vessels have come under fire over the past two weeks, according to ship tracker Kpler. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said Tuesday that two "non-compliant" oil tankers had been set ablaze in the strait after hitting mines laid by its naval unit, Iranian state-affiliated news agency Tasnim reported. Meanwhile, Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said at a weekly news conference on Tuesday that Tehran would respond to any American strike "in equal measure, if not more forcefully," according to Tasnim. U.S. President Donald Trump said earlier this month that American forces will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Tamas Varga, analyst at PVM Oil Associates, told CNBC in an email on Tuesday that front-end WTI strength ahead of the contract expiry is a sign of tightness in the global crude oil market. "It is a reflection of falling export volumes from the Middle East as tanker attacks and Houthi strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure intensify," he said. "Secondly, the U.S. decision to exempt Russian shadow fleet from sanctions will push freight rates possibly lower, which was a prohibitive factor to increase demand for U.S.-sourced crude." "With this hurdle removed, at least temporary, U.S. crude oil grades are back in play as replacements of Mideast crude oil," he added. "Thirdly, U.S. commercial oil stocks are expected to have declined last week."
