events.title: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, but also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions. The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from US government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said . The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the US and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models. China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added. The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems. Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week . The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares. The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report. In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude. events.title: No wonder the White House wants Warsh to cut: A 1% Fed rate hike costs the Treasury an extra $95 billion a year in national debt interest
events.summary: There are many—none particularly surprising—reasons politicians and policymakers push central banks for a lower base interest rate. It makes borrowing cheaper and stimulates the economy, potentially leading to more jobs and home purchases. It also, conveniently, makes the government’s own borrowing costs cheaper. While leaders the world over have lobbied for lower base rates for these reasons, none have done quite so forcefully as President Donald Trump and his team: First, going to extraordinary lengths—including personal insults and a criminal investigation—against previous Fed chairman Jerome Powell, and now the broader Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) led by new chairman Kevin Warsh. Trump and his team have suggested that rates are too high, hurting consumers’ chances of owning a home as a result (mortgage rates are tied to long-dated rates). But Bank of America has also put a figure on the cost to the government of elevated interest rates. “Clients are concerned about U.S. fiscal deficit risks. We are too,” wrote BofA analysts Meghan Swiber, Stephen Juneau, Mark Cabana, and Ralph Axel. “Higher rates become increasingly costly the longer they persist. The near-term deficit outlook has changed little, but the rates backdrop has changed the longer-run fiscal math.” “Higher yields compound into materially greater interest expense and Treasury financing needs over time, while raising the risk that the eﬀective interest rate on the debt eventually exceeds nominal growth. Debt spiral starts when interest costs exceed nominal growth.” Treasury payments to service the $40 trillion national debt surpassed $2 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, the department recently announced. In a recent analysis , the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) forecasted the alterations to projected service payments on the debt under two interest rate scenarios. In the first, rates were 150 basis points higher than current projections between 2026 and 2036, and in the second, rates were just 50 basis points higher. In the first scenario, in which interest rates are 1.5% higher than forecasts, deficits are $6 trillion larger, with a $4.9 trillion increase in net interest costs. A 0.5% increase results in $1.9 trillion added to current debt projections, with an extra $1.6 trillion added in net interest costs. “Even if primary deficits remain largely unchanged, the growing interest burden materially increases the government’s financing needs,” the analysts wrote. “We estimate that interest expense rises $95 billion a year for every 100bps of Fed hikes,” the team wrote. Rising concern Bank of America and its clients aren’t the only ones concerned that the U.S. fiscal picture is at something of a tipping point. Over the weekend, Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s, wrote that global investors are digesting the U.S. spending habits and “appear to be demanding a higher rate to compensate for the mounting risk.” He explained: “The 10-year Treasury yield is up about a percentage point this year, among the biggest increases of any major economy, and the countries with the heaviest interest burdens have generally seen the biggest increases. “A vicious cycle threatens to take hold, with higher rates adding to the interest payments and debt load, which in turn pushes rates up even more.” BofA’s team seems inclined to agree, writing that the bottom line means an unchanged deficit picture is becoming a “bigger financing problem.” They added: “As elevated yields feed through to the debt stock, interest expense compounds, financing needs rise and the fiscal trajectory becomes less sustainable.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Former OpenAI exec has quietly built $1.5 billion startup, betting AI can revive U.S. manufacturing
events.summary: Former OpenAI employee Bob McGrew has been quietly building a startup called Arda, which raised capital at a $1.5 billion valuation. McGrew, who spent parts of his career at Palantir and PayPal, said Arda is building an AI assistant for manufacturing and has already been working with Anduril. "It's a user interface and an agent that does for manufacturing engineers what Claude or Cursor does for programmers," McGrew told CNBC. OpenAI's former research chief has been quietly building a startup that aims to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. using AI. Bob McGrew's newest company, Arda, has raised $230 million at a $1.5 billion valuation, the company told CNBC in an exclusive interview Tuesday. The round was led by Altimeter Capital, Accel and Khosla Ventures. Arda makes AI software to help automate manufacturing. McGrew, who was also Palantir's product and engineering lead for over a decade, said Arda's AI models have already been deployed with military tech company Anduril. "It's a user interface and an agent that does for manufacturing engineers what Claude or Cursor does for programmers," McGrew told CNBC. He pointed to the "human-intensive" nature of manufacturing, and the time it can take to adapt production to a new design for a weapon or drone. "When a design changes, you can retrain a human in a day — but it takes three to six months in order to change the automation to reflect the new design," McGrew said. "We've built a software and AI product that basically allows manufacturing engineers to build assembly lines much faster." McGrew joined OpenAI in 2017 and worked on the reasoning capabilities of early models before the launch of ChatGPT. He left during a 2024 wave of other high-profile exits, including chief technology officer Mira Murati and co-founder and chief scientist Ilya Sutskever. "OpenAI is an amazing place," McGrew said. He said he remembers being in rooms with CEO Sam Altman , Dario Amodei, who left to start Anthropic , and Sutskever, "talking about what it would look like when a model could write your email for you." McGrew stayed through the famous weekend in November 2023 when Altman was abruptly fired and then rehired. McGrew said he wanted to stay to ship OpenAI's reasoning product, which he called the "last key breakthrough left before AGI," or artificial general intelligence. "I said, if I could just ship that, I'd be happy with my career at OpenAI, and I'd be ready to move on to something else," he said. McGrew, who hasn't spoken publicly about Arda until this week, said the company is using a combination of its own proprietary models, open-source models and some frontier models to run the software. Arda's other co-founders include Augustus Odena, who helped start Adept and previously worked at Google and Meta , and former Palantir engineers Alex Mark and Jakob Frick. Altimeter's Apoorv Agrawal led the recent funding round. He met McGrew when they both worked at Palantir. Manufacturing largely happens overseas, Agrawal said, but there's a market for bringing it back. "Manufacturing globally is a $16 trillion industry. In the U.S. alone, it's $3 trillion," Agrawal said. "We think that Arda, and the vision that they've outlined, will continue to capture a significant portion of that. Yes, the price is steep today, but the long-term opportunity is very high." McGrew said robotics is next on the product roadmap, and automating factories could help bring more manufacturing — and more jobs — to the U.S. "If your design changes very frequently, the only place you can really build your product is in East Asia, because you need an army of human workers who can be retrained quickly, and you can't wait for automation to catch up," he said. McGrew also highlighted the economic opportunity as the Trump administration looks to onshore manufacturing. "No one has ever successfully built a smartphone in the U.S.," he said. "Never successfully assembled one, and so if you can build a smartphone in the U.S. that is not taking away American jobs. That is bringing American jobs."

events.title: More than 250,000 displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated: UNHCR
events.summary: UNICEF says escalating fighting in Taiz is threatening its water systems, serving an estimated three million people. More than 250,000 people have been internally displaced in Yemen since the country’s war reignited in July, the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) has said, as fighting between Houthi rebels and forces loyal to the internationally recognised government rages across several fronts. The city of Taiz in southwestern Yemen is at the centre of the displacement crisis, accounting for 76 percent of departures and hosting 52 percent of those newly displaced, UNHCR said in a statement on Tuesday. list 1 of 4 GCC condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as Yemen fighting intensifies list 2 of 4 Iran support for Houthis probed as Yemen war re-erupts and Saudi cities hit list 3 of 4 Houthi attack on Yemen army camp in Shabwa kills at least 53: reports list 4 of 4 US leaving oil-for-security approach, not Middle East: Envoy Tom Barrack Lahij in southwestern Yemen hosts 23 percent of the newly displaced population, followed by Aden in the south with 13 percent, UNHCR said. “Shelling intensified in Taiz, including in residential areas and around health facilities, while insecurity and restrictions along key routes continue to constrain humanitarian access and movement,” the agency said in a statement. The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, the interim capital of the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government. “The most immediate needs that we’ve been able to identify are around shelter, food, and multi-purpose cash assistance,” UNHCR spokesperson Matthew Saltmarsh told a news conference in Geneva, Switzerland. The agency said about 33,700 families still require shelter assistance amid severe underfunding of the humanitarian response to the war. Separately, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said in a statement that escalating fighting and fuel shortages in Taiz are threatening its water systems that serve an estimated three million people, including at least 1.6 million children. “Already one of Yemen’s most water-scarce areas, Taiz is now facing renewed pressure on its most essential services for thousands of displaced families,” said Akhil Iyer, UNICEF’s Yemen representative, at a press briefing in Geneva. The warnings come as fighting intensifies between Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthis. The death toll from a Houthi ballistic missile strike on a military training camp in Yemen’s Shabwa governorate increased to at least 58, local authorities said. The Yemeni government described the site as a security training centre away from the front lines, while Houthi forces said they targeted Saudi-backed forces. Hospitals faced blood shortages in Ataq as medical teams responded to casualties and families searched for missing relatives. The attack was followed by retaliatory strikes by government forces near Taiz, raising further concerns over the worsening humanitarian crisis in Yemen. Reporting from the capital, Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said, “The Houthis are not backing down. Their military spokesman says they are continuing to conduct more missile attacks deep inside Saudi Arabia.” “As cross-border attacks grow, Yemenis fear the war is coming closer to home, especially as both sides threaten to escalate their attacks, while Saudi Arabia steps up its air campaign,” Mawry added. Meanwhile, Yemen’s Saudi-backed coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said on Tuesday that its forces have destroyed 127 Houthi weapons depots and missile launch platforms. Separately, the United Kingdom said it would deploy Royal Air Force jets ⁠on defensive missions to help protect Saudi Arabia from increasing Houthi ⁠attacks. The British Ministry of Defence said in a statement that the Typhoon warplanes would operate in a “defensive role” and not carry out attacks against the Houthis. Tensions have soared in Yemen since July, when the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi ports, and fighting escalated sharply last month when they seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the government along the Red Sea coast. Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded to the losses with a counteroffensive and launched Operation Dawn of Yemen, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including Sanaa, seized by the group in 2014.

events.summary: The General Motors Technical Center in Warren, Mich., still looks the way Eero Saarinen drew it in the 1950s: low glass-and-steel boxes set on a grid, end walls of glazed brick in saturated colors, massive man-made lakes, everything in its right place. The campus was dedicated in 1956 and has been a National Historic Landmark since 2014. As Fortune walked around on a recent site visit, it felt like a massive public high school. Fitting in like a bright Lego set is the $900 million investment in the Battery Cell Development Center (BCDC), a massive light-gray rectangle, and the Innovation Center, which resembles a blue-and-yellow battery pack sitting on top of a historic building. If GM is a giant campus, longtime GM battery engineer Andy Oury is the cheerful science teacher, polo shirt tucked into his blue jeans, driving around in his large (all-electric) Silverado. Just the weekend before, he said, he drove it 220 miles to Traverse City, where he powered his camper off the truck all weekend and towed a wood chipper around town.  courtesy of General Motors Oury joined GM in 1999 and became interested in batteries about a decade later, as GM began work on the Chevrolet Volt. This plug-in hybrid convinced him GM was serious about electric transportation, he told Fortune . Oury reports to Kurt Kelty, a battery lifer who spent over a decade each at Panasonic and Tesla . About a decade ago, Oury said, he noticed on LinkedIn that Kelty was leaving Tesla, and he called his boss at the time: “Hey, you’ve got to try to hire this guy.” Kelty, now GM’s vice president of battery and sustainability, told Fortune that the battery operations and research labs have been a massive investment at a time when Detroit is largely reeling from a failed bet on EVs. The federal EV tax credit expired at the end of September 2025, and GM took about $7.6 billion in EV-related charges last year, although that was a fraction of Ford’s and Stellantis’ similar charges in their EV divisions ($19.5 billion and $26.5 billion, respectively). GM says these charges are not comparable as it is sticking with EVs as its end-game scenario. The battery plant is still very much a work in progress, expected to come online as fully operational later this year. Anselmo “Mo” Gallegos is the director of battery cell development, responsible for rapidly scaling up science class into an industrial process. If Andy is the cool teacher, then Mo is the brainy grad student, grinning from behind his glasses or safety glasses, and he’s also prone to food metaphors. Every battery maker has a proprietary formation protocol, the final charging process that brings a cell to life, he said: “a recipe to get the perfect donut at the end of it.” courtesy of General Motors Walking me around the ovens and mixers, some of them a tangle of pipes and wires that recall the bombastic 1960s art of Marvel Comics great Jack Kirby , Gallegos casts himself as a chef seeking just the right mix of ingredients. Batteries, he said, are “a mix of chemistry, mechanical interfaces [and] dark, dark black magic.” The ovens are where the proverbial cake can be overbaked. “Is it going to stick? Is it going to crack?” he said. “You get your cake out of the oven and sometimes it’s got cracks along the top. We hate that.” Mo’s team is ramping up to make a couple thousand full-size cells a day, and Gallegos’ job is to work out the process so that every one of them comes out smooth, no cracks. Before building the BCDC, GM couldn’t build a cell like this at all. Engineers drew one on paper, took it to a partner like Samsung or LG and asked, in Oury’s words, “pretty please, will you put this together?” What the plant is built to prove is a big bet on chemistry. Much of the world’s cheap EV battery supply runs on lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, a chemical that China dominates. GM is betting that its next generation of electric trucks and full-size SUVs will run on something else: lithium manganese-rich, or LMR, cells, which swap out much of the nickel and cobalt for cheaper, more plentiful manganese and extra lithium. GM’s LMR cells use about 30% to 40% nickel, Oury said, compared with roughly 85% in the high-nickel cells currently being used. GM says LMR can deliver roughly a third more energy density than leading LFP cells at comparable cost — and Gallegos and Oury are scrambling to start commercial production with partner LG Energy Solution in 2028. Kelty explained that GM has been working on LMR for more than a decade and considers it homegrown. “We’re not licensing this from China,” he said. “We’re developing this here.” If it works, GM gets a cheaper, longer-range battery for its biggest vehicles that doesn’t depend on Chinese technology. If it doesn’t, GM will have wagered on a chemistry that, by Kelty’s own account, most of the industry considers a long shot. courtesy of General Motors “Our data showed one thing,” Kelty said: “that this actually made sense.” The question inside GM became why the company wasn’t already moving. “It took a voice saying, the reason we’re not doing LMR is because it’s us. It’s our own broken mentality. So let’s fix that,” Oury recalled. The hurdle, he said, was “actually more momentum-based or emotion-based rather than data and business-based.” When GM made the call, Kelty said, the team had supporting data to get it perhaps 60% to 70% of the way to the decision. “What we had to do was make that last leap and say, ‘You know what? We’re going to get the next 30% or 40% of the data and make it there.’” He called it a “testament to the trust in the team.” GM hasn’t fully abandoned LFP; in July 2025, it announced it would convert its Spring Hill, Tenn., cell plant to produce LFP cells, but GM chose LMR for its biggest vehicles.  It’s been a big change for America’s No. 1 automaker, which has long produced, to recall Alfred P. Sloan’s famous phrase, “a car for every purse and purpose”  — and whose employees pride themselves on being A students who know all the answers. Leaders at GM told Fortune they’re trying to grow a different kind of high achiever: someone who challenges inherited constraints, works from incomplete information, admits what won’t get done and uses early failures to learn faster, without missing core deliverables. But it’s not easy to accept a few Bs when you’re used to being an A student.  courtesy of General Motors Red light, green light When Kelty joined GM in February 2024, he began a new quarterly process with his team. At the start of each period, he spends an hour one-on-one with each direct report, agreeing on goals. He describes his job in three parts: “set the direction, set the priorities, and then remove obstacles.” At the end of each quarter, the work is marked red, yellow or green. “At the end of the quarter, when we look at it, there should be some red lights on there,” Kelty said in an interview with Fortune . “And if there isn’t, then to me that means that they didn

events.title: Eka is worth $1.45B thanks to a physical AI model that has experts raving
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Robots still aren’t that good at picking things up, despite billions of dollars of investment and endless videos fed into deep learning models. That may be about to change, thanks to a manipulation architecture built by Eka Robotics, which encompasses a force-sensitive gripper and a new kind of deep-learning model. Founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, the startup just closed an $150 million Series A round that values it at $1.45 billion post-money, led by venture funds a16z and F-Prime. “They are already exceeding superhuman performance for certain tasks, and so we think over the next few months there will be superhuman performance in many dexterous manipulation tasks,” Raghu Raguram, the a16z general partner who co-led the fundraising round, told TechCrunch. In an era of never-ending robotic demonstrations, Eka’s capabilities are shocking veteran robot builders. Kris Hauser, a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said it had a “wow factor” compared to other robot demos he saw recently. The Eka robot “was able to adapt to a large number of different objects without retraining,” Hauser said, adding that it also had an aspect of “humanness, creepy humanness that it would try over and over again if it failed the first time.” Another roboticist, who asked for anonymity because of their work at a frontier lab, told TechCrunch that seeing Eka’s robot in action was an emotional experience, comparable to when robots first achieved reliable legged locomotion five to ten years ago. Take a look for yourself: What’s notable here? How smoothly and rapidly the robot moves. It can pick up about 1,500 objects that weigh up to 1 kg in an hour, compared to about 600 for a human; Eka says it reliably picks up objects more than 95% of the time. And the robot arm is strong enough to hurt itself as it moves that quickly. That indicates, per the frontier lab observer, that “they have a lot of trust in their algorithm not breaking the robot. I wonder how many robots they broke along the way?” When the frontier lab roboticist met Eka’s robot, they handed it a raspberry, the lab’s apparent favorite test item. “The experience of a big, heavy robot rushing towards my arm and then slowing down just in time and very gently touching me is a feeling that I am, as we speak, carrying this feeling in my body,” they told TechCrunch. These capabilities are a consequence of how the foundational model was built. Rather than a vision-language-action model — which is trained to understand the relationship between language, visual inputs, and actions — the schema here is a vision-force-action model, which focuses on the relationship between language, force inputs, and actions. Critics of the current direction of generative AI robotics models, like Rodney Brooks , say that they will fail without an attempt to represent force and touch; Eka’s results suggest such critics have a point. “Vision is not the primary way in which you close this last millimeter problem,” Eka co-founder Agrawal told TechCrunch. “Vision tells you roughly where the object is, what the pose is, but the actual grabbing, the actual searching is happening through forces.” Eka had to design a unique robotic hand that was more flexible than traditional grippers, and included more force sensors; it reacts to contact, which is why it doesn’t crush the raspberry. The founders are cagey about how they achieved that for obvious competitive reasons, but it comes down to using a physics simulator to model the multiple forces the robot will encounter as it attempts to grasp something, and using that to create a reinforcement learning environment that can be run at scale. They say they can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes. “Rather than being limited to the data that you’re collecting from, say, human demonstrations, Eka is pushing through reinforcement learning this approach where the robot can surpass any kind of demonstrations that are given to it,” Hauser said. “What’s really exciting is that they’re able to not be limited to the data that is presented to them for training.” Agrawal and Haarnoja, who first met in graduate school at the University of California, Berkeley, are leading researchers in the field of reinforcement learning for robotics control. Eka’s key bet was that this technique could be done at scale through simulation, rather than relying on videos collected by gigworkers or robot operators performing tasks over many hours. Simulation was key to achieving their robot’s reliable manipulation, a feat that in the past that has proven more difficult for tasks that require interacting with objects, rather than avoiding them.

events.title: Inspired Capital closes $450M fourth fund as New York pushes back on Silicon Valley’s gravitational pull
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Inspired Capital, the early-stage firm founded in 2019 by Alexa von Tobel and Penny Pritzker, has closed its fourth fund with $450 million in commitments. The new capital will bring the firm’s assets under management to nearly $1.4 billion, von Tobel tells TechCrunch. The raise comes as venture dollars are piling up on the West Coast. Between 2020 and the end of 2025, the Bay Area had raised $352 billion for VC funds — roughly 46% of all U.S. venture capital, according to PitchBook. Last year, that percentage shot up even higher, with Bay Area firms locking down 55% of the total new commitments to U.S. venture funds. New York-based Inspired’s new fund is a reminder that capital is accruing elsewhere, too. In fact, Inspired is growing: it closed a $330 million third fund in early 2024, following a $281 million second fund and its $200 million debut fund. Despite having money to invest, von Tobel says the firm is sticking to its formula. Inspired backs roughly 10 companies a year, which can be anywhere between “napkin” stage and Series A, writing checks between $1 million and $15 million. Pritzker, the former U.S. Commerce Secretary, remains an active co-founder in the firm. With six years of investing experience under her belt, von Tobel is now willing to talk about results, too. She says that 12 companies across the firm’s first two funds have become unicorns, representing about 15% of the portfolio. “Ten of them have passed $100 million in revenue, four have crossed $400 million and one has crossed $500 million,” she says. Perhaps more relevant to the firm’s limited partners, Inspired counts more than 10 exits, including MosaicML (acquired for $1.3 billion in June by Databricks), DeepTune (which Mercor acquired in July for an undisclosed amount), and Saturn ( snapped up last year by Snap). Another portfolio company, TeamShares, a fintech startup that buys up other businesses , went public in June through a special purpose acquisition vehicle . Von Tobel claimed the firm’s second fund ranks in the top 5% of its cohort by all metrics, though she declined to share cash-on-cash returns, citing the relative newness of the firm. To be clear, Inspired is not squarely focused on New York. Its portfolio is split roughly 45% East Coast, 45% West Coast and 10% elsewhere. That balance reflects the way that startups grow, she says. “A company that’s getting quite big in Silicon Valley often wants and needs a second talent footprint, and New York becomes really important,” she says. Of course, for others, New York is the only choice. On that front, von Tobel says she has been pitched by at least 10 founders in recent weeks who selected New York specifically to avoid hiring job-hopping employees who have little allegiance to any one company, as is often the case in San Francisco. Von Tobel definitely doesn’t dismiss the Valley. She says that someone from her team is on the ground in the Bay Area every week, and that she’s in the area routinely, too. “We have to pay extreme attention to both [coasts],” she says. As for strategy, she describes a firm that picks themes early and avoids the herd as much as possible. While many companies chase AI applications, for example, Inspired has backed physical AI and quantum computing startups, she says. Inspired came upon the creator-commerce platform ShopMy by following that thesis. Where Inspired isn’t so different is in its penchant for backing serial entrepreneurs. Von Tobel says roughly a third of the firm’s portfolio is by repeat founders. Asked about her stance on secondaries, she says Inspired will sell “a few chips” once companies reach multi-billion-dollar valuations, but it tends to keep more than 90% of its ownership, mostly using secondaries to add to positions in breakaway portfolio companies. That said, Inspired will lead later primary rounds if it misses an early one, and it has written checks for companies that are already valued above $100 million, according to von Tobel. Von Tobel, who launched her online financial learning platform LearnVest on the TechCrunch 50 stage in 2009 and sold the company six years later to Northwestern Mutual for a reported $375 million, insists that Inspired’s strongest edge is patience and its ability to combine the best of both coasts. “We bring West Coast ambition with East Coast financial discipline,” she says. A couple and a 17-year-old are among those killed by Israeli air attacks and gunfire in the Gaza Strip. At least four Palestinians, including a couple and a 17-year-old, have been killed in Israeli air attacks and gunfire in separate incidents in the Gaza Strip, health officials said. An Israeli air strike killed Akram Yassin and his wife Dina Abu Baker in an apartment in Gaza City, medics said on Tuesday. list 1 of 3 Trump’s approval ratings plummet: what that means for the US midterms list 2 of 3 Zelenskyy to hold talks on Russia-Ukraine war with Witkoff, Europeans list 3 of 3 US leaving oil-for-security approach, not Middle East: Envoy Tom Barrack In Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, a 17-year-old boy was killed by Israeli gunfire near the Qizan an-Najjar neighbourhood. Another person was killed by Israeli gunfire in the Zeitoun suburb east of Gaza City. The Israeli military also carried out artillery attacks in other areas south of Khan Younis, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported. Al Jazeera’s Tareq Abu Azzoum, reporting from Deir el-Balah in Gaza, said there has been a surge in Israeli attacks across Gaza overnight and into the early hours of Tuesday. “We can see that the attacks have been pretty much concentrated on Gaza City, where a residential flat was targeted without any warning,” he said. “We are seeing very distressing scenes, and footage coming from the site of the attack shows the scale of destruction that has been inflicted upon the whole residential area,” he added. “We also saw a clear activation of Israeli drones and fighter jets through the early hours of this morning across the central areas of the territory.” Palestinians inspected the aftermath of the strike on the apartment in Gaza City before gathering for the couple’s funeral. “We’re supposed to be in a ceasefire period, but honestly, we are not seeing a ceasefire or anything. The war is still going on, assassinations are continuing, and the shelling has not stopped,” Mahmoud Yassin, whose brother was killed, told the Reuters news agency. Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza has killed at least 74,480 people since October 2023, with another 175,539 wounded, according to the Gaza health authorities. Since the so-called “ceasefire” in October 2025, 1,522 Palestinians have been killed and 5,421 wounded in Israeli attacks, and 839 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble. About 82 percent of structures in Gaza, roughly 200,000 buildings, have been damaged, with about two-thirds of them destroyed since the start of the war, according to the United Nations.

events.title: ‘Every day could cost lives’: UK government blocks Gaza families’ reunion
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Britain’s reopened refugee resettlement scheme offers no escape for Palestinians in Gaza. When his three-year-old son asks why they cannot be together, his Palestinian father tells him the border is closed. “He asks me, why don’t you open it?” the father, who requested anonymity, told Al Jazeera. “He thinks I own an airplane. He is always asking me, can you come and take us?” list 1 of 4 FIFA set for rule change after Balogun red card row at the World Cup: reports list 2 of 4 Fighting in Yemen intensifies: What’s the latest on the battlefield? list 3 of 4 Syrian authorities arrest main suspect in 2013 Baniyas mass killings list 4 of 4 US-Iran stalemate: What are Trump’s next military options? Separated by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, they speak over WhatsApp whenever the internet connection allows. The father has been granted protection in Britain, while his wife and their two children, remain trapped in a tent in Gaza. “When I can’t get in touch with my wife, I feel so stressed. I am so scared that something bad has happened to her or the children.” Sometimes, he goes to the park to clear his head, and sees children playing with their parents. “My heart hurts when I see that,” he said. “I am incredibly lonely. Without my family it is impossible to enjoy anything. I worry about them all the time.” Lawyers and rights groups estimate there are between 250 and 300 people who are seeking through the courts to have their immediate family join them from Gaza but remain separated. On September 30 , an Upper Tribunal ruled to reunite the families in the UK, but the Home Office is appealing the decision and is refusing to waive the requirement for the families to provide biometrics, despite there being no registration facility in Gaza. This is prolonging their separation as Israel continues to bombard the enclave despite a so-called ceasefire agreement in October 2025. A second family that spoke to Al Jazeera also requested anonymity. Earlier this month, shrapnel from an Israeli bomb damaged their home. The mother told Al Jazeera they have since been displaced again. “Where we are now, there is no safety. They bombed the area next to us last night,” she said. “I sat in the corner and I brought all three children to my body. They were all screaming and crying and I kept telling them everything will be OK.” Asked what she would like most in the world, her youngest daughter answers: “To go to my baba with my sisters and my mama.” Decla Palmer, a solicitor at Greater Manchester Immigration Aid Unit who represents the families, told Al Jazeera: “To hold your children and keep them safe from harm is the most basic wish of any parent. What these families are going through is every parent’s worst nightmare”. “The fathers, in the UK, are facing the prospect that they may never hold their children again.” Both families applied before the government suspended new applications under the refugee family reunion route on September 4, 2025. Their lawyers say the families meet the requirements, but what keeps them apart is a bureaucratic catch-22. They cannot obtain visas without providing biometrics. But Gaza’s visa application centre, where families would register physical characteristics such as fingerprints, has been closed since October 2023, so they cannot leave Gaza. More flexible biometric requirements are given for those who need to be medically evacuated from Gaza, while the government has helped scholarship students leave Gaza and complete biometric checks in Jordan. But lawyers say the Home Office is refusing to provide the same guarantees for separated family members to make that journey, even though they would still have to undergo UK and Israeli security checks. Palmer said: “The Home Office is actively keeping these families apart, leaving them stranded in Gaza in grave danger.” “The judge made the right decision in our case, ruling that the Home Office should apply its unsafe journeys policy lawfully to allow the mothers and children we represent, who are eligible to come to the UK under the Immigration Rules, to leave Gaza and reunite in the UK,” Palmer added. “Instead, the Home Office is doing everything possible to delay and to defend its unlawful decisions, taking a policy position that blocks people in Gaza who are eligible to come to the UK from being able to do so.” No safe and legal route for families inside Gaza Activists say a dedicated Gaza family scheme could overcome these barriers, pointing to earlier arrangements that allowed eligible Ukrainians to provide biometrics after arriving in Britain. A petition calling for such a scheme attracted more than 100,000 signatures and was debated in parliament in May 2024. In its December 2023 response, the government said it had no plans for bespoke arrangements, directing people towards existing visa routes.

events.title: UK to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi cities from Houthi attacks
events.summary: The U.K. will send RAF Typhoons to help Saudi Arabia defend against Houthi drones and missiles. The support comes after Houthi attacks on Riyadh and Aramco as Yemen’s civil war intensifies. The U.K. says its jets will fly defensive missions, while its refuelling support also covers strikes on Houthi targets. The U.K. said it would provide defensive military support, including fighter jets, to support Saudi Arabia as attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels escalate. The Houthis, a Yemeni militant group, have launched a series of strikes on Saudi targets in recent weeks. Airport attacks in the capital city of Riyadh led to multiple fatalities, flight cancellations and property damage, while facilities belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco were targeted last week. "The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region," U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said in a statement on Tuesday. New deployment adds to Britain's existing Saudi mission He added that Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles. "This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks," Streeting said. The U.K. Ministry of Defence also said that the fighter jets would operate only in a defensive role and would not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis. It said the Royal Air Force would also provide an Airbus A400M Atlas jet "to support the movement of defence materiel within Saudi Arabia," while U.K. military advisers will also give support to Saudi staff officers. "Escalating violence in the Gulf can have a serious impact at home in the UK — driving up the cost of living, disrupting energy supplies and costs to British businesses. It is also causing devastation to the civilian population in Yemen," the MoD said. "We unequivocally condemn the Houthi attacks on civilian targets like King Khalid International Airport and are clear that Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen have the right to defend themselves." Fighting in Yemen intensifies as Iran war reverberates Yemen's civil war has returned to full-scale fighting between the Houthis and the country's internationally recognized government amid a wider regional escalation linked to the U.S.-Iran war. Al Jazeera reported Monday that at least 53 people were killed when the Houthis launched three ballistic missiles at a military camp in southern Yemen. CNBC was not able to independently verify the reports.

events.title: ‘Horizontal revolt’: Why Albania’s young protesters want PM Rama to go
events.summary: From the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ to street clashes in Tirana, an inside look at a leaderless youth uprising challenging Edi Rama’s decade-long rule. For several days, the streets of Tirana have witnessed a wave of antigovernment demonstrations, with demonstrators engaged in fierce clashes with security forces, while police have fired tear gas on thousands of young protesters to prevent them from scaling barricades. Protests escalated last week after school and university students joined them, citing rising tuition fees and crumbling infrastructure. list 1 of 4 Photos: Antigovernment protesters clash with police in Albania’s capital list 2 of 4 Fire engulfs Albania’s Supreme Court as protests enter fifth day list 3 of 4 Albania’s protests explained list 4 of 4 How has the cost of living changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal? What initially began as a targeted environmental protest in May has rapidly escalated into one of the most serious political challenges facing Prime Minister Edi Rama in his more than a decade in power. Yet, as the unrest reaches a boiling point, a fundamental question remains: Who is behind this movement, and can it force systemic political change? ‘A horizontal rebellion’ spurred by social media Contrary to claims by government officials that the unrest is being orchestrated by political opponents or external actors, analysts and journalists on the ground emphasise that the movement is largely decentralised and youth-driven. Fatos Hakorja, editor-in-chief of TV Klan and Klan News, told Al Jazeera that the demonstrations have evolved organically into a broad coalition of high school students, university students, environmentalists, and aggrieved citizens. “So far, what can be said with certainty is that the protests have been organised mainly by young people themselves,” Hakorja told Al Jazeera. “What began as the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ gradually developed into a broader student and youth protest… There is no clear evidence that a single consolidated structure stands behind the protests,” he said, referring to the May protest against a luxury resort that threatens the protected coastline. Hakorja noted that coordination takes place dynamically across digital platforms such as WhatsApp, Telegram, and Snapchat, rather than through formal organisational hierarchies. Albanian political analyst and publicist Ben Andoni echoed this view, describing the situation not merely as a standard protest, but as “a genuine, horizontal revolt”. “The protest has turned into a rebellion for the past seven days. It was a protest before, but it has never taken on the character of a movement. If it were so, there would be a leadership group and some short-, medium-, and long-term goals,” Andoni told Al Jazeera. “It is a horizontal movement, where people are mobilised by TikTok groups and social networks, but not by true cultural and political organisations. That is also a handicap or a source of pressure for Rama’s government, which seeks to negotiate, but finds no single counterpart standing in its way.” From the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ to broad structural discontent The roots of the current unrest are multifaceted, blending localised grievances with deep-seated frustration over governance, economic stagnation, and corruption. The initial spark – dubbed the “Flamingo Revolution” – was ignited by environmental opposition to controversial luxury development projects, notably in the protected area of Zvernec and the planned resort investment on Sazan Island by the firm of Jared Kushner, United States President Donald Trump’s son-in-law. The flamingo, native to these coastal lagoons, quickly became a symbol of resistance against the perceived commodification of public lands. However, environmental concerns swiftly converged with student anger over high tuition fees, inadequate dormitory conditions, and low educational competitiveness. Beneath these immediate triggers lies a much deeper structural crisis. “Problems of corruption, nepotism, and a lack of perspective are the main reasons that drove people to protest,” Andoni explained. “The protest summarised the entire range of problems that Albania has, and brought them to the doorstep of a government that has crossed lines regarding corruption, inequality, and particularly a lack of empathy for the people. “Among some protesters, especially on social media, there is also a narrative that Rama is placing the country’s interests at the service of private interests, his personal hold on power, or foreign interests, including Israeli interests. These claims have not been proven, but they seem to have increased the anger of some young people and part of the wider population,” Hakorja added. Rama has strongly rejected the allegations, calling them conspiracy theories and dismissing them as manipulated disinformation spread through social media by “foreign hands”, aimed at destabilising the government and undermining the country’s public institutions.

events.title: Investors look to earnings to reset the bull market. The key level to watch on the S&P 500
events.summary: The key level traders are watching on the S&P 500 that could mean an even bigger decline is ahead. Warren Buffett’s answer for how one should become inflation-resistant. Investors' collective cash cushion against an adverse market surprise is running low. Get Mike Santoli's Market Memo in your inbox first. SUBSCRIBE HERE In a previous life, when I routinely shut down New York City bars, the end of Daylight Saving Time was an annual bonus, as 2am on a Saturday night instantly became 1am, leaving three more hours until closing time. The financial markets now are undergoing several forms of late-cycle unease, and Wall Street is now looking for earnings season and the passage of the midterm elections to turn back the clock before last call. To be clear, this remains a bull market, the S&P 500 's uptrend unbroken, with constant rotations between AI tech and remainder of the market fitfully supporting the tape, with pullbacks limited to 3% for half a year. Still, the index is now chopping around a flattish 50-day moving average at levels first reached 11 weeks ago, the AI-hardware cohort has badly broken stride, bank stocks are trading poorly off their results, and credit markets are getting colicky. Late last week, the urgent selling in semiconductors and data-center equities and debt resembled the sort of forced-unwind rhythms from July, when a big upstart tech hedge fund was in the process of being all but liquidated. A tentative bounce in semiconductor stocks Monday was minimally reassuring, in that it meant we didn't get the further disorderly purge many had braced for over the weekend (when S&P 500 "perpetual" futures on Hyperliquid had a sudden head-fake drop late Saturday). Jason Hunter, technical strategist at JP Morgan, sets out the crucial question for a market sending mixed signals: "With the bearish seasonal window now closing, we are left wondering if the market is in the terminal phase of a sequence of rolling corrections ahead of a typical late-year rally. Or are the plentiful amounts of bearish internal, momentum, and intra-market divergences that have formed as the S&P 500 index has decelerated below longer-term channel resistance setting the market up for a larger and more correlated setback?" He leans toward a more cautious interpretation, keeping the S&P 500 on a short leash that extends about 2.5% lower to 7500, a break of which would lose the tape the benefit of the doubt. Based on precedent and circumstance, the market "should" be setting up for a comeback that could reset the clock in bulls' favor. The fourth quarter after a midterm election year, historically, is overwhelmingly positive. Earnings growth projected to exceed a 20% year-over-year growth rate again this quarter can hardly be viewed as anything but a positive at least to bolster the fundamental case. Still, against most probabilities, 2018 happened. By which I mean a 19% S&P 500 peak-to-trough decline in the fourth quarter of a midterm-election year, one that saw total S&P 500 earnings grow by more than 20%. The 2018 tailspin had followed a massive momentum crescendo and reversal several months earlier, which gave way to an erratic tape that couldn't absorb what seemed at the time relatively unthreatening Federal Reserve tightening actions. Financial conditions have now been tightening by means of higher Treasury yields, somewhat wider corporate-credit spreads, an uptick in volatility and a stronger U.S. dollar. It's become common to hear investors insist that "the market is doing the Fed's tightening for it," suggesting Chairman Kevin Warsh himself should show restraint in further hiking rates despite the recent upturn in inflation. Sure, but the reason the markets are tightening is, in part, because Warsh himself expressed resolve in fighting inflation and investors therefore believe he'll take short-term rates up a bit more. How Warsh treats these market shifts after next week's Fed meeting is another node of disagreement on the Street. Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave says the markets are testing the Fed's pain threshold with the Nasdaq retreating 5% and credit spreads flaring a bit. The market has taken recent Fedspeak to suggest very low chances of an October rate hike, even though Warsh himself has decried forward guidance and said the Fed shouldn't suppress normal market volatility. Bhave is maintaining his non-consensus prediction for an October hike, conceding it's a close call. Morgan Stanley equity strategist Mike Wilson takes the other side on the Fed's response to the recent tensing up of markets: "We think some acknowledgement of this tightening by Warsh would be well received by rate-sensitive areas that have already derated notably. Conversely, an indifference to this tightening may invoke memories of Powell's 2018 'auto-pilot' remarks in reference to that tightening episode.

events.title: Novo's next-generation obesity drug shows 25% weight loss in women in late-stage analysis
events.summary: Novo released new evidence that its experimental CagriSema injection can improve upon the weight loss with its blockbuster GLP-1 obesity injection, Wegovy. The Danish company said its next-generation obesity drug showed 25% weight loss on average at 68 weeks among adult women in a new analysis conducted after a late-stage trial. A second analysis found that the drug was associated with significant weight loss across menopause statuses. Novo on Tuesday said its next-generation obesity drug, CagriSema, showed 25% weight loss on average among adult women in a new analysis conducted after a late-stage trial. The Danish company said further work is needed to confirm the hypotheses of two post-study analyses. Still, the results are the latest evidence that the experimental injection can improve upon the weight loss and other benefits offered by Novo's GLP-1 drug semaglutide, the active ingredient in its blockbuster obesity shot Wegovy and diabetes counterpart Ozempic. CagriSema, a combination of semaglutide and another drug called cagrilintide that targets the amylin pathway, is expected to launch early next year. Obesity drug leaders Novo and Eli Lilly have built new treatments around amylin , which involves a hormone released in the pancreas alongside insulin that helps regulate hunger and fullness, hoping it will give them a new revenue stream beyond existing GLP-1s. In an analysis of roughly 2,300 women with obesity or who are overweight, CagriSema caused 25% weight loss on average at 68 weeks compared with 3% with placebo. The results are based on an ideal scenario in which all patients stayed on treatment without interruptions. A second analysis of around 1,900 women assigned by their menopausal status found that weight loss reached 26.7%, 24.8%, and 23.1% in premenopausal, perimenopausal and postmenopausal women, respectively, at 68 weeks, if all patients remained on the drug. That compares with approximately 2% across menopause groups with a placebo. Across both analyses, CagriSema was linked to reductions in abdominal fat, based on waist circumference, among women overall and across menopause stages, Novo added. The results suggest that women may experience slightly more weight loss on CagriSema than a broader population of both men and women with obesity saw in the phase 3 trial. Initial results from the study showed that CagriSema helped adults lose 22.7% of their weight on average at 68 weeks versus 2.3% in the placebo group. However, the majority of patients in the trial — around 67% of roughly 3,400 — were women. Weight gain is very common for women during menopause. Declining estrogen levels can contribute to a slowdown in metabolism, making it easier for women to gain weight and harder to maintain muscle mass. After menopause, estrogen generally remains low and does not return to previous levels. More than 86 million women in the U.S. are 40 and older, according to the U.S. Census Bureau , which are the years in which perimenopause, menopause and postmenopause occur. "Many women with obesity or overweight experience weight gain as they move through menopause, and it is important to explore investigational products such as CagriSema across the reproductive lifespan," said Michelle Skinner Moore, Novo's interim head of clinical development, medical and regulatory affairs. Wall Street has not appeared particularly excited about CagriSema, whose previous late-stage clinical trial results disappointed investors because the drug showed weight loss efficacy below their expectations. Novo, however, maintains CagriSema is effective and differentiated enough from its other drugs to draw significant demand. Analysts expect CagriSema to generate $11.84 billion in sales for obesity specifically in 2028, according to a consensus estimate compiled by FactSet.

events.title: Russian aerial blitz kills 7 in Ukraine as Zelenskyy meets US and European officials in Norway
events.summary: Officials say Russia has launched another missile and drone attack on Ukraine and that at least seven people have been killed KYIV, Ukraine -- Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least seven people, officials said Tuesday, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy scrambled to ensure more American and European help during his visit to Norway. U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff , who along with Jared Kushner has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement and end their war , was also in Oslo. Kushner, who is U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, was to attend the meeting with Zelenskyy by videoconference. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb were also due to meet with Zelenskyy in Norway's capital. “We are maintaining all contacts that can help bring peace,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X after he arrived in Oslo. He said officials gathered in Norway will discuss strengthening Ukraine's air defenses and joint production of weapons . Meanwhile, Russian spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters the Kremlin hopes that a meeting in Russia with the U.S. envoys can be organized soon, though he didn’t give any indication about where or when. He said Russian President Vladimir Putin’s meetings with Trump's envoys — potentially as early as Wednesday — would be “very important,” adding: “We highly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators.” With further U.S. support for Ukraine in doubt as relations between Zelenskyy and Trump sour again , the Ukrainian leader said that he spoke with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is on a trip to Asia. That conversation came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers on Monday that he believes “some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us.” Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russia’s ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said that the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine. Zelenskyy also said that he sought Rubio’s help to ensure that the United States continues to share vital intelligence with Ukraine after Kyiv had received none or belated warnings about Russian missile attacks in recent days. Also, Zelenskyy said that speed restrictions were still in place on Kyiv’s use of the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX’s satellite internet service, hampering battlefield operations . Trump has also waived sanctions on Russia , a move which Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow’s full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February. Zelenskyy said that he had “a substantive conversation” with Rubio. “I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position,” Zelenskyy said on social media. With the Russian army held up on the front line, Putin is trying to bomb Ukraine into submission while robbing it of vital U.S. support, Western leaders and analysts say. European countries, worried by Russia’s plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to take up the slack of any falloff in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are American-made. 2 dead, 11 injured after Kansas mother drives onto soccer field during game: Police Iran updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs' Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say European countries and European Union institutions have allocated 237 billion euros ($266 billion) to supporting Ukraine, compared with 115 billion euros ($129 billion) from the U.S., according to Germany’s Kiel Institute, which tracks assistance to Kyiv. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday questioned whether U.S. negotiators have been honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace. “Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now, why Ukraine hasn’t surrendered on Putin’s terms is because Europe has been supporting Ukraine,” Kallas said. “Ukraine wants peace more than anybody because they have been under this bombardment for already four years now,” she told EU lawmakers in Strasbourg, France. “The only one who doesn’t want peace is Russia.” Four people were killed and 27 others wounded, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said. Three were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged, police said. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, while hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police.

The unplanned downtime for customers began at 0608 UTC when europe-west-2-b, one of three local availability zones in the London region, started playing up. According to an update on its status page , Google Cloud said at 1158 UTC that full recovery workloads should be “completed, tentatively” by 1300 UTC. Customers can expect another update at that point, with Google either giving the thumbs up, thumbs sideways or having to admit engineers are still working on a fix. Services that went AWOL included BigQuery Data TransferService, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, Google Cloud NetApp Volumes, Google Kubernetes Engine, and Managed Service for Apache Kafka. We are seeing the recovery of services and are prioritizing the recovery of existing workloads.Customers may not be able to yet create new workloads." The Register has asked Google for further elucidation but it said the only information is available on the status page. The "fragility" of the cloud model is again on display, Dr Amro Al-Said Ahmad , a lecturer in computer science at Keele University told The Register . He estimates that a total of 38 services were down and out for the count. "The incident highlights the dependency effect of modern cloud ecosystems. When a core cloud region experiences failures, the impact extends far beyond the directly affected services. Applications, APIs, databases, authentication systems, payment platforms, analytics pipelines, and third-party SaaS products that depend on those services can all experience cascading failures." "A problem in a single cloud region can therefore propagate through an entire digital supply chain, affecting organisations that are several layers removed from the original outage. While this is a regional outage centered on europe-west2, the breadth of affected services highlights a key cloud engineering lesson: resilience is not achieved by simply moving to the cloud. events.title: Best Buy launches new gaming hub ahead of 'Zelda' and 'Grand Theft Auto VI'
events.summary: Best Buy is launching a new gaming experience for customers as it leans into the fast-growing business, the company told CNBC exclusively. The announcement comes ahead of some of this year's biggest launches, including "Grand Theft Auto VI" next month. Chief Revenue Officer Patrick McGinnis told CNBC the timing of the launch is "pretty perfect," though the new experience has been in the works for over a year. The company has previously said gaming is a large driver of its overall performance each quarter. Best Buy is tapping further into a growing customer cohort: gamers. Chief Revenue Officer Patrick McGinnis told CNBC exclusively that the electronics retailer is launching a new experience Tuesday for customers featuring gaming content, new technology and special offers, among other features. The online destination is called Best Buy Gamers and is launching in a beta version. "Gamers are a customer that are really like no other in terms of their passion for not just the tech, the titles, but also how they want to work with each other as a community," McGinnis said. "So for us, being relevant for that customer wherever and whenever they want to interact with the thing that they love is really important." Best Buy says millions of gamers shop at the retailer each year, including trying out games in the store and seeking advice from in-store experts. The new gaming experience, created in partnership with video game website IGN, will offer members gaming articles and reviews, live Best Buy event updates for launches and deals on new technology. The announcement comes ahead of some of the biggest launches in gaming this year, including the Nov. 5 release of "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time," a remake from Nintendo , and the Nov. 19 launch of Take-Two Interactive 's highly anticipated "Grand Theft Auto VI." McGinnis said the timing of the rollout is "pretty perfect" given the slate of new video games over the next month, though Best Buy has been developing the new platform for over a year. "We want to be relevant for our gaming customers, not just during the important, big tentpole periods of the calendar, like when we have these big gaming launches coming up, but really every day," he said. "We want to be there when they discover new titles and connect with the community, and not just when they're buying a big console or a new gaming title." Best Buy has been leaning into gaming as it sees growing demand from its customers. For its fiscal first-quarter results reported in May, the company said gaming and computing was one of its biggest drivers of growth. On a call with analysts to discuss Best Buy's fiscal second quarter in August, incoming CEO Jason Bonfig said the company expects that demand for "Grand Theft Auto VI" will boost the gaming category. Best Buy has been looking for growth drivers as the retailer tries to revitalize its business performance under Bonfig. The company has seen slumping sales and was hit by tariffs and lower consumer confidence, among other factors. Tapping into gaming could help revitalize the retailer. McGinnis said the new gamer experience is an example of the company's strategic goals coming together. "If you think about what those priorities are, the Gamers [beta] community is definitely a way that we're expanding and growing our reach, reaching that gaming customer," he said. "Providing a place for them to again pursue what they're most passionate about certainly is elevating our experience." Best Buy is also leaning into in-store experiences around gaming, starting with a location in Torrance, California, next month, where Sony , Nintendo and Microsoft will come together to offer gaming experiences and activations for customers. With the combination of physical retail and the online platform, McGinnis said, Best Buy hopes to sit at the intersection of technology, entertainment and culture within the gaming community. He said the company plans to tweak its new online experience based on feedback from its customers and continue innovating to meet its audience where it is, especially as the gaming segment continues to be one of the company's strongest performers. "We recognize the gaming customer as incredibly passionate and wants to engage with what they love in a lot of different ways," he said. "There's observations of gaps that exist in the places and spaces where gamers are engaged, and we thought that we could build something that would really complement what they're engaging with today from a social platform perspective, not to replace those types of experiences in any way, shape or form."

events.title: US inequality is getting worse in ways you might not expect
events.summary: Billionaires like Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai and Elon Musk, pictured here at President Donald Trump's 2025 inauguration, have seen their wealth soar thanks to the stock market boom and beneficial tax changes. Chip Somodevilla/Pool Photo via AP The buzzword of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections may be affordability , but growing anger over inequality is behind the sentiment. A Pew Research survey released in October 2026 found that roughly 6 in 10 Americans – including 4 in 10 Republicans – believe there’s too much inequality in the U.S. And a growing share from both major political parties state that the economy needs to be fundamentally rebuilt to address this. This sentiment has, however, been difficult to convert into political results. Public support for California’s proposed wealth tax on billionaires has been waning ahead of the midterms, for example, and in 2025, Republicans passed President Donald Trump’s sweeping legislation that included tax cuts for the wealthy while cutting safety net programs. I’m an economist who has been studying inequality for about two decades. My research confirms the trend of rising inequality since 1980, driven by the wealthiest pulling away not just from the middle class, but also from the “merely wealthy.” Overall, recent research underscores how policy choices – including taxation and public spending – enabled this 40-year rise in inequality. Some policies enacted more recently appear to be accelerating this trend. An analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%. Inequality by the numbers Recent federal data shows that wealth inequality continues to grow . The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion. That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 – and from 27.4% in 1999. These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class – the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% – who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group that’s 40 times larger than the top 1%. And the middle’s share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data. But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows. This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth – almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%. Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026. Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories. Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is disproportionately boosted by corporate profits, which are up sharply overall . The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfolios’ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability that’s driving up stock prices – especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom. How taxes play a role Since President Ronald Reagan’s tax cuts in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become less and less progressive , often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats. The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research – including international studies – doesn’t back that up. A 2025 Brookings report notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth. Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trump’s sweeping policy and tax bill, which included provisions making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent. Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the lowest corporate tax rate since 1940 . While many voters cite affordability as a top concern, concerns over inequality have increasingly been part of this debate. AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib It’s also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because the composition of their wealth is different. They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from. Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%’s wealth portfolio consists of corporate and business ownership , allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways – including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability. Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can borrow against it for cash , usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares. By contrast, below that elite, real estate is a much more important component of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share. For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%. The new drivers of inequality Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played. But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed. One example is a provision in Trump’s 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse. Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by about 5 million due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs. The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point. They disproportionately affect low- and middle-income consumers but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy – while boosting the profits of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil. This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which has pushed up the global price of oil. Then there are tariffs, which are fundamentally a consumption tax on imports. Economists at the New York Federal Reserve have found that these levies have inflicted a heavy hit on many common consumer goods. They estimated that prices for these items, which make up a much larger share of household budgets among the nonwealthy, would have fallen on average by 1% over the year without the tariffs. Instead, they have risen by 2.9%. This acceleration in the redistribution of wealth from the middle class to the very top, in short, has an array of drivers. But they’re not inexorable forces of history. As economist Thomas Piketty put it in “ A Brief History of Equality ,” published in 2022: “Inequality is first of all a social, historical, and political construction.” Markus Schneide
