events.title: Why Rubio is visiting Reliance’s oil refinery in India, the world’s largest
events.summary: Reliance is central to Washington’s efforts to punish Russian energy buyers and contain oil prices amid the war on Iran with a crucial midterm election looming. New Delhi, India — United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has arrived in India for a two-day visit, during which he is set to tour the Jamnagar refinery complex in Gujarat, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, a major player in global oil markets. Reliance’s crude refinery in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s home state is the world’s largest single-site refinery. In many ways, Reliance Industries’ businesses sit at the crossroads of the ongoing global energy crisis. The conglomerate is central to Washington’s efforts to punish Russian energy buyers, while also trying to contain oil prices amid the war on Iran, on top of rising diesel costs in the US, where a crucial midterm election looms. Reliance has also only recently committed to a major investment in the US, which President Donald Trump’s administration has cited as an example of its successes in luring global capital. Rubio is skipping the capital, New Delhi, at a time when the US-India bilateral relationship has been rocky, strained by a string of friction points — and an elusive trade deal. So why is the top US diplomat visiting the world’s largest single-site oil refinery? After meetings in Mumbai, India’s financial hub in the western state of Maharashtra, Rubio will fly to Jamnagar in neighbouring Gujarat, near the Gulf of Kutch. Jamnagar opens into the Arabian Sea and is home to Reliance Industries’ refining complex, a major hub for crude processing and fuel exports, which processes 1.4 million barrels per day (bpd). Rubio had visited India earlier this year too, but this trip “is a little more business-focused”, the US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor, told reporters last week. A readout from Rubio’s office noted that he would “meet with business leaders to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation”. “[At Jamnagar] he will meet some of the folks at Reliance,” Gor said. The world’s largest single-site oil-refining complex has a combined crude-processing capacity of 1.4 million bpd. That is nearly 1.5 percent of global refining capacity, according to the company. The complex comprises two refineries: the original facility, commissioned in 1999 with a capacity of 660,000bpd, and a second, export-oriented refinery commissioned in 2008, adding 580,000bpd, which operates in a special economic zone. Jamnagar imports crude from international suppliers and exports refined products to global markets. The refinery can process heavy, sulphur-rich crude that many facilities cannot handle efficiently, converting oil into higher-value products. Reliance said last month that the complex has processed more than 216 crude grades, claiming to be “perhaps the only refinery to achieve this feat”. The Jamnagar refinery’s capacity is also driving a sharp revival in imports of Venezuelan crude — taken over by the US earlier this year after abducting then-President Nicolas Maduro — as Washington seeks to reshape global oil trade. Reliance is expected to account for roughly 350,000bpd to 370,000bpd of the October intake, according to estimates from analytics firm Kpler. “We will talk with Reliance about refining more Venezuelan crude,” Rubio told reporters in brief remarks on Tuesday. Why is the refinery significant for global energy supplies? Reliance is a central player in keeping global oil markets stable, as one of the world’s biggest suppliers of refined petroleum products. In September, for instance, six of the seven large cargo ships that docked at European Union ports carrying oil products were bearing Reliance goods. Reliance’s biggest export is diesel, which Trump has been particularly worried about, with prices reaching historic highs in the US ahead of midterm elections early next month. Though the data on exports by category is not public, an analysis by the Reuters news agency from trade sources noted that Reliance Industries exported 21.66 million tonnes of refined petroleum products in the first half of 2025 from Jamnagar. Diesel accounted for the largest share at 9.81 million tonnes, followed by petrol at 6.14 million tonnes and jet fuel at 2.06 million tonnes. Europe accounted for the biggest share of the company’s exports, making up 28 percent of Reliance’s refined products during the period. Buyers include BP, ExxonMobil, Glencore, Vitol and Trafigura. The Jamnagar refinery also shipped about $143m worth of oil products to the US last month, according to data cited by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a think tank in Finland. CREA noted in its report that the EU’s ban on importing petroleum products made from Russian crude from January 2026 does not adequately prevent products from refineries in third countries from entering Europe when those refineries also process Russian crude.

events.title: A scuff on your bag, a dent in your mug – and suddenly it feels like time for a new one
events.summary: Would this bother you? 500px/Getty Images Imagine you have a bag you really like. It felt like “the one” when you bought it. Over time, it starts to look worn. There are some scuffs on it. Nothing is actually wrong with the bag, and it still works exactly as it should. Yet, once you notice those imperfections, you start thinking about buying a new one to replace it. Consumers do this all the time. They replace phones that still work , furniture with a scratch and sweaters with a small snag. Often, what has changed is how people see these items. We are marketing researchers who study why people buy, use and get rid of stuff. This obsession with perfection began when one of us, Aprajita Gautam , moved from India to the U.S. in 2019. She was struck by how different the culture of buying and owning things was in the two countries. In our peer-reviewed research paper , published in August 2026 in the Journal of Consumer Research, we identified one reason for this pattern: Some people care much more than others about having flawless things. We call this penchant a desire for perfect products. Not the same as perfectionism We began by interviewing 17 people in Austin, Texas, in 2023. They included real estate agents, entrepreneurs, stay-at-home mothers and people employed by an nonprofit that promotes reuse. We asked them about their possessions and what made things seem perfect or imperfect. We then surveyed about 540 more people, some online and some in a university research lab. The results suggested that people who strongly preferred flawless items had more elaborate ideas about what their ideal product was and were sensitive to even small deviations from those ideas. Their standards also kept rising. Seeing something better than what they owned could raise the bar further for them. Next, we developed questions to assess how much people care about having flawless possessions. We used people’s answers to determine how strongly they desired perfect products. We also found that this tendency is related to but distinct from perfectionism . While perfectionists hold themselves to high or even impossible standards, people who want perfect stuff hold what they buy and own to lofty standards. You might easily shrug off a bad day at the office but be far less forgiving of a scratch on your new coffee table. For people who feel they have to own perfect products, even a small imperfection can overshadow everything else they like about something they own. Finally, we conducted 12 experiments where we recruited participants – University of Texas at Austin students and online workers participating in crowdsourcing marketplaces – to test the behavioral effects of the desire for perfect possessions. It can affect how you shop In our first online experiment, we asked 402 consumers across the country to imagine booking a hotel in California’s Napa Valley using filters like those on travel websites, such as star rating, Wi-Fi or a spa. Consumers who desired perfect products used more filters and set higher cutoffs, narrowing their search to hotels that came closer to meeting their standards. Newness itself also had value for them. In another online experiment with 301 consumers, those who cared most about owning flawless possessions were quicker to upgrade to the latest iPhone, even when it offered little real improvement over the previous one. This urge can be costly. It can mean paying extra for something new when the old one works fine, or spending more time searching for a product that meets every standard that may not actually matter. If you can live with imperfections, you can buy some of your stuff used. Moment/Getty Images Makes people less open to repairs This preference also affects what people do with the stuff they already own. In our next online experiment, we asked 1,004 U.S. participants to chose between two options: an insulated coffee mug and an insulated water bottle. When told that the product they chose had a small dent on the bottom, those who were most bothered by flaws in their possessions were more likely to swap it for the other option. We found a similar pattern with repairs . In an online experiment with 601 consumers, we found that those who want to own perfect products were less interested in fixing a broken keyboard when the replacement key wouldn’t match the color of the other keys. This highlights a problem with repairs that isn’t usually part of discussions about sustainable consumption : Fixing something can restore its function without necessarily making it look as good as new. A factor for donations Consumers with exacting standards for their things also applied their high standards to items they were getting rid of. In an experiment we conducted in a university behavioral lab, we asked 339 students to help with a “Clean Out Your Closet” drive. They examined pieces of clothing that others had discarded and sorted them into two bins: one to donate and one to recycle. Those who strongly preferred flawless items were less likely to donate imperfect but still usable clothing. This attitude can shorten a product’s useful life. That finding has implications for sustainability . Much of the academic research about sustainable consumption focuses on what people buy. But another way to consume less is to keep products in use longer. That becomes harder if small imperfections make otherwise useful products seem less valuable. Learning to value imperfection Our research suggests that how someone responds to flaws in their possessions can vary depending on what those flaws mean to them. We were inspired in part by the Japanese concept of wabi-sabi , which finds beauty and value in imperfection and change. In our final online experiment, 1,203 consumers learned about hoodies with subtle variations in color and pattern. When those variations were described as making each hoodie unique, consumers who love having perfect products responded less negatively to them. A mark on a well-used object can be seen as a flaw, but it can also become part of its history. And replacing products because of minor imperfections can lead consumers to waste their money. None of this means consumers should keep everything forever. Mugs break and clothing and shoes get worn out. Sometimes people simply want something new. But consider that bag again. Its scuffs could mean it is no longer the perfect bag you originally bought. Or they could mean you’ve carried it hundreds of times because you like it. The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

events.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
events.summary: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through Web links, researchers reported Monday. Like many online services, Muse allows users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. A single query is all that's required Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. events.title: Iran denies collapse is close as US claims IRGC running out of money
events.summary: Iranian authorities have remained defiant despite the financial strain, saying they want to lift the US blockade and pressure on their terms. Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have rejected claims that Iran is unable to support its regional allies, but acknowledged that the United States’ sanctions and the war have created financial challenges. US Central Command chief Brad Cooper claimed last week that a combination of military attacks and a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports “has dealt severe blows” to the country. list 1 of 3 Hezbollah funding plan indicates a new challenge to Lebanon’s government list 2 of 3 Iran support for Houthis probed as Yemen war re-erupts and Saudi cities hit list 3 of 3 How Israel’s 2026 election works The admiral said the US had prevented at least $25bn in Iranian crude exports and helped freeze approximately $350m in cryptocurrency assets. This means the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) are now unable to pay their soldiers and Iran-linked regional groups suffering from financial shortfalls. “The financial strain on Iran’s military has become so significant that there are reports of Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments to their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also is not paying its troops,” Cooper said. This is being portrayed as a victory for the US in its war with Iran, which so far has shown very few tangible victories for Washington. Michael Knights, head of MENA research at US-based intelligence and geopolitical risk advisory firm Horizon Engage, said Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen have suffered financially during the past few years. “The national economies feeding the Hezbollah and Houthi movements are badly broken, so they continue to receive stipends and in-kind funding – in fuel products – from Iran,” Knights told Al Jazeera. For decades, the IRGC Quds Force has supplied money, weapons, components, training and manufacturing expertise to regional allied groups. It has enabled partners at loggerheads with the US and Israel to assemble or produce a number of weapons locally, according to United Nations experts and US officials. The axis groups also draw on businesses, including oil exports, as well as donations and local resources to fund their operations. Some Iraqi factions have been integrated into the official security forces and receive government funding through the Popular Mobilisation Forces. Allied commercial networks in Iraq are selling Iranian commodities and distributing proceeds through intermediaries and exchange houses, the US Department of the Treasury has claimed. This has put them in a better financial position than their “poorer cousins” in Hezbollah and the Houthis, Knights said, with some money allegedly flowing from Iraq towards Iran in recent years. “Some Iraqi militiamen and government civil servants are indeed paid late at the same time that Iraqi militias send funding overseas to help Iran, the Houthis and Lebanese Hezbollah,” he told Al Jazeera. The US Treasury alleged in September that Kataib Hezbollah , a prominent Tehran-backed Shia Muslim armed group in neighbouring Iraq, siphoned Iraqi resources to support Iran. The Treasury also described substantial earlier transfers from the Quds Force to Hezbollah, depicting flows in both directions. A report by the Reuters news agency earlier this month cited unnamed sources as saying Hezbollah received $200m from Iran in September . The US State Department rejected the report at the time, saying Hezbollah was “trying to save face with fake stories about cash influxes from Iran”. Iran’s economy has taken hit after hit in recent years due to war, domestic mismanagement and sanctions . This has led to runaway inflation, low-paying jobs, a depreciating national currency and isolation from the global community for 90 million Iranians. There appears to be little sign of the situation improving, with the World Bank reporting earlier this month a projected 7.7 percent contraction of the economy in the fiscal year 2026-27. The authorities emphasise that does not affect their resolve. They have also challenged US Treasury assessments that economic pressure could result in losing control within months . “Despite all these pressures, the Iranian economy has demonstrated very good resilience, and the claim that Iran’s economy is collapsing is nothing more than an illusion,” Central Bank chief Abdolnaser Hemmati said earlier this month. President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged on Sunday that military attacks and the maritime blockade had created substantial problems for the country. But he said his government was relying on domestic capacities to withstand the pressure. He claimed consumption management had now removed the need for petrol imports that would otherwise cost $12bn, if US pressure allowed imports at all.

events.title: Apple adds U.S. titanium supplier for iPhone Duo as supply stays tight
events.summary: Apple is adding a U.S. titanium supplier for its new iPhone Duo and expanding domestic production of camera components for the iPhone 18 Pro. It's part of the company's push to manufacture more critical components in the U.S. Apple said it's committing up to $100 million over three years to Pennsylvania-based Perryman Company, which will produce titanium used in Apple products including the $1,999 iPhone Duo. Apple is adding a U.S. titanium supplier for its new iPhone Duo and expanding domestic production of camera components for the iPhone 18 Pro as part of a push to expand manufacturing in its home country. The company said Tuesday it will commit up to $100 million over the next three years to Perryman Company, based in Houston, Pennsylvania, for the production of titanium used in Apple products, including the $1,999 foldable Duo. Since the start of President Donald Trump's second term, Apple has been vocal about its efforts to invest more in the U.S., even as the final assembly of most iPhones remains overseas. In August of last year, Apple launched the American Manufacturing Program (AMP), increasing its plan for domestic spending by $100 billion to a total of $600 billion. Tim Cook , Apple's CEO until last month, appeared at the White House for that announcement, as Trump was pushing the iPhone maker and other tech giants to bolster production in the U.S. The latest announcement comes as Apple faces severe supply constraints for its first foldable phone, which goes on sale in stores Friday. Telephone switch operators and PCs show why Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption Always on, always listening: New AI devices are pushing legal limits and could put users in jeopardy Online delivery estimates for some Duo models stretched to roughly 14 weeks on the first day of preorders, according to Morgan Stanley, the longest wait the firm has recorded for a new iPhone in a decade. Apple said Friday that preorder demand had been "nothing short of extraordinary," but hasn't said whether it plans to increase production. JPMorgan analysts estimate Apple will ship roughly 8 million to 9 million Duo devices this year, below earlier expectations of about 10 million, because of supply constraints. Apple didn't say whether the agreement with Perryman would increase near-term capacity. Perryman will melt, forge, and roll grade 5 titanium, which Apple said will contain at least 80% recycled material. Titanium is used for the Duo's enclosure, providing durability, according to Apple. In addition to the Perryman announcement, Apple said Tuesday that it's expanding its partnership with Delaware-based Qnity Electronics , which will manufacture advanced films used in the variable-aperture camera system on the iPhone 18 Pro. The feature allows the phone's main camera to adjust how much light enters the lens depending on conditions, giving users greater control over light and depth. Apple said nearly 100 components used in the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro are produced by American companies across more than a dozen states. "We're thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America," Sabih Khan, Apple's operating chief, said in a statement. Apple also highlighted investments with other AMP partners, including Broadcom for U.S.-made chips, Corning for specialty glass used in iPhones and Apple Watches, and Amkor , which is constructing a semiconductor packaging and testing facility in Peoria, Arizona. For the Duo, questions remain about whether Apple can produce enough phones to meet demand for a phone facing unusually long wait times before hitting stores. —CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed to this report WATCH: First impressions of the foldable iPhone Duo — Apple's biggest iPhone redesign ever

events.title: Advancing digital sovereignty with greater control and choice
events.summary: Oct 20, 2026 | Douglas Phillips - President and Chief Technology Officer, Microsoft Specialized Clouds Across my conversations with leaders in government, critical infrastructure and regulated industries, one priority consistently rises to the top: putting technology to work on their most important systems while maintaining the control those systems require. This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change. Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate. Last year, we introduced Microsoft Sovereign Cloud to give customers more choice in how they address these requirements. Since then, we have continued to turn our commitments into practical capabilities across public cloud and customer-operated environments, while expanding how we enable partners to address sovereignty requirements in their local markets. Today, we are sharing the next stage of that work. A continuum of control, built around the workload Our approach to digital sovereignty starts with the workload. Each workload carries different requirements for data, operations, technology dependencies, continuity and risk. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed to make it easier for organizations to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload without forcing every application into the same deployment model. Those needs can vary widely across organizations. A public-facing digital service may benefit from the scale and pace of innovation in the public cloud. A system supporting essential operations may need to continue running locally if connectivity is disrupted. An AI workload handling highly sensitive data may require models, data and processing to remain within a customer-controlled environment. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed around this workload-based approach, providing a continuum of management, control and options across Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and the Sovereign Partner Ecosystem. Organizations can apply the level of control appropriate to each workload while maintaining a consistent approach to governance and operations across their digital estate. Sovereign Public Cloud adds capabilities for workloads that require greater control and transparency while continuing to benefit from the scale and innovation of Azure. Sovereign Private Cloud extends cloud capabilities into customer-operated environments, including connected and disconnected operations. The Sovereign Partner Ecosystem broadens the continuum through independently operated environments, specialized partners, locally relevant expertise and technologies that support customers’ sovereignty requirements. These are not isolated destinations. Customers can combine public cloud, private cloud and partner capabilities across their digital estate, applying different levels of control to different workloads as their operating needs evolve. Making control more visible in Sovereign Public Cloud For many workloads, the public cloud provides a combination of scale, innovation, integrated security and compliance. Organizations can benefit from these capabilities while applying additional sovereignty controls for residency, confidentiality, operator access, policy and continuity. Our work in Sovereign Public Cloud makes these controls easier to understand, apply and demonstrate. Sovereign Control Panel , entering public preview at Microsoft Ignite, brings these signals together in a unified Azure portal experience. It helps organizations understand their sovereignty posture, apply and manage controls, identify gaps and risks and take action to address them. It also supports business continuity readiness by helping customers understand workload dependencies and assess portability across operating environments when required. This visibility complements controls across the operator-access lifecycle. Just-in-time Access and Customer Lockbox give customers additional control over access to their environments. For customers in the European Union (EU) and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), we are rolling out Data Guardian , which adds European-resident oversight by a trusted EU partner for qualifying Microsoft engineer remote access to in-scope production systems. Production Touch Ledger , also launched with phased rollout in the EU and EFTA, creates tamper-evident records of that access and the actions performed. Azure Key Vault Managed Hardware Security Module (HSM) already gives customers dedicated, single-tenant protection and control over the encryption keys used by supported Azure services. Last year, we committed to extending that control beyond Microsoft infrastructure. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, allowing customers to keep the root encryption key in hardware they own and operate on-premises or through a trusted third party. This gives organizations another option for workloads that require physical control of key hardware outside Microsoft infrastructure. Azure confidential computing helps protect supported data while it is processed in a hardware-based and attested trusted execution environment. We are also increasing transparency into the technologies that underpin that trust. Azure Confidential Clean Rooms , now in limited preview, applies confidential computing to approved multiparty collaboration, allowing participants to analyze shared sensitive data while limiting broader exposure of the underlying information. Together, these capabilities provide additional technical and operational controls that can support a broader digital sovereignty strategy aligned to an organization’s legal, policy, security, resilience and business requirements. Designing for resilience and operational independence For some workloads, digital sovereignty also means maintaining critical operations as connectivity, geopolitical and operating conditions change. Resilience must be designed from the start so essential workloads can continue operating through disruption. To help customers prepare for these scenarios, we are publishing new sovereign business continuity guidance and architecture patterns . These resources help organizations translate resilience requirements into architectures they can plan, implement and test before they are needed. For many workloads, the scale and geographic reach of the public cloud provide a strong foundation for resilience across locations and operating conditions.

events.title: Monetary policy could turn accommodative as AI productivity gains take hold: MAS chief economist
events.summary: While AI-related investments are driving economic growth, the technology has yet to deliver significant productivity improvements across the wider economy, says MAS chief economist Edward Robinson. MAS chief economist Edward Robinson said central banks should stay restrictive for now, as AI investment is boosting demand but has not yet lifted economy-wide productivity. He warned that misreading the shift could raise inflation risks, after MAS tightened policy in April and July 2026 before holding rates in October. Robinson said AI is helping Asia, especially electronics exports, and could lift productivity by up to 0.6 percentage point a year if adoption, skills and infrastructure improve. SINGAPORE – Central banks may be able to ease monetary policy once artificial intelligence delivers widespread productivity gains, but they should keep policy appropriately restrictive for now as the AI investment boom fuels demand, said Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) chief economist Edward Robinson on Oct 20. While AI-related investments are driving economic growth, the technology has yet to deliver significant productivity improvements across the wider economy, he said. Speaking at the Beijing Financial Street Forum, Robinson cautioned that misjudging this transition could carry risks, calling for a gradual, data-dependent approach to monetary policy. MAS tightened monetary policy in April and July 2026 amid rising inflation risks, before leaving its policy settings unchanged in October. In its latest monetary policy statement on Oct 14, the central bank warned that domestic inflation could remain elevated if the AI-related boom generated broader economic spillovers and pushed up unit labour costs. Still, Robinson noted that the AI boom has been particularly beneficial for Asia, with AI-driven electronics accounting for more than 70 per cent of the region’s export growth this year. Beyond manufacturing, Asian economies – including China – are also making progress in developing AI technologies, ranging from advanced chips to large language models. However, Robinson, who is also MAS deputy managing director for economic policy, said growth in industries producing AI-related technologies has largely been driven by increased investment and more intensive use of existing resources, rather than improvements in efficiency. New data centres are being built, advanced equipment is being used more intensively, and workers and machines are effectively “working harder”, rather than “working smarter”, he noted. “AI is diffusing across the wider economy faster than the personal computer and the internet did,” he said. “While early evidence points to efficiency gains in specific applications, it remains too soon to identify a decisive economy-wide step-up in productivity.” Nevertheless, Robinson pointed to the potential for substantial gains over time, drawing parallels with the introduction of electricity a century ago. The productivity benefits of electrification became substantial only after factories and workflows were redesigned around the technology, he said. Similarly, AI could require widespread adoption, investments in skills and infrastructure, and changes to how organisations operate before its full economic benefits emerge, he added. With sufficiently broad adoption and appropriate investment, AI could raise total factor productivity growth by up to 0.6 percentage point annually, Robinson said, pointing to estimates from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. “This could meaningfully offset the negative effects from demographic ageing and other structural headwinds in Asia,” he noted. THE BUSINESS TIMES

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Staffing software giant calls in CrowdStrike as customers face login headaches and questions remain over possible data theft 'Password1' and a forgotten test account land Welsh outfits in hot water 25 minutes ago Google Cloud says a 'power event' caused today's outage 1 hour ago Microsoft admits that Always On VPN problems were not fixed in the October Security Update 2 hours ago Whitehall shuts the front door on digital ID but leaves the back open 3 hours ago UK finance watchdog wants firms to report AI failures and close calls 4 hours ago Bullhorn is the latest tech giant finding itself on the wrong end of a cyberattack, forcing the recruitment software provider to shut down its platform while it investigates. The US-based company, which serves more than 10,000 customers worldwide, says its systems are now back online in the UK, US, and Australia. Unfortunately for customers hoping to get back to work, online doesn't necessarily mean working. In its latest status update, published on Tuesday , Bullhorn confirmed that some users were still struggling with single sign-on (SSO), password resets, and customizations, while several products continued to report degraded performance. Things started going sideways on Friday, October 16, when Bullhorn flagged problems getting job postings onto Indeed. By the following morning, the platform was suffering a full-blown outage, and Bullhorn confirmed later that day that it was dealing with something rather more serious than a technical hiccup. "We have detected a cyber incident on the Bullhorn Platform. We have temporarily disabled access to our systems in order to contain the activity while we investigate further," the company said, noting that it had roped in cybersecurity specialists from CrowdStrike to help investigate the attack and restore its services. For recruitment agencies using Bullhorn, the outage meant losing access to candidate records, job applications, placements and, in some cases, the systems used to get people paid. Services began returning on Monday, but recovery has been anything but seamless. As of Tuesday morning, Bullhorn's status page still listed degraded performance across several products, including its automation tools, Talent Platform, Onboarding365 and Time & Expense. While Bullhorn is making progress getting customers back into their accounts, it has yet to answer arguably the bigger question: whether the attackers stole anything. In its customer FAQ , it said a forensic investigation is ongoing, and has not yet determined whether attackers exfiltrated customer data. Bullhorn says it will contact affected customers if the investigation finds their information was compromised, and it also warned people to watch out for opportunistic crooks looking to exploit the chaos. "Threat actors may pose as Bullhorn personnel via email, text, or phone calls, using the incident as a pretext to request credentials or sensitive information," it warned on Tuesday, stressing that its employees would never ask customers to disclose passwords, multi-factor authentication codes, or verification tokens. The company has also required password resets for users who don’t log in through SSO, while customers using API integrations have been instructed to rotate their credentials. The cause of the intrusion remains unknown, and Bullhorn has not publicly identified the attackers or confirmed whether ransomware was involved. The company didn’t respond to The Register ’s questions at publication time. The outage may be coming to an end, but Bullhorn's investigation into what the attackers actually did is far from over.

Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced. I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. We discussed what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet. Read the exclusive interview to find out what Cammarata’s claims could mean for AI . —Will Douglas Heaven Making the internet better for AI agents might make it worse for everyone else Until recently, you could split internet users into just two categories: bots and people. But personal AI agents are slowly but surely disrupting that divide by taking on online tasks, from booking flights to reserving hotel rooms. Meta’s Muse alone was downloaded 5 million times in its first month. The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents.  If that demand keeps rising, the internet could be redesigned for agents rather than people. events.title: France PM promises more curfews as authorities seek to regain control
events.summary: Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu says local authorities will coordinate with mayors to decide whether to impose curfews. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has said new curfews will be imposed where necessary in parts of the country, as authorities sought to restore order after weekend demonstrations over the cost of living and issues in the education system descended into riots. In a post on X on Tuesday, Lecornu said local authorities would coordinate with mayors to decide whether to impose curfews in their respective prefectures. list 1 of 3 ‘Anger and shame’: Macron denounces France’s nationwide rioting, looting list 2 of 3 French protest violence: A ‘Christmas present’ for Le Pen’s far right? list 3 of 3 French protests: Is it game over for Macron’s centrists before elections? More than half a million people gathered across France on Saturday for demonstrations that brought together students demanding better education conditions and groups rejecting the high cost of living. The protests descended into looting and arson in numerous locations, with more than 2,500 people arrested. Monday night passed without any major incidents across France, police have confirmed. The government is due to hold a series of meetings as it intensifies efforts to contain the unrest, which followed weeks of student protests over education standards. French Digital Minister Anne Le Henanff is due to meet social media bosses on Tuesday to discuss the protests. In a post on X on Monday, Henanff said goods looted over the weekend were being sold online and called on platforms to remove such listings. Demonstrators have called for further protests this Saturday, but France’s main trade unions have not backed the call, with union officials due to meet Lecornu on Wednesday. On Thursday, Lecornu will hold talks with political parties about the protests, which come before presidential elections due to take place in April and May next year. Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right National Rally, currently leads the polls. Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, who leads La France Insoumise, is currently in second place. President Emmanuel Macron cannot stand because of France’s two-term limit. Le Pen and Melenchon have both been accused of exploiting the protests before next year’s vote. Alice Cohen-Morzadec, a spokesperson for the French Student Union, told Al Jazeera that the demonstrations were an “outburst” of anger in response to Macron’s policies, which she said had “destroyed” students’ living conditions. “One student out of two cannot eat properly. One student out of three doesn’t have a permanent house to live in. We cannot study in these conditions,” Cohen-Morzadec said.

events.title: Is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space?
events.summary: Analysts say a Russian craft’s close pass of a commercial radar satellite is a first and a warning to Kyiv’s backers. A Russian military satellite has manoeuvred to within metres of a US-registered radar satellite believed to provide intelligence to Ukraine, according to space-tracking data reported by The War Zone, a US defence news site. Cosmos 2612 may have passed ICEYE-X36, a satellite owned by the US arm of the Finnish company ICEYE. list 1 of 4 Finland seeking one million land mines as it eyes Russian threat list 2 of 4 Children among six killed in Russian drone strike on Ukraine park list 3 of 4 US-Ukraine relations sour as Trump, Zelenskyy clash over talks, arms list 4 of 4 South Korea to pull more embassy staff from Ukraine after POW row LeoLabs, a US space-tracking company, put the closest approach at about 500 metres, according to Breaking Defence. ICEYE has supplied radar imagery to Ukraine since 2022, Defence News reported. So is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space? Al Jazeera spoke to analysts to find out: A Russian satellite has deliberately positioned itself close to a Western one, after months of manoeuvring. Cosmos 2612 is one of six satellites the Russian military launched in April, The War Zone reported. In May, four of them moved close to an ICEYE satellite. ICEYE-X36 is a commercial satellite, owned by a private company rather than a government, but ICEYE sells radar imagery to militaries and supplies data to the US and its allies. ICEYE’s chief executive, Rafal Modrzewski, told the Reuters news agency the company then moved its own satellite, which appeared to prompt further Russian manoeuvres. Then, between Thursday and Friday last week, Cosmos 2612 closed in from more than 320km (200 miles) from ICEYE-X36 to about 4.8km (3 miles), the space-tracking company LeoLabs told the news site Axios. Over the weekend, it moved between positions ahead of and behind the ICEYE satellite, at times coming within roughly 500 metres, LeoLabs said in a report on Monday, adding that the estimate was uncertain and, by Monday, it had begun to move away. A Ukrainian official told Axios that Ukraine’s military works with ICEYE and uses its capabilities, but said it was unclear whether ICEYE-X36 itself supports Ukraine. Has Russia done this before, and what is the purpose? In the past, Russia has mainly carried out such manoeuvres against Western military satellites, rather than commercially owned ones, Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer in the defence studies department at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera. In early 2020, two Russian satellites moved close to USA 245, a US spy satellite. In September 2025, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said two Russian Luch-Olymp satellites were tracking two Intelsat satellites used by the German military. Dr Marco Langbroek, a lecturer in optical space situational awareness at TU Delft Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, said: “At geostationary altitude, we have seen two Russian satellites (LUCH/OLYMP-K 1 & 2) repeatedly approach western communication satellites to distances of a few tens of kilometres in the past few years, likely with the intention to eavesdrop on communications and data transfers. And we have seen the Russians practising very close approaches in Low Earth Orbit – similar to what they now did to ICEYE-X36 – with their own satellites as test targets.” However, this incident is different, because “approaching another satellite this close without the cooperation of the owner or operator of the other satellite, is widely considered ‘not done’ as it is dangerous, with a risk of collision or interference. “It is equivalent to placing your car on the freeway within 10 cm of another driving car: highly unsafe.” Langbroek said it is not known what the purpose of the Russian manoeuvre was, however, “it could be a dry run for a future attack, it could be provocation or scare tactics to ruffle the feathers of Ukraine and its allies, and/or a test to see how the satellite operators react to a threat like this.” This sort of manoeuvre, therefore, falls into the pattern of “hybrid warfare” – “the same kind of provocations and inciting reactions like what Russia does when they fly a drone into Polish airspace or zoom a NATO warship at low elevation in the Baltic Sea”. Close approaches have happened for years, but not like this. Hilborne said this is “the first time that a country has done such a manoeuvre … against the commercial satellite without any consent”. It was also “incredibly close”, he said, with some reports putting the distance at less than 30 metres. Far more common is interference that does not require going near a satellite at all. This is mostly done through jamming, which drowns out a satellite’s signals, often from the ground. Western military officials told Reuters that Russian interference with Western space systems has increased significantly since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

events.title: Yemen: Maps show 10 years of changing control
events.summary: A decade of war has shifted Yemen’s front lines, but the Houthis still hold the capital, Sanaa, and no side controls the country. Looking at maps of who controls which areas of Yemen over the past 12 years of war reveals changing alliances and coalitions, all while the country faces poverty and malnutrition. The Houthi armed group, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized the capital, Sanaa, on September 21, 2014, after advancing south from their heartland of Saada in northern Yemen. list 1 of 4 Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi missile launched towards Riyadh list 2 of 4 Iraq’s PM tells Saudi crown prince Iraqi territory will not be used for attacks list 3 of 4 Two scenarios for the Yemen war list 4 of 4 Renewed fighting risks ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ in Yemen, aid groups warn The Iran-allied group used antigovernment grievances to gain support after July 2014 fuel subsidy cuts triggered anger. The Houthis mobilised protests demanding the reversal of the government’s decisions, and subsequently its resignation. They allied with forces loyal to former President Ali Abdullah Saleh, which helped them capture military positions and state institutions. Then-President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi fled to Aden in February 2015. When forces aligned with the Houthis and Saleh advanced towards the southern port city, Hadi took refuge in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. In March 2015, Saudi Arabia launched a military intervention to restore his internationally recognised government. Over the next decade, alliances broke and front lines shifted. In this visual explainer, AJLabs uses seven maps to track how Yemen has been fragmented, and how no side has been able to control the whole country. By late 2016, two years after the Houthis seized Sanaa, Yemen was split into rival zones of control. The Houthi-Saleh alliance controlled Sanaa and much of the northern and western heartlands, home to most of Yemen’s population. Pro-government forces held territory across the south and the east, supported by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) also challenged government authority across parts of the south. The antigovernment alliance in Yemen went through its most significant fracture after Saleh appeared close to switching sides in the conflict, leading to a short outbreak of fighting with the Houthis, who then killed Yemen’s former longtime president in Sanaa in December 2017. This left the Houthis, a primarily Zaidi Shia group, in sole charge of much of northwestern Yemen, including Sanaa and the port city of Hodeidah. Some pro-Saleh forces switched sides, and pro-government and anti-Houthi forces controlled territory across the south and the east while AQAP retained pockets of influence. Nearly three years into its intervention and despite a heavy air campaign, the Saudi-led coalition had failed to restore the internationally recognised government of Hadi in Sanaa. The Houthis continued to hold Sanaa and much of the northwestern highlands. Government-aligned forces held extensive territory across the south and the east while AQAP maintained pockets of influence. The December 2018 Stockholm Agreement halted a pro-government offensive against Houthi-held Hodeidah, a major entry point for food, fuel and aid. Neither side had been able to achieve a decisive victory. Divisions among the Houthis’ opponents further weakened efforts to establish government authority. The UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC), which seized Aden in 2019, held territory separately from government forces. Despite officially being part of the anti-Houthi, Saudi-led coalition, the STC fought the government several times. Hadi was forced to transfer his powers to an eight-member Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), ending his presidency without reclaiming the capital. Saudi-Houthi negotiations raised hopes of a settlement and led to a truce in April 2022, but Yemen remained divided as it had been for years. While the Houthis retained their control over Yemen’s northwest, the STC continued to undermine Yemen’s internationally recognised government as it tried to increase its own power in the south in the hope that this would eventually lay the foundations for an independent state. Government forces controlled broad areas of the east, which separatists also wanted to claim for any future state. The Hadrami Elite Forces, a UAE-backed group, controlled coastal Hadramout. The National Resistance Forces (NRF), led by Saleh’s nephew Tareq Saleh and supported by the UAE, held part of the Red Sea coast. By 2025, the Houthis had held Sanaa and most of Yemen’s northwest continuously for more than a decade. Government-aligned forces operated across the south and the east. Houthi attacks on shipping, which the group said were launched in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza, drew attacks from Israel, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Text of this article October 20, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Apple announces new American Manufacturing Program partners for iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro From U.S. titanium to advanced camera technology, American suppliers are producing key components in the latest iPhone lineup CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced new and expanded partnerships with American companies that are supplying critical materials and components for iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro. Through its American Manufacturing Program (AMP), Apple is partnering with Perryman Company, a Pennsylvania-based titanium producer, to supply titanium for Apple products, including iPhone Duo. Apple is also expanding its partnership with Qnity Electronics, headquartered in Delaware, to produce technology for the new variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro camera system — the most advanced Apple has ever made. Apple works with suppliers in all 50 states and supports more than 450,000 American jobs. We’re proud to work with Perryman and Qnity Electronics to continue expanding our American Manufacturing Program and support U.S. jobs.” The grade 5 titanium enclosure on iPhone Duo is exceptionally strong, providing amazing durability to the first foldable iPhone. Apple will commit up to $100 million over the next three years with Perryman, a family-owned business and a global leader in manufacturing specialty titanium products. At its site in Houston, Pennsylvania, Perryman melts, forges, and rolls titanium with a minimum of 80 percent recycled content for iPhone Duo. Apple is also expanding its partnership with Qnity Electronics to build key camera technology for iPhone 18 Pro in the U.S. Qnity, which joined the American Manufacturing Program in March, will produce advanced films essential to the new variable aperture camera system on iPhone 18 Pro. Variable aperture is at the heart of the new 48MP Fusion Main camera, which enables incredible light and depth control. It’s powered by on-device intelligence that automatically lets in more light for darker settings and helps get sharper detail in brighter ones. Nearly 100 components in iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro — from wireless chips to the silicon that powers key functions across the devices — are produced by American companies and drawn from suppliers in more than a dozen states. events.title: Draymond Green says he's 'not Steph Curry,' wants to play another year even if he leaves Golden State Warriors
events.summary: Draymond Green wants to retire with the Golden State Warriors but says he plans to keep playing next season, even if it means joining another team. The four-time NBA champion is entering his 15th season with Golden State after signing a one-year deal in July. Green says he would have no “ill feelings” if the Warriors move on from him and remains grateful for his career with the franchise. Four-time NBA champion Draymond Green said he would love to retire as a member of the Golden State Warriors, but he plans to keep playing next season, even if that means joining another team. Green was drafted by the Warriors in 2012 and has spent all 14 seasons of his career with Golden State. He signed a one-year deal with the team in July. In an interview with CNBC Sport, Green said he plans to approach this season as though it could be his last with the Warriors. "I would love to retire a Golden State Warrior. However, I'm also not Steph Curry, right? So I don't have every luxury that Steph Curry has, and that's okay," Green said. "It's such a rare thing to be on one team your entire career. And if I can accomplish that feat, I would love to." Curry expressed a similar desire to stay with the franchise when he spoke with CNBC in September. "I want to be a lifer with the Golden State Warriors," Curry said on CNBC's Squawk on the Street . Shortly after that interview, Curry signed a two-year contract extension worth a reported $116 million that keeps him with Golden State through the 2028-29 season. But Green acknowledged that his future with the Warriors is less certain. He said he won't harbor any "ill feelings" toward the franchise if his time with the team ends after this season. "I would love to play basketball next year...if that's not here, I'm not going to retire," he said. Green said he understands that the Warriors will weigh business considerations when deciding his future and hopes he fits into the team's plans. "If I don't, great. But I'm extremely grateful for the journey that I've been on here," he added. Last season, the Warriors power forward averaged 8.4 points, 5.5 rebounds and 5.5 assists per game. Golden State went 37-45 and missed the playoffs. This season, head coach Steve Kerr has made adjustments to the offense that include playing faster and spacing out the floor differently. Green, who won NBA Defensive Player of the Year in 2017, is being asked to get down the floor faster and not trail the play. Green said he doesn't take entering his 15th season with the Warriors for granted and feels "blessed" to have spent his entire NBA career with the franchise. "I don't know how many years I have left in the NBA, let alone at this place," he said. "For me, it's all about enjoying what's in front of us." Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes. Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these. The streaming service first previewed the idea at its Investor Day in May, where it also introduced AI capabilities that let listeners ask questions about what they’re listening to or watching and debuted new tools for managing creator sponsorships. As the company explained at the time, memberships would help to “create a natural path to go deeper, unlocking new and exclusive experiences for fans and new revenue opportunities for creators.” The feature is now rolling out to 34 markets globally , including the U.S. The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube. Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode. Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment. To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes. Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases). A handful of shows will offer memberships at launch, including “The Adam Friedland Show,” “Making Sense with Sam Harris,” “Shawn Ryan Show,” “The Sculpt Society,” “Two Hot Takes,” as well as YMH Studios, which is bringing memberships to 12 shows across its network. Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics. events.title: Oura adds new fitness metrics to show how workouts impact your body
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. As competition in the smart ring market escalates , Oura is introducing two new features to give people more insight into their workouts and how they impact their bodies. The company announced on Tuesday it’s rolling out Cardio Effort and VO₂ max metrics to expand workout tracking beyond exercise duration and heart rate zones. While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating. By launching more advanced workout metrics, Oura is looking to differentiate itself from competitors. With Cardio Effort, users will be able to see how much a workout taxes their cardiovascular system. This measurement is aggregated over the week relative to each user’s individual baseline to provide more insights. Oura explained that this metric shifts users’ focus from “How many minutes did I move?” to “Am I maintaining my fitness, building it, or overdoing it?” Since Cardio Effort accounts for both intensity and duration, a shorter, more intense workout can yield a similar score to a longer, less intense one, the company says. Oura notes that the metric has two components: Workout Cardio Effort and Weekly Cardio Effort. The first metric evaluates the impact of an individual workout, while the latter aggregates effort into a weekly total, categorized as “Light,” “Fair,” “Maintaining,” “Building,” or “Reaching.” Oura measures elevated heart rate relative to each member’s long-term resting heart rate, avoiding the variability associated with maximum-heart-rate estimates. Weekly effort levels are then determined using personalized ranges based on recent activity patterns. Cardio Effort is rolling out to Oura Ring Gen3 and later models. As for VO₂ max, the metric shows how workouts contribute to long-term fitness. It measures how effectively the heart, lungs, and muscles work together to deliver and use oxygen during exercise. Previously, measuring VO₂ max typically required a lab test or a six-minute walking test. Oura can now estimate it passively using GPS-enabled workouts. After completing five qualifying activities, users receive an initial VO2 Max estimate. Within the My Health Heart Hub, they can view their current VO2 Max estimate in ml/kg/min, their fitness category (Low, Fair, High, or Peak), how their estimate has changed over time, and when it was last updated. Users also receive insights highlighting meaningful changes in their VO2 Max or indicating when their estimate remains consistent. VO₂ Max is launching in Oura Labs, the company’s hub for experimental features, for members with Gen3 and newer Oura Ring devices. Oura says these two new features are designed to work together to show users how hard they’re working and how that effort is adding up over time. events.title: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
events.summary: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line. As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn’t a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie. The AI adoption spectrum by industry Recent survey data from TripleTen highlights just how stark the current adoption curve is across different sectors of the economy (see Figure 1). Figure 1: The AI adoption curve remains steep across industries, but non-tech industry adoption rates are increasing. Source : TripleTen , 2026 While tech leads the way, finance emerges as a clear second: 48% of finance workers have been asked to use AI chatbots, and 32% have been asked to automate parts of their workflow. This demonstrates how rapidly knowledge work integrates AI once clear use cases emerge. By contrast, sectors like healthcare (18% asked to use chatbots) and education (25%) reflect lower initial exposure. Because these broad industry categories encompass a mix of specialized hands-on professionals, clinical or instructional personnel, and back-office administrative staff, universal adoption was never going to happen overnight. Integrating automated tools into compliance-heavy or human-facing operations requires a more deliberate pace, which is reflected by the lower numbers. The AI skills workers are being asked to learn Across all surveyed industries, 79% of workers report being asked to learn at least one skill they didn’t previously have. Looking at the specific competencies demanded in tech today offers a preview of the skill sets likely to shift into other sectors (see Figure 2). Figure 2: Workforces across industries are learning new skills. Source : TripleTen , 2026 Although some of these sound like niche skills confined to tech, many of them will translate to frontline work across sectors—from hospital systems managing patient logistics to school districts processing administrative reporting. One skill gets less attention than it should. Only 30% of managers and owners call judging whether AI output is right or wrong an absolute must, which puts it sixth on a list of seven. As AI tools reach more industries, this is the skill that catches mistakes before they cause problems. It is also where work experience helps most: To spot a wrong answer, you need to know what the right one looks like. How early AI adoption helps your career Early AI adoption offers clear professional leverage: TripleTen’s survey data shows that when managers learned a new skill or automation process from an employee, 88% of those employee-led AI innovations became standard company practice. In early-adopting industries, employees who identify repetitive administrative tasks and use AI tools to streamline them have a voice in shaping organizational policy. As healthcare networks, educational institutions, and retail operations begin broader rollouts of AI-enabled software, workers who understand how to validate outputs, prompt models, and automate routine tasks will hold a strong advantage. Being the person who can streamline administrative overhead promises better chances for retention, promotions, and wage growth. Ana Riabova, the AI strategy and enablement lead at TripleTen, says, “Everyone talks about saving time, but the real win with early adoption is expanding what you can actually do. People who get ahead are using it to handle things they used to have to hand off. It doesn’t matter how senior or junior you are. You keep your core skills, but suddenly you aren’t boxed in by them anymore.” The AI resource gap: Who pays for training and how workers learn If non-tech industries absorb these tools more gradually, the challenge for workers lies in getting access to quality learning resources. Workers’ out-of-pocket investment in training varies significantly by industry: Tech: $1,758 average (13% spent $0) Finance: $1,664 average (24% spent $0) Healthcare: $990 average (45% spent $0) Education: $883 average (42% spent $0) Nearly half of healthcare and education workers spent nothing out of pocket on professional development last year. Furthermore, tech workers actively leverage a larger variety of learning channels (see Figure 3). Figure 3: Professional development efforts mirror the AI adoption curve. Source : TripleTen , 2026 Tech workers are nearly twice as likely as all workers to use AI chatbots as learning tools (48% vs. 27%), and more than twice as likely as workers outside tech (21%), effectively using AI to accelerate their acquisition of other skills. However, ask workers whom they trust most to teach them a new job skill, and they choose someone currently doing that job (31%). Fewer pick an official certification program (19%), an AI tool (16%), or a university professor (6%). Conclusion The difference in AI adoption rates across industries is not a story of who is succeeding and who is failing. Rather, it’s a timeline of how technology diffuses through an economy. Tech and finance are testing the mechanics of AI integration today. For workers in healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing, the current phase provides a valuable window to observe which skills generate real productivity gains—allowing them to build those competencies before they become standard industry expectations. events.title: Yemen’s critically ill are trapped as war closes the country’s airports
events.summary: A re-ignition of Yemen’s war has left the chronically sick and needing treatment trapped in the country. Sanaa, Yemen – Rajaa Ghirsan, a 50-year-old seamstress from Sanaa, Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital, can barely speak or breathe due to obstructions in her airway. Her vocal cord paralysis and severe complications in her larynx have left her dependent on a device fitted around her neck to keep air flowing and stave off suffocation. The device has to be replaced every two months and costs $100 each time. list 1 of 3 Cholera cases surge in Yemen as conflict intensifies, WHO says list 2 of 3 Why Iran-US negotiations keep failing list 3 of 3 Houthi attack on Yemen army camp in Shabwa kills at least 53: reports She has undergone six operations in Egypt and India since 2006 in an attempt to try to help her breathe normally, but she now needs another complex operation abroad to open her airway. As Yemen’s conflict-weakened health system lacks the infrastructure and specialist care required, she will need to head overseas for treatment. After registering with the Higher Medical Committee in Sanaa, the body responsible for arranging medical treatment abroad, she spent seven years trying to secure a seat on a once-weekly flight to Amman, where Yemeni patients have been treated. But repeated closures and air attacks have kept that flight out of reach, and she cannot afford the long overland journey to Aden airport, which is her only alternative out of the country. “The device helps her breathe a little, but it has worn her out and taken away her rest for years,” says Nouran al-Salawi, 28, Ghirsan’s daughter, who has cared for her mother for the past decade while raising two children of her own. “She is waiting for the moment she can have the last operation and be free of it, or she is waiting for death instead.” Ghirsan is among the many Yemenis who depend on Sanaa International Airport to get the medical care they need abroad. The airport is the main air link for millions living under Houthi control in the north, but it has been repeatedly shut since the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis closed it to commercial traffic in August 2016. A United Nations-brokered truce allowed a limited number of flights to resume in May 2022, but Israeli air attacks in 2025 damaged the airport and destroyed aircraft. In July, Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia struck its only working runway to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing. As of today, no regular flights leave the capital, while Aden, the seat of the internationally recognised government and the main alternative for patients in the north, has also come under attack. Anis al-Asbahi, spokesperson for the Houthi-run Ministry of Health in Sanaa, told Al Jazeera that repeated closures of Sanaa airport over the past decade have affected about 400,000 patients, including 250,000 who need treatment abroad. The flight disruptions have also affected more than 125,000 people with cancer who face shortages of medicine. “It has led to shortages of more than 1,600 types of medicine, including 12 cancer drugs that are barred from entering the country,” he said. “Additionally, more than 40,000 patients with thalassemia and haemolytic anaemia face shortages of iron chelation drugs and the intravenous solutions needed for their treatment.” Yemen’s Houthis have unilaterally released 159 war prisoners loyal to the Saudi-backed government of Yemen, according to a statement by the head of the Houthi Prisoner Affairs Committee, Abdul-Qader al-Murtada [Yahya Arhab/EPA] Fighting between government and Houthi forces has reignited in recent months, leading to new restrictions on the movement of aid and people. This month, UN envoy Hans Grundberg told the Security Council that the country had slid back into full-scale war. Aden’s airport has been hit twice this month , most recently on October 16, when two missiles landed about 500 metres (550 yards) from a Yemenia plane preparing to take off for Cairo. With Sanaa airport out of operation, Aden’s under attack, and unrest this year in Seiyun, a city in the eastern province of Hadramout that hosts another airport, patients in northern Yemen have limited options. Mohammed Shajara, 30, tried to reach Tehran for treatment for his paraplegic five-year-old daughter in June. But he was left stranded in Tehran when the government blocked Iranian flights to and from Sanaa in July, so they returned without treatment. Aden was his next option, but the journey from Sanaa takes about 14 hours and involves crossing dozens of checkpoints on both sides of the front lines. With the airport coming under repeated attack, he is holding off for now. Abdulkarim Abdullah, 60, had kidney failure and relied on weekly dialysis in Sanaa. The regular treatment has strained his family’s finances, so they have looked for a treatment to fix the problem.

events.title: Taobao invests $19 million in Singapore promotions for 11.11 sale launching Oct 20
events.summary: Pursuit Of Jade star Zhang Linghe fronts Chinese e-commerce giant Taobao’s 11.11 sale with a shopping livestream and special merchandise, in addition to its advertising around Singapore. Taobao is spending 100 million yuan (S$19 million) on Singapore’s 11.11 sale, with free shipping vouchers, public transport ads and shopping vouchers to grow its market share. The company has widened free shipping, added air express delivery and PayNow, and says Singapore is a key hub for Chinese brands entering South-east Asia. Taobao is using AI tools and local recommendations to stand out from rivals like Pinduoduo, while English AI features are due next year and Alibaba faces profit pressure. HONG KONG – Chinese e-commerce giant Taobao is investing 100 million yuan (S$19 million) in Singapore’s promotions for its 11.11 Singles’ Day sale , which kicked off on Oct 20. The e-commerce company’s biggest sale of the year – which runs till Nov 13 – is part of Taobao’s efforts to expand its presence here. The 100 million yuan includes free shipping vouchers, physical advertising on public transport in Singapore, and shopping vouchers for customers, said Cora Cai, Taobao’s Singapore country head, at a press conference on Oct 16 in Hong Kong. The physical advertisements in Singapore include about 200 big screens in the central business district and residential areas, with spending double that of 2025’s 11.11 season, Cai said. This is part of Taobao’s continued investment in the Singapore market and its overall expansion into foreign markets, Cai said. Since introducing free shipping with $0 minimum spend in August 2026, Taobao has expanded eligible products across fashion apparel, sports and outdoors, and maternity and baby products categories, with the majority of trending fashion apparel now eligible for free shipping. Taobao has also introduced air express delivery, allowing users to upgrade eligible parcels to air shipping for as little as $1, to receive their purchases as quickly as in five days. The e-commerce platform also started accepting payments via PayNow in October. “Singapore is one of the countries we’re expanding in as the appetite for Chinese brands is high in Singapore,” said Cai. “Singapore has become a hub for Chinese brands to go overseas in South-east Asia – they often pick Singapore as their first stop in the region.” She said 70% of Singaporean online shoppers buy clothing from Taobao, while furniture is emerging as the fastest-growing category among Singaporean homebuyers. Taobao faces fierce competition from other Chinese e-commerce platforms, such as Pinduoduo, which competes on price by offering heavily discounted products. Cai said that Taobao intends to differentiate itself through its large variety of products and its technical capabilities to help consumers find what they want. “Consumers nowadays don’t buy an item just because it’s cheap; they buy it because they actually need it,” she said. “We aim to upgrade our overall shopping guide capabilities so consumers can find what they want faster. Simultaneously, through AI and curation, we ensure that products genuinely suited for the local market are visible.” . The app’s new AI features include a localised recommendation algorithm and enhanced AI shopping assistants, said Ye Tian, general manager of Taobao Tmall Overseas. Currently, many of these advanced AI tools are optimised only in the Mandarin version of the app. AI functions in other languages, including English, are in the pipeline over the next year, as the platform targets broader demographics across the Asia-Pacific region, said Taobao. Taobao declined to comment on how much it invested in its latest AI upgrades. Its parent company, Alibaba Group, on Aug 20 reported higher revenue of its most recent quarter, boosted by the global artificial intelligence frenzy driving demand for its products. However, net profit plunged 76 per cent year on year to 10.5 billion yuan, reflecting the impact of large strategic investments and economic pressure in its home market.
