events.title: TSH Resources yet to respond to SGX’s haze queries; First Resources pledges cooperation
events.summary: Agribusiness companies have come under increasing scrutiny over their potential links to the transboundary haze. SINGAPORE – Plantation company TSH Resources has yet to respond publicly to queries from the Singapore Exchange (SGX) over fires in Indonesia amid growing attention on agribusiness firms’ operations as transboundary haze affects the region. The company, which has a primary listing on Bursa Malaysia and a secondary listing in Singapore, had not published a response as at 6pm on Oct 20. It also did not respond to queries from The Straits Times. In response to ST's queries, a spokesperson for Singapore Exchange Regulation said it was engaging TSH Resources to seek information on the impact of the fires on its operations, and would require the company to disclose any material information. Under SGX's regulatory framework, companies with secondary listings in Singapore are required to simultaneously publish on the SGX website any announcements made in their home markets. Unlike companies primarily listed in Singapore, those with secondary listings generally follow the rules of their home exchanges, although SGX may impose additional requirements. A spokesperson for Bursa Malaysia told ST on Oct 20 that it was aware of the issue and monitoring developments closely. The spokesperson did not confirm whether Bursa had queried TSH Resources, but said it would engage relevant parties where there were valid and verifiable grounds to do so. Recent bourse filings, including one on Oct 20, showed that TSH Resources had been buying back its own shares. TSH Resources was among seven listed companies named by Senior Minister K. Shanmugam during a media doorstop on Oct 19 as having received queries from SGX. He said companies could not just rely solely on statements about their fire prevention policies. The Government would ask for the full facts from companies, seeking evidence on where the fires started, who owned the affected land, and what steps were taken to contain them. In response to his remarks, First Resources said on Oct 20 that it welcomed a thorough, evidence-based examination of the ongoing fires and haze situation, and reiterated that it strictly enforces a longstanding zero-burning policy across its operations. It said it is confident that an objective review of the available evidence would show that it does not clear land using fire, either directly or indirectly. It added that it was open to constructive suggestions from regulators, customers, investors, civil society organisations and other industry stakeholders on strengthening fire prevention and management. Other companies including Golden Agri-Resources, Indofood Agri, Kencana Agri, Wilmar and Bumitama Agri had not published additional statements, after responding to SGX’s queries last week. The Indonesia Stock Exchange has also queried listed companies over the fires and haze, prompting disclosures on their fire prevention measures and the impact on their operations. Most of the companies said the fires had not materially affected their operations or financial performance. Among those who have responded were Astra Agro Lestari, PP London Sumatra Indonesia (LSIP) and Salim Ivomas Pratama, which have ownership links to Singapore-listed companies. Astra Agro Lestari said in an Oct 16 disclosure that fire mitigation protocols were in place across its concessions. But the company acknowledged that its subsidiary, Subur Agro Makmur, located in South Kalimantan, had been affected by forest and land fires. The company, which is controlled by Astra International, a subsidiary of Singapore-listed Jardine Cycle & Carriage, said the fires had not resulted in any operational shutdowns or materially affected its production targets or financial performance. It also noted that the fires had been extinguished . Astra Agro Lestari also noted that employees at Subur Agro Makmur were being questioned by the law enforcement authorities, although the company said it had not received any “administrative sanctions” over the incident. Meanwhile, LSIP said on Oct 15 that it was monitoring its operating areas in Sumatra and Kalimantan, with no unplanned shutdowns or material asset write-downs arising from forest fires. It added that it strictly enforced a zero-burning policy and used mechanical methods to clear unproductive plantation areas. LSIP is majority-owned by fellow Indonesia-listed plantation company Salim Ivomas Pratama, which is in turn controlled by Singapore-listed Indofood Agri. In a separate disclosure on Oct 15, Salim Ivomas Pratama said it strictly enforced a zero-burning policy and used mechanical methods to clear unproductive plantation areas. The company said its plantations were also equipped with firefighting vehicles and equipment, while designated employees underwent regular training in fire prevention and emergency response. It added that it had not experienced any material business interruptions or adverse operational impacts from the fires.

events.title: UK to deploy Typhoon jets to help defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
events.summary: Ministry of Defence says warplanes will operate in ‘defensive role’ and not be used to attack Yemeni group. The United Kingdom has said it will deploy fighter jets to help protect Saudi Arabia from attacks by Yemen’s Houthis. In a statement on Tuesday, the British Ministry of Defence said the Typhoon warplanes would operate in a “defensive role” and not carry out attacks against the Iranian-backed armed group. list 1 of 3 Egyptian parliament delays vote on military support for Saudi Arabia list 2 of 3 Saudi Arabia cancels 2026 ‘Davos in the Desert’ amid Houthi attacks list 3 of 3 US leaving oil-for-security approach, not Middle East: Envoy Tom Barrack “The UK will fly defensive counter air missions to support the protection of Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure against aerial attack, using RAF Typhoon fighter jets,” it added. The support includes an extension of air-to-air refuelling support for Saudi air operations, the ministry added. The announcement comes amid heavy fighting between the Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia. In recent weeks, the Houthis have carried out missile and drone strikes against the kingdom, including oil facilities and Riyadh’s main airport, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government has launched air attacks on Houthi positions. “The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region,” UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said. “That’s why today I have approved further UK military support. RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles. This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks,” he added. Reporting from London, Al Jazeera’s Camille Nedelec said the UK government’s decision was partly driven by growing concerns over rising energy prices. “What’s happening in the Gulf has a direct impact on people’s homes,” she said, adding that the move “shows increasing engagement by the UK” in the region. The UK announcement came a day after Egypt’s parliament delayed for a second day a vote on President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s request to authorise military support for Saudi Arabia, if the kingdom asked for its support. State media said the new session would be held on October 26.

Windows command prompt puts in a surprise appearance 2 days ago Microsoft has been forced to admit that the Always On VPN glitch – which it said it had fixed in an update on October 13 – was not actually fixed after all. We've all been there. You fix that bug, or tweak the configuration setting, and you're pleased with yourself, but it turns out it didn't take, and you have to send the "er, about that fix" follow-up email of shame. The same has happened to Microsoft. After proudly declaring the problem resolved as part of its last security update , the company had to roll back its triumphant trumpeting to a sad little parp from a clown's horn in the message WI1482218: "This disclosure was mistakenly updated to Resolved status on October 13, 2026. We have returned its status to Mitigated. "We apologize for any inconvenience or confusion." The bug in question concerns the operating system's Always On VPN functionality, a useful bit of code that quietly opens a VPN connection in the background without tiresome prompts for authentication. It dates back to Windows 10, and Microsoft alerted administrators to problems after the September 2026 Windows security update inadvertently broke it. The issue affects Windows 11 versions from 24H2 through 26H2. The problem could occur when the VPN was set to try a different connection method if the initial connection failed (Microsoft gave the example of using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP). According to Microsoft: "Affected VPN connections might remain in a 'Connecting' state or repeatedly attempt to connect without succeeding. Subsequent connection attempts might also display the error: 'The specified port is already in use'." This is not ideal for administrators. The workaround Microsoft highlighted back on October 13 was to change from automatic protocol selection to a single protocol, which would at least get affected users up and running. The workaround remains the same. The bad news is that, because last week's fix did not work, affected administrators will need to apply the workaround for a bit longer. events.title: Myanmar’s detained ex-leader Suu Kyi receives package from King Charles III
events.summary: Military-backed government says it delivered two books and diplomatic correspondence to Aung San Suu Kyi. Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has received a package from King Charles III, its military-backed government said, releasing the first pictures of the detained Nobel laureate in two months. Home ministry officials met the country’s former leader on Monday to deliver the parcel containing two books about soil and sealed diplomatic correspondence from the British monarch, Myanmar’s presidential spokeswoman said on her Facebook page. Britain is Myanmar’s former colonial power and King Charles is known to have a keen interest in gardening and the environment. list 1 of 4 Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing visits Malaysia amid concerns over repatriations list 2 of 4 China sentences three people to death for running Myanmar scam centres list 3 of 4 UN Human Rights Council elects 15 members in uncontested vote list 4 of 4 Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president wins back neighbours despite war Accompanying the statement were two images of Suu Kyi meeting two men with their backs to the camera. The pictures appeared to be in a similar room to the last released images of her, when she met a Red Cross representative in August, her first publicised meeting with a foreign official since she was ousted more than five years ago. Myanmar authorities referred to Suu Kyi as a “special female prisoner” on Tuesday, the first time they have used the term to describe the pro-democracy and human rights advocate, whose global reputation suffered after she rejected accusations of genocide committed against Myanmar’s Muslim Rohingya minority. Suu Kyi was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED. The coup leader and former military government chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April following elections that did not include Suu Kyi’s party, and she was moved to house arrest soon afterwards. Suu Kyi remains detained on charges rights groups say were concocted to return power to the military, which has historically ruled Myanmar since independence. “I have been extremely lenient toward her,” Min Aung Hlaing said in an interview with Time magazine published last month. The international community, including Britain, has called for Suu Kyi’s release and access to her as part of efforts to resolve the country’s political crisis, but the government has rejected those calls.

events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Meeting note-taking tool Otter.ai announced on Tuesday that it has raised $320 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund (CVF), which provides capital to startups without diluting equity and gets returns on the results of marketing spend. Otter.ai said that it will use these funds for enterprise growth, go-to-market strategy, international expansion, and product innovation. The startup, which has been around for nearly a decade, has raised $50 million in total funding with its last round in 2021, according to PitchBook data. Last year, Otter hit a revenue milestone after crossing $100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR) . The company said it’s now approaching new milestones, but didn’t provide updated figures. The company said that 40 million users have used its product to date, up from 25 million last year. However, given the crowded space among meeting note-taking products, a pertinent challenge for Otter would be to have its customers stick around. Unfortunately, the startup didn’t provide any numbers around its monthly active users or churn. “Voice is one of the biggest untapped opportunities in enterprise AI, and Otter is at the forefront of it – a conviction that’s only deepened watching Otter’s growth,” said Pranav Singhvi, Partner and Co-founder of CVF, General Catalyst. “When Otter enables enterprises to capture critical voice data and turns it into actionable business insights, teams move faster, decisions get sharper, and productivity compounds across the organization, and that’s why it’s a strong partner for CVF.” There is a lot of competition in the market with well-funded meeting notetakers like Fireflies.ai, Granola , and Read AI ; new entrants like Calendly , Wispr , and Superhuman, which acquired Fathom ; and other notetakers like Circleback, Talat, and Quill. Most of these notetakers want to connect to enterprise systems and, based on data captured in meetings, automate workflows. Otter is also heading in that direction. In the last few years, it introduced a meeting assistant , a search function that works across apps , and integration with other AI tools . Otter’s newly appointed CMO, Alex Gay, who comes from Superhuman, told TechCrunch at a sit-down at the HumanX conference last month that the company sees a big opportunity in turning transcripts into an actionable roadmap for people who are in back-to-back meetings. “When we start thinking about what is actually the bigger problem that people are facing right now, we saw this large pain point in meeting-heavy roles, where people are back-to-back in conversations. These meetings are the work for them. That’s either customer conversations or, from a sales standpoint. That’s where strategies are discussed. But meetings are terribly inefficient because when you come into a meeting, you spend the first twenty minutes recapping what was said before to catch everybody up,” he said. The company is now experimenting with providing insights before, after, and during meetings. It has been testing a feature to send a pre-brief to users with details and background information, with context from previous conversations across surfaces. Plus, it is also trying out a Live Assist feature to let users ask questions to the AI assistant during the meeting to get knowledge. events.title: France’s growing debt woes: How bond markets set countries’ borrowing costs
events.summary: France’s rising debt is unnerving investors, but countries such as the US and Japan owe even greater sums. France’s borrowing costs have surged amid the worst social unrest in the country in decades. Yields on French bonds have risen to their highest levels in nearly a quarter of a century as investors demand higher returns for taking on government debt. The surge reflects a growing conviction in bond markets that lending to France is becoming an increasingly risky proposition. list 1 of 4 Hegseth meets Netanyahu on unannounced Israel visit list 2 of 4 Rashida Tlaib demands arrest of Israeli soldier tied to Hind Rajab killing list 3 of 4 ‘Release Epstein files’, protester interrupts JD Vance’s speech list 4 of 4 Saudi Arabia cancels 2026 ‘Davos in the Desert’ amid Houthi attacks While France is grappling with a widening gap between government spending and revenues, the country’s fragmented political landscape is bitterly divided on how to plug the hole. Meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of protesters, some of whom have participated in rioting and looting, have taken to the streets to oppose proposed budget cuts and demand greater spending on cost-of-living relief and public services such as education. France’s national debt is now at its highest level since the immediate aftermath of World War II, nearing 120 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). How do bonds work and why are France’s borrowing costs rising? Bonds are a type of loan to a government or corporation. Countries routinely borrow from bond markets to allow spending that is not covered by tax revenues. In exchange for buying a bond, an investor is paid regular interest payments, plus the original borrowed sum at a set date in the future. These bonds can be traded on the bond market to other investors in the meantime. Bond prices are influenced by interest rates, inflation and confidence in the issuer’s ability to repay the loan, among other factors. When bond prices rise, bond yields fall, and vice versa. France’s 10-year bond yield has risen more than 130 basis points since June, topping 4.9 percent. France’s borrowing costs now stand at their highest levels since 2002, swallowing up a growing share of tax revenues that could otherwise be directed towards essential services such as education and healthcare. While France’s debt levels are relatively high, the amount that a country owes is just one consideration for investors pricing the risk of its bonds. Market confidence in a country’s ability to meet its obligations is shaped by a range of factors, including the economy’s strength, the amount of its external debt versus domestic debt and the ability of the political system to govern effectively. “The sustainability of sovereign debt is rarely determined by its absolute level alone,” Victor Lequillerier, president of BSI Economics, a think tank in Paris, told Al Jazeera. “It depends far more on its trajectory, structure, and broader economic and financial context.” In France’s case, the paralysis of the country’s political system is a key driver of concern in the bond markets currently. In the fragmented National Assembly, French Prime Minister Ssbastien Lecornu, who was appointed by President Emmanuel Macron under the country’s semi-presidential system, is mired in a legislative battle to pass a budget for next year that includes 54 billion euros ($61bn) in savings. Marine Le Pen of far-right National Rally and Jean-Luc Melenchon of far-left France Unbowed, the two leading candidates in next year’s presidential election, are opposed to Lecornu’s proposals, though the government could invoke a constitutional clause to bypass parliament if deemed necessary. Antonio Fatas, a professor of economics at INSEAD in Fontainebleau, France, told Al Jazeera: “Are the French numbers much worse than other countries? No, but marginally they are worse, and the real difficulty here is that the political situation is such that the current government does not have an easy path to put together a budget that makes sense from a debt sustainability point of view.” He added: “That’s what makes France a special case now, that’s why markets are very much worried about what France is going through and why you see a lot of the noise.” What is the state of France’s finances? France’s national debt, at about 3.6 trillion euros ($4 trillion), is equivalent to 119 percent of GDP, up from 98 percent in 2019, the year before the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. Of greater concern to markets than the total debt is France’s ballooning deficit, however, which is expected to reach 5.4 percent of GDP in 2026 – far above the European Union average of just more than 3 percent. This is the amount by which a government’s spending exceeds its income. France, which has a strong tradition of left-wing politics and activism, has long had one of the biggest public sectors in the developed world.

events.title: Whitehall shuts the front door on digital ID but leaves the back open
events.summary: Britain's national digital ID scheme may be dead, but Whitehall appears to have forgotten to tell the infrastructure. Despite the government scrapping its controversial plans , officials told MPs on Monday that work continues on GOV.UK One Login, digital wallets, and a growing collection of digital credentials designed to help people prove who they are. The abandoned scheme was one of Keir Starmer's flagship policies, originally pitched as a compulsory digital ID card to crack down on illegal working. Privacy campaigners weren't impressed, warning of surveillance and government overreach, and ministers eventually made it voluntary before Andy Burnham, decided to bin the whole thing. But scrapping the scheme hasn't dented Whitehall's digital identity ambitions. Officials told MPs this week that more than 80 types of documents are earmarked for the government's digital wallet, including proof of benefits, driving test certificates, and Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) certificates. That's quite a lot of paperwork for something that's supposedly dead. The revelations came during a Public Accounts Committee hearing on Monday, where MPs wanted to know what exactly had been scrapped. "But is it not the case, based on the answers you've given us this afternoon, that the infrastructure of digital ID in the public sector is still being pursued?" asked Sarah Green, Liberal Democrat MP for Chesham and Amersham. Susannah Storey, DCMS permanent secretary, was keen to draw a line between the national scheme ministers had scrapped and the digital identity projects Whitehall had no intention of abandoning. One Login already allows people to prove who they are online, she said, but "that is not the same as a national digital identity strategy." Rod Latham, DCMS director for cybersecurity and digital identity, had a convenient explanation for why so much of digital ID was still standing: the government had only scrapped plans for a new identity product. "We already had One Login and the Gov Wallet," he told MPs, adding that work on the digital identity trust framework was also underway before the national scheme was announced. Whitehall isn't wasting time putting that technology to use, with officials confirming that testing is already underway to enable digital credentials to work with private businesses. Natalie Jones, the senior responsible owner for GOV.UK One Login, revealed that the government had opened a testing environment for private sector providers to integrate with its digital wallet technology. This would let people use digital driving licenses to prove their age in pubs , collect parcels, or verify their identity online. "We've got a bit of a chicken and egg situation. A digital driving license is only useful if there are people ready and shops and businesses ready to receive it,” Jones said, noting that further testing is planned for December, with a national rollout of digital driving licenses targeted for 2027. MPs also pressed officials on privacy, particularly whether citizens would have to consent before their information was shared between government departments. "In the confines of digital ID used in digital services, then consent is the model," said Christine Bellamy, interim director general for digital products at the Government Digital Service. There's a catch, of course. Government departments can already share data without asking permission, and officials couldn't quite explain how that squares with their promises about consent. "The strategy needs to be fully finished," Bellamy admitted, which might not be the reassurance MPs were hoping for. Jones insisted that One Login was "not a big data lake," saying it stores identity information separately and cannot see what users do inside government services. "One Login does not issue a single identifier to people," she added. Rupert Lowe MP remained unconvinced, warning that Britain could end up getting digital ID "by the back door rather than the front door." Officials maintained that the canceled national scheme was fundamentally different from the services still being developed, and that people would retain alternatives to digital identification. National digital ID may be officially dead, but between One Login, digital wallets, and dozens of planned credentials, Whitehall still has plenty of identity-related work to keep it busy. ®

events.title: HSBC CEO warns the AI boom won’t make every data center a good bet
events.summary: HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery told CNBC that data center deals hinge on the quality of tenants and contract pricing. Global data center spending could reach $7 trillion by 2030, McKinsey estimates. Hyperscalers’ growing bond issuance is adding to competition for financing, Mohamed El-Erian has said. AI is a transformational technology worth investing in — but investors must be selective when investing in data centers, according to the head of one of the world's biggest banks. Speaking to CNBC's Dan Murphy on Tuesday, HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery called artificial intelligence "a major enabler to re-engineer and reimagine all our businesses, all our activities." "It's going to put a lot of power back in the hands of our colleagues because of the level of productivity it gives them, so it's going to be transformational, and we're certainly very much on a journey to adopt it," he said, adding that AI would help to "re-engineer the bank." But when it comes to investing in infrastructure underpinning the technology, he advised discernment over an all-in approach. "One has to be selective," Elhedery said. "You have to look at the quality of the tenancy agreements. You have to look at the pricing of these contracts. Not all of them are of that level of virtuosity that you can support strongly. Some of them may be more challenging." HSBC was ranked as the seventh-largest bank in the world and the biggest lender in Europe by S&P Global last year, with assets worth close to $3 trillion. The bank — headquartered in London — is both a financier and operator of data centers. In its 2025 annual report, HSBC said it intends to become "the leading bank for fast-growing transition ecosystems," noting that its customer base spans areas including data centers and the AI sector. Data center campuses house the servers that power AI and cloud computing, and have seen a multibillion-dollar boom in recent years. Global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030, according to McKinsey, with Big Tech increasingly tapping private credit and taking on debt to fund the development of the facilities. But AI borrowing is becoming a source of tension in financial markets, as the cost of capital soars and corporations add to huge debt piles as they race to finance AI and the build-out of data centers. Speaking at LSEG and Eurasia Group's GZERO Summit in London earlier this month, Mohamed El-Erian, chief economic adviser of Allianz and former CEO of PIMCO, highlighted the competition for financing between governments and AI-related companies as a source of pressure in bond markets. "Governments are borrowing what they're borrowing, plus they're refinancing debt at a higher level of rates," he said. "[And] you have hyperscalers who last year raised $200 billion in bond financing, and are probably going to raise a trillion in bond financing this year. They are yield insensitive. They are spread insensitive because they are betting on something that is truly transformational." Bond yields issued by various major economies have hit multi-decade highs in 2026, amid concerns around elevated government deficits and mounting debt levels alongside fears of sticky inflation and more hawkish central banks. JPMorgan Chase estimated earlier this year that $4.1 trillion in AI-related debt will be issued by the end of the decade, as data center and other AI-adjacent companies splurge on building capacity.

events.title: Oil prices hit five-month high as Houthi escalation worsens supply and inflation fears
events.summary: Oil prices hit a five-month high on Tuesday after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen continued attacking Saudi Arabia, further stoking concerns over supply and higher inflation that could prompt interest rate increases. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was trading 1.52 per cent higher at $111.30 per barrel at 2.27pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 2.30 per cent to $100.80 a barrel. Crude prices were last at these levels in mid-May. On Friday, Brent hit $110 for the first time since May, while WTI topped $100 for the first time in a month. The Houthis claimed responsibility for renewed strikes on ⁠Saudi energy, airport and military targets ⁠on Monday, escalating tension in the region and bringing down stock markets in the Gulf. The rebels claimed to have carried out six attacks on the kingdom, which included strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, a military airbase near Abha International Airport, a naval task-force camp and a Saudi radar in Bir Askar. With the US-Iran conflict continuing, crude supplies from the Middle East remain choked, prompting moves to ensure adequate supplies globally. The International Energy Agency last week said it had agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel to the market amid a surge in diesel prices. Gulf oil producers, meanwhile, have pushed tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashed prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around the Strait of Hormuz buckles under congestion and persistent attacks . The fighting has kept energy prices elevated, nudging inflation upwards and, in turn, raising the probability of another interest rate increase by the US Federal Reserve, which is scheduled to meet next week. Analysts are now expecting a second straight raise as Fed officials seek to tame inflation. "Brent crude hovering near five-month highs following geopolitical tensions in the Middle East has reignited fears of sticky inflation," analysts at US energy company Duncan Oil said. "Surging energy costs have led investors to believe the Fed will keep interest rates higher for longer to tame inflation." Ship movements in the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war made up a fifth of the world's energy exports, remain under pressure. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Monday that Washington was willing to allow oil tankers placed under sanctions to begin a process to legitimately ship crude. Analytics firm Kpler said easing sanctions on the shadow fleet would have little effect on record freight rates. It estimated that, as of Monday, only 24 of the nearly 160 vessels under sanctions from the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control could return to mainstream trade after taking into account their age and ownership restrictions. Wholesale diesel, meanwhile, already surpassed $200 per gallon in Singapore and hit roughly $220 in Europe and the US, the Paris-based IEA said last week.

( Reuters: Andrew Kelly ) Google says a "power event" at a London data centre has disrupted cloud services across Europe. The outage has affected banks, websites and court live streams. The technology giant says its engineers are working to fix the problem. Google Cloud services have failed across Europe after a "power event" at a data centre based in London, according to the tech giant's website. The issue has reportedly affected banks and other websites across the continent. The Google Cloud website is not reporting serious issues in any other region, but said that services in parts of Europe could experience "elevated errors and intermittent network issues". "Due to a power event we had suffered an outage within europe-west2-b zone," the Google Cloud website said. Google said the incident began shortly after 6am UK time and that its engineering teams were investigating. Customers of major UK banks were reporting issues accessing their accounts. ( Reuters: Phil Noble ) Banking giant Revolut is among the institutions believed to have been affected by the outage. "We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services," the bank said in a statement on social media. "We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe." Another major British bank, Halifax, wrote on X that customers were "having issues with our app and online". Court live streams, including that of the ongoing trial of comedian Russell Brand, were also reportedly down as a result. events.title: Zelenskyy to meet with U.S. envoy as tensions with Trump mount
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is travelling to Norway to meet with U.S. envoys and other European leaders. U.S. President Donald Trump once again called for a new leader in Ukraine on Monday. Zelenskyy has criticized the U.S. government for restricting access to critical satellite services. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is set to meet with U.S. special envoys on Tuesday after U.S. President Donald Trump aimed a fresh spate of criticism at the wartime leader. Zelenskyy will arrive in Norway on Tuesday and meet with the country's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr and President of Finland Alexander Stubb in Oslo later in the day. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will also take part in the discussions. The meetings come as tensions mount between Zelenskyy and Trump, while the U.S. has recently eased some pressure on Russia, which invaded Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine requested that Witkoff and Kushner join the meeting in Oslo, Norway, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said in a statement. "Diplomatic efforts have previously taken place in several countries, and Norway and Finland are pleased to be able to continue this work. The aim is to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path," he said. Trump responded to criticism on Monday that he waived sanctions against Russia recently and is on the "wrong side" of history . "Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said to reporters outside the White House. "Zelenskyy is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago." "I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine," Trump said, echoing previous calls for a "new president" in Kyiv. "If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago, and he'd have a million people living from his side." Trump also said he would meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to figure out how to end the Ukraine war, which reportedly could exclude Zelenskyy. "Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump said. Last week, Zelenskyy hit out at the U.S. government over restrictions on access to satellite services offered by SpaceX 's military satellite system, Starshield, which is critical to Ukraine's defense against Russian strikes. "No explanation for either of these issues has been provided to Ukraine by the American side," Zelenskyy said on Monday. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had shifted the blame to the U.S. government and Trump, who he said are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that the U.S. is responsible, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Zelenskyy to be "very careful about making statements like this that aren't true." Trump said Monday that he doesn't know who restricted the Starlink service in Ukraine, "but I'd like to find out." events.title: Europe to see 'biggest-ever' increase in air fares next year, Ryanair chief says
events.summary: Ryanair Holdings chief executive Michael O’Leary has forecast a record increase in European air fares next year as the Middle East war continues to push up oil prices , forcing airlines to pass on their fuel costs to consumers. Ticket prices are set to increase by as much as 20 per cent next year, Mr O’Leary told a news conference in Brussels on Tuesday. As a result, airline margins will be squeezed because even the jump in fuel surcharges won’t make up for the higher oil bill, he said. “You’re going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say in history, in Europe in the next 12 months,” Mr O’Leary said. “The question is, will that increase in airfares be enough to cover the dramatically higher oil bills? I don’t think it will be.” The comments by the head of Europe’s largest budget carrier add to the more pessimistic outlook for the aviation industry, which has been forced to contend with a dramatic rise in costs even as travellers continue to splurge on air tickets. Mr O’Leary said most European airlines, including his own, lack significant hedging next year to protect against higher oil prices. In addition, there’s less capacity in the market as some airlines struggle, while higher taxes are further dimming the picture for the industry. “We’re 85 per cent unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” he said. Ryanair's shares dropped as much as 2.1 per cent, bringing the decline to 25 per cent for the year. At that rate, that would be the worst annual stock return since 2018. The chief executive used his news conference to dish out against regulation in markets such as France and Belgium, where Ryanair will reduce its footprint in response to higher taxes. He repeated that the European aviation industry will continue to consolidate as weaker players struggle to survive in a high-cost environment. Air Baltic and Spain’s Volotea are the latest European carriers to undergo restructuring as higher costs take their toll. Last week, Deutsche Lufthansa won the race against Air France-KLM to acquire a stake in Portugal’s state-owned TAP. Meanwhile, US private equity firm Apollo Global Management is laying out the framework to take over EasyJet. Airlines across the world have suffered from soaring jet fuel costs since the Iran war began in late February. Ryanair’s most recent earnings in July showed the conflict hit its profit and caused later bookings amid concern about jet-fuel supply availability. Mr O’Leary said separately that he aims to receive the first delivery of the carrier’s Boeing Max 10 aircraft in January, with about 16 more expected up to April.

events.title: Netflix hunts for its next big hit after US$135b stock market wipe-out
events.summary: Netflix is among the top 10 worst performers in the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index. Netflix is under pressure after losing more than US$135 billion (S$173 billion) in market value in 2026, as weak engagement and fewer hit shows hurt growth. It is changing its content team, cutting about 1,000 jobs, and may focus on “more premium, conversation-driving originals” and higher 2027 spending. Investors will watch the Oct 20 earnings call for signs of recovery, but analysts say proof of better engagement and ad growth is still needed. NEW YORK – Netflix needs to prove that it can produce hit movies and TV series again to stop a slide that has erased more than US$135 billion (S$173 billion) in market value in 2026. The streaming giant reports earnings after the close on Oct 20, and investors will likely be more attuned to what content executives say is coming over the next six months than to the company’s third-quarter numbers. The stock is down 26% in 2026, putting Netflix among the 10 worst performers in the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index and on track for its worst year since 2022, and it is coming off a 14% decline in September. The reason is no secret to anyone following the company: User engagement has stalled owing to a lack of popular content despite heavy spending driven by a crowded, competitive entertainment landscape. Netflix won the fewest Emmy Awards in a decade in 2026, and the company is not growing fast enough , according to co-chief executive officer Ted Sarandos. “The content’s getting very expensive, and there are just still too many players,” said Ken Mahoney of Mahoney Asset Management. “I think there are so many better tech stories out there than Netflix that have sticky customers.” Netflix is taking steps to improve its content and raise its audience numbers. On Oct 19, it announced that the head of its film division, Dan Lin, was leaving, and last week replaced its chief content officer, Bela Bajaria, with Peter Rice, the former chairman of Walt Disney Television. The company also plans to cut about 1,000 positions in various departments globally in a bid to reduce costs. For investors, however, the issue is that this earnings report will not reflect those moves. And even if executives give a solid revenue outlook, it is unlikely to quell the debate around engagement, according to Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Geetha Raganathan. “A stronger (fourth-quarter) slate could revive viewing and ads, but investors will want proof that engagement can improve without derailing margin expansion,” she wrote in an Oct 19 note. The addition of Rice signals a potential pivot towards “more premium, conversation-driving originals and higher 2027 content spending”, she added. Analysts following the company expect it to report a 12% rise in revenue in the third quarter to US$12.9 billion, and a 39% jump in earnings to 82 US cents a share, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Its gross margin is expected to be 51%, down slightly from the second quarter. Wall Street remains generally bullish on the stock, with an average price target of about US$92 suggesting a 32% rise over the next 12 months. And while sentiment has weakened, with two analysts putting sell-equivalent ratings on the shares in September, bulls see a vibe shift coming. “While total viewing is still weak, quality has improved as reflected in hour/top-10 title and the number of sequels is increasing” through the end of 2026, Oppenheimer analysts led by Jason Helfstein wrote in an Oct 14 note. Three months of US price increases and one month of higher ad rates should give revenue a boost, and the recent headcount reductions will allow for more spending on marketing or content or provide upside to margins, they added. Management may offer some indications for what it expects in 2027, but the company is unlikely to offer thorough guidance, according to Mark Mahaney of Evercore ISI. He was particularly enthusiastic about Netflix’s recent release of East Of Eden. “East Of Eden looks very promising to us,” Mahaney wrote in a note to clients on Oct 16. “Steinbeck is BACK!” Ad revenue may be more important to investors than audience engagement, according to Wedbush’s Alicia Reese, who says the segment is on track to double to roughly US$3 billion in 2026. “Netflix is actively making changes that should address both its engagement issues and shift dollars from heavy infrastructure to more focused content spend,” Reese wrote in an Oct 16 note. One argument for buying the stock would be valuation, considering it is priced at less than 19 times earnings projected over the next 12 months, the lowest valuation since 2022 and a steep discount to its 10-year average of 49. That helps explain why KeyBanc Capital Markets analyst Justin Patterson believes the Netflix bear case is already priced into the share price. “The bear case on slowing engagement and more modest margin expansion is arguably priced in,” he wrote in an Oct 12 note.

events.title: Free trade agreements may be out of fashion, but APEC can further existing deals: Jeffrey Siow
events.summary: Second Minister for Finance Jeffrey Siow said on Oct 20 that APEC can build on existing regional trade agreements such as the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership. Singapore urges APEC to build on existing regional deals like RCEP and CPTPP to keep trade open, as free trade agreements may have fallen out of fashion. Jeffrey Siow said regional cooperation could include digital partnerships, such as ASEAN’s DEFA. Siow spoke at the APEC finance ministers' meeting in Hong Kong. SINGAPORE – Countries should continue to pursue economic openness and collaboration through forums and platforms like the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) grouping, even as the global consensus that has sustained openness has weakened, said Second Minister for Finance Jeffrey Siow. Speaking at the APEC finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong on Oct 20, he noted that inking free trade agreements may no longer be in trend. This comes as strategic competition is increasingly driving countries to impose trade restrictions and distribute industrial subsidies to protect their critical sectors and secure supply chains. Against this backdrop, Siow said: “We need more forums and platforms like APEC for economies to come together, build common ground, and advance cooperation. “Free trade agreements may have fallen out of fashion, but we can build on existing regional trade agreements such as the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP).” The ASEAN-led RCEP is the world’s largest free trade agreement, comprising around 30% of global gross domestic product and around a third of the world’s population. It involves 15 countries, namely Indonesia, Singapore, Brunei, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam, Australia, China, Japan, South Korea and New Zealand. Meanwhile, the CPTPP is a free trade agreement among 12 countries: Japan, Australia, New Zealand , Singapore, Brunei, Canada, Chile, Malaysia, Mexico, Peru, the United Kingdom and Vietnam. Siow added that like-minded countries can work together to advance topical interests through plurilateral arrangements involving more than two parties but fewer states than multilateral agreements. He cited digital economy agreements including ASEAN’s landmark Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) , that is expected to be formally signed in November to lay the groundwork for closer digital integration across South-east Asia. He also mentioned Green Economy Agreements, which Singapore has advocated to accelerate its transition towards a green and sustainable future. He also named the Future of Investment and Trade Partnership, known as FIT-P, as an example of flexible cooperation between like-minded countries. The grouping of 20 small and medium-sized, trade-dependent economies allows some of them to move on initiatives “while the door remains open for others to join later”, he said. For instance, 10 FIT-P members endorsed a joint declaration on strengthening the rules-based trading system on March 16, before three more members joined at a later date. Siow also said that open economic cooperation must come with domestic support, as the benefits of globalisation, which have been enormous on aggregate, have not always been evenly shared. “Workers and industries have borne the costs of rapid technological change. The advent of artificial intelligence will add to these pressures,” he added. At a session on the global and regional outlook at the APEC meeting, Siow said that while the global economy has remained resilient amid the ongoing Middle East conflict, growth has been unevenly distributed and heavily dependent on AI investment. He said: “If the productivity gains from AI fall short of expectations, financial markets could experience a correction, and economies could find ourselves exposed to bigger risks.” Siow added that for growth to be sustained, AI investments must be translated into wider productivity improvements and good job opportunities. This is a focus of Singapore’s Economic Strategy Review, Siow said, where the country is growing industries generating high-value jobs which are assisted by technology. He said semiconductor firms like Micron and GlobalFoundries are expanding their operations in the Republic, with new roles in engineering and operations tapping AI, robotics and smart manufacturing technologies. Singapore’s workforce is also being equipped with future-ready skills. In accountancy , for instance, AI is being used to analyse large volumes of financial transactions, identify anomalies, and prepare detailed reports. “But accountants must still interpret the findings, exercise professional judgment and advise businesses,” Siow said. “ Singapore has launched a programme to help accountants develop the skills to work effectively with AI.

events.title: France curfews calm unrest as Macron faces criticism over Gulf trip
events.summary: French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Tuesday that some areas would remain under curfew after a weekend of violent rioting. Criticism is growing of President Emmanuel Macron's decision to embark on a tour of the Middle East amid the turmoil at home. Parliament is in the thick of negotiating a 2027 budget, as analysts warn of the need to bring down the deficit to cool rising borrowing costs. Curfews contributed to a "calm" night across France, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Tuesday, even as public discontent remained high following the weekend's mass protests, looting and violent scenes . Certain areas of several French cities were under curfew overnight, including Place de la République and Les Halles in Paris, and parts of central Lyon. Lille and Nice were among the cities to impose curfews for minors. The unrest comes at a particularly fragile moment for France, where public anger over living costs and deteriorating services is colliding with political instability and a fiscal crisis that threatens to turn into a debt crisis as government borrowing costs rise to the highest level in decades. The country faces a divided parliament with no majority and presidential elections in April 2027. In a statement on Tuesday, Lecornu said local officials would impose new curfews where required. Meanwhile, criticism is mounting over President Emmanuel Macron's decision to embark on a three-day tour of the Middle East as France suffers its most severe riots in many years. Riots followed weeks of demonstrations over the country's education system , the cost of living and other issues. While hundreds of thousands of people marched peacefully, pockets of violence erupted, shocking the country, as protesters smashed shopfronts and set Limoges Town Hall on fire. Political commentator Christophe Barbier on radio station RTL said on Monday there was "no longer a pilot in the plane." At the same time, newspaper La Dépêche du Midi wrote in a scathing editorial that Macron had "to see if the misery of a reviled president is less painful in the Persian Gulf sun" as France "sinks deeper into crisis." Macron said on Sunday he was looking to address high fuel prices and secure French energy supplies through the trip to Kuwait, the UAE, Bahrain and Qatar, while strengthening defense and security cooperation. There is also public anger over claims that police lost control of the situation at the weekend as disorder and looting escalated. Police were earlier this month accused of excessive force in their response to student protests, after a 15-year-old ​boy's hand was blown off by a stun grenade. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez' offered to quit his post on Monday after claiming responsibility for what unfolded. Macron declined his resignation, saying immediate leadership of law enforcement was needed. "The lack of enforcement means that more than 3,000 shops have been sacked, and for the economy today we awake with a feeling that the state cannot do the basic duty that it is supposed to do, and this is now creating somehow lack of trust," Fabrice Le Saché, vice president of business group MEDEF, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday. "This is dangerous because we have been used to... riots in our country — remember the Yellow Vests and other movements — but this one has passed, I think, the level of the previous ones, and we cannot continue to keep going with that same type of situation every time we have social unrest," Le Saché said. French businesses have one of the highest tax burdens in the euro area but now feel they cannot receive basic security in return, he added. Lecornu said Monday that a support fund would be established for damaged or looted businesses, and that the government would talk with insurers to speed up assessments. "The scale of the damage suggests this weekend's riots could ultimately prove more costly than the unrest that followed the death of Nahel Merzouk in 2023," which generated around 1 billion euros ($1.12 billion) in insured losses, Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft, said by email. "Further violence is not inevitable, but protests linked to the underlying grievances, including cost-of-living pressures and discontent over public services and education, are likely to persist, putting continued pressure on the government to demonstrate that it can maintain order," Middleton said. French markets came under pressure on Monday after the weekend scenes, with bonds, stocks and the euro all selling off, amid growing skepticism about the country's ability to bring down its deficit to a sustainable level. Fierce debate is underway over the 2027 budget, with the government targeting an overall decline in the deficit to 5% of GDP from 5.4%.

events.title: Walmart launches joint membership with Sam's Club as it leans into delivery, gas discounts
events.summary: Walmart is now offering a joint Walmart+ membership with Sam's Club Plus for $120 per year as the retailer further leans into convenience. Both stores will continue to offer standalone membership options. The announcement comes as Walmart has been emphasizing value to grow sales, especially as consumers face high gas and food prices. Walmart on Tuesday announced a new joint membership combining its namesake chain and its subsidiary Sam's Club, as the retailer leans further into convenience and value to win over cash-strapped shoppers. The membership, which combines Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus, will cost $120 per year, according to the company. That price is nearly $100 less than buying individual annual memberships to each retailer, though there is no monthly payment option for the new deal. Both stores will continue to offer standalone options. "We're giving people a reason to expect more from their memberships," Walmart CEO John Furner said in a statement. "For $120 a year, we're raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own." The membership gives customers access to Sam's Club warehouses, free delivery from both chains, a subscription to Peacock or Paramount+ streaming services, gas savings and 2% Sam's Club cash on eligible purchases. Customers who already have accounts at both stores can link their accounts to receive the discount. While Walmart's customers often shop for routine, everyday essentials, Sam's Club warehouses offer more opportunity to stock up on bulk purchases. A joint membership could allow the store models to complement one another, according to the company. The announcement comes as Walmart bets on convenience to drive sales, especially as consumer wallets are squeezed by high gas and food prices. In August, as Walmart reported fiscal second-quarter earnings, the company raised its outlook for the year, with Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey telling CNBC that consumer spending remained strong despite higher fuel prices. Even so, its stock fell at the time as its sales outlook disappointed Wall Street. Rainey said in August that the company was lowering prices across various categories, including beef, adding that it's well positioned to weather economic uncertainty because of its emphasis on value and its scale. Meanwhile, Sam's Club saw a 26% increase in e-commerce sales in the fiscal second quarter, driven by increased transactions and membership growth. The retailer, which also operates its own gas stations, reported net sales of $25.7 billion, including fuel, during that period. The membership business — which is part of Walmart's push to grow sales with higher profit margins — is already strong. Walmart reported a 17% increase globally in revenue from its membership in the fiscal second quarter with Walmart+ net adds notching a record second-quarter high. For Sam's Club, that revenue number grew 6%. Walmart added Tuesday that employees at both stores will also receive joint memberships as part of their benefits. The company said any costs related to the changes in the membership program are not expected to materially impact the company's fiscal third-quarter or full-year guidance.

events.title: How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
events.summary: Andrew Haverdink, a tall grad student in a rain bib and rubber boots, wrenched a double-handed drill from the frozen soil that underlies much of Alaska’s Denali National Park and then unclipped the hollow barrel from the end of the bit.  He knelt in front of a blue tarp, lined the barrel up with a plastic tray, and pushed a rod through the opposite end. A perfect solid, cylindrical core of ancient soil emerged—dark, rich permafrost at least a foot long. On that late morning in early July, Haverdink was among a team of Northern Arizona University students and staff gathering samples and data from a research plot, divided by surveyor’s tape unspooled atop tussocks, alders, and fireweed.  In late June of 2013, a lightning strike sparked a fire in this stretch of mostly treeless tundra, in the northern backcountry of the park. Whipped by the Chinooks , intense downslope winds created as moist ocean air surmounts and then descends the Alaska Range , the fire ripped across nearly 35,000 acres . It burned through much of the vegetation and deep into the topsoil, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves the frozen permafrost, a massive storehouse of carbon that underlies 85% of Alaska.  During their first survey, in 2016, the researchers found that in places where the fire burned hottest and deepest, the thawed soil above the permafrost (known as the active layer) extended between a foot and nearly two feet deeper than in plots outside the burn scar—an indication of deep thawing. Northern Arizona University graduate student Andrew Haverdink drills out permafrost cores in the northern backcountry of Alaska’s Denali National Park. JAMES TEMPLE Crucially, the fire also crossed two sets of survey grids that the National Park Service established in 2001, including the one where the researchers stood that morning. That pre-fire snapshot offered the Northern Arizona group a rare opportunity to study how the blaze has altered the vegetation, carbon, and permafrost across time, says Xanthe Walker, one of the principal investigators on the project, who was watching over Haverdink’s work that morning. These direct observations from high-latitude fires are helping scientists to better understand the impacts of wildfire and permafrost loss on climate change, she says. “There’s a lot of uncertainty,” Walker says. “These are huge biomes with massive fires that no one’s ever been to or ever looked at.” They’re among a growing group of researchers striving to untangle what happens in the aftermath of fires in the Arctic-boreal region as they occur more often, burn hotter than before, and expose the landscape and frozen permafrost to a warming climate.  The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects: As warming temperatures fuel more frequent and severe fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires, and permafrost loss .  Understanding just how powerful these effects are, how they compound, and to what degree other transformations of the landscape may mitigate them is essential to gain a clearer picture of our climate future. Notably, past modeling suggested that the carbon dioxide uptake from expanding trees and plants may largely offset the release of carbon from warming soils and melting permafrost, at least over long periods and under moderate levels of warming. But the improving observations and analyses have revealed worrisome signs about the impacts of rising Arctic-boreal emissions in the immediate decades ahead, as the world struggles to keep global warming within relatively safe boundaries.     The permafrost problem  Permafrost makes up 15% of the land surface of the Northern Hemisphere and holds about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon, roughly twice the amount in the atmosphere. Most of it formed during the last ice age, but it’s been thawing at an accelerating rate during the last half-century, amid rising temperatures and worsening fires. As it melts, microbes begin to break down that organic matter, releasing it into the air in the form of carbon dioxide and methane. Both are powerful greenhouse gases that fuel climate change. The impacts of permafrost loss, however, aren’t as straightforward as they may initially seem. Notably, there has been a long-running scientific debate over what would have the strongest effect on the exchange of greenhouse gases over the next few centuries: the loss of carbon in soil and permafrost or the carbon uptake from so-called “Arctic greening,” which describes the spread of carbon-absorbing plants across the landscape as temperatures rise.  Thawing permafrost itself can contribute to the latter phenomenon as the unfrozen soil layer deepens and makes more nitrogen, phosphorus, and other nutrients accessible to plants. Carbon-sucking trees and shrubs with deeper root systems can take hold and thrive in places where they wouldn’t have been able to in the past. A riverbank exposes ice-rich yedoma permafrost along the Itkillik River in northern Alaska. MIKHAIL KANEVSKIY; UNIVERSITY OF ALASKA FAIRBANKS But as more Arctic-boreal fires ignite and more permafrost melts, researchers have been able to closely study what exactly happens in the aftermath, using on-site surveys like those conducted by the Northern Arizona University team, satellite observations, lidar flights, a widening network of greenhouse-gas-measuring towers, and other tools.  The findings have alarmed many researchers.  In particular, permafrost seems particularly prone to abrupt thawing rather than the gradual version that major climate models have simulated. A 2020 paper found that this could release far more carbon than previously understood, doubling the emissions from thawing permafrost and offsetting the carbon uptake from future plant growth.  In addition, even if carbon levels eventually net out through Arctic greening, the emissions from high-latitude fires and permafrost loss appear to be accelerating warming right now.   Susan Natali, an Arctic climate scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, and her colleagues have published several papers in recent years concluding that the combined emissions from these feedback effects will push the planet past 2 °C faster than currently predicted. She and other researchers  also found that about 40% of the Arctic-boreal zone has already flipped from a carbon sink into a carbon source, when the emissions from permafrost melting, fires and other forces are taken into account.  “The more we learn about processes like abrupt thaw, deeper-burning fires, and cold-season emissions, and the more we see disturbances increasing, the more likely it is that the sink will weaken and source areas will expand,” Natali said in an email. events.title: 'Gulf security is our security', says former UK defence secretary
events.summary: Britain should do more to help its allies in the Gulf, including considering strikes on the Houthis , because Washington's priorities have changed and its partners must now stand together, former UK defence secretary Michael Fallon has told The National . The US , he said, is “shifting its priorities to homeland defence, to the Indo-Pacific. And therefore, it means that in terms of Washington, perhaps Europe and the Middle East count for less than they used to”. That shift is structural, not a passing mood. “We've also seen a change in the United States,” Sir Michael said, recalling a country that “helped us win two world wars in Europe”. With the Gulf and Europe pushed down Washington's list of priorities, the burden falls on the allies. “I think we should be doing more,” he said. “These are our partners and friends, and we should be helping more.” For Britain, that means being ready to act against the Houthis . “That means, if necessary, we should be prepared to consider strikes as we did two years ago” he said, alongside the US and other European nations, as in the joint US-UK air campaign against Houthi targets that began in January 2024. Sir Michael, who served as the defence secretary from 2014 to 2017 under prime ministers David Cameron and Theresa May, was speaking in Dubai on the sidelines of the inaugural Middle East chapter of Signum Global Advisors, chaired by Charles Myers and launched by Raha Moradi, where he took part in a closed-door, onstage discussion. Sir Michael was careful with his words about the White House. Asked whether US President Donald Trump was an unreliable, unpredictable partner for the Gulf and Europe, he pointed to Moscow instead. “The most unreliable person clearly is President [Vladimir] Putin.” It is, to borrow the Irish, a mé féin foreign policy in Washington: me, myself and I. For America's allies, the old guarantees are no longer a given. However, he was clear that the ground had moved. “You have an unpredictable element now,” he said. “Policy shifts suddenly.” 'Gulf security is our security' “Gulf security is our security,” Sir Michael said. “It's our economic security. It's our energy security.” The trade and energy flowing through the region, he said, fed straight into the British economy and inflation, “and in the end, affects interest rates back in the UK”. “So we have a huge interest, as well as friendships and historical ties,” he said. The pressure on those ties is rising. Since July, the Houthis have been in direct conflict with Saudi Arabia , declaring a naval blockade of the kingdom and attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, while threatening to close the Bab Al Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. The Strait of Hormuz has already been disrupted by the US-Israel war with Iran. Britain has stepped up, but only so far. In April, the RAF deployed its Rapid Sentry air-defence system to Kuwait. Last month, in the first substantial foreign policy decision of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government, London agreed to a Saudi request for an RAF Voyager tanker to keep the kingdom's Typhoon jets in the air for longer. Ministers described it as a strictly defensive, “time-limited commitment”. “Well, we've responded to Kuwait's call for assistance,” Sir Michael said. “The Saudis asked us for help.” The most obvious step, he said, is to make sure the Houthis cannot disrupt the Bab Al Mandeb strait in the way Hormuz has been disrupted, which means tackling Houthi strikes “at source”. Asked whether strikes would be a big step for Mr Burnham, he said: “It would be, and clearly, they've considered it.” Labour has been reluctant before. In February, under Keir Starmer, the government initially refused to let the US use British bases, including Diego Garcia, for strikes on Iran, before reversing course. Sir Michael said the government had now “reversed that decision and said they can use Diego Garcia, but I think we should be doing more than that”. Gulf states, he said, are “with us, by the way, in the long-term battle against international terrorism ”, as they were in the international coalition against ISIS. Europe's turn to do more The same logic applies in Europe, where, Sir Michael said, the continent had been too slow to carry its share of the pressure on Moscow. He called Washington's diesel deal with Russia a misstep. This month, the US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027, and on Friday, Mr Trump signed an executive order pausing new Russia sanctions passed by Congress. “I'm afraid it's a miscalculation,” Sir Michael said. The volumes are too small to bring down diesel prices in the US and the deal is unlikely to move a ceasefire any further forward, he said. Mr Putin, he argued, would read it as weakness. “He's given up nothing in return,” he said. Russia has kept up its attacks on Ukraine 's civilian infrastructure, he added, and “he hasn't come to change any of his negotiating position about the future of Ukraine”. Asked whether it undermines sanctions as a weapon globally, he said it does. “You're either all in on sanctions or you're not.” Mr Trump, he conceded, has a point: “Where Trump is right, that our sanctions haven't been fully applied.” Europe has been far too slow to cut its dependence on Russian oil and gas, to police the shadow fleet and to use sanctioned Russian assets to help Ukraine, Sir Michael said. “Europe keeps passing new packages of sanctions, which rather casts doubt on the previous packages.” The EU adopted its 22nd package on October 12, the largest single round of listings yet at 1,569 individuals and entities. Brussels is already drafting a 23rd. Yet EU countries still bought €817 million ($917 million) of Russian pipeline gas and €615 million of Russian LNG in September. Pressure on Kyiv The stakes are highest in Ukraine . “I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Bloomberg this week. “I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war” against Russia “could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks.” A capitulation would not only encourage Mr Putin, Sir Michael said. It would put Russia's near neighbours “in the firing line, whether it's Moldova, the rest of Georgia, even the Baltic states, even though they're part of Nato ”. Moscow regards those countries as its “near abroad”, he said, “and they will be much more exposed. events.title: Singapore-based semiconductor firm Mi Material to expand into US, Malaysia in $215m IPO
events.summary: Mi Material CEO Kevin Tan said that the company will focus on maintaining healthy earnings post-IPO, as it looks to grow its specialty alloy business to support the semiconductor industry. Mi Material launched a $215m SGX IPO offering 77.5 million shares at $1.80 each. Trading on the mainboard is expected to start on Oct 28. The Singapore-based firm is a top-two global solder sphere supplier, with 24% of the 2025 serviceable market. FY2025 revenue was US$65.3 million and net profit was US$10 million. Most IPO funds will build a US R&D centre, with more work in Singapore, Taiwan and Malaysia. Chief executive Kevin Tan said growth stays strong, with 28% CAGR and a focus on earnings. SINGAPORE – The future of chip manufacturing lies in producing customised chips with specialised materials that improve reliability and heat management, and Mi Material sees enormous potential as a major supplier in this sector ahead of its listing on the Singapore Exchange. The Singapore-based semiconductor materials firm is looking to raise $215 million through its mainboard share offering, including $139.5 million from the initial public offering (IPO) launched on Oct 19 and $75.5 million from the placements to cornerstone investors. The offer of 77.5 million shares at $1.80 per share comprises a public offer of 6.2 million shares here and 71.3 million shares offered to institutional and overseas investors. OCBC is the issue manager, and serves as joint bookrunner and underwriter with CGS International. A separate cornerstone tranche of 41.9 million shares has also garnered interest from seven fund managers, which will account for the remainder of the funds raised. These include three under the Equity Market Development Programme – Amova Asset Management, Fullerton Fund Management and Manulife Investment Management (Singapore). Mi Material’s public offer closes at noon on Oct 26, and its shares are expected to commence trading on Oct 28 at 2pm. The solder sphere supplier is one of the two largest in the world, accounting for 24% of the global serviceable market in 2025. Solder spheres are tiny spherical pellets that connect semiconductor chips to circuit boards and packaging in mobile and wearable devices, and in more demanding applications in data centres, edge AI and renewable energy. Mi Material’s parent company, Bursa-listed Mi Technovation, builds die-sorting and inspection machines for outsourced semiconductor assembly and test companies (OSAT) that handle the final post-fabrication stages of chip-making. The materials business began as Taiwanese firm Accurus in 1998 before it was acquired by German chemicals giant Henkel in 2006. Following a management buyout in 2010, the firm pivoted to its current business of patented solder sphere manufacturing, which Mi Technovation subsequently took over in 2021. Mi Material’s total revenue for FY2025 was US$65.3 million, with net profit at US$10 million. Three of its largest customers – which are end-market chip designers in the premium consumer electronics, AI application-specific integrated circuits, and high-bandwidth memory sectors – made up 50% of its revenue in the financial year ended Dec 31, 2025. Meanwhile, its top five direct customers, including OSAT and fabrication companies, contributed around 46% of its revenue. Chief executive Kevin Tan said at a media briefing on Oct 19 that the company has seen its compound annual growth rate (CAGR) rise to around 28% over the last three years, which is rare for a company that has been established for close to three decades. “Bear in mind that we are not a vanilla IPO where we started from a start-up – in those cases, a few hundred per cent increase is very normal. But we are already the top two in the world for this technology, and to grow at 28% CAGR is actually a very difficult thing.” The company has two facilities in Tainan, Taiwan, and Ningbo, China, and its third facility in Senai, Malaysia, is close to completion, with trial production runs under way . It is expected to have seven production lines by next year. Most of the IPO’s $168.2 million proceeds will be invested in a research and development centre in the US, which will also serve as a demonstration platform for Mi Material’s US-based clients. The company will also set up an R&D laboratory in Singapore, bringing it closer to its clients’ regional headquarters, and upgrade its existing facility in Taiwan. Asked whether the lacklustre performance of recent IPOs on the SGX was a concern, Tan said the company’s priority is to ensure healthy earnings. “No matter what we tell the investors about the equity story, at the end of the day, we must be able to recognise it in terms of earnings,” he said, adding that higher earnings will naturally convince the market about its business performance and sustainability.

events.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
events.summary: At the world’s biggest chipmaking complex, Samsung is building the fabs it needs for the AI memory boom. Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes . In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment. Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banners that hang from the highest girders read, “Even if the work runs late, don’t rush.” A giant LED scoreboard announces the winners of a contest for writing a poem about safety. Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street. Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips. Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.” Popular Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason Thore Graepel Don’t be fooled by this summer of AI hype Timnit Gebru Emily M.
