events.title: These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
events.summary: In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge set up a six-foot folding table in the cafeteria of Cane Bay High School in Summerville, South Carolina, to conduct a taste test. When the first rush of about 150 hungry students hit, he was waiting with slow cookers filled with steaming marinara sauce and meatballs.  Kids love a taste test, but they’re also discerning, and Dodge wasn’t sure what they would make of his product, a blend featuring both meat and mushrooms. As students swarmed the table and tapped out their opinions on an iPad or scanned a QR code to use their phones, Dodge asked those who lingered to guess what kind of vegetable might have been mixed into the meat. Few of them could—the meatballs had tasted like moist, flavorful beef.  The school enrolls a few thousand students, and Dodge estimates that the majority of them came by. In the end, the survey showed that 92% of those who tried the meatballs wanted them on the menu; they easily cleared the bar to be added for the 2026–2027 school year. Comments described their flavor as “bussin’.”  Through his consulting company, K–12 Food Solutions, Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The proprietary blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the most intractable challenges of the climate crisis, at least on the individual level: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef. Livestock production accounts for somewhere between 10% and 20% of all greenhouse-gas emissions related to human activity, and nearly two-thirds of that comes from ruminants like cows raised for meat and dairy products. Beef herds create four times the emissions of dairy herds per kilo of food produced. And for US households, food makes up as much as 30% of emissions .  Unlike other polluting sectors, such as electricity and transportation, cattle farming has little potential for a big fix. Ruminants produce about 30% of the methane associated with human activity, and this gas has 28 times more global-­warming potential than carbon dioxide. What’s more, it would be virtually impossible to raise them in a perfectly climate-­neutral manner. “We don’t have a technical solution to change the stomach of a ruminant,” says Fredrik Hedenus, a professor in sustainability and systems analysis at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden. Technologies to dampen the impact of their burps have been in the works for a while but have yet to scale. They also fix only part of the problem with red meat: Cows need a lot of land for pasture and for feed, which has made livestock a top driver of deforestation in the Amazon and elsewhere around the world. Even if the world stopped burning all fossil fuels tomorrow, emissions from agriculture would push the planet past 2 °C over preindustrial temperatures by 2070, Hedenus says. According to his research, more efficient livestock farming methods would still leave agriculture eating up over half of humanity’s carbon budget by that time. Only with the addition of dietary changes does his model show a winning scenario.  He’s far from alone in his conclusions: A 2024 survey of more than 200 climate scientists, conducted at Harvard, found that the vast majority believe reducing emissions from livestock is important to meeting climate goals. People have to eat less beef. “Essentially, you need a culture shift,” Hedenus says. Yet the culture has proved intractable. Not only do people like the taste of meat, but across most of the world, meat-eating tends to be associated with status. As societies have grown wealthier, it has increased. A United Nations report showed that global meat production quadrupled between 1961 and 2022 , while vegetarianism has held steady at about 4% of the population in the US since 1999.  What could move the needle is a carbon-light and delicious meat replacement. But from a food-tech standpoint, all we have to show is a menu of mostly failed solutions. Lab-grown meat has generated endless headlines since the 2000s but has yet to become commercially available (and affordable) at scale. And while breakthroughs in taste and texture inched plant-based meats from companies like Impossible Foods and Beyond Meat toward mass adoption, the hype—and the appetite—has somewhat fizzled.  So instead of asking people to change their preferences, startups like Joyn are trying a different tack. They’re creating what are broadly referred to as blended meat products, which combine plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat. Paul Shapiro, cofounder of the startup BMC Ingredients, which markets a plant protein related to mushrooms, says the math is easy to understand: If we imagine that Impossible Whoppers at Burger King account for about 2% of sales, that’s only a 2% reduction in meat. But if a conventional Whopper were 20% plants, that would be a 20% cut right off the bat.  Those aren’t quite the numbers climate models are calling for, but some estimates say they could lead to outsized gains relative to the status quo: A 2022 study in Nature found that replacing 20% of beef globally could halve the annual rate of deforestation. And unlike the other solutions tried thus far, this particular Hail Mary is one a lot of omnivores seem open to giving a try.  The idea of blending meat and vegetables together is, of course, nothing new. Food cultures from around the world boast an array of dishes that combine small amounts of meat with plants. Today, home cooks still add veggies and legumes to dishes to stretch tight grocery budgets or to sneak extra greenery into their children’s supper.  But in the mid to late 2010s, however, the focus was largely on companies that appeared to have cracked the code for ditching meat entirely. When Impossible debuted its namesake burger in 2016, it impressed with an ingredient called heme, an iron-rich molecule in the protein soy leghemoglobin that allowed all-plant burgers to “bleed” like beef.  Impossible and its biggest competitor, Beyond, swaggered through the media and the markets. In 2019, Impossible’s founder told the New Yorker he intended to wipe out all animal agriculture by 2035. Beyond’s 2019 IPO was the most successful since the 2008 financial crisis. A flood of imitators followed. But within a few years, tastes shifted. In 2023, Impossible employees’ stock values tumbled 89% from a 2021 high. That same year, Beyond laid off 20% of its staff, and a bruising Businessweek feature labeled the entire sector a fad . Sales have been slipping for years, with a 10% year-over-year drop in 2025 , according to the Good Food Institute, a think tank focused on alternative proteins.   Any quest to wipe out animal agriculture could now seem farcical. In 2025, Americans downed $45 billion worth of beef. Several factors were likely at play. Megan Krogius, a spokesperson for Impossible Foods, sa

events.title: How Trump’s FBI Purge Saved Lindsey Graham and James Clyburn From a Bribery Investigation
events.summary: Beatrice Caciotti for ProPublica. Source images: Getty Images, Hawaii News Now, South Carolina Department of Transportation. On March 3, 2020, Sen. Lindsey Graham walked into a private dining room at Charlie Palmer Steak in Washington, D.C. Graham’s time was expensive. He was meeting with two executives and a lobbyist from a Hawaiian naval defense contractor called Navatek. And he had required them to commit to $40,000 in campaign contributions for a 45-minute meeting. Navatek’s CEO, Martin Kao, was confident that was all the time he needed. “Shoot all he has to really do is stop by and say ‘yes,’” Kao wrote to a Navatek lobbyist and a fellow executive the day before, in an email seen by ProPublica. “That should only take a minute and he’s on his way. We don’t need to pretend we give a shit about each other.” At the dinner, Graham ate little and talked a lot. But Kao got the “yes” he was hoping for: Graham agreed to steer a $10 million government contract Navatek’s way in his native South Carolina, Kao later recounted to the FBI. In exchange, he said, Graham asked Kao to pledge a total of $100,000 to his reelection campaign. “Paper Trail” Podcast Hear the reporters discuss their reporting on the FBI on ”Paper Trail.” In early 2025, the FBI opened a sweeping investigation into bribery on Capitol Hill with Graham’s steakhouse dinner at the center. Kao confessed to federal agents that his business model consisted of bribing public officials in exchange for government contracts, and that the research Navatek was providing to the government was often worthless. The scheme involved some of the most powerful figures in Congress, he said — in both parties. In South Carolina, Kao told agents, Navatek made a campaign cash-for-contracts deal not only with Graham, but also with the state’s top Democrat, Rep. James Clyburn, and another influential Republican, Rep. Joe Wilson. Kao told agents that Graham in particular left little room for ambiguity: “This is how much I want, and how much I am going to give you,” Kao remembered Graham saying, according to notes one agent took during their debrief in late 2024. Kao’s admissions would constitute a vast criminal bribery scheme if they could be proved in court — a challenge, given recent Supreme Court rulings that have made it more difficult to win corruption cases. Kao himself posed another hurdle. He was facing prison for fraud and campaign finance violations and was speaking to the FBI in the hopes of reducing his sentence. But the FBI agents who took Kao’s confession — two experienced anti-corruption investigators — could see that much of it lined up with a trove of records they had seized from Navatek. They forged ahead. The FBI took the formal step of naming two former Navatek executives who had worked with Kao as subjects of a bribery investigation. The agency did not designate Graham, Clyburn and Wilson that way, but the agents were actively investigating their interactions with Kao. The agents indicated to their superiors that the lawmakers could become subjects in the future, according to records viewed by ProPublica. The details of this investigation have not previously been reported. President Donald Trump returned to the White House and almost immediately gutted the specialized FBI and Department of Justice teams dedicated to taking on public corruption — an act of revenge for having previously investigated him. The two experienced agents on the case were swept up in the purge, and the career prosecutor assisting them quit after Trump appointees forbid the DOJ’s anti-corruption section from filing any new cases . Today, there is no one left to look into Kao’s explosive allegations, as the Trump administration has abandoned any pretense of prosecuting public corruption. The case is dead. ProPublica has unearthed the investigation by reviewing thousands of pages of legal documents, internal company emails, evidence the FBI used to vet Kao’s claims and dozens of interviews with people who saw how Navatek operated, including an eyewitness to Graham and Kao’s secret steakhouse dinner. This story is part of a series based on our reporting. Last month, ProPublica reported that the FBI had probed the conduct of Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who steered millions in government funding toward Navatek while Kao gave her illegal campaign donations. Collins denied wrongdoing and dismissed Kao as a “convicted liar.” Kao is indeed the only person involved to serve prison time. He pleaded guilty to making illegal campaign donations and a loan fraud scheme in 2022. In 2025, he was sentenced to 87 months in prison. Graham died at 71 earlier this year. His sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill his seat, retained most of his senior staff, including those who dealt with Navatek. She even took up some of his committee assignments, including appropriations. Darline Graham is running for a full term in office this November. Clyburn, 86, is one of the most powerful Democrats in Washington. He is widely credited with tipping the scales for Joe Biden during the 2020 Democratic presidential primary. Wilson remains influential on national defense spending from his senior perch on the Armed Services Committee. James Clyburn, left, and Lindsey Graham speak during an event at the White House to celebrate the 2023-24 University of South Carolina Gamecocks NCAA women’s basketball championship team. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images “Whatever a donor may think or say, a donation would never cause Congressman Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s request,” Jami LaRue, Clyburn’s communications director, wrote in response to detailed questions. “The Congressman has always striven to assist the University of South Carolina and all of the colleges and universities in his district when called upon to further their important missions. The crimes and lies of an imprisoned fraudster will not cause the Congressman to waver in his support for these fine institutions.” David Snider, Wilson’s communications director, did not address a detailed list of questions sent by ProPublica. “Congressman Wilson does and has always abided by campaign donation regulations set forth by the Federal Election Commission,” Snider said in an email. In an emailed statement, Taylor Reidy, who was Lindsey Graham’s communications director and now holds the same post for his sister, wrote that “any allegations of quid-pro-quo behavior or wrongdoing by the late Senator Lindsey Graham or his staff are simply false.” She said the accusations were the “ravings of a convicted felon” and that her office was never contacted by the FBI about the matter. After Kao’s arrest, they disgorged his donations, she added. The two executives who were subjects of the FBI investigation, Duke Hartman and Joshua Knight, were never charged. Hartman, the other executive at the dinner meeting with Graham, is now the CEO of a new naval research company called Integer Technologies that he co-founded with Knight

events.title: Europe faces record airfare surge in 2027 as war drives up fuel costs, warns Ryanair boss
events.summary: Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary forecasts a 20% increase in ticket prices as airlines reel from soaring costs. BRUSSELS – Ryanair Holdings chief executive Michael O’Leary predicted the highest increase in European airfares in history in 2027 as the Middle East war continues to drive up oil prices, forcing airlines to pass on their fuel costs to consumers. Ticket prices are set to increase by as much as 20% in 2027, O’Leary said on Oct 20 during a news conference in Brussels. As a result, airline margins will get squeezed because even the jump in fuel surcharges will not make up for the higher oil bill, he said. “You’re going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe in the next 12 months,” O’Leary said. “The question is: Will that increase in airfares be enough to cover the dramatically higher oil bills? I don’t think it will be.” The comments by the head of Europe’s largest budget carrier add to the more pessimistic outlook for the aviation industry, which has been forced to contend with a dramatic jump in costs even as travellers continue to splurge on air tickets. O’Leary said most European airlines, including his own, lack significant hedging in 2027 to protect against higher oil prices. In addition, there is less capacity in the market as some airlines struggle, while higher taxes are further dimming the picture for the industry. “We’re 85% unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” he said. Ryanair dropped as much as 2.1%, bringing the decline to 25% for the year. At that rate, that would be the worst annual stock return since 2018. O’Leary used his expletive-laden news conference to dish out against regulation in markets like France and Belgium, where Ryanair will reduce its footprint in response to higher taxes. He reiterated that the European aviation industry will continue to consolidate as weaker players struggle to survive in a high-cost environment. Air Baltic and Spain’s Volotea are the latest European carriers to undergo restructuring as higher costs take their toll. Last week, Deutsche Lufthansa won the race against Air France-KLM to acquire a stake in Portugal’s state-owned TAP. Meanwhile, US private equity firm Apollo Global Management is laying out the framework to take over EasyJet. Airlines across the world have suffered from soaring jet fuel costs since the Iran war escalated earlier in 2026 , leading to lower consumer demand. In September, Ryanair cut its annual passenger target for the fiscal year, saying it will fly fewer seats in the quieter winter season. BLOOMBERG

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Rooftop rent cuts, planning refusals and congestion leave Ookla ranking the UK’s capital last for speed and latency UK finance watchdog wants firms to report AI failures and close calls 4 hours ago Uber dodges £340M cabbie lawsuit after drivers miss legal deadline 23 hours ago Metropolitan Police's unchecked use of shoplifting platform lands force in trouble with data watchdog 5 days ago London cabbies want Sadiq Khan to slam the brakes on robotaxis 8 days ago BT Tower's rooftop pool plan brings swimmers back down to earth 27 days ago London's mobile network performance has slipped behind other European capitals as operators struggle to add capacity fast enough to meet demand. The city ranked seventh out of 18 in the continent for median download speed in 2021, but traffic has since expanded faster than available capacity. Other metropolises have improved; London now has the slowest speeds and the highest latency under load, according to mobile network testing firm Ookla . The research points to obstacles mobile operators face in adding extra capacity: applications for new street masts in London have fallen since 2022, and about three quarters of those filed since 2019 were refused. The Big Smoke was among the first European capitals to get 5G coverage, yet when Ookla's Q3 2026 tests found the city now has the slowest median download speed (109.43 Mbps), the slowest median upload speed (11.40 Mbps) and the highest latency under load - a measure of how the network copes with heavy use. Ookla's records show London’s 5G medina speed peaked at 200 Mbps in Q2 2021, fell as low as 102 Mbps in Q3 2023, then recovered slightly. Paris, by contrast, has stayed above 225 Mbps since mid-2021. The cause is congestion. In Central London, performance slumps on weekdays as commuters arrive: median download speed falls to 80.07 Mbps through the morning, 27 percent below weekend levels at the same hours. Part of the problem is that UK mobile operators own few of their antenna sites, many of which sit on rooftops in built-up areas, says Ookla. Under the Electronic Communications Code, and changes introduced in 2017, a London rooftop is worth about £1,000 ($1,333) a year to its owner, down from £21,000 ($28k). That givers landlords little motivation to host antennas, and many prefer solar panels. Operators can also receive notices to quit when a building is redeveloped, and it is estimated that this keeps about 7 percent of London’s rooftop sites out of action at any time. Planning rules compound the problem as applications for new masts are more likely to be refused in boroughs with conservation areas, such as Westminster. Street mast applications peaked in 2020, early in the first 5G build, and have fallen by more than four-fifths since 2022. Three quarters of applications for new street masts since 2019 were refused, against one in five upgrades. "Planning restrictions, particularly in conservation areas, make it harder to install and upgrade the mobile equipment London needs," Ookla lead industry analyst Luke Kehoe told The Register . "Notices to quit can also force rooftop sites offline during redevelopment long before replacements are ready, leaving operators trying to restore lost capacity while demand keeps growing." City Hall has noticed, and a draft plan for the capital drawn up by the Mayor of London observes that notices to quit "have eroded London’s overall mobile connectivity compared to other equivalent cities." The plan, due tor adoption in 2028, would require developers to keep mobile service running during construction, put masts on taller buildings and in the public realm; and ask boroughs to work with operators on sites in conservation areas. Other experts blame different factors for London’s poor mobile service.

events.title: Why cyber resilience is now a boardroom priority for UK public services
events.summary: The UK public sector has reached a cyber resilience inflection point. A new Prime Minister has taken office, and significant machinery-of-government changes have already been announced, including the scrapping of DSIT, the department that had become the center of government digital, technology and cyber policy. Its responsibilities are now being redistributed across other parts of Whitehall, creating a new policy and delivery landscape for public sector leaders to navigate. For years, cyber security was treated as a specialist operational discipline that was essential but largely delegated to technical teams. That model is no longer sustainable. Pressure is now coming from three directions at once, as policy raises expectations for boards and senior leaders, organizational reform reshapes how services, systems and suppliers connect, and technology change, from cloud and hybrid work to AI, expands both opportunity and exposure. Together, these forces mean cyber resilience can no longer sit below board level. Public services, from healthcare and benefits to transport, education, local government and emergency response, are now so digitally dependent that a cyber incident is not simply an IT outage. It is a risk to public trust, public safety and the continuity of government itself. Recent history shows what this means in practice. The 2024 ransomware attack on Synnovis, a pathology services provider to parts of the NHS, significantly reduced the capacity to process blood, urine and specimen tests, caused disruption across south-east London and contributed to delays affecting more than 11,000 outpatient and elective procedure appointments. Incidents like this turn abstract cyber risk into real-world service disruption, making resilience a boardroom issue rather than a back-office concern. Cyber resilience is no longer a technical aspiration, but a leadership obligation shaped by policy, organizational and technology change. Policy change has made cyber resilience a leadership obligation The direction from government and the National Cyber Security Centre is clear. The Cyber Resilience Pledge asks organizations to make cyber security a board-level responsibility, register for NCSC Early Warning and take a risk-based approach to Cyber Essentials across their supply chains. The NCSC’s Cyber Governance Code of Practice reinforces the point that cyber risk must be governed like any other material organizational risk. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will further expand expectations across essential and digital services, strengthening incident reporting and bringing more critical suppliers into scope. This matters because the scale and impact of cyber threats facing the UK are increasing sharply. The NCSC handled 204 nationally significant cyber incidents in the year to September 2025, up from 89 the previous year. That means the UK is now experiencing an average of four nationally significant cyber attacks every week. Policy has therefore changed the boardroom question. Leaders should no longer ask only whether an organization has invested in security tools. They need to ask whether they can prove resilience, evidence accountability and continue delivering critical services when systems are under pressure, suppliers are compromised, data access is disrupted or attackers are already inside the network. Organisational change is creating hidden cyber risk The second force is organizational change. Local Government Reorganisation is redrawing structures and responsibilities across England. Rail renationalization and other shifts in public ownership are changing who owns, manages and secures critical data and systems. Departmental priorities and delivery models are also evolving under a new Prime Minister, with DSIT being dismantled and functions including digital transformation, public sector AI adoption, information resilience and online harms moving into different departments and central government structures. Every one of these transitions creates potential gaps. Systems need to be integrated. Identity and access privileges need to be reassessed. Data needs to move between teams, agencies and suppliers. Contracts and responsibilities need to be redefined. During periods of change, the attack surface expands, and accountability can become blurred. This is why cyber resilience must be built into public sector reform from the outset. The question is not simply how to restructure services efficiently. It is how to ensure citizens can continue to access those services securely throughout the transition. Reorganization without resilience is a risk to the public. Technology change demands continuous assurance The third force is technology change. Public sector work now happens across hybrid environments, shared services, cloud platforms, partner ecosystems and complex supply chains. Traditional security models were built for a more stable world of fixed offices, predictable networks, known users and clearly defined organizational boundaries. That world no longer exists. AI makes this problem more urgent. AI is already being used across the public sector to improve productivity, analyze information and support better service delivery. But without governance, organizations can quickly lose track of which tools are being used, what data they can access and whether sensitive information is being exposed. Shadow AI is not a future risk. It is a present governance challenge. Resilience in this environment requires continuous assurance. Access should not be granted simply because a user is on a trusted network. Every request should be verified based on identity, context, device posture and risk. Users should only receive the access they need, when they need it. Applications should be protected from unnecessary exposure. Data should be segmented so that compromise in one area does not automatically spread across the organization. What public sector boards should do now Making cyber resilience a board-level priority does not mean every director needs to become a technical expert. It means senior leaders need the right governance, evidence and accountability to respond to the three forces reshaping risk across the public sector. That starts with treating cyber resilience as a standing board agenda item, linked directly to service continuity, citizen trust, regulatory exposure and reform delivery. It also requires boards to understand which critical services depend on which systems, suppliers and datasets, where single points of failure exist, and how disruption in one part of the ecosystem could affect citizens’ ability to access essential services. Supply chain assurance must be part of that same conversation. Public services are delivered through ecosystems, so resilience cannot stop at the boundary of a single department, council, agency or trust. events.title: Landholders and politicians push for tougher laws on renewable energy developments
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Landholders push for more regulations amid renewables rollout Glenn Franz and his parents own a property next to Wambo Wind Farm. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) About 12 community action groups have come together to discuss the challenges landholders face amid growth in the renewable energy sector. The group is calling for a minimum 3-kilometre setback from residences and up-front decommissioning bonds. Regional Voices Queensland will continue advocating for better protections for those impacted by renewable energy projects. A coalition of rural community groups is demanding tougher laws governing renewable energy developments, including mandatory turbine setbacks, stricter decommissioning rules and stronger protections for neighbouring landholders. Regional Voices Queensland (RVQ), a loose alliance of about 12 community action groups representing communities affected by renewable energy projects across the state, brought landholders, farming industry representatives and politicians together for its first major meeting today at the Franz family farm beside the Wambo Wind Farm at Diamondy, 280 kilometres north-west of Brisbane. The meeting, co-organised by Member for Maranoa David Littleproud, focused on reforms to planning laws, with more than 70 participants travelling from communities including the Southern Downs and other parts of regional Queensland. Regional Voices Queensland members are demanding tougher laws governing renewable energy developments. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) RVQ chair and Property Rights Australia board member, Jim Willmott, described the alliance as a "supergroup" formed after community organisations dealing with individual projects identified common concerns. Queensland's wind farm code has not allowed developers to comply simply by meeting a specified separation distance since 2024. Projects must meet all of the code's performance outcomes, including noise criteria at neighbouring dwellings. David Littleproud says affected landholders wanted clarity around the issue. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) Mr Littleproud said affected landholders were seeking practical safeguards rather than opposing renewable energy outright. "They're not asking for anything irrational," he said. "They're actually being quite considered and it's coming from a lived experience." Farm co-owner Glenn Franz, who does not host the turbines, said the experience of living beside the wind farm had highlighted gaps in existing protections, particularly around visual amenity and the financial risks associated with dismantling turbines at the end of their operational lives. "We've got 13 wind turbines surrounding us within a 3km zone," Mr Franz said. "There's got to be safeguards for the future. "It'd be nice to have the security up front, not as a pay-as-you-go-down-the-track sort of scheme." Karl Stefanovic interviewed landholders at the meeting. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) The Wambo Wind Farm, a joint venture between state-owned Stanwell and energy infrastructure group Cubico, received planning approval in 2020. Mr Franz said while the project was well advanced, other communities were at the start of the process and could learn from the Diamondy community's experience. Anna Lethbridge and Brendan Taylor from AgForce attended the meeting. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) AgForce policy adviser Anna Lethbridge said safeguards needed to extend beyond project hosts to neighbouring producers, including protections against contamination and impacts on agricultural accreditation. "From an AgForce perspective, we're not opposed to renewables," Ms Lethbridge said. Queensland regulates wind farm developments through its planning and environmental assessment framework, including State Code 23 and applicable approval conditions. Since 2025, new wind farm applications must undergo impact assessment and provide financial security for decommissioning. However, RVQ is concerned the wording is vague and could still leave landholders or taxpayers liable. Developers must now also negotiate a community benefit agreement with the relevant council before lodging an application.

events.title: Oil wavers near five-month high as Iran threats vie with flows
events.summary: Hostilities have recently flared up in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent oil stayed near a five-month high at just below US$110 a barrel as traders weighed Iran’s threats in the Strait of Hormuz against strong crude flows from the Persian Gulf. Iran said it had “no choice” but to assert control over Hormuz, while US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Gulf flows had recovered to about 80% of prewar levels. Geopolitical risks keep prices high as attacks on tankers continue; Brent has risen about 80% in 2026, and Iraq’s exports have topped 3.4 million barrels a day in October. Brent oil fluctuated near a five-month high as traders weighed the risk of further Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz against robust crude flows from the Persian Gulf. The global benchmark was just below US$110 a barrel, near the highest since May, while the most-active West Texas Intermediate contract was close to US$99. Iran has “no choice” but to assert control over Hormuz to safeguard the country’s security, First Vice-President Mohammad Reza Aref said on Oct 19 , according to a report from state-run news agency IRNA. Despite a recent flare-up in hostilities around the waterway , crude exports from the Gulf have continued at an accelerated pace. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox News that flows had recovered to about 80% of their prewar level, although refined-product shipments remained constrained. Brent has surged about 80% in 2026 as widening conflicts in the Middle East and between Russia and Ukraine disrupt energy supplies. Refined products have rallied even harder, with European diesel futures surging. Renewed attacks on tankers and energy infrastructure are keeping geopolitical risk elevated even as Persian Gulf crude flows recover. “The risks to oil prices clearly lie to the upside,” said Hamad Hussain, a commodities economist at Capital Economics. The escalation in attacks on ships raises the possibility of a “renewed fall in oil supply and a continued rise in prices”, he added. Iran’s Aref said the Islamic Republic could ensure safe passage through Hormuz for friendly nations, but warned that the “the US is now the cause of the current situation and must pay the price”. He made the comments during a meeting in Tajikistan with Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin. Iraq is among Persian Gulf producers that have ramped up crude flows, with the country’s oil minister saying exports have exceeded 3.4 million barrels a day so far in October . Shipments are now close to prewar levels after the OPEC member offered deep discounts to regional benchmarks. Meanwhile, the Trump administration is authorising the sale of sanctioned oil tankers so they can legitimately ship crude, according to Wright. The move is aimed at expanding capacity as the US-Iran war strains supply and drives up freight costs. He estimated there are about 1,600 vessels in the global “dark fleet”. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Cumulative impacts of data centre gas plants overlooked, court hears
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Data centre developer takes Southern Highlands power plant fight to court Gundungurra man Dane Shanahan voiced his opposition to the project during the open-air Land and Environment Court hearing. ( ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt ) Nakar Property is appealing in the Land and Environment Court after its application to build a 16-megawatt gas-fired power plant in the Southern Highlands was refused. Community members urged the court to consider all three of the power plants proposed for the site. Lawyers for the applicant and the council will present evidence in coming days. A court has heard the "cumulative impacts" of a series of gas plants proposed to run data centres in the Southern Highlands are being ignored as a result of fragmented planning decisions. Seven community members gave evidence at the site of the development in Moss Vale on Tuesday morning, kicking off a three-day hearing in the Land and Environment Court. The court is considering developer Nakar Property's appeal of a refusal by Wingecarribee Shire Council for one of its projects on the site. The application was for a 16-megawatt gas-fired power plant and battery storage system to power data centres. Separately, the developer has secured approval for another gas-fired plant on the site, a 14MW facility, and is seeking state government approval for a third, 673MW plant. More than 100 community members gathered on the site ahead of the Land and Environment Court hearing. ( ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt ) A crowd of more than 100 community members, Land and Environment Court Commissioner Nicola Targett, and representatives for the council and the applicant gathered in an open field in Moss Vale for the first day of the hearing. The first community member to address the court was Dane Shanahan, who introduced himself by his Gundungurra name, Mullyang. The emerging knowledge-holder for the region's traditional landowners told the court his name meant "eagle" and, as he outlined his community's concerns about the project, two wedge-tailed eagles appeared in the sky above the open-air court. After the proceedings, Mr Shanahan described the appearance of the birds as an "ancestral presence". He was one of several speakers to urge the commissioner to consider the application for the 16MW facility in the broader context of the development. "Each piece is being presented as small — each piece is being assessed on its own and no-one is looking at the whole," Mr Shanahan told the court. The court is only assessing the appeal lodged by Nakar Property for the 16MW facility and battery, but Gabby Kent, who lives 1 kilometre from the proposed site, agreed with Mr Shanahan's argument. "The planning processes may be separate, but the cumulative impacts to my family … and my community are not," she said. Will McCarthy says the project needs to be looked at as a whole. ( ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt ) Will McCarthy, whose home overlooks the development, echoed those sentiments. "At some point the planning system needs to stand back at look at the development as a whole," he told the commissioner. The court heard the applicant had submitted an amended plan for the development to speakers and parties ahead of the hearing. That submission included changes such as painting exhaust stacks green to address visual amenity, and adding some onsite solar power generation. Mr Shanahan told the court no Gundungurra people had been consulted as part of the development application's Aboriginal Heritage Assessment, despite the cultural significance of a waterway that would be cut off by the project. "It is as significant to the Gundungurra as Genesis is to Christians," he said. "The applicant has proposed to reshape an ancestral waterway without asking the people [whether] it will scar." The power plant and battery would provide power to data centres on Cloud Carrier's Moss Vale site. ( Supplied: Cloud Carrier ) Jacqueline Duc raised concerns about the health impacts of pollutants, telling the court carcinogens from gas power-plants had been linked to lung and childhood cancers. She also raised concerns about the project being located within the Sydney water catchment, saying its tributaries eventually flowed into Warragamba Dam, which supplied 80 per cent of the city's drinking water. The applicant's lawyer, James Smith, did not question any of the community speakers. The court will hear from the applicant's attorney and the council's representative, Michael Staunton, in coming days.

events.title: Gulf states to boost diesel shipments to struggling France
events.summary: The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain are to sell France the equivalent of 10 per cent of its usual diesel consumption in the coming weeks, French government sources said, as President Emmanuel Macron started the second day of his Gulf tour. The aim is reduce European energy prices, which have drawn protests and public anger in France and elsewhere. “The greater the quantity, the lower the price. It’s quite simple,” an adviser to French President Emmanuel Macron said. A large part of the deal was negotiated by Mr Macron during a tour of the Gulf that started with visits to Kuwait and the UAE on Monday. He landed in Bahrain on Tuesday, before travelling on to Qatar. France previously obtained guarantees from Saudi Arabia to sell the country 95,000 tonnes of diesel in October and November, bringing the total to 190,000 tonnes over the two months. In addition, the UAE and Bahrain are in the coming weeks expected to separately sell 100,000 tonnes of diesel to France for an unknown duration. “These are political commitments obtained from countries in the region because they know us and they know we are reliable – because we have been there during every critical moment, notably by deploying air defence capabilities,” the adviser said. Sales are to go through French energy company TotalEnergies, whose chief executive, Patrick Pouyanne, has accompanied Mr Macron on his Gulf tour. “Our mission is primarily to secure supplies because there is a risk. We have a diesel deficit, as we are a major importer,” Mr Pouyanne said. “We are in contact with [...] national companies and we are going to sign a contract specifically for France. The commitment in Saudi Arabia is to ensure that supplies continue beyond November.” The announcement is a political win for Mr Macron, who is under pressure in France, which is in the grip of large-scale protests over a cost-of-living crisis. Some demonstrations have turned violent. Authorities have imposed a curfew in central Paris and other parts of the country. European diesel is currently trading at almost $200 a barrel amid the war in Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. That compares with about $80 at the start of 2026, with refined products rallying much harder than crude prices this year. AI and tech deals During Mr Macron's stop in the UAE on Monday, France and the UAE signed deals in energy, artificial intelligence and advanced technology as the countries strengthen investment and economic ties. The preliminary agreements were signed in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Mr Macron in the UAE capital. Three agreements focused on AI and advanced technology were signed with French start-up AMI Labs to strengthen research and technological co-operation and explore new applications across several fields, Abu Dhabi Media office reported. Emmanuel Macron visits UAE on Gulf tour – in pictures The deals cover Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Abu Dhabi’s G42 and computing company Analog. MBZUAI is to focus on strengthening co-operation with AMI Labs in AI research and development, while G42 aims to establish a framework for strategic co-operation in cloud computing infrastructure and AI models. Analog’s deal with AMI Labs is related to exploring opportunities to integrate AI models into robotics and physical AI applications and opening new avenues for developing intelligent systems and expanding their use in industrial and technology sectors. AI is a cornerstone of French-Emirati relations. During a visit by Sheikh Mohamed to France in February 2025, the UAE announced that billions of euros was to be investment in an AI campus and date centre project near Paris. The UAE and France will also boost co-operation in the energy sector, with Adnoc Gas and Schneider Electric signing an initial pact to assess advanced technology and opportunities for operational improvements to help enhance efficiency and improve the performance of energy systems. Adnoc Refining and Technip Energies also signed two contracts relating to a refining capacity enhancement project and a sustainable aviation fuel project. “These agreements demonstrate both countries’ commitment to broadening economic and investment co-operation, strengthening integration between their industrial, technological and research capabilities, and opening new avenues for public-private partnerships to support the development of innovative and sustainable solutions in shared priority sectors,” Abu Dhabi Media office said.

events.title: Oil majors face spending test from Iran war windfall cash
events.summary: The severe disruption of the Strait of Hormuz has pushed energy prices to multi-year highs. Oil majors are set for a big third-quarter profit jump after the US-Israeli war on Iran lifted energy prices and refining margins. Investors want to see whether Shell, BP, TotalEnergies, Chevron and Exxon keep spending discipline or start a costly spending spree. BP is using cash to cut debt, while Shell and TotalEnergies may raise buybacks; BP plans a strategy update on 15 December. LONDON – Oil majors are set to post a big jump in third-quarter profit as the US-Israeli war on Iran has boosted refining and trading results, while investors will monitor how wisely they use their cash piles and whether they resist a spending spree. The severe disruption of the Strait of Hormuz since US-Israeli airstrikes began the war in February has pushed energy prices to multi-year highs, allowing trading desks to profit from the volatility. In a sector notorious in the past for boom and bust, the majors have all promised this time to refrain from losing control of costs in what is one of the highest-earning years for global oil producers in recent memory. Shell, BP and TotalEnergies all expect refining margins to increase three- to fourfold in the third quarter from a year ago, with Shell guiding for a record high of US$42 a barrel. TotalEnergies expects cash flow from its refining and chemicals business to double to around US$4 billion (S$5.11 billion) from the previous quarter. Exxon signalled that higher refining margins in the quarter could boost downstream profit by US$4.5 billion versus the previous quarter. Are majors adapting their spending plans? As oil majors report third-quarter results at the end of October, investors are asking whether they will stick to their existing spending plans in times of exceptional earnings, wrote RBC Capital Markets analyst Biraj Borkhataria in a research note. So far, Chevron and Exxon have used the money to pay down debt. Investors in Chevron will monitor investment in Venezuela and its progress towards extending its contract to operate the TCO joint venture in Kazakhstan, which is developing the country’s largest oilfield, analysts said. HSBC expects Shell to announce a US$3.5 billion buyback for the fourth quarter, after it reduced the pace of its buyback programme to a quarterly US$3 billion earlier in 2026. After the oil major’s trading update last week, investment bank TPH called BP its favourite name among European majors. It said BP’s underlying profit could exceed US$7 billion, versus US$5.7 billion in the second quarter, boosted by refining and gas marketing and trading. That cash is going towards repairing BP’s balance sheet. Citi data shows BP’s net debt to operating cash flow falling from 1.7 times at the end of 2025, the highest of the five biggest majors, to an expected 0.8 times by the third quarter. BP is likely to discuss its future capital allocation during its third-quarter earnings announcement, HSBC said, as BP hits a target to reduce its net debt about a year early, also helped by pausing its buyback programme in 2026. BP has flagged a strategy update on Dec 15. “We believe the priority will remain firmly on deleveraging, with stable capex and no buyback resumption before 2028,” said HSBC’s Kim Fustier and Sadnan Ali in a note. Shell and Total are due to report on Oct 29 while BP, Chevron and Exxon are due on Oct 30. REUTERS

events.title: WA woman's 'harrowing' ordeal stranded in Bali hospital after fall
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts WA woman stranded in Bali hospital after horror fall while on holiday Estelle Ravenscroft is being treated at a hospital in Bali after having a fall. ( Supplied: Marilyn Jones ) A 79-year-old woman is in a Bali hospital in a serious condition after breaking multiple bones when she fell at a restaurant. Estelle Ravenscroft's family are fundraising to bring her home because she is not covered by insurance. The Insurance Council of Australia is urging travellers to persist in efforts to obtain insurance before heading overseas. A West Australian grandmother is facing a potential bill of $100,000 to return home to Australia after falling down stairs at a Bali restaurant. Estelle Ravenscroft, 79, and her husband Keith remain in Bali, where Ms Ravenscroft is in the intensive care unit at a local hospital. Ms Ravenscroft broke both her legs in the fall. The harrowing ordeal has been exacerbated by mounting medical expenses as Ms Ravenscroft is not covered by insurance. Mr Ravenscroft said it was difficult to obtain travel insurance, because of their age. Indonesia is not among the 11 countries with which Australia has a reciprocal arrangement for publicly-funded emergency care. Ms Ravenscroft's family said the 79-year-old had gone for lunch at a restaurant and fallen down the stairs, which had no rails. Speaking this morning, Mr Ravenscroft said his wife had pulled through after a nine-hour operation at a local hospital. "She's sitting up now, but there are some difficulties breathing, and issues with transfusions, but she's pulled through the operation OK, which is really fantastic." Estelle Ravenscroft broke multiple bones when she fell at a restaurant. ( Supplied: Leonie Walsh ) The couple's family has appealed to the community for help with expenses through an online fundraising website. Mr Ravenscroft said travel insurance was increasingly difficult to obtain as people aged. "When you get a certain age, you'll find having the insurances that you think you can have, are not available," he said. "I'd prefer not to go into that, because I'm here at the moment to make sure that my wife is OK. I want to get her home. The family wants to get her home." Ms Ravenscroft's sister Marilyn Jones said the family was grateful for the support offered by the WA community. Estelle Ravenscroft was on holiday with her husband in Bali when she fell at a restaurant. ( Supplied: Marilyn Jones ) "The amount daily is climbing," she said. Ms Jones said she was aware of commentary around the couple's lack of adequate travel insurance. "It's pulled us down terribly," she said. "There are some not very nice people out there, but there are also some wonderful people out there. National Seniors Australia chief executive Chris Grice urged older Australians to investigate all options for travel insurance before travelling overseas. ''So I just feel so badly for someone who is caught in a foreign land, who perhaps can't get home because of the costs involved." He said he was aware of seniors who struggled to get travel insurance as they aged, but urged people to persist. "It depends on age and existing conditions," he said. "It doesn't mean they can't get cover. It all depends on how they are being treated." He said people needed to try and speak directly to an insurer, rather than apply online, if they had concerns. An Insurance Council of Australia spokesperson said its thoughts were with the Ravenscrofts and acknowledged the strain many households were under. "While cost of living is putting pressure on household budgets, a single overseas medical emergency, evacuation, or trip cancellation can cost far more than the premium of even a comprehensive policy," she said.

events.title: Blackwall quadruples valuation to $2.2B as websites wrangle an increasingly crowded internet
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Estonia-based Blackwall , which builds web traffic security tools for hosting providers, said on Tuesday that it has raised $100 million at a $2.2 billion valuation. It builds products that helps websites grapple with the skyrocketing volume of bot traffic, especially AI agents. The Series C was led by AVP, with participation from existing investors Dawn Capital, MMC Ventures and Tera Ventures. Blackwall’s executive chairman, Roi Carthy, told TechCrunch this funding round increased the company’s valuation by 4 times since its previous fundraise in 2025 . Over the past few years, web infrastructure companies like Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva and Blackwall have found themselves in an increasingly valuable but difficult space: They’re on the frontlines, dealing with DDoS attacks, indiscriminate scraping, botnet farms, malicious requests, and these days, even swarms of AI agents going rogue . But it’s also a chance to make a killing by helping hosting providers and websites deal with all the potentially unwanted traffic. Blackwall, however, isn’t interested in competing with the bigwigs in its space. Instead of selling its platform directly to websites, the company uses a “channel” approach, working with web hosting, managed service and cloud providers to understand their needs, and then handing over a bundle of tools which they can customize. Those providers can then offer Blackwall’s security tools to their own clients under their own branding and retain control of that relationship. There’s money in it for both sides. Co-founder and CEO Nikita Rozenberg told TechCrunch that hosting companies can mix and match security components to build their own solution according to what they want to provide to their end customers, set the prices, and share a cut of the revenue with Blackwall. The company initially gives its customers a free tier showing the traffic and threats hitting their network, but charges for any protection or tools to address the threats. In addition to providing services like threat intelligence, certificate management, DDoS protection and traffic routing, Blackwall examines its customers’ web traffic to differentiate actual visitors and legit AI agents from malicious bots, intruders, and disruptive traffic. Rozenberg said the company uses techniques like digital fingerprinting to identify the software sending a request — for example, Microsoft Office or Codex — to filter out bots. In addition, the company uses its own AI models at customers’ endpoints to analyze the intent and behavior of the requests coming in to differentiate agents sent by a person for a real request versus a malicious bot. In the coming years, Rozenberg sees a big opportunity emerging as AI agents begin interacting and transacting with websites on behalf of their users. This should eventually require systems to manage which agents get access, and on what terms, and how they are authorized to make payments. Blackwall isn’t alone in eyeing that opportunity. Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control lets website owners allow or block individual AI crawlers, and there’s also an option to charge them for access. But Rozenberg argues that Blackwall’s advantage lies in letting hosting providers offer such traffic management services themselves instead of handing the customer relationship to another security provider. Blackwall plans to use the funding to expand its operations across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, and develop more security tooling for hosting, cloud and managed service providers. events.title: Hiring in the UAE rebounds in third quarter despite uncertainty fuelled by Middle East conflict
events.summary: Hiring in the UAE rebounded in the third quarter of the year to growth of 4 per cent, the highest across the Gulf , as business demand recovers, a report has found. After hiring in the country dropped by 4 per cent in the second quarter, demand recovered from the mid-year slowdown and by September new export business was growing at its fastest pace in almost two years, Cooper Fitch said its third quarter employment index. Companies remain cautious about the year ahead, the report added. Across the Gulf, hiring returned to growth in the third quarter, rising 2 per cent following a 3 per cent decline in the previous quarter. In Saudi Arabia, recruitment rose 1.5 per cent, while Oman recorded 0.5 per cent growth. Hiring, however, fell by 1 per cent in Qatar , 2 per cent in Kuwait and 2 per cent in Bahrain. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has had a significant impact on regional economies, with the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz affecting oil-exporting countries. The International Monetary Fund, in a report this month, projected the UAE 's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, as long as shipping routes normalise and the strait reopens. The fund also expects Saudi Arabia 's economy to contract 3.3 per cent this year, while Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3 per cent, 16.7 per cent and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. Oman is the only Gulf member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent. However, all the six states are anticipated to post growth in 2027, the IMF said. The contraction in Gulf hiring "lasted a single quarter and the market is now back within the modest growth range seen through 2025", Cooper Fitch said. "Growth extended across a wider range of functions than in the previous quarter, with paused mandates resuming in sectors such as energy." Sectors hiring Hiring in energy recorded the sharpest increase at 7 per cent across the Gulf in the July-September period. Mandates stalled during the regional tensions returned steadily as conditions eased, the report said. "Clients resumed searches where they left off. In the UAE, growth came from across the energy market, including nuclear and renewables," it added. The delivery of Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 pipeline also supported the sector's growth. "Project directors, commissioning specialists and contracts leaders remained difficult to secure. Candidates with scarce technical skills continued to receive multiple offers, keeping the market firmly in their favour," the report added. Hiring in finance grew 5 per cent, strategy rose 6 per cent – its first increase of 2026, while real estate and software employment was up 4 per cent. Recruitment in sales and marketing rose 3 per cent in the third quarter, "reflecting cautious confidence rather than a broad hiring rebound", while human resources grew 2 per cent, the report said. However, hiring in banking declined 4 per cent, while investment management fell by 5 per cent "after a strong run of hiring earlier in the year, driven by regional platform expansion and fund activity". While hiring picked up in the third quarter, it remained selective, Cooper Fitch said. "Clients focused on advancing active searches and securing specialist capability rather than broad expansion, and several markets and parts of financial services saw lower activity," it said. Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, it remains to be seen whether the improvement can be sustained. "Business demand has provided a firmer base, but costs remain elevated and visibility on trade and shipping is still limited," the report said. "Competition for scarce specialist talent has also intensified, adding pressure on employers seeking to secure critical capability."

events.title: Inquiry urges halt to plan to burn Sydney's waste in regional towns
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Energy-from-waste inquiry recommends moratorium on proposed incinerators Topic: Recycling and Waste Management There has been strong opposition in Parkes to a proposed energy-from-waste facility. ( ABC News: Joanna Woodburn ) A NSW parliamentary inquiry into waste-to-energy facilities has handed down 22 recommendations. The committee advised that two incinerator proposals in Parkes and Goulburn should be halted pending an independent review. The NSW government has until early 2027 to respond to the recommendations. A New South Wales parliamentary inquiry into energy-from-waste facilities has recommended that the state government reject plans to burn Sydney's waste in regional communities. The select committee on proposed energy-from-waste technology made 22 recommendations after holding seven hearings across 2025 and 2026. The committee recommended that development applications to build incinerators in Tarago near Goulburn and Parkes be knocked back. The chair of the committee, Nationals MLC Nichole Overall, today told NSW parliament it was clear the technology was not appropriate to be built in the communities. "Given the absence of numerous critical elements, significantly the lack of social licence and community acceptance including from local councils and Aboriginal land councils," Ms Overall said. Nichole Overall chaired the select committee's inquiry into energy-from-waste facilities. ( ABC News: Lisa Glenday ) Environment Protection Authority regulations limit the construction of energy-from-waste facilities to four locations in NSW: Tomago, West Lithgow, Parkes, and the southern Goulburn-Mulwaree precinct. "The government, proponents and advocates state that these facilities are safe wherever they are located," Ms Overall said. Existing landfill capacity in Greater Sydney is expected to be reached by 2030, with advocates for incinerators highlighting the technology as a potential solution. The scoping report for the proposed $1 billion Parkes Energy Recovery facility in the New South Wales central west was published by the NSW Planning Department on Tuesday. A sign shows opposition to the proposed Parkes waste-to-energy facility. ( Supplied: Parkes Clean Future Alliance ) If approved, the site would have capacity to process 732,000 tonnes of waste per annum by thermally treating household and industrial rubbish. Almost all of the waste processed would be transferred by rail from Sydney to the site, before being converted into up to 80 megawatts of base load power daily. If approved, the Parkes Energy Recovery facility would have capacity to process 730,000 tonnes of waste per year. ( Supplied: Parkes Energy Recovery ) Ms Overall said the committee heard from residents in opposition to the development throughout the hearings. "Waste is best managed as close to its source as possible," she said. "Transporting hundreds of thousands of tonnes of metropolitan waste to regional facilities, hundreds of kilometres away adds to cost, emissions and impacts." Parkes resident Erik Lensson welcomed the committee's recommendation for the state government to reject the incinerator proposal. "It is entirely unsuitable," he said. Ed Nicholas says the project is safe and, if approved, will deliver benefits to the region. ( ABC News: Laurence Curson ) In a statement, Parkes Energy Recovery director Ed Nicholas said while the technology is new to Australia, it has been embraced in developing countries around the world. "It's a pity that the inquiry wasn't able to visit an operating facility as part of their investigation," Mr Nicholas said. "Had they done so, they would have seen for themselves how best-practice facilities, such as the one we are proposing for Parkes, work in both rural and urban areas to strict environmental standards. "We are committed to listening to feedback … and demonstrating the real benefits this project can bring at every stage." Veolia is proposing to build the Woodlawn Advanced Energy Recovery Centre near Tarago. ( Supplied: Veolia ) Veolia is proposing to process 380,000 tonnes of non-recyclable waste from Sydney each year at the company's existing Woodlawn site near Tarago. If approved, it would generate enough electricity for up to 40,000 homes. The proposal is before the NSW Planning Department and is awaiting a response to submissions from Veolia. Veolia have been contacted for comment. The committee received more than 1,400 submissions, the majority in opposition to the technology's development.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72 Thu, 3 Sept 40 72 → Fri, 4 Sept, 7:40 pm, Final score, Cats 107, Blues 74 Fri, 4 Sept 107 74 → Sat, 5 Sept, 3:15 pm, Final score, Swans 141, Lions 88 Sat, 5 Sept 141 88 → Sat, 5 Sept, 7:35 pm, Final score, Crows 90, Bulldogs 68 Sat, 5 Sept 90 68 → Fri, 11 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 120, Cats 106 Fri, 11 Sept 120 106 → Sat, 12 Sept, 7:35 pm, Final score, Lions 144, Crows 91 Sat, 12 Sept 144 91 → Fri, 18 Sept, 7:40 pm, Final score, Swans 71, Dockers 83 Fri, 18 Sept 71 83 → Sat, 19 Sept, 5:15 pm, Final score, Hawks 122, Lions 131 Sat, 19 Sept 122 131 → Sat, 26 Sept, 2:30 pm, Final score, Dockers 89, Lions 96 Sat, 26 Sept 89 96 → Whyalla Football League clubs face unclear future in wake of steelworks job losses Robert Brereton says there are not enough players and volunteers for all six clubs in the Whyalla Football League to continue. ( ABC News ) Whyalla's six football clubs are facing an uncertain future in the wake of job losses at the steelworks. Members from the clubs say it is unlikely the Upper Spencer Gulf city will have enough players and volunteers to keep all six clubs, with future mergers possible. More certainty is expected for the town after a decision on a buyer is made. Football in Whyalla is facing an uncertain future as the region grapples with the flow-on effects of mass redundancies at the steelworks, with local clubs concerned a drop in player numbers could lead to their demise. Last month, the state government revealed that the steelworks' blast furnace, which had been shut down for months, would not be restarted and, as a result, the plant's direct workforce to be reduced from 1,700 to 1,200 people . A further 300 contractors were also expected to be impacted, and it is unknown how many workers will chase employment opportunities elsewhere and consequently leave the Upper Spencer Gulf city. Last week, more than 250 workers who accepted redundancies finished up at the steelworks . Roopena Football Club is one of the six which make up the Whyalla Football League, and president Robert Brereton said each club was bracing for player shortages. "I think every club in Whyalla at the moment probably doesn't fully understand what season 2027 is going to look like for them," he said. The blast furnace at the Whyalla steelworks has been shut down, resulting in job losses. ( ABC News: Brant Cumming ) He said it was not just players clubs could lose, but volunteers. "Every one of those teams has a level of volunteer support and we've noticed over the journey that it's difficult to find the volunteers needed to keep all the sports on the park." The steel city's population peaked in the mid-1970s, when about 33,000 people were living in the region, but the latest figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics show it had fallen to about 21,400 in 2021. Greg Flanegan from the North Whyalla Football Club said it was likely the number of clubs in the league needed to reduce. "With the expansion of Whyalla getting so strong we went to six clubs, and Port Augusta and Pirie just stayed the same. I don't know that we'll ever get back to that." Greg Flanegan says Whyalla may need to drop down to four clubs. ( ABC News ) President of the Central Whyalla Football Club, Richard Wallace, said he felt "a little bit nervous" about the future of the league. "In the current form — six teams, and we're one team that's been struggling a little bit, if you lose too many people it's pretty hard to keep your club going so it doesn't look good but we're going to hang in there. Whyalla hangs in," he said. He said amalgamation was not on the table for his club "at the moment", but the concept was "not completely a bad thing", noting clubs like Woodville-West Torrens and the Brisbane Lions had won premierships in the years following mergers. "I'm hopeful for the future of footy, and Whyalla. I've got to be," he said. Richard Wallace says the next couple of years will be tough for Whyalla and its football clubs. ( ABC News ) Mr Brereton said the South Australian National Football League had "basically given clubs two options" if considering mergers. "One is one club consumes the other completely, or both clubs fold and form a new club. And the appetite for either of those two options is not high," he said. "All clubs have struggled a bit with that understanding that potentially in a merger one club disappears and 100 years of history goes with it, or they both lose their 100 years of history and a new club forms and they continue on like that.

events.title: Former Google chief Eric Schmidt’s 1% Anthropic stake set to reap huge windfall
events.summary: Eric Schmidt invested tens of millions of dollars in Anthropic’s Series A fundraising round. Eric Schmidt owns about 1% of Anthropic from an early Series A bet, which could add billions to his wealth if the AI firm goes public at a huge valuation. Anthropic is preparing an IPO, with marketing due around 9 November and a debut expected by end-2026. Investors see a possible US$1.8 trillion to US$2 trillion value. Big backers include Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia and Microsoft. The company’s latest US$65 billion funding round pushed its value above OpenAI for the first time. WASHINGTON – Former Google chief executive officer Eric Schmidt owns around 1% of Anthropic thanks to his early investment in the start-up, according to sources familiar with the matter, setting him up for one of the largest individual windfalls from the company’s imminent public market debut . Schmidt invested tens of millions of dollars in Anthropic’s Series A fundraising round, according to the sources, who asked not to be identified because they were not authorised to discuss private matters. It is unclear if he has sold any part of his stake since the initial investment. Schmidt and Anthropic declined to comment. Anthropic’s highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO) is set to generate massive windfalls for its employees and investors. The start-up’s seven co-founders are already worth US$8 billion (S$10.2 billion) each based on its last funding round, fortunes that propelled them onto the Bloomberg Billionaires Index of the world’s 500 richest people. When Schmidt, 71, made his first bet on Anthropic in 2021, it was valued at US$461 million, according to data company Pitchbook. Investors indicated earlier in October that a fair valuation for the company is in the US$1.8 trillion to US$2 trillion ballpark; the high end of that range would value Anthropic at more than 4,300 times its Series A funding round. At that value, the Anthropic stake would boost Schmidt’s net worth by about one-third to nearly US$80 billion, according to Bloomberg’s wealth index. Even using Anthropic’s most recent valuation of US$965 billion, Schmidt adds nearly US$10 billion to his existing fortune of US$57.5 billion. Schmidt has become a prolific technology investor over the past decade and a half, across several investment platforms including TomorrowVentures, Innovation Endeavors and his Hillspire family office, which Pitchbook associates with hundreds of different venture capital bets. His early portfolio focused on consumer internet, software and financial technology, but more recently artificial intelligence has been a major focus, with investments in Mistral AI, Reflection AI and World Labs, as well as Anthropic. If Anthropic’s public stock debuts at a US$2 trillion value, his bet on the company would beat Innovation Endeavors’ own early bet on Uber Technologies in 2011. By the time that company went public in 2019, its value had increased about 1,400-fold to US$82 billion. Anthropic is set to begin formally marketing its IPO as soon as the week of Nov 9, putting it in line to begin trading before the US Thanksgiving holiday, sources familiar with the matter said earlier in October. It is expected to make its debut no later than the end of 2026. The start-up’s major backers include Alphabet, Amazon.com, Nvidia and Microsoft, which have all poured billions into the Claude chatbot maker. Venture firms Altimeter Capital, Dragoneer, Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital also each put more than US$2 billion into the company when they led a US$65 billion funding round in May that tipped Anthropic’s valuation higher than its rival OpenAI for the first time. The company – whose other backers include Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital – expects to match or beat the size of SpaceX’s record-setting US$1.77 trillion June IPO, sources familiar with the matter have said. events.title: Software upgrades eat nearly a third of companies’ IT budgets, survey finds
events.summary: Vendor-driven upgrades can add costs and operational risks for information technology companies in the AI race. A survey by Origina found large US and British firms spend 28% of software budgets on vendor-driven upgrades, migrations and licence changes they did not choose. The study said 95% paid for upgrades they expected to worsen results, while 80% feared leaving a major vendor would disrupt business. Companies also lost time and money: 84% of senior engineers worked on forced changes, and the latest change cost US$12.87 million a year on average. Large US and British companies spend 28% of their software budgets on average to pay for vendor-driven upgrades, migration and licensing changes they would not have actively chosen, adding avoidable costs and operational risks in the race to adopt artificial-intelligence solutions, a survey by software maintenance provider Origina showed on Oct 20 . These hard-to-avoid recurring costs and operational disruptions were described as a “software tax” in the study that surveyed more than 2,000 companies. “When the alternative to an unwanted upgrade is losing support on systems the business runs on, saying yes is often a rational response,” Origina chief executive Tomas O’Leary said. The report showed 95% of respondents said they had paid for a vendor-driven upgrade they expected to worsen outcomes, while 80% said leaving a major software vendor would significantly disrupt their business. Another 84% said senior engineering staff “always” or “often” devoted time to vendor-driven software changes rather than innovation or business-focused development. Some 91% said they had retired fully functional hardware in the past three years to comply with vendors’ support deadlines, sacrificing 1.65 years of remaining useful life on average. O’Leary said the issue was largely universal and also applied to other regions, with older companies with more entrenched technology stacks facing the biggest challenges. According to the report, the most recent vendor-driven software change resulted in an average annual cost of US$12.87 million (S$16 million) for the surveyed organisations. REUTERS
