events.title: Hegseth makes unannounced trip and other Mideast news
events.summary: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is in the Middle East U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is in the Middle East. Meanwhile, Israeli police have arrested 10 suspects in a wave of settler violence that targeted a U.S. journalist and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank, and Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced attacks in Yemen and across Saudi Arabia. Here's the latest news from the Middle East on Monday. Read our full coverage here . U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has made an unannounced trip to the Middle East. Hegseth announced on social media late Monday U.S. time that he was in the Middle East visiting troops that were on an unspecified, “historic mission.” However, the post also came several hours after Axios reported that Hegseth was in Israel visiting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. When asked about the visit and the reports, the Pentagon declined to comment. Saudi Arabia has executed a Bangladeshi man and woman after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” in a mosque in the Muslim holy city of Mecca. Bangladesh said that it wasn't informed before the sentences were carried out and has sought information from Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Interior Ministry said the Bangladeshis were executed because of “the gravity and seriousness of their actions in violating the sanctity of both time and place.” It did not elaborate. Police said 10 suspects were arrested on Monday following violent attacks by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank that prompted heavy criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government. Israeli police didn't identify who attacked the people who had come to support Palestinians during their annual olive harvest. Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine was beaten Friday by a crowd of young male settlers while documenting the scene, leaving her with several broken ribs and vertebrae. Masked settlers also attacked a group of European diplomats on Saturday. Palestinians have been subject to surging attacks, rarely leading to arrests or punishment, rights groups say. Netanyahu’s main rival in the Oct. 27 elections, Gadi Eisenkot, said “a handful of criminals is burning up the last shreds of legitimacy left to the state of Israel.” A money shortage has forced the World Food Program to deny food and cash assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza and 200,000 people in the West Bank, according to its acting director Carl Skau, who urged international donors to provide $450 million to fund hot meals and food parcels for the next six months. Skau said Monday in a video briefing that “life in Gaza remains absolutely brutal” and incredibly dangerous, with U.N. teams recording about 50 attacks per day in the past week, while in the West Bank, he saw burned olive fields, camps and villages. There have been more settler attacks over these first two weeks of the olive harvest than during all of last year, he said. Israel's military said Monday that it would resume coordinating the entry of commercial trucks into Gaza, but warned that future reports of merchants paying taxes to Hamas would lead to their licenses being revoked. The suspension since Wednesday cut off the flow of needed food and goods. COGAT, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza, cited disagreements between Hamas and the merchants over taxes, and claimed to be communicating a decision made by the merchants. Truckers in Gaza said Israel was using the disagreement as a pretext to fight Hamas’ taxation efforts. They said officials in Gaza called the money a “donation” to pay civil servants rather than a tax. COGAT said Monday that Hamas had withdrawn its demands. 2 dead, 11 injured after Kansas mother drives onto soccer field during game: Police Iran updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs' Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Iran-backed Houthi rebels killed at least 53 soldiers in ballistic missile strikes on a Yemeni military camp on Monday, making it one of the deadliest attacks on the Saudi-backed government’s forces since rebels shattered a 2022 ceasefire in Yemen’s civil war . The strikes on the al-Alam military camp also wounded 200 recruits, the Shabwa provincial government said. The Houthi rebels also claimed Monday to have carried out six military operations targeting oil infrastructure, airports and military sites across Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities say recent Houthi missile and drone attacks have killed 19 people and injured more than 350 others. The Saudi Civil Defense issued more danger alerts across parts of the kingdom Monday. Three separate Israeli strikes hit Gaza City, killing at least two people, according to Shifa Hospital, and two 17-year-olds were killed in another strike on Khan Younis in southern Gaza, according to Nasser Hospital. The Israeli military said it struck Hamas militants in each of the attacks on Gaza City. It did not comment on the other attack.

events.title: Japan’s 20-year bond auction sees strongest demand on record
events.summary: Japan’s super-long yields have recently approached multi-decade highs, as a global bond selloff driven by escalating tensions in the Middle East and higher oil prices added to inflation and fiscal concerns. Japan’s 20-year bond auction drew record demand, with a bid-to-cover ratio of 5.84. Higher yields and easing fiscal worries brought back domestic buyers. The auction helped push the 20-year yield down by as much as 6 basis points to 3.710%. BNP Paribas said the result showed stronger demand from life insurers and other investors. Markets still worry about Japan’s finances and future bond supply under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. Traders now await the Bank of Japan meeting next week for rate clues. TOKYO – Japan’s 20-year government bond auction on Oct 20 saw the strongest demand on record, as elevated yields attracted renewed buying from domestic investors. The bid-to-cover ratio was 5.84, compared with 4.01 at the previous sale, and a 12-month average of 3.73. In another sign of robust investor interest, the tail, or gap between average and lowest-accepted prices, was 0.07, compared with 0.15 in September . The yield for the tenor fell as much as 6 basis points to 3.710% after the results. Ryutaro Kimura, senior bond strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management, said the “positive outcome” was “a reflection of recovering demand from domestic investors, driven by high interest-rate levels and easing fiscal concerns”. Life insurers have strengthened their net buying of super-long bonds again since June, underscoring the recovery in demand, he said. Earlier in October , the 20-year JGB yield climbed to levels last seen in the mid-1990s, while the 30-year yield hit a record high. The rise in yields reflects persistent concerns over Japan’s fiscal outlook , as investors are focused on how Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will fund her planned sales-tax cut on food and soft drinks without further straining the nation’s finances. Takaichi has sought to ease market concerns, saying her administration aims to build a strong economy and achieve fiscal sustainability, while pledging to appropriately manage JGB issuance in next fiscal year’s budget. Against that backdrop, investors have been watching to see if elevated yields will draw demand from domestic institutional buyers. Fukoku Mutual Life Insurance, the first life insurer to outline its plans for the fiscal second half, said it sees scope to move a bit more from foreign bonds into yen bonds as yields have risen more than expected. Mark Cranfield, Bloomberg’s markets live strategist, said: “That’s stunning demand for a 20-year JGB auction; indeed, it is the best on record for the duration and sets up a faster pace of yield curve flattening. “It is exceedingly rare to see any JGB auction with a bid-to-cover above 5.0, and it’s even more remarkable in 20-year, which has seen a decidedly mixed record over the past two years.” He added: “There is a very large unknown component in the buying, which suggests that foreigners have stepped up to participate. Showing confidence that the BOJ will deliver on a steady path of interest rate hikes.” A major test for Japanese bonds will come at the Bank of Japan’s policy meeting next week. While markets widely expect the central bank to keep rates unchanged, with overnight index swaps pricing in about a 6.2% chance of a hike, traders will look to Governor Kazuo Ueda’s post-decision press conference for signals on the pace and scope for further tightening. events.title: Arada enters Saudi Arabia with $3.8bn Riyadh project
events.summary: UAE developer Arada is launching a Dh14 billion ($3.8 billion) residential project in Riyadh and plans to build 100,000 homes in Saudi Arabia over the next three to five years as it expands in the kingdom, its chief executive has said. The company will also launch projects in Jeddah and Makkah as the Saudi market opens for foreign investment. “We have a good pipeline coming, and we will probably announce another project by the end of the year,” Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said. “As a group we plan to have 200,000 homes in the next three to five years, with half of that coming in Saudi Arabia.” Arada is jointly owned by Saudi businessman Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed’s KBW Investments and Sharjah-based Basma Group. Following the Saudi announcement, Arada’s pipeline is valued at Dh185 billion across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, the UK, Australia and Syria, comprising more than 70,000 homes. It has completed 17,000 homes so far. Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s largest economy, has overhauled its property sector, allowing foreigners to buy in designated zones in Riyadh and Jeddah, while introducing “special requirements” for home ownership in Makkah and Madinah from January. It also introduced land tax rules last year to help free up undeveloped land and spur building activity. Riyadh debut Arada’s debut project will be built in the Al Rimal district in Riyadh's north-eastern growth corridor on a plot covering 2.5 million square metres. Apart from 3,500 villas and town houses, it will also have a school, retail outlets and a community centre, as well as sporting facilities and green areas. The project is inspired by Arada's Masaar, a Dh8 billion woodland community development in Sharjah. Units will be sold for between 1,000 and 1,400 Saudi riyals ($267 and $373) per square foot, with construction starting in mid-2027 and completing in five years time, Mr Alkhoshaibi said. Arada KSA, set up in partnership with Saudi property investor Xtopia, will spearhead its expansion in the kingdom, with Mohammed AlDhabaan, chairman of Xtopia as the new chairman of Arada KSA. Arada KSA has access to a significant 10 million square metre land bank across Saudi Arabia with a collective value of Dh49 billion, spanning key strategic locations including Riyadh, Jeddah and Makkah, it said in a separate announcement. Meeting domestic demand Demand for housing in Saudi Arabia is strong as the government pushes to increase home ownership among Saudis. Demand from expatriates following the opening of the sector to foreign buyers is also supporting the market, he said. “The real demand is by the Saudis who need a home, and this is driven further by the government, [which is] pushing for higher home ownership for the Saudis.” “The government's initiative, which we're trying to support, is that they want to provide 300,000 homes delivered in the next three years.” Saudi Arabia has set a target of raising home ownership rates among locals to 70 per cent by 2030 under the Sakani programme – a joint initiative between the Ministry of Housing and the Real Estate Development Fund. By the end of last year, Saudi citizens owning homes exceeded 66 per cent, with one million beneficiaries of government housing support programmes, the Saudi Press Agency reported in January, citing Minister of Municipalities and Housing Majed Al Hogail. Saudi Arabia’s property market was mixed in the second quarter, with nationwide residential transaction values contracting by 26.9 per cent year-on-year to 37.67 billion riyals and the total deal count falling 14.2 per cent, according to the latest CBRE report. The National Residential Price Index, however, grew 2.6 per cent on an annual basis, supported by a 1.1 per cent rise in apartment prices during the quarter. The Al Rimal project will be funded through a Capital Market Authority-regulated investment structure managed by Al Rajhi Capital, an asset-management firm in the kingdom. “We have partnered with Al Rajhi, who will provide the fund management and will also provide the funding. So there is obviously certain equity we put in, but [the] majority is through the fund and the bank,” Mr Alkhoshaibi said. The company is also entering Syria with plans to build a $7 billion “UAE-style” mixed-use real estate project in Damascus in phases over 10 years. The company's property sales are ranging between Dh400 million and Dh700 million a month despite uncertainty over the Iran war, he added. “The external factors will have an impact, but it will be mitigated or reduced by delivering a great product in a great location at a reasonable price, and that's what we've been doing.”

events.title: Sea plans IPO for financial services arm Monee, memo says
events.summary: Sea Limited’s financial services arm Monee offers mobile wallets, payments processing, credit and banking services. Sea Limited plans to list its financial services arm Monee, founder Forrest Lee said in an internal memo reviewed by Reuters. Lee said going public would give Monee the “resources and the room to go further and faster than it can today”. It runs mobile wallets, payments, credit and banking in eight markets. Sea will also launch an AI-first enterprise platform called Sea Cloud. Lee said quarterly revenue has grown more than 80 times in nine years to US$7.8 billion (S$10 billion). SINGAPORE – Singapore-headquartered tech conglomerate Sea Limited is planning a public listing for its financial services arm Monee and will also launch an artificial intelligence enterprise platform business, according to an internal memo sent on Oct 20. Founder Forrest Li, in the memo to employees that was reviewed by Reuters, said he believed going public would give its financial payments and services business the “resources and the room to go further and faster than it can today”. The business operates in Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Taiwan and Brazil and offers mobile wallets, payments processing, credit and banking services. Sea did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The memo said the tech group would also launch an AI-first enterprise platform named Sea Cloud. In the memo, which was sent on the ninth anniversary of the group’s public listing in New York, Li said the quarterly revenue for the group had grown more than 80 times over that period to US$7.8 billion (S$10 billion). AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Publishers call for better verification of domain name registrants, and ICANN is on the job with a new policy ICANN testing tech to let law enforcement access non-public WHOIS info 11 hours ago ICANN vows to work faster, improve transparency 1 day ago No shame in the Domain Name game: DNS is doomed, literally 7 days ago ICANN reveals bids for new top-level domains 12 days ago AWS Route 53 DNS service reimagined...as a file system? August 28, 2026 A website registered by “David Beckham” was the world’s second-most-visited source of pirated Japanese manga in February 2025, leading publishers to call for better verification of who buys domain names to address the problem. The “Beckham” who registered the site was of course not the famous footballer and spokesmodel. However Tatsuo Ninoseki, an attorney with the Shin Hirakawa-Cho Law Office who represents the Japan Publishers manga Anti-Piracy Conference (JPMAC), put fake Becks in play today during a session on DNS abuse at ICANN’s annual meeting in Bali, Indonesia. Ninoseki said miscreants routinely create unauthorized English translations of manga and post them on websites that include ads. The lawyer said such sites can attract hundreds of millions of users and cost publishers $17 billion in revenue each year. JPMAC has decided its best course of action is not to pursue copyright abusers, but instead to go after commercial-scale pirates. That means it tries to act against pirate websites like those registered by “Beckham,” by sending them stern legal letters and using other legal means. But those pirates have trained to get around defenders. Ninoseki said pirate manga sites maintain a set of domain names – he said they’ve registered names in 158 top-level domains and frequently “domain hop” between them. The pirates’ pools of domains include some common naming elements, so even though Google has stopped indexing these pirate sites, users figure out that a theoretical piratemanga.XXX site will soon reappear at piratemanga.YYY. Pirate sites also redirect from domains they’re not using to host content to another that is full of pirated comics. Sometimes they use several sites at once and direct users across a fleet of live sites, so traffic flows to each site stay small and don’t cause suspicion. Ninoseki said 82.4 percent of domain hops happen within 15 days of the last move, suggesting pirates know how long enforcement actions or takedown requests will take and move to a different site before they run into trouble. “Many domain hops do not appear to be a reaction to legal countermeasures,” the attorney said. Ninoseki said JPMAC feels more comprehensive verification of domain name registrants would be a big help, especially checking physical addresses provided by registrants which he feels would weed out more pirates. The lawyer spoke during an ICANN session on DNS abuse, which the governance body defines as using domain names to facilitate malware, botnets, phishing, pharming, and spam. ICANN is currently working on a policy called PDP1 to address DNS abuse, one element of which would require registries to consider all domains held by their customers if just one is found to conduct DNS abuse. That policy would mean that once a registrant named “David Beckham” is connected to a single piracy site, all other domains registered by fake Becks would be checked in case they’re also committing DNS fouls.

events.title: Indonesia battles to stabilise market after MSCI expulsion threat
events.summary: Jakarta’s benchmark index rose 3% on Oct 20, after hitting a six-year low in the previous session. Indonesia’s stock market rebounded 5.3% after a US$82 billion sell-off, triggered by MSCI’s warning it could be downgraded to “standalone” status. The exchange will remove highly concentrated stocks from its benchmark index, and cut daily price limits, to reduce selling pressure and improve investor confidence. The rupiah stays weak and all eyes are on Bank Indonesia’s rate decision, as officials push reforms on transparency, liquidity and market rules. SINGAPORE/JAKARTA – Indonesian stocks rose on Oct 20 as the authorities in Jakarta introduced measures to restrict selling after a record two-day US$82 billion (S$104.9 billion) rout sparked by index provider MSCI’s warning of possible removal from its global indexes. Jakarta’s benchmark index advanced 5.3% on Oct 20, after hitting a six-year low in the previous session as the world’s worst-performing stock market this year dropped 14.8% over Oct 16 and Oct 19. T he index is down about 40% in 2026. The selloff was sparked by MSCI’s warning on Oct 16 that Indonesia could be reclassified as a “standalone” market from “emerging markets”, a harsher-than-expected downgrade that stunned investors and policymakers and raised fears of large-scale passive fund outflows. The index provider cited Indonesia’s failure to improve ownership transparency and curb coordinated trading, turning what had been a downgrade risk to “frontier” market status into a full-blown crisis of investor confidence. Relegation to “standalone” status would mark a major setback for South-east Asia’s biggest economy as investors grow increasingly uneasy about the country’s fiscal health and the autonomy of its central bank under President Prabowo Subianto. Foreign investors have already pulled nearly US$5 billion from Indonesian equities this year, with Goldman Sachs estimating a removal by MSCI could spur US$5.6 billion of passive outflows. After an online meeting with MSCI on Oct 19, the Indonesia Stock Exchange said it would exclude from its benchmark index any stocks with a high concentration of ownership by any person or entity. “We are doing what is best for our market,” IDX President Director Jeffrey Hendrik said, adding the exclusion would provide a more accurate picture of the index’s movements. He said the affected stocks account for roughly 18% of the total index weight. Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments, said excluding tightly held stocks should help address some investability concerns, but implementation would be key, given the potential for domestic pushback. “From here, we think the bigger incremental risk to flows is likely to come from active rather than passive funds,” he said. MSCI’s warning has weighed on the rupiah, which strengthened slightly to 17,980 per US dollar on Oct 20 but remained close to the record low of 18,190 hit in June ahead of a policy decision from Indonesia’s central bank . Bank Indonesia (BI) is expected to hold rates steady on Oct 21, although some economists have raised the prospect of a rate hike to defend the currency, which is down 7% in 2026. George Xu, a director in Fitch Ratings’ sovereigns team, said the latest concerns and substantial market selloff reinforced the risks the rating agency identified when it revised the outlook on Indonesia to negative in March. “From sovereign rating perspective, we do not anticipate the consultation announcement itself to have material immediate credit implications,” he said, but said external pressure could raise the government’s borrowing costs and erode external buffers. ‘Please pray,’ watchdog urges amid investor unease To stem the rout, the stock exchange this week halved the daily down limit on stock prices to 7% from 15%, while setting a 1 rupiah down limit on shares priced at 14 rupiah or less. Market watchers said the move to remove stocks with highly concentrated ownership from the benchmark index was a constructive step, but noted investors would still have some exposure to those firms through direct ownership and investment products such as mutual funds. “We must ensure that even if a stock is delisted from the Jakarta Composite Index, concentration risk does not continue to accumulate within products purchased by the public,” said Liza Camelia Suryanata, head of research at stockbroker Kiwoom Sekuritas Indonesia. Also on Oct 19, Prabowo held talks with finance chiefs, including the head of the Financial Services Authority (OJK), the finance minister and the BI governor. After the meeting, OJK chief Friderica Widyasari Dewi said the regulator would continue to advance Indonesia’s capital market reforms, particularly regarding transparency, liquidity, and law enforcement against various forms of violations. “The stock market has started to rebound today; the important thing is to keep building confidence,” said OJK’s Friderica in a separate event.

events.title: CPF maintains A grade in global ranking of pension systems for second year; overall score goes up
events.summary: The CPF was the first pension system in Asia to secure an A grade, with its overall score rising from 80.8 to 82 on the Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension Index. Singapore’s CPF kept its A grade in the Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension Index for a second year, and its overall score rose from 80.8 to 82. The report said ageing populations and longer lives are straining pension systems. Singapore’s CPF is “fully funded” by employer and employee contributions, unlike pay-as-you-go systems. Experts said retirement systems must stay flexible as people work longer. Singapore is moving towards a retirement age of 65 and a re-employment age of 70 by 2030. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s Central Provident Fund has retained its A rating for a second consecutive year in an annual global ranking of pension systems. The CPF was the first pension system in Asia to secure an A grade, with its overall score rising from 80.8 to 82 on the Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension Index. It was given a B+ grade in 2024. In 2026, Australia’s social security system also achieved an A rating, meaning the Asia-Pacific region now has two top-tier retirement systems. Other countries that earned the top rating for their pension systems are the Netherlands, which obtained the highest score of 85.8, as well as Denmark, Iceland and Israel. “First-class” retirement income systems that are robust, sustainable, deliver good benefits and have a high level of integrity get an A from Marsh. The professional services firm has collaborated with the CFA Institute, the global association of investment professionals, on the annual index since 2008 . Previously called the Mercer CFA Institute Global Pension Index, it was renamed in 2026 after Mercer adopted the Marsh brand in September as part of a corporate rebrand by its parent company, Marsh McLennan. In 2026, the index examined the impact of falling birth rates and rising life expectancies on 55 retirement income systems worldwide, up from 52 in the 2025 index. The study covered pension systems in 66% of the world’s population, including the US, Britain, China, India, South Korea and Japan. Reflecting the focus on the ageing population globally, the report adjusted the Adequacy sub-index to consider the levels of income available at retirement and at age 80. This recognises the fact that more people will live past 80 and into their 90s, needing financial support throughout their long retirement years. The Adequacy sub-index measures whether a pension system provides a sufficient level of income for retirees to maintain a decent standard of living. It is one of three sub-indexes that make up a pension system’s overall index score. Singapore’s Adequacy score jumped from 79.4 in 2025 to 82.8 in 2026, but its Sustainability sub-index score dipped from 75.5 to 75.3. The Sustainability sub-index assesses a pension system’s long-term viability and its ability to meet future pension obligations. Meanwhile, the Integrity sub-index rounds out the overall score by measuring the level of public trust and assessing whether the pension system earns the confidence of those who depend on it. On this front, Singapore held its 90.4 score. Rising life expectancies strain government budgets Mirroring the global trend of population ageing, Singapore became a super-aged society in June 2026, when 21.4% of its citizens were 65 or older. The United Nations classifies any nation with 21% of its population aged 65 and above as super-aged. Marsh highlighted in its report that ageing populations are placing increasing strain on government budgets. Public pensions, especially those that operate on a pay-as-you-go basis, will not be sustainable because they rely on taxes from the current working population to fund the retirement payouts of today’s retirees. As the population ages, there will be a smaller workforce to pay for the retirement benefits of a growing pool of retirees. Marsh noted that growing financial strain will prompt many countries to review the funding of their pension systems. Governments will either have to cut retirement benefits or encourage their population to save for their future payouts in advance. Marsh noted that Singapore’s CPF, unlike other pension systems, is “fully funded with contributions from both employers and employees”. These CPF contributions are invested primarily in special Singapore Government Securities, which allow the CPF Board to pay interest of at least 2.5% on Ordinary Account savings and at least 4% on Special Account and Retirement Account (RA) savings. Walter Theseira, associate professor of economics at the Singapore University of Social Sciences, added that because CPF payouts are based solely on one’s own retirement savings, they will not be affected by government tax constraints or public finance challenges. CPF Life, the national longevity insurance annuity scheme, pays out income from each member’s CPF personal retirement savings pot for as long as they live.

events.title: Brisbane council to embrace early morning culture with new dawn plan
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Brisbane City Council to develop economic plan to embrace locals' early-morning habits The Brisbane City Council will conduct a survey about residents' early morning habits. ( ABC News: Brian Hurst ) The Brisbane City Council has launched a survey of residents' early-morning behaviours to inform a new Dawn Economy Plan. The council says the plan will help improve park facilities and public transport options as Brisbane leans into its reputation as a city of early risers. The survey will be open until November 22. The Brisbane City Council hopes to take advantage of residents' tendency to wake up early with the development of a new Dawn Plan, set to highlight early-morning economic opportunities. To inform the plan, the council is encouraging locals to take part in a survey about their experiences in Brisbane between 4am and 7am. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said the responses would help improve park facilities, pathways and public transport options in the early hours. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner says Brisbane has a thriving dawn economy. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) "The reality is there's a thriving dawn economy at the moment," Cr Schrinner said. "People are voting with their feet. They want to get up early, they want to get out and about, and they want to get active." Analysis by University of Melbourne research fellow Dr Anna Edwards found Brisbane has one of the most active early-morning trading hours in Australia . About 13 per cent of Brisbane cafes are open between 5am and 6am. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston ) The research showed 13 per cent of Brisbane food and drink businesses are open between 5am and 6am, and by 8am, about half are serving customers. Dr Edwards said it was "wonderful" to see the Brisbane City Council "drawing on this strength and building on it". "We do a lot of planning of places by space, but we don't necessarily always think about timing. "Things have shifted quite considerably over the last five to 10 years, and I think we need to be thinking about this, but mornings generally have been quite overlooked." Blaine Swanborough co-owns a cafe in Mitchelton that opens at 6am. ( ABC News ) Blaine Swanborough co-owns a cafe in Mitchelton which opens at 6am, and said the community is often out and about by then. "We really see a drop off in trade later in the mornings as it heats up, especially in summer," Mr Swanborough said. "We really try and make the most of it in the early morning. "Our balance is with staff as well … but we try and find that line of providing what the community wants." The council says survey responses will help improve park facilities, pathways and public transport options. ( ABC News: Giulio Saggin, file photo ) Committee for Brisbane chief executive Jen Williams said the dawn economy plan was about playing to Brisbane's strengths. "For a long time, Brisbane has shied away from acknowledging that it is an early-rising city," Ms Williams said. "Whereas now, we can see with the global wellness movement and a focus on health, that people really do want to embrace the mornings. "The dawn economy doesn't come at the expense of the night-time economy. It is really about building a 24-hour city." Council opposition leader Jared Cassidy said the dawn survey was unnecessary. "It's shocking that our Lord Mayor, who has served in Council for over 20 years, has just realised Brisbane residents start their day early," Cr Cassidy said. "It's simple — we need investment in the infrastructure and services necessary to improve our uniquely Brisbane way of life. "Early morning public transport services and lighting in parks and bikeways to support active travel in the winter months would be a great start." The dawn economy survey will be open until midnight on November 22.

events.title: UAE tax rules: What businesses can claim for employee expenses
events.summary: Giving employees the tools they need to do their jobs effectively is a timeless business requirement. Whether a company has standard lists of equipment and resources for different grades and functions, which it should to make onboarding easier, most businesses could produce such lists without much difficulty. There are, however, tax considerations, particularly corporation tax and VAT . Thankfully, Federal Tax Authority Decision No 17 of 2026 has helpfully brought together answers to many of the questions businesses might have. There are five main sections, starting with transport provided for staff. It's critical that employees are not charged for the service and that transport is provided only between their homes and workplaces. Could there be a collection point for several employees, provided it is a reasonable distance from their homes? I would imagine so. Cash payments instead of transport cannot be offered, and there should be no identifiable non-business benefit. Could one employee who fails either test affect the entire arrangement? The decision says nothing about separating qualifying and non-qualifying cases. Best not be the person who tests the rules. What about pooling transport between two neighbouring companies? If the company providing the service changes according to a weekly schedule, would that complicate matters? A strict interpretation would require whichever company provides the service to invoice its commercial neighbour. I don't see how this can be avoided. Anything more complicated might best be outsourced for simplicity. Next is the provision of food and beverages. This is permissible where employees live so remotely that returning home is impractical. What constitutes remote is not defined, although I would interpret it as being unable to reach home within a reasonable time, given an individual's circumstances. This raises the possibility that only a small proportion of the workforce might qualify. No guidance has been provided on whether a minimum number of employees must meet the conditions. The provision must be linked to an employee's role and circumstances, including their workplace or residence. Suitable facilities should not be available at their accommodation or workplace, nor should local food outlets be reasonably accessible. Again, cash payments instead of food and beverages should not be an option. Moving on to company-provided accommodation, this must be an operational necessity. Perhaps the work site is in the Empty Quarter, 100 miles (160km) from the nearest town. Difficult access could make it reasonable to accommodate employees on or near the site. Accommodation and communication Accommodation should be suitable but not luxurious. No swimming pools, expansive manicured gardens, extensive household staff or additional reception rooms. The rules for onboarding new employees are a little more relaxed. Accommodation can be provided for up to 30 days, and the expense claimed, provided it is not ostentatious. Notably, the decision does not exclude employees who have already been living in the country, regardless of how long they have been here. I recall benefiting from such an arrangement when starting a role in the late 2000s. I believe there were two reasons for it. First, treating new starters differently would have been inconvenient. Second, with international personnel flying in and out of the region, putting everyone in the same hotel helped employees become familiar with the business and encouraged social interaction. Mobile phones are another area where guidance already existed, and the new decision restates and expands on it. Devices must be required for work and used only for business purposes. Each invoice should be reviewed, with personal calls identified and excluded from VAT or corporation tax claims. A company may decide to absorb the non-deductible cost rather than introduce an internal system for recovering personal expenses. Sometimes the administrative cost can outweigh the value of recovering small amounts spent on company assets. The new requirement is for a formal standard operating policy. This must be communicated to everyone affected, reviewed periodically, updated when necessary and demonstrably enforced. For businesses without standard operating procedures, this would be a good place to start. If I could, as an accountant, give human resources departments one task, it would be to map every business process and identify the roles and individuals responsible for each. This would strengthen both control and continuity. I can think of few projects more valuable when reassessing internal efficiency, particularly in an AI-driven world where automation is the mot du jour . Lastly comes parking, which is subject to the same requirements as mobile phones.

( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) The mother of Complainant A in the Alan Jones trial has told a court her son's "mood was different" when he returned home from a trip to the veteran broadcaster's private farm. Complainant A says when he was a 17-year-old schoolboy he was indecently assaulted by Mr Jones at the farm. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching related to five male complainants. A mother has told a trial she trusted Alan Jones as a mentor to her son before the broadcaster allegedly indecently assaulted the 17-year-old schoolboy at his private farm. One of Mr Jones's five alleged victims, known as Complainant A, alleges the radio host kissed him, put his tongue in his mouth and touched his buttocks when he visited Mr Jones's property in the Southern Highlands as a 17-year-old schoolboy. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexually touching, relating to several alleged incidents against five males between 2003 and 2020. The court previously heard the complainant was 13 years old when he sent a letter to the then-2GB radio host, requesting help for his single mother and their serious financial struggles. Emails read to the court show Mr Jones developed a relationship with the boy over several years, and that the prominent media figure helped wipe $600,000 off the mother's home loan and provided $100,000 to assist with the completion of their home. Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching related to five male complainants. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Giving evidence at the trial on Tuesday, the boy's mother told the court her son met up with Mr Jones on several occasions including for private breakfasts at his Circular Quay apartment and lunch at a pub, but that she was never invited. She recalled when her son was 17 and had been invited by Mr Jones to spend two nights at his Fitzroy Falls farm and that she felt "really comfortable" with him going because she "trusted" the radio host. "[Someone] who saw that my son was intelligent as he is." Mother breaks down reading son's note NSW Sexual Violence Helpline on 1800 424 017 NSW Victims Services on 1800 633 063 Bravehearts (support for child sexual abuse survivors) on 1800 272 831 Child Protection Helpline on 132 111 MARS Australia (for men affected by rape and sexual abuse) on (07) 3857 1222 National Survivors Foundation on 1300 124 433 Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. The woman told the court that when her son returned home from the trip, "his mood was different" and she "knew straight away something was up". "He wasn't sleeping, he was just staying up," she said. She said her son wrote her a letter 10 days later, saying "something happened at Fitzroy Falls" and that "someone did something they shouldn't have" but did not go into explicit detail. The mother broke down several times in the witness box, including when her son's letter was placed in front of her during her testimony. The woman said after receiving the note she asked her son if he wanted to report what happened to police. "He [my son] said to me that 'I wasn't raped'," she said. Mother tells court of her 'dire' financial situation The mother told the court that, before the alleged assault that she was in a "dire" situation, with a $1.3 million mortgage hanging over her head and the builder of her unfinished home walking off the job. The trial heard the woman's partner had also left the country and would often miss child support payments. The woman said a family friend suggested she reach out to the broadcaster for help because "he's influential and there might be people he knows who can help you". The mother said she provided information to her son to send to Mr Jones, who replied with an email saying, "you sound a special sort of young man," and asking for additional information. "When he [my son] told me that, I was incredibly grateful that someone of his stature was interested in what we were doing because we got such a prompt reply," the mother said. "I was desperate, people who are being served repossession papers are not cruising along in life." Court told Mr Jones put mother in contact with head of major bank The woman told the court that Mr Jones organised for the head of the Commonwealth Bank at the time to call her to understand more about her circumstances and try to find a "manageable" situation for the family.

events.title: Hong Kong’s rail company MTR bets $6.3 billion on a city that doesn’t exist yet
events.summary: For much of MTR’s history, the government has used the “rail-plus-property” model to subsidise construction. MTR is spending at least HK$38.9 billion on the Northern Metropolis rail link, a project built before the city around it exists. The company is borrowing upfront and waiting years for land value returns. The Northern Metropolis plan aims for 500,000 new homes, 2.5 million people, and a tech hub by 2030 and 2034. It marks a shift towards Hong Kong’s border area and away from Victoria Harbour growth. The project brings big risks for MTR, including high interest rates, property market weakness, and past cost overruns. Ratings stay strong, but success depends on on-time delivery and government backing. HONG KONG – Hong Kong’s MTR has built the city’s railways in one of two ways: The government handed over land around new stations, or paid directly. Either way, the money arrived with the track. The Northern Metropolis is different. MTR is putting up at least HK$38.9 billion (S$6.3 billion), borrowing to do it, and will wait years to find out whether the land it receives in return – under a funding model that has never been tested at this scale – is worth what the lines cost. “In the past, for some projects, we developed the area and then we built the railway,” said Dominic Law, head of project delivery for phase one of MTR’s Northern Link. “But moving into the Northern Metropolis, we are focusing on the infrastructure first.” At 300 sq km, the Northern Metropolis covers more than a quarter of Hong Kong’s total land area and is 2½ times the size of San Francisco. Under the government’s plan, half a million new homes will be constructed, helping increase the area’s population to 2.5 million from 980,000 over a roughly 20-year period. The economic centrepiece of the project is a tech hub designed to be Hong Kong’s Silicon Valley. To facilitate this, MTR will build 17km of underground rail track and seven new stations for the Northern Link and spur line. Some works have already started. The project is scheduled for completion in 2034 and will be financed upfront by the company. To help pay for the construction, the company has raised more than HK$130 billion in bonds and loans since early 2025, much of it earmarked for capital works including the Northern Metropolis, according to Bloomberg data. In turn, the government has granted MTR development rights for 10 plots of land along the upcoming lines. The government, which owns virtually all the land in Hong Kong, typically sells plots at a large premium to factor in development potential. In the case of the Northern Link, the government has deducted HK$39.05 billion from the premium MTR owes – roughly equal to the company’s targeted outlay. MTR was established in 1975 with the British colonial government as sole shareholder to build the city’s metro system after the population swelled by almost four million in three decades. In 2000, the government divested a 23% stake to investors when the company was listed on Hong Kong’s stock exchange. For much of MTR’s history, the government has used the “rail-plus-property” model to subsidise construction. That model – selling homes around its stations – has made MTR one of the most profitable railway businesses by net margin. In recent decades, however, three major projects – the West Island line, the high-speed rail link to mainland China and the Shatin to Central line – were directly funded by the government as part of a massive wave of spending on infrastructure. The Northern Metropolis was formally unveiled in 2021 by the city’s then leader Carrie Lam to help it better integrate with mainland China, solve a housing shortage, develop advanced tech industries and create jobs. The project signals a notable shift away from the intense development around Victoria Harbour towards the historically underdeveloped, mostly rural land adjacent to the mainland border – as well as reducing Hong Kong’s reliance on the finance and real estate industries for growth. The city’s new five-year plan announced in September sets a binding target of having 900ha of land in the Northern Metropolis ready for construction by 2030, underscoring the strategic importance of the development. All this shows the pressure on MTR to complete the railways on schedule and on budget, at a time when the outlook for the property market is unclear. Existing home prices are down 16% from their 2021 high, and a currency peg with the dollar means the city’s interest rates move in sync with those in the US. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s base rate is 4.25%, more than double the 1.8% average since 2008. “To fully unleash the potential of this development, we really need the Northern Link to be in operation at the right time,” said MTR’s Law. “It is a very complex project covering a big area and affecting a lot of different stakeholders.” The company’s recent record shows the challenges.

events.title: Shares stumble, oil rises as markets await AI sector results
events.summary: Brent rose to US$109.64 per barrel. Asian shares fell as investors waited for results from Meta, Tesla and chipmakers. AI earnings are seen as a key test of market strength and spending plans. Oil prices rose as Trump’s Russia energy order and French riots lifted safe-haven demand. Brent and WTI both gained, while gold fell. French unrest, weak Asian markets and cautious central bank signals weighed on sentiment. Traders also watched speeches from the ECB and Bank of England, plus crypto losses. TOKYO – Asian stocks retreated broadly on Oct 20 while oil rose as geopolitical risks rattled sentiment ahead of key results from artificial intelligence bellwether companies. The euro recouped some losses from the previous session that were spurred by escalating riots in France. Crude prices resumed their climb as markets weighed an executive order from US President Donald Trump that waived some sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy. The spotlight now turns to corporate earnings, with investors seeking fresh evidence that consumers and the broader economy remain resilient. Quarterly earnings are due from SpaceX and Netflix on Oct 20, with results from AI heavyweights such as Meta and Tesla scheduled for later in the week. “The market is happy to cover shorts and unwind defensive trades, but that’s very different from having the conviction to rebuild aggressive exposure to AI,” Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone, said in a note. “French sovereign risk is clearly being priced into European equities, but the euro’s resilience suggests traders aren’t yet treating it as a systemic European problem.” The MSCI Asia ex-Japan index fell 1.14 %, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 0.98 %. South Korea’s KOSPI tumbled 3.92 %. In early European trade, the pan-region Euro Stoxx 50 futures slipped 0.57%, German DAX futures dipped 0.33% and FTSE futures lost 0.47%. US stock futures, the S&P 500 e-minis, rose 0.12% to 7,743.5. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, fell 0.16% to 101.80, with the euro up 0.17% at US$1.1229. The Japanese yen strengthened 0.16% to 158.24 per dollar, and sterling rose 0.21% to US$1.3327. Overnight, the French authorities set curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, Lille and Nice, after a weekend of riots and looting stemming from nationwide anti-government protests. And in the Middle East, dozens were killed and more than 200 were injured after an attack by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security forces training camp in Yemen’s Shabwa province. Netflix is expected to report slowing revenue growth in the third quarter, while SpaceX is forecast to report US$12.74 billion (S$16.3 billion) i n quarterly revenue. General Motors, Hasbro, Halliburton, and 3M are among the more established names due to report on Oct 20. Along with quarterly results, markets are increasingly focused on the massive spending plans of the major AI players. Facebook operator Meta is one of five AI hyperscalers expected to increase combined capital expenditure to about US$1.2 trillion (S$1.5 trillion) in 2027, according to Goldman Sachs. “Investors are fine with AI being used more. What they’re questioning is whether every dollar of AI capex earns more than it costs to finance,” said Ninghui Liu, head of investment strategy and research for APAC at State Street Investment Management. “AI has gone from an earnings story to a balance-sheet story, and now a unit-economics story to some extent.” US crude rose 0.18% to US$103.85 a barrel and Brent rose to US$109.64 per barrel, up 0.08% on the day. Spot gold rose 0.13% to US$4,145.25 an ounce. An executive order issued by Trump on the night of Oct 16 waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs, including duties on the country’s goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas. However, Trump said on Oct 17 that he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter. Inflationary pressures from elevated oil prices have put most major central banks on a tightening bias, though with a careful eye on whether economies are resilient enough to absorb higher interest rates. Recent comments from Federal Reserve officials, including Chair Kevin Warsh, suggest policymakers are in no rush to hike rates again. The US Census Bureau is due to release September figures, with housing starts expected to rise to 1.305 million from 1.275 million in August, while building permits are seen at 1.395 million compared with 1.403 million. European Central Bank (ECB) policymaker Martin Kocher is due to speak later on Oct 20, as well as ECB policymaker and Finnish central bank governor Olli Rehn. Bank of England Monetary Policy Committee member Megan Greene will deliver a speech at the London School of Economics. Euro Stoxx 50 futures fell 0.71%, DAX futures slipped 0.40% and FTSE futures dropped 0.44%. S&P e-minis were flat at 7,734.25. In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin gained 0.22% to US$82,117.01, and ether rose 0.63% to US$2,413.64. REUTERS

events.title: ICANN testing tech to let law enforcement access non-public WHOIS info
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Single sign-on to help address imminent threats to life, critical infrastructure, or kids 'Password1' and a forgotten test account land Welsh outfits in hot water 25 minutes ago Bullhorn sees red after cyberattack knocks recruitment platform offline 1 hour ago Whitehall shuts the front door on digital ID but leaves the back open 3 hours ago UK finance watchdog wants firms to report AI failures and close calls 4 hours ago Why cyber resilience is now a boardroom priority for UK public services 6 hours ago ICANN has started testing authentication schemes that will allow law enforcement agencies to make urgent requests for non-public WHOIS information – when needed to address threats to life, critical infrastructure, or child exploitation. Domain registrars collect information about their customers and in the past that data was publicly available in WHOIS records. Some domain registrars offer services that substitute their own contact details, to preserve customer privacy. In recent years, laws like GDPR mean registrars are sometimes required to hide WHOIS data. That’s fair enough but makes it hard for law enforcement to contact a domain holder if their resources are being misused – intentionally or otherwise – for purposes such as hosting malware, acting as command-and-control infrastructure for malware, or facilitating phishing. ICANN’s definition for the kind of behaviour it thinks justifies urgent requests for WHOIS info is “imminent threat to life, of serious bodily injury, to critical infrastructure, or of child exploitation.” The org has convened an Input Group on Law Enforcement Agency Authentication Mechanisms to consider the issue, and that group yesterday explained its progress during ICANN’s annual meeting in Bali, Indonesia. At this point, readers may have concerns that this proposal could allow law enforcement authorities to make inappropriate requests for WHOIS information. Several factors may ease such concerns. One is that representatives of domain registrars Namecheap and Verisign spoke during the session about the proposal, and both were supportive. Another is that the Input Group’s work is largely technical. Once it devises a mechanism to allow requests, other groups within ICANN dedicated to policy will work out acceptable use and related issues. This is the way internet governance gets done! Specialists work on their own bits of a problem and then collaborate to create a robust system that works at a technical level, is practical, and enforceable in multiple jurisdictions. At this point, ICANN’s preferred approach is to use Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) so that authenticated users at law enforcement agencies can log into the governance org’s Registration Data Request Service (RDRS) and file requests to access non-public WHOIS info. ICANN is already testing this approach with the FBI and Interpol but is open to other authentication mechanisms to allow other agencies access RDRS. The Input Group’s aim is to publish a spec those agencies can conform to. ICANN will pass requests filed in RDRS to whichever registrar sold the domain. The registrar will have 24 hours to consider the request – or up to 72 hours for complex queries. Registrars will also be able to deny requests if they feel the query does not meet the urgency threshold. Register readers might worry that a colossal agency like the FBI could flood RDRS with requests from thousands of individual agents, swamping domain registries. ICANN’s plan is to avoid that by requiring law enforcement agencies to nominate certain personnel who are permitted to make requests, and to enforce that permission using a token shared during SAML handshakes. The content of that token is the kind of policy question that the Input Group expects others at ICANN to finalize later.

events.title: Walmart’s Flipkart is quietly building a food delivery challenger in India
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Flipkart, the Walmart-owned Indian e-commerce giant, is preparing to challenge India’s food-delivery duopoly of Zomato and Swiggy. It is entering a fiercely competitive market that has defeated even previous attempts by Amazon and Google to break in. The Bengaluru-based company is testing its food-delivery service internally and has expanded the trial from a few hundred employees to upwards of 8,000, according to two people familiar with the matter. It has also deployed a dedicated fleet of riders through its logistics arm, Ekart, separate from the riders who handle its quick-commerce deliveries, as it prepares for a public launch. The employee-only service appears as a separate tab on Flipkart’s main shopping app, alongside its Minutes quick-commerce offering and travel bookings, TechCrunch has learned. It draws on restaurants listed through ONDC, a government-backed network that connects online buyers and sellers across different platforms , as well as restaurants that Flipkart signed up directly. Riders wearing jerseys bearing the “Eat-in by Minutes” branding have also begun fulfilling orders on the streets of Bengaluru, the southern Indian city where Flipkart is headquartered. As Flipkart expands its food-delivery operations, it is entering a market that the brokerage firm Bernstein estimates is growing 18% to 20% a year. Online delivery, though, still accounts for just over 15% of India’s broader food-services industry. Zomato, owned by Eternal, and Swiggy together serve an estimated 85 million to 95 million paying customers a year, per Bernstein. That figure shows how dominant the two are, and how much room newcomers have to grow online food ordering in the world’s most populous country, which has more than a billion internet subscriptions. Flipkart is not the only company trying to shake up India’s food-delivery market. Ride-hailing company Rapido, which has already given Uber and its Indian rival Ola a tough fight, has been expanding Ownly, its food-delivery service that charges restaurants zero commission. Meanwhile, Swiggy has launched Toing , a separate app aimed at customers looking for cheaper meals. Both moves reflect growing pressure on the industry’s existing pricing model and the commissions that restaurants pay. “Monopoly is bad, but duopoly is more pathetic,” said Sagar Daryani, president of the New Delhi-headquartered National Restaurant Association of India, which represents over 500,000 restaurants nationwide. “What one does, the other follows suit.” Daryani argued that restaurants have long needed alternatives to the two dominant platforms. Flipkart is not the first deep-pocketed company to try breaking into India’s food-delivery market. In 2020, Amazon launched a food-ordering service in Bengaluru , but it shut the service down two years later . Google’s Areo app, which offered food ordering alongside other services, also failed to gain traction. Uber also left the market in 2020, selling its Uber Eats business in India to Zomato. Daryani sees one important difference between Flipkart and the companies that tried food delivery before it. Zomato and Swiggy built their businesses around delivering meals before expanding into quick commerce. Flipkart is doing the reverse, using its established e-commerce business and growing quick-commerce operations as a springboard into food delivery. “Flipkart’s quick commerce benefit will get passed on to food delivery, so it will be leaner, more efficient,” Daryani told TechCrunch. Restaurants are also hoping that new entrants will bring down the cost of selling meals online. Daryani, also co-founder and CEO of the dumpling chain Wow! Momo Foods, said Flipkart has proposed a base commission of about 10%, compared with the 20% to 25% that restaurants typically pay Zomato and Swiggy. Commissions are only part of the expense, though. Once advertising, discounts, and other promotional costs are factored in, restaurants can end up spending 40% to 50% of an order’s value on the established platforms, Daryani told TechCrunch. He expects Flipkart to keep that total cost closer to 15% to 16%, which could mean restaurants keep more money from each order. Nonetheless, getting restaurants on board is one thing and winning over customers is another. Bernstein estimates that new entrants could save customers just ₹20 to ₹30 (around 20–30 cents) per order by operating more efficiently, which may not be enough to draw customers away from Zomato and Swiggy. The two incumbents could also offer deeper discounts to keep them. Flipkart is not planning to stay in Bengaluru for long. MONTREAL – Honeywell Aerospace said on Oct 19 it expects 9,950 new business jet deliveries worldwide between 2026 and 2035, raising its forecast by 4.4% from 2025 as higher aircraft utilisation and fleet growth support demand. The forecast includes about 4,200 turboprop deliveries through 2035, bringing total aircraft deliveries to roughly 14,000, while the global business aviation fleet is expected to grow about 29% over the next decade. Growing demand for charter and fractional ownership is driving higher aircraft utilisation, helping support business jet demand despite economic uncertainty and geopolitical volatility . Honeywell Aerospace expects global business aviation flight hours to increase about 34% through 2035, outpacing fleet growth as operators make greater use of shared-use models. “Business aircraft owners and operators are consistently flying more, ordering new business jets, expanding fleets and investing in innovations that are driving growth across the sector,” said Linnea Whisler, president of Commercial Original Equipment at Honeywell Aerospace. The company said North America remained the largest business aviation market, while demand was growing in Latin America and parts of Asia-Pacific, including India. However, it noted that conflict in the Middle East has disrupted flight operations and paused development activity in the region. REUTERS

events.title: S’pore-listed First Resources pledges cooperation with authorities over haze
events.summary: The Singapore Exchange-listed company said it welcomed a thorough, evidence-based examination of the ongoing fires and haze situation. SINGAPORE – Palm oil producer First Resources has pledged to cooperate fully with any inquiries or investigations by the authorities, following statements that Singapore intends to pursue all available legal and regulatory measures against companies linked to the current haze. In an Oct 20 press statement, the Singapore Exchange (SGX)-listed company said it welcomed a thorough, evidence-based examination of the ongoing fires and haze situation, and reiterated that it strictly enforces a longstanding zero-burning policy across its operations. It added that it is confident that an objective review of the available evidence would show that it does not clear land using fire, either directly or indirectly. In its statement, First Resources said assessments of where fires originated should be based on verified facts, scientific evidence and a comprehensive understanding of conditions on the ground. The group, which has a market value of $6 billion in Singapore, welcomed documentary and technical reviews, as well as on-the-ground verification where necessary, to provide an accurate picture of the situation. Evidence may include the chronology of hot-spot detections and fire progression based on satellite imagery, documentary evidence of the actions taken to suppress and extinguish fires, and spatial analyses demonstrating the continued protection of conservation areas, it said. First Resources also said it was open to constructive suggestions from regulators, customers, investors, civil society organisations and other industry stakeholders on strengthening fire prevention and management. “Addressing the complex challenge of transboundary haze requires sustained collaboration among governments, companies, local communities and other stakeholders,” it said. First Resources ’ statement comes after the company said on Oct 16 that fires from outside its boundaries had spread into areas under its management, and had not originated from its concessions. It said some fires had become too large and fast-moving to contain despite its firefighting efforts. Other SGX-listed companies, including Golden Agri Resources, Bumitama Agri, Wilmar International, Kencana Agri, Indofood Agri, have also issued similar statements after receiving queries from SGX RegCo over their operations and potential ties to the haze. TSH Resources has yet to respond. Senior Minister K. Shanmugam told reporters on Oct 19 that statements from the companies – no matter how well drafted, are not good enough. Shanmugam, who is also Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs, added that the Government will “ask for the full facts, consider all evidence fairly and act based on the facts”. Kang Wan Chern is deputy business editor at The Straits Times.

events.title: Mamdani says feds have abdicated on AI, urges New Yorkers to push back
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Two of New York’s sweethearts, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and activist and “Broad City” star Ilana Glazer, spoke about AI at Webster Hall in Manhattan on Monday night, with Glazer posing questions to the mayor about the future of AI in society. Mamdani encouraged New Yorkers to resist the overwhelming feeling that AI is inevitably coming for their jobs, their kids’ minds, and their dignity, and to take back control instead. His message came at a moment when the federal government is doing little to regulate AI, leaving cities to act on their own. At The People’s AI Assembly, an event hosted by the AI Now Institute , a think tank that explores the social implications of AI, Mamdani argued that the technology’s rapid rollout is not inevitable and that public officials should hold AI companies accountable. Last month, Mamdani ordered a ban on AI use in elementary and middle schools. Glazer, a parent, said the technology’s arrival in classrooms unsettles her. “It just makes me nervous. It feels so non-consensual, as though…this has to be in schools. It wasn’t two years ago. Why does it have to be in schools?” she said. Over the summer, the mayor also introduced a policy that would require landlords, brokers, and real estate platforms to clearly disclose when a property’s listing photos or videos are made with AI. The policy is aimed at protecting New Yorkers from getting “house-phished,” or tricked by misleading listings. Both moves challenge the assumption that schools and the public must simply accept AI as it arrives. “Nothing has to be,” Mamdani said at the event Monday. “There’s a creep that comes with this, and there’s an intent to overwhelm that leaves people feeling as if there is simply no option.” He said there has been a “reckless adoption of technology without any kind of a reckoning with the limitations of that technology,” citing the U.S. military’s February strike on a school in Iran that killed more than 150 people, including at least 123 children . Officials involved in the Pentagon’s internal investigation have told Bloomberg that overreliance on AI in targeting was one factor in the attack. “There is this desire to speak about [AI] as if it is infallible, as if it cannot be questioned, as if the only people who can regulate it are the ones who are currently developing it,” Mamdani said, noting that Facebook made similar arguments back in 2008. “What it really is,’ he continued, “is an attempt to escape any kind of accountability at any level, without also jeopardizing the potential valuation from an IPO.” Anthropic is expected to debut on the public markets this year, and OpenAI has said it will go public in 2027. Mamdani criticized the “complete abdication of federal law” when it comes to AI. “At a national level, when the conversation is about artificial intelligence, it’s so often framed in this language of an arms race with China, and any of the humanistic concern, we just push to the side in a language of national competition,” the mayor said. President Donald Trump’s Superintelligence Task Force , announced earlier this month, largely focuses on allowing powerful AI companies to self-regulate, rather than creating new federal restrictions. That comes despite growing fears about AI’s effect on every facet of human life, including warnings from whistleblowers at Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI that AI could lead to human extinction. “As we are looking at what comes after this federal administration, there has to be a very different kind of framework in how we think about AI, talk about AI, the accountability we’re willing to bring forward when it comes to that,” Mamdani said. events.title: DeepSeek deep-sixed at all US federal civilian agencies
events.summary: The US Department of Homeland Security on Monday issued an order directing federal civilian agencies not to use technology products from Chinese AI lab DeepSeek, and to remove any existing implementations. The order [PDF] is broad, as it requires agencies to ditch "all DeepSeek and DeepSeek-affiliate products, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations." Complying will be tricky as it is not clear which third-party products and services have been developed using DeepSeek's wares. Nor is it clear whether "developed using" means providing ongoing access to DeepSeek models via API or simply refers to any app vibe-coded with the help of DeepSeek. It also leaves open the question of AI gateways. Services such as OpenRouter and Vercel AI Gateway make DeepSeek's models available through APIs. And those using gateway services may find themselves using DeepSeek models without meaning to do so. OpenRouter, for example , "routes requests to the best available providers for your model." It selects what the service deems to be the best fit provider of AI services. Vercel AI Gateway does the same by default . So federal civilian agencies could be using DeepSeek models inadvertently, if they haven't taken steps to constrain their AI providers. A DHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. US officials have contemplated a ban on DeepSeek since the China-based AI lab released DeepSeek-R1 in early 2025. On February 6, 2025, US Representative Darin LaHood (R-IL) and US Representative Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) introduced the No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act. The lawmakers characterised DeepSeek as a national security threat because its AI models purportedly capture data on US citizens and provide it to the Chinese government. The bill never made it out of committee, but various government agencies followed through. The US Defense community and lawmakers have already exiled DeepSeek. The Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) started blocking DeepSeek on the Pentagon’s IT networks in January 2025. The US Navy , NASA , and the US House of Representatives took similar steps. So did various US states. While the DHS announcement has taken a long time to reach civilian agencies, its timing may be a boon for American AI companies which, like Anthropic, hope to soon go public. That's because open weight models represent competition, and those from China have proven particularly popular both in terms of capabilities and cost. Government agencies that cannot deploy such models (and the taxpayers who fund those agencies) may be stuck paying the prices set by favored US model makers. Concerns about the security and privacy of DeepSeek's iOS mobile app surfaced shortly after DeepSeek-R1 debuted . Several months later, a December 2025 report on the DeekSeek mobile app for Android and iOS cited similar concerns, including plaintext information leaks, links to servers run by Chinese tech firms, and shortcomings like lack of SSL pinning. These issues, however, are mainly mobile security problems that afflict many apps, particularly those that integrate third-party advertising SDKs from companies based outside the US. They don't really address the additional risks posed by the capture of text prompts and responses, or how local secrets and other sensitive information can be ingested by AI agents. Katie Moussouris, founder and CEO of Luta Security , told The Register in an email that while there are legitimate national security reasons to keep DeepSeek's app and servers away from government systems, the way this particular order is written exceeds that requirement in ways that aren't practical. "Banning DeepSeek's own app and API is workable," said Moussouris. "The problem is the ban on 'third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations.' The order doesn't say what 'developed using' means. It could technically cover any model derived from DeepSeek and more importantly, any software whose developers used DeepSeek to write or test code. An AI software bill of materials doesn't record which tools developers used, so it would be no real help. Every vendor would have to attest that nothing it relies on ever touched DeepSeek. There's no practical way to verify that." Moussouris also took issue with the breadth of the order, noting that applying the rules to US-hosted versions of DeepSeek's models goes too far. "The risks the order cites are mostly about data flowing to DeepSeek's servers in China, its data collection, and its app," she said. "US hosting avoids most of those. "For the model itself, the order says only that it may contain malware or vulnerabilities, which is true of all software. NIST found DeepSeek more vulnerable to prompt injection than US models , though every model has that problem. NIST also found it easier to jailbreak , but jailbreak guardrails often get in the way of defenders." ®

events.title: Embedded AI evaluators won’t be an easy solution, Hugging Face’s policy chief says
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking — the supposedly neutral and accurate system of evaluations that are designed to measure whether one AI product is better than another. However, the methods behind these evaluations are complicated and still maturing, said Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s chief policy officer, during a discussion at TechCrunch Disrupt last week. Testing needs to come together into a more consistent science if the industry is to rely on them in the future. With that in mind, can we trust the current tests that are being released? “Trust is such a weighted term,” said Solaiman. “In terms of whether we can trust results, one big part [of that] is can you reproduce the results of an evaluation? Do you have the level of access that you need to the model itself — this is where open weights come in in a big way,” she added. Reproducibility in model evaluations has long remained one of the stickier aspects of benchmarking — and remains a topic of significant debate in the industry. Outside of an individual test’s validity, there’s also the added question of how that test compares to other evaluations. “They are an evolving science — where we don’t know how to meaningfully compare them to each other,” Solaiman said. “They start to get ineffective relatively quickly, and we don’t have as much of a thriving ecosystem as we need,” she added. “There’s this hunger for an embedded evaluator ecosystem now, but the qualifications that determine who is an effective evaluator across what tasks need a lot more standardization.” The idea of embedded evaluators — in which supposedly “neutral” third-party observers are placed inside AI organizations — has been popularized over the last several months, as AI labs grapple with a rash of safety incidents that have spurred concerns over the potential harms of their technology. Hugging Face was famously the target of one of those incidents. Instead of active government regulation to identify and mitigate model safety concerns, labs have pushed for the third-party solution. However, doubts remain over how neutral or effective those evaluators will actually be. Anthropic’s decision to hire Accenture as its first evaluator spurred a good amount of backlash, with some critics mocking the idea that the consulting firm was qualified to do the task at hand. Evaluations are now moving from merely a test of the model itself to a test of the entire system around the model — including the harness and agent. The harness — or the tool the user is using to access the model — specifically, has a lot to do with a model’s performance, and a weaker model with a better harness could easily outperform a frontier model, Solaiman shared. “Agentic evals are really hard and really expensive,” said Solaiman. “We have just more evaluations for models. … We don’t have as many evaluations for harnesses, and we are developing better evaluations for the holistic agent — because that’s what a lot of folks are getting value out of,” she added. In other words, the evaluation space is a bit of a free-for-all at the moment, and if benchmarking is going to continue to be seen as a useful tool for industry leaders, a more uniform, industry-wide approach — where everyone is on the same page — may be necessary.
