events.title: He Tried to Set Limits on His State’s School Vouchers. Billionaires Helped Bankroll a Campaign to Unseat Him.
events.summary: PACs targeted former West Virginia Delegate Vernon Criss following his proposal to rein in state spending on school vouchers.  Will Price/West Virginia Legislature On a cold February morning at West Virginia’s Capitol, children in winter jackets, holding signs and their homework, clogged the hallways outside the House Finance Committee room. Delegate Vernon Criss, the committee’s chairperson, popped outside his office, then promptly walked back in.  Five days earlier, the Republican lawmaker had proposed to limit payouts from a voucher program that diverts public tax dollars to private education. Since then, families had shown up each morning, and with them lobbyists and organizers posting inflammatory assertions that the proposal would kill the program. Criss didn’t want that. Five years earlier, he voted to create the Hope Scholarship program, the nation’s first educational savings account program to have no income requirements. Since then, 11 other states have passed similar legislation.  In the first year of the Hope program in West Virginia, it cost the state $9 million. Now, as 2026 was beginning, it was set to expand, with estimates that it could cost $200 million or more a year. And Criss was concerned that unchecked growth of the program, coupled with a spree of tax cuts, could put the state budget into a tailspin. The state and its lawmakers needed “to face the music,” as Criss would later say. On that February day in Charleston, a staffer unlocked the committee door. Parents and media filed in, taking seats along the narrow benches lining the committee room’s walls. Kids lay on the floor. A delegate asked if the Hope Scholarship bill would be discussed. When Criss said no, the parents and their kids stood up and filed out.  Within the next few days, lawmakers would stop the effort to curtail spending on vouchers. And Criss would soon be fighting for his political life. Criss greets constituents supporting the Hope Scholarship. Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislature The money and organizing behind the demise of the bill, as well as the targeting of Criss, can be traced to “school choice” advocates at the local and national levels and their ability to spend huge sums to have their way. When Republicans assumed control of the West Virginia Legislature in 2015, school choice — their preferred terminology for voucher-style programs — became a rallying point for an array of political nonprofits. Through lobbying and supporting sympathetic lawmakers, they helped establish the Hope Scholarship six years later.  The first year, a little more than 2,300 students enrolled in the program , which was designed to permit more students over time. Today, 26,000 students are taking part , more than the enrollment in the state’s largest public school district. West Virginia has been part of a nationwide push, partially funded by billionaire-backed political groups , to use taxpayer dollars to fund private schools. Among the proponents of these programs are the influential Koch family network and Pennsylvania billionaire Jeffrey Yass, who has spent more than $350 million since 2015 on political campaigns, including a push for public funding for private education. In West Virginia, Arkansas and Texas , proponents have been eager to challenge anyone who got in the way, including fellow Republicans who voiced concerns. Basic guardrails or efforts to cap spending have been met with intense resistance. During the 2026 West Virginia primary, three political action committees spent heavily on independent advertisements, targeting 10 incumbent Republicans. They succeeded in ousting four, all of whom had disagreements with the governor; most expressed reservations about the Hope Scholarship. Their biggest victory was unseating Criss, the long-serving incumbent and high-ranking Republican. One of the three PACs working to defeat Criss is affiliated with the Koch family. Yass has contributed to the two others: School Freedom Fund and the Sugar Maple PAC. David McIntosh, president of School Freedom Fund and the affiliated Club for Growth, was jubilant afterward. “These elections are a warning to Republican leaders like Vernon Criss — if you oppose school freedom, expect to be held accountable,” he wrote in a press announcement at the time. Help ProPublica Report on Education Have you had trouble finding a school or using a voucher-style program? Do you have concerns about schools — public or private — in your area? Help us understand how families across the country are navigating their school options. Get in Touch Criss had been unopposed in his 2024 primary. In 2026, the three PACs spent more than $145,000 to help a 23-year-old defeat him. Criss’ proposal to put financial limits on the Hope Scholarship program came as West Virginia public schools arrived at a dangerous crossroads. The program directs dollars away from public schools, adding to funding shortfalls created by enrollment drops. Since 2019, 70 public schools have closed throughout the state, with the system losing more than 30,000 students. By the end of this school year, up to 20 more schools could close.  During the same legislative session this year, when lawmakers passed emergency legislation to help one school district stay open, there was little drama — no crowds in the hallways or the galleries.  The Rise of Hope  In 2021, as West Virginia lawmakers worked on the bill that would create the Hope Scholarship, they got some help from the outside: a lobbyist and political operative named Jason Huffman.  Huffman has been the director of Americans for Prosperity-West Virginia since the mid-2010s. The group is part of the larger Americans for Prosperity, which was set up by the billionaire industrialist David Koch and supported by his brother Charles, longtime donors to conservative causes. Americans for Prosperity advocates for low taxes, school choice and loosened environmental regulations throughout the country.  In shaping the West Virginia legislation, Huffman said, one goal was to create a school voucher program that other states could model. While other states had already passed voucher-style programs, they hadn’t made them open to all residents regardless of income. Jason Huffman is the director of Americans for Prosperity-West Virginia. Courtesy of Jason Huffman Among those advocating in West Virginia were members of Cardinal Institute, a homegrown conservative think tank. Founded in 2015, the group made public funding for private schooling one of its first policy planks. Over the last decade, Cardinal has received significant donations from organizations that also have received funding from Koch entities and Yass.  To support the Hope legislation, Cardinal’s leaders distributed research, published columns in newspapers and linked up with other groups, like Americans for Prosperity and the Institute for Justice, which litigates libertarian causes, to push the is

events.title: Rubio is in Uzbekistan to promote US ties and trade with Central Asia
events.summary: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is in Uzbekistan promoting trade and ties with Central Asia U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was in Uzbekistan on Monday to promote trade and ties with Central Asia, during a trip that came amid rumblings that America’s top diplomat is ignoring pressing matters in favor of politically safer visits and meetings. The trip, which involves a stop in India later this week, seeks to promote U.S. economic and security ties with Central and South Asia . But it has only tangential links to the Trump administration’s current main foreign policy dilemmas in the Middle East and with the Russia-Ukraine war . Rubio has brushed aside suggestions he is eschewing the most difficult issues in favor of taking on lower-hanging diplomatic fruit with less risk of failure and political damage, and the State Department pushed back on the criticism of his schedule. In Samarkand, Rubio was meeting with his counterparts from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan under the C5+1 diplomatic forum, which brings together the five Central Asian countries and the United States to discuss security, trade and other shared concerns. Speaking to reporters ahead of the meeting, Rubio said “the United States wants to be a strong partner in Central Asia.” “Central Asia has just not gotten the level of attention from our policymakers over the last 20 years that it deserves. But that’s changing. That’s why we’re here now,” he said. Despite repeated assurances from multiple administrations that the U.S. would become more actively involved in Central Asia, the region has often languished as a foreign policy priority in Washington. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the newly independent Central Asian nations saw a brief surge in U.S. interest, but that waned until after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States, which turned America’s attention once again toward Afghanistan and its neighbors. The U.S. established a military presence in several countries mainly as transit points for equipment, materiel and provisions needed by U.S. and allied forces fighting the Taliban and al-Qaida in Afghanistan. As the U.S. wound down its 20-year operation in Afghanistan, the Trump administration, in both its first and second terms, has sought to elevate its ties with Central Asia due to its location between Russia and China, but also as an underdeveloped area ripe for U.S. business opportunities. Rubio’s trip, which has been heavily promoted by the U.S. ambassador to India and special presidential envoy for Central Asia, Sergio Gor, is perhaps the most ambitious U.S. attempt in decades to boost economic and commercial ties with the region. Speaking to reporters in Samarkand, Rubio described “an incredible delegation” with representatives of almost 300 American businesses joining. events.title: Ken Paxton’s Anti-Abortion Influence Already Extended Beyond Texas. He Could Take It Further in the Senate.
events.summary: Photo illustration by Lisa Larson-Walker/ProPublica. Source images: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images, skaman306/Getty Images, Mike Klein/Getty Images. Early in his tenure as Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton issued a statement commemorating what he believed was a national tragedy. “It’s impossible to fill the void of more than 50 million missing human beings,” he said in 2016. He was marking the 43rd anniversary of Roe v. Wade, the Supreme Court ruling that protected abortion rights — and had long stood in the way of efforts to ban terminations in early pregnancy, when most abortions occur. Paxton spent the years that followed testing Roe’s limits and ultimately prevailed where others had failed: In 2021, he defended a near-total abortion ban that Texas legislators had designed to evade conventional legal challenges. The U.S. Supreme Court allowed it to take effect while Roe remained in force. After the justices overturned Roe the following year, Paxton kept pushing, pursuing new ways to extend the reach of Texas’ restrictions. He prevailed against the Biden administration, picked fights with states that protect abortion access and pioneered strategies that his peers later adopted or expanded. While Paxton’s tenure as attorney general has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum for his personal scandals and alleged misuse of the office , detractors and allies alike agree that his signal achievement as the state’s top legal official has been advancing restrictions on abortion. A close look at his record shows a clear pattern in his successes: He relentlessly tests the limits of the law and employs novel legal strategies to advance his goals. Paxton’s national role as an anti-abortion warrior would change if he wins his U.S. Senate race. As Texas attorney general, he has been able to act largely on his own authority. If he prevails in November, he would become one of 100 senators in a chamber where most legislation needs 60 votes to overcome a filibuster. But allies who have witnessed his victories see an opening. “He’ll have the ability to use some of the laws that he’s defended in Texas as influence to draft legislation in the U.S. Senate,” said Mary Elizabeth Castle, director of government relations at Texas Values, a Christian advocacy group that supports a national abortion ban. Legal experts and advocates on both sides expect he could join colleagues who are pressuring the Food and Drug Administration to revoke its approval of the abortion drug mifepristone. Anti-abortion activists at the state and federal level are also trying to secure legal rights for fetuses, which could have implications for reproductive care like birth control and in vitro fertilization. Paxton, who has called himself a strong supporter of IVF, recently said he was open to restrictions intended to prevent the loss of fertilized eggs. His litigation has also raised questions that experts expect the Supreme Court to confront, including whether a federal law, which mandates hospitals provide stabilizing care to patients having an emergency, overrides state abortion bans; whether to treat a fetus as a separate patient that has its own emergency care rights; and how far states can go in pursuing out-of-state doctors who prescribe abortion medication to patients in states where it’s banned. During the current race, abortion has played a far smaller role than questions about Paxton’s ethics. His Democratic opponent, James Talarico, has said that he supports restoring a federal right to abortion and that his Christian faith calls for an end to “extreme” laws that Paxton has defended and that have forced women to flee the state for emergency abortion care. Lately, Paxton has said little about abortion — an issue on which he has defended restrictions more stringent than many Texans say they want . But those who have watched Paxton extend the reach of Texas law beyond its borders are paying close attention to his Senate bid. Dr. Jennifer Villavicencio, an abortion provider, said she has felt compelled to move her family twice to states with strong laws shielding doctors from out-of-state litigation, partly out of concern that Paxton is creating a blueprint for targeting providers like her. “It’s very disheartening and scary to think that it’s maybe coming to the U.S. Senate,” she said. Photo illustration by Lisa Larson-Walker/ProPublica. Source images: Drew Angerer/Getty Images, Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images. Paxton successfully defended a near-total abortion ban before Roe v. Wade was struck down. When Paxton became Texas attorney general in 2015, there was no ambiguity about where he stood on abortion. Raised by an anti-abortion activist , he married his sweetheart from a Christian college, who spoke proudly about the fact that she was adopted , saying her birth mother “ chose life .” She campaigned for Paxton, but he had his own bona fides. A law he’d co-sponsored as a state senator banned almost all abortions after 20 weeks. Similar 20-week bans had taken root across the country as decades of court rulings chipped away at Roe, but no state had managed to enforce a ban as early as six weeks. More than a dozen tried, passing laws that prohibited abortion when cardiac activity could be detected. One after another, they were blocked by judges. Then, in 2021, a Texas lawyer named Jonathan Mitchell worked with legislators to craft a law that would withstand similar challenges. Instead of having state officials enforce their “heartbeat law,” the new act, referred to as Senate Bill 8, allowed citizens to sue physicians they suspected were providing abortions. The law offered up to $10,000 if they won. When abortion providers and President Joe Biden’s administration separately challenged the law in federal court, Paxton’s office argued that state officials couldn’t be ordered to stop enforcing it because they had no power to do so in the first place. Only private citizens could. “Because the executive officials are expressly prohibited from enforcing SB 8,” his office wrote to the Supreme Court, “there is nothing for a federal court to enjoin.” The Supreme Court agreed that Paxton couldn’t be sued because “the petitioners have not identified any enforcement authority the attorney general possesses in connection with S. B. 8 that a federal court might enjoin him from exercising.” The law remained in effect, becoming the first enforceable six-week ban under Roe. Legislators in Idaho and Oklahoma subsequently passed similar laws. For Dr. Sam Dickman, who worked at a San Antonio Planned Parenthood, the implications were clear: “I was going to need to either entirely change the type of medicine I was providing or leave the state,” he said. He opted for the latter, moving to Montana, where abortion is legal until viability, or roughly 24 weeks. events.title: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
events.summary: In the middle of an especially warm July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks.  The blaze, possibly sparked by lightning, burned across the dry carpet of feather mosses and lichen before climbing into the crowns. By the time fire agencies responded, flames had reached 12 feet in length and sent up a 500-foot column of smoke.  A few days shy of the five-year anniversary of the Yankovich Road Fire, I followed three members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium into the boreal forest, walking along cross-country ski trails lined by feathery field horsetail. In 2024, the organization, which hosts presentations to keep wildfire managers abreast of new developments in fire science, helped turn the area into an educational walking trail, with interpretive signs posted along the route. About a half-mile in, the horizon opened up as we reached a sparse stand of naked, blackened tree trunks, stripped of needles and neighbors.  Hilary Shook, the coordinator of the consortium, stepped off the trail with her thaw probe, a T-shaped pointed metal rod used to detect the upper boundary of the permafrost, the ancient layer of frozen soil that underlies 15% of the land around the Northern Hemisphere and stores roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere. A test of the ground just outside the burn scar hit the concrete-like layer about a foot below the surface. But as Shook applied pressure here, where the fire had burned away the moss and organic-rich topsoil that insulates the permafrost, the probe plunged at least three times deeper into the ground. “That was an immediate effect of the fire,” said Alison York, the outgoing coordinator of the organization, who was standing nearby. “When we monitored right after, it had already thawed quite a bit.” Researchers Eric Miller (left) and Alison York (right) record thaw depth at the site of the Yankovich Road Fire. LEIF VAN CISE This rudimentary tool, offering a measure of depth from a single point in the earth, reveals an escalating problem across the far north. As climate change fuels increasingly frequent and severe fires in the planet’s northern latitudes, they’re accelerating the thawing of more and more permafrost. This allows the organic matter to break down and release powerful greenhouse gases that contribute to a spiraling climate feedback effect, propelling more warming, more fires, and the loss of still more permafrost.  Most dramatically, intensifying wildfires in Canada released more carbon than the nation’s combined fossil fuel emissions in 2023. As in Alaska, many of these megafires occur in vast remote areas where the policy is to let them burn so long as they don’t threaten human habitats. Yet if intensifying fires and warming are left unchecked, the world’s boreal forests and permafrost could increasingly transition from giant carbon sinks into massive sources of atmospheric carbon.  Now, international teams of researchers across the US, Canada, and elsewhere are scrambling to understand what’s at stake, financially as well as ecologically. They’re looking at preventive measures, like controlled burns, and studying the potential to rapidly detect and extinguish wildfires before they grow out of control. They’re even exploring what was once unthinkable: sending in human firefighters not to save lives or structures, but to protect one of our planet’s great stores of carbon. “We need to figure out a better way to live with wildfire,” says Brendan Rogers, a senior scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, one of the main organizations driving the loosely collaborative research effort. “I do think that it can make a meaningful difference.” Woodwell scientist Brendan Rogers (above) has been studying the impact of Arctic-boreal fires on permafrost, as well as what could be done about it. PHILIP KEITH (PHOTOS), WOODWELL CLIMATE RESEARCH (MAPS) Woodwell, the University of Victoria’s Polis Institute for Ecological Governance, and the nonprofit Alaska Venture Fund are now partnering on a multimillion-dollar initiative known as North Fire to study and raise public awareness about the potential benefits of these interventions, MIT Technology Review can report.  The idea is complicated and controversial for a number of reasons. Wildfire is a natural and necessary component of healthy forest ecosystems. Preventing or suppressing fires across huge stretches of largely unmanaged Arctic-boreal forests and tundra would take vast resources. And it’s not yet clear how much of a difference such interventions would make in emissions. Ultimately, the mere fact that researchers are considering such extreme interventions into natural systems is a grim reflection of the dangers we’ve placed ourselves in by continuing to generate more and more greenhouse-gas emissions each year. Those threats are forcing us to grapple with increasingly difficult questions that involve ever steeper trade-offs: What’s the best way to spend our finite resources and dwindling time to avoid the worst dangers of climate change? And when, if ever, is it okay to put people in possible danger to reduce broader risks to the world? ‘A massive blind spot’ Emissions from forest fires have risen 60% around the world since 2001—but they’ve nearly tripled across the boreal forests in the far north.   This stretch of the globe is warming as much as four times faster than the rest of the planet, drying out the landscape. In addition, lightning strikes that set off fires have ticked up sharply as warmer air increases the convective energy in the atmosphere, driving the updrafts that trigger thunderstorms. In that sense, humans have already interceded in these otherwise natural ecosystems by producing the greenhouse-gas emissions that are increasing temperatures, subjecting forests to fire patterns well outside healthy historic norms. “To me, that outweighs the existential dread of ‘Should we or should we not intervene?” says Kate Hayes, an assistant professor at Western Washington University, who is working with Woodwell to study the emissions benefits of fire interventions. “We’ve already intervened, arguably. And so from here, it’s a little bit of a Band-Aid on a bullet wound.” The permafrost that encircles the northern latitudes, underlying large stretches of Canada, Greenland, Siberia, Scandinavia, and other Arctic nations, stores around 1.5 trillion tons of carbon, much of which froze in place millennia ago. The steady global rise in temperature, however, has already shrunk the footprint of Arctic permafrost by about 12 % since 1850, with that loss rapidly accelerating during the last 50 years. By 2100, fire-driven thawing of permafrost could release about the equivalent of nearly 80 billion tons of carbon dioxide, under high warming scenarios. That’s more than half the emissions that fires will release

events.title: Microsoft’s second-hand licensing appeal gets the brush-off
events.summary: Microsoft has failed to win permission to appeal to the UK Supreme Court in the long-running legal spat with ValueLicensing after the Court of Appeal refused its application. The US megacorp was challenging a November 2025 ruling in ValueLicensing's favor that VL may resell pre-owned software licenses. That judgment was unambiguous, but Microsoft told The Register at the time that it would seek permission to appeal. That request was rejected last week in blunt terms. No reasons were given for the refusal, just the words "It is ordered that the application is refused." It isn't quite the end of the road. Microsoft could apply to the Supreme Court itself, but it would need to file within 28 days and show a compelling reason why the Court of Appeal was wrong to refuse its appeal. Things are looking dicey for Microsoft in the case that started in 2021 when ValueLicensing sued Microsoft for £270 million over claims that the Windows maker choked off the supply of surplus Office licenses. Microsoft denied any wrongdoing and Instead attempted to reframe the case as a copyright dispute. The UK's Competition Appeal Tribunal rejected Microsoft's arguments and a subsequent appeal. A recently published Consent Order adds to the pressure. It demands documents from past and present Microsoft bosses, including a potentially explosive internal deck titled "Second-Hand Software Presentation" (SHS). The contents of the file are unknown, but the Consent Order refers to it as a "Known Adverse Document." It dates back to 2013, a few years after Office 365 was launched. The order also asks why Microsoft waited until the end of 2025 to disclose the document’s existence, a few years after Office 365 launched. To add a little more spice, Alexander Wolfson is listed as an intervener on the appeal refusal. He is the proposed class representative in a separate claim filed on behalf of millions of UK customers seeking between £1.3 billion to £3.5 billion in compensation from Microsoft over its conduct regarding pre-owned licenses. ValueLicensing and Microsoft declined to comment on the latest development. Appeals aside, the next stage will be a Witness Statement from Microsoft explaining who knew what and when, followed by further disclosure. ®

events.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
events.summary: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block. When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log.  Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground. AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning.  “There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed. The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it.  Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.” COURTESY MIT CSAIL As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience. They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.) Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work  meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures. But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning.” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it.  “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.” Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans. Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore.  Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop. Just continue doing whatever you want to do.”  “It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.” As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations.  “There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.” “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter.

events.title: Trump Appointees Asked a Federal Cybersecurity Agency to Secretly Acquire a Voting Machine — and Hack It
events.summary: Photo illustration by Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica. Source images: Christopher Mark Juhn/Anadolu via Getty Images, Erlon Silva - TRI Digital via Getty Images, Mironov Konstantin via Getty Images. A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it. The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.  The proposition was shocking to CISA’s career staffers, according to one of the former officials. CISA typically worked to thwart hackers. Moreover, the agency had been directed not to alert the voting machine company if it uncovered flaws, contrary to its standard practices. The request made the CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. “My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any [election] results they don’t like,” one of the former officials said. “This goes against everything CISA represents.” The CISA employees repeatedly told the political appointees that their request was impossible, in part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation had just been laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative. The appointees eventually stopped pressing CISA. Though not acted on, the request shows how the Trump administration has tried to use the agency for its own ends while draining it of resources for one of its critical missions: protecting the nation’s voting systems.  In Trump’s second term, his administration has laid off or pushed out more than 1,000 CISA employees, shrinking the agency by about one-third. The president’s 2027 budget proposal would reduce funding for the agency by another $700 million, which could necessitate 900 additional layoffs.  In response, Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into CISA’s ability to do its job and demanded answers as to why federal funds are not being used to support election security as directed by Congress. Since Trump signed the CISA Act in 2018, the agency has worked with state authorities and voting machine vendors to help protect election infrastructure from cyberattacks. During Trump’s second term, though, CISA has abandoned much of this work. Several state election authorities said the agency provided them no assistance — and no explanation for its absence — during the most critical planning stages for the upcoming midterms. “There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA. In 2025 and through mid-September 2026 — when the bulk of preparations for the election typically would have been completed — “they were nonexistent. Literally nonexistent.” While Trump has repeatedly warned that America’s elections are vulnerable to hacking, in some cases repeating disproven claims, experts said his administration is undermining the federal government’s role in helping secure them. Though CISA re-emerged in September with a last-minute security plan for the election, some state officials told ProPublica they fear that what is left of the agency has been compromised by a conspiracy-obsessed presidential administration. In recent months, in reviving debunked theories about the 2020 election, the Trump administration has declassified troves of records, including sensitive material that state officials provided to CISA. Some state authorities said they no longer trusted the administration enough to share information with CISA, a key to the agency’s success in past elections. “They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments on national security. “There’s no fucking way they’re ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.”  A spokesperson for the White House declined an interview request but defended Trump’s handling of election security in an emailed statement. “President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections,” said Lauren Bis.  Bis referred specific questions about CISA’s handling of elections to DHS. DHS and CISA did not respond to interview requests or to a detailed list of questions. “There’s no fucking way [state governments are] ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.” A former federal cybersecurity official who advises state governments Current and former CISA employees and state election officials describe an agency that has become significantly less equipped to help states fight legitimate cyber threats. State leaders say they have used their own resources to shore up gaps left by CISA, such as paying for sensor technology that can detect unusual activity in election networks. But some services, like intel on foreign actors, can’t be replicated. Some people interviewed said they were worried that Trump and his allies continue to ratchet up rhetoric about voting security, particularly about threats to voting machines. Officials in one large voting jurisdiction said they have met privately with machine vendors to come up with a contingency plan if the federal government seizes their machines or declares them unusable. “I don’t pay attention to what the president says. I pay attention to what his administration does,” Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said. “And what they’ve done is basically cut us off and left us on our own.” Defending elections from hackers wasn’t always part of DHS’s remit. Throughout the mid-1990s and 2000s, a series of cyberattacks rocked the federal government, demonstrating the emerging threat. In 2007, hackers broke into the Pentagon and stole terabytes of sensitive data. The digital heist, by an unknown foreign adversary, was so damaging that one intelligence leader later described it as an “espionage Pearl Harbor.” Under George W. Bush, DHS underwent a reorganization to more effectively combat terrorism and respond to disasters like Hurricane Katrina. The department dedicated resources under an office called the National Protection and Programs Directorate to help fortify advanced cyber defense systems and important infrastructure. The office’s work ranged from helping secure events like the Super Bowl to protecting chemical plants to issuing cybersecurity warnings to the private sector and the public. In 2018, Trump signed a bill making the office a stand-alone agency, allowing for more federal funding and transforming it into, essentially, the ultimate tech support desk for anythin

events.title: Tropics attract city dwellers in regional migration trend
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tropics welcome city dwellers in regional migration trend Small rural towns like Atherton on the Tablelands near Cairns are seeing an influx of residents from capital cities. ( ABC News: Nathan Morris ) The Regional Australia Institute says new data shows city-to-regional migration is on par with pandemic levels. The Sunshine Coast was the most popular destination for people moving to regional Australia, while other areas of Queensland recorded significant annual growth. Sydney and Melbourne recorded the largest losses of residents to regional Australia. City dwellers are moving to regional Australia at rates not seen since the COVID pandemic, according to new data. The movement of people out of Sydney and Melbourne is captured in data from Commonwealth Bank, which the Regional Australia Institute (RAI) has analysed to track migration trends. Sydney accounted for 52 per cent of the net population outflow to Australian regions in the June 2026 quarter. ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) The not-for-profit organisation said migration from capital cities to regional Australia during the June 2026 quarter matched the record set in June 2021. Those moving to the regions outnumbered those moving to the cities by 30 per cent, and Sydney and Melbourne recorded the largest losses of residents. Sunshine Coast is the region that city movers are favouring most. ( Supplied ) The Sunshine Coast remained the most favoured region for those leaving capital cities, followed by Greater Geelong in Victoria. In the 12 months to the June 2026 quarter, the Sunshine Coast received 8.7 per cent of total net migration share. Victoria's Central Goldfields and the New South Wales Snowy Mountains were the most popular for movers already living in regional Australia. Beyond the stand-out markets, the RAI highlighted significant growth in north Queensland in the 12 months to the June 2026 quarter. Geelong trailed the Sunshine Coast with the second-largest share of total net internal migration. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) The sugarcane and horticultural mecca of the Burdekin, south of Townsville, saw a 238 per cent annual increase in the number of city movers choosing the region. Retail operator Candace Young moved from Dalby to the Burdekin in 2023. She said since the move, she had noticed a stream of southerners moving to the shire of 17,000 people. "We are getting a lot of city people coming up here, customers coming to the shop who have moved from Victoria or Tasmania," she said. "Here, you can drive five minutes in any direction and take the kids fishing or camping, and those things are free activities. The Atherton Tablelands region, south of Cairns, received a 131 per cent annual increase in residents from capital cities. RAI chief executive Liz Ritchie said the latest quarterly data showed people still wanted to move to regional Australia in droves, years after the pandemic-inspired tree and sea changes. "It is those southern states that are really feeling the pinch in terms of how people are measuring their lifestyle and what they're hoping for," she said. "It is a good-news story for Queensland." Liz Ritchie says one in three city dwellers were planning a regional move within five years. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Ms Ritchie said the RAI was lobbying to establish a national population plan to assist regional planning. "We continue to under-project population in regional Australia, and our regional communities suffer because of that," she said. "People on the ground know when their town is growing, and they know when they're feeling the pinch.

events.title: AI’s epic cash call is matched only by its ability to strangle revenue streams
events.summary: As it was written , so it has come to pass. A while back, we suggested that given how good AI was at code analysis, it would become possible to clone large applications. And then where would we be? Here, that’s where. An industrious individual has released source code and binaries for Claude-copied Microsoft Office and Adobe Creative Suite programs, disappointingly not calling elements of the latter Fauxtoshop . They’re in pre-alpha states of incomplete bugginess, but with substantial functionality, which is proof of how insanely productive AI can be given a task needing zero creativity and wearing "This is what a proof of concept looks like" and "Unintended Consquesences" T-shirts. They could also add Karma Police to their wardrobe. It’s clear that Microsoft and Adobe are facing some competition from what their rival describes as "clean-room reimplementations." It’s also unclear that there is any law against it. You can’t copyright functionality, the code has been generated in Rust with claimed clean-room conditions, and while there may be something in claiming that the works are substantially derivative, there’s a big problem here. Companies that sell AI trained on the biggest theft of IP in history are going to need unmatched legal dexterity to claim that AI shouldn’t be allowed to sully their own IP. Chutzpah used to be defined as a child on trial for murdering their parents begging for mercy on the grounds that they’re an orphan. We’ll have to update that. The post-codeclone world is going to be interesting. Everything becomes effectively open source, which closes down substantial revenue streams for big companies who had assumed lock-in. The motivation to build ab-initio alternatives may go away, in open source as well as closed. The push to subscription-only cloud-hosted products, where nobody can get their thieving AI prompts on binaries, seems an obvious counter move, but AI can control and scrape a web interface, which is all it needs. It's an arms race that won’t be won by humans. Code cloning is just the latest case of AI being so disruptive it threatens its creators. Another is the doom loop that Microsoft-OpenAI acknowledged in internal emails : by siphoning away the ad revenue that pays for content, AI chokes off the data it depends on. It's deforestation by companies that built their business on other people's IP. The biggest potential point of failure is the money. How revenues will hold up against cheaper or free Chinese models is a concern, given the high importance assigned by Beijing to develop AI as a global influence vector. The models themselves are very efficient, in part because of export regulations on high-end silicon and something of a glut of older datacenters. This wouldn’t be the first time restricting access to technology is an evolutionary driver with a poor outcome for those doing the restricting. A much bigger issue is: where will the money come from to build the infrastructure that is needed to support the claims AI is using to justify its growth. Gartner says that there’s not enough return on investment to drive that growth, while a much more engaging SemiAnalysis podcast predicts total capex by 2030 of $11 trillion and asks where it’s going to come from. If you’re interested in understanding AI and aren't following SemiAnalysis, you’re not interested in understanding AI, and while the outfit is relentlessly optimistic it’s also wildly well-informed. In this case, the structure of the investment market for AI is picked apart. It is very weird. Neocloud is made up of startups with a voracious appetite for cash, but no investment grade status . Thus, Nvidia backstops them, guaranteeing to rent unsold capacity for a fixed price for long enough to guarantee enough revenue to attract other investment. Other cash-rich big tech companies do similar things. This backstopping, also known more wryly as "balance sheet as a service," effectively shifts more risk to investment-rated companies. It's an increasingly important capex enabler, but as SemiAnalysis says, it’s necessarily limited, especially if AI itself has blown a hole in the enterprise. Or take the residual value of the older compute. Normally, the book value and revenue capabilities of datacenter chips depreciates over five years or so to some nominal value. That’s not happening here, where chips of that vintage are suddenly producing the same or more revenue than they did when they were new. Such are the peculiarities of a supply-constrained market used to rapid obsolescence. Surely a good thing, though? No. It’s another strange and hard-to-model factor in a market defined by strange and hard-to-model factors. Don’t even mention AGI. Or models too dangerous to use. Or model collapse. Many investors do not like the strange and hard to model, including huge pools of institutional funds. There are models that can blend in risk-averse investors to speculative investments, but those who remember the clever models that blew up the global economy nearly twenty years ago are not yet all dead. The tl;dr of the answer to where do you get enough money to make AI work as promised, is: nobody knows. What happens if the capex has no cap to ex? See previous answer. It may be an infantile affliction to have animation clips come to mind when considering AI, but it can’t be helped. Agentic AI? Mickey Mouse as the sorcerer's apprentice in Fantasia. Big Tech pushing out AI as fast as it can? Wile E Coyote sawing through the branch he’s sitting on. AI investment market? Any of Caine’s quests in the Amazing Digital Circus. We’re all along for the ride, whether we like it or not. ®

events.title: AI inference is running into a memory bottleneck. Huawei wants to tackle it with OceanStor M900
events.summary: As organizations move from straightforward AI interactions towards longer conversations, complex reasoning and autonomous agents, the demands on their infrastructure are changing. Processing increasingly large amounts of context places significant pressure on memory capacity, while keeping accelerators supplied with data becomes just as important as raw computing power. One particular challenge is the key-value (KV) cache, which stores information generated during inference so models can reuse previous computations rather than repeatedly processing the same context. As context windows expand and multi-turn interactions become more demanding, these caches grow considerably. GPU memory and system memory provide fast access but are expensive and capacity constrained. Traditional storage offers greater capacity, yet its longer, CPU-mediated data paths can introduce latency that leaves valuable accelerator resources waiting for data. Huawei believes addressing this gap requires a different approach to storage. Bringing context memory closer to compute At HUAWEI CONNECT 2026 in Shanghai, Huawei introduced OceanStor M900 Context Memory Storage, designed to support AI inference across hyperscale datacenters and its Ascend SuperPoD infrastructure. The platform introduces what Huawei describes as a dedicated Context Memory Storage layer, extending KV cache beyond accelerator and system memory into a shared, multi-tier storage pool. Using Huawei's UnifiedBus high-speed interconnect, OceanStor M900 enables KV cache resources to be shared across a cluster, with Huawei claiming capacity of up to 64PB and substantially more context available per NPU. Its innovative ASU disk also integrates CPU, networking and storage controller functions. Combined with native KV semantics, this allows NPUs to access stored cache data in a single hop, avoiding conventional protocol conversion and CPU forwarding. According to Huawei, this approach reduces access latency to 60 microseconds, potentially doubling token throughput and halving time to first token in typical AI coding workloads. Cost and durability are also part of the proposition. Huawei's KV-aware adaptive storage technology manages data placement according to cache lifecycles, with claimed endurance of up to 24 drive writes per day, or 16 times that of conventional SSDs. The company argues this could reduce replacement and maintenance costs over time. The wider significance of OceanStor M900 lies in Huawei's approach to AI infrastructure. Rather than treating storage as a separate supporting component, the company is positioning memory, networking and compute as increasingly interconnected elements of inference performance. As agentic AI workloads grow, how efficiently infrastructure retains, shares and retrieves context may become as important as how quickly its accelerators can process it. Sponsored by Huawei

events.title: Six-year plastics factory fight takes toll on Moss Vale residents
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Moss Vale residents tell court of personal toll after six-year plastics factory fight Hundreds of residents gathered at the proposed Moss Vale plastics recycling factory site as the Land and Environment Court began hearing an appeal against the project's rejection. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Hundreds of Moss Vale residents have gathered as a developer appeals the rejection of a proposed plastics recycling factory. The court heard emotional accounts of how six years of uncertainty has affected local families. The hearing will continue for another nine days, with council offering live stream access at the Moss Vale Civic Centre from Tuesday. A mother described fearing for her children's health, a doctor recounted the psychological toll on families, and a retiree told of plans for a quieter life put on hold. They were among the eight residents who addressed the NSW Land and Environment Court at Moss Vale on Monday, as hundreds gathered for the opening of an appeal hearing into a proposed plastics recycling factory. Developer Repoly is appealing the Independent Planning Commission's decision to reject the project last year. The proposed factory would process up to 120,000 tonnes of mixed plastic waste a year at a site on Beaconsfield Road. For Jean McKern, who lives immediately beside the proposed site, the dispute has overshadowed what she hoped would be peaceful retirement years. Jean McKern (sitting) surrounded by people who also spoke at the appeal hearing. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Now in her late 80s, she told the court she was a healthy, active 83-year-old when the proposal first emerged in 2020. She described disrupted sleep, mounting stress and health problems she believes have been exacerbated by the uncertainty. Ms McKern became emotional as she described fears about noise, lighting, pollution and fire risks, saying she could be forced to leave the home where she has lived for 30 years. Another neighbouring resident, Graham Horden , said he and his wife had downsized in retirement, hoping to restore native vegetation on their property and spend time with their grandchildren. "From a feeling of justified satisfaction in our retirement years, we have regressed to a situation of prolonged stress and anxiety," he told the court. He said the uncertainty had also raised concerns about their financial position as self-funded retirees. Families living in 'suspended animation' Moss Vale mother Natalie Swainston described watching her two young sons play cricket at nearby Lackey Park on Saturday and worrying about potential pollution if the factory were operating less than a kilometre away. Natalie Swainston told the court she feared the potential impacts of the factory on children attending a nearby childcare centre. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Her children had previously attended a childcare centre about 300 metres from the proposed development, where they spent much of their days playing outdoors. "It's quite hard to explain what it's like to live in suspended animation for this long," she told the court. "You put your life on hold and wait for the next amendment, the next deadline, the next hearing. You think you can finally rest and then there's an appeal." Palliative care doctor Jacqueline Duc, speaking on behalf of local health professionals and Doctors for the Environment Australia, raised concerns about potential health risks and the psychological toll of the prolonged dispute. She urged the court to adopt a precautionary approach. Dr Duc also shared a deeply personal account of how the dispute had affected another member of the community. Jacqueline Duc told the court years of uncertainty over the proposed factory had affected the wellbeing of local families. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) She told the court the family's daughter's eighth birthday wish was for the factory proposal to go away. She said their daughter is now 11, and the dispute continues. The Independent Planning Commission refused approval in January 2025, citing concerns including fire risks and the suitability of the location. Repoly has since amended its plans, including moving one building further from neighbouring homes and proposing to transport process wastewater offsite for disposal. Wingecarribee Shire Council maintains the location remains unsuitable. More than 500 people attended the appeal hearing at the site of Repoly's proposed facility in Moss Vale.

events.title: UAE amends e-invoicing regulations as implementation deadline draws closer
events.summary: The UAE's Ministry of Finance has made amendments to its e-invoicing system that will apply to value-added tax filing in the country from next year. Authorities are introducing a temporary exclusion for business transactions between entities that are members of the same tax group for two years, starting from January 1, 2027, the Ministry of Finance said on Monday. Such transactions will be treated as "excluded transactions" throughout the 24-month period, "giving businesses greater flexibility and more time to adapt to the system", the ministry said. David Daly, a partner at Gulf Tax Accounting Group, said the move was "welcome", but more clarity would be needed to understand specific details. For instance, in a scenario where each entity also issues invoices to non-tax group members, it still needs to be known whether these must be managed through the e-invoicing system, he said. The ministry's latest decision also amends article 11 on the storage of electronic invoice and electronic credit note data. Under the amended provision, entities must retain all electronic invoices, electronic credit notes and any associated data for the period prescribed under the Tax Procedures Law, and ensure that such records can be provided to the Federal Tax Authority on request, the ministry said. The decision "removes the previous requirement that such data be stored within the UAE, thereby shifting the focus from the location of storage to the retention and accessibility of records for tax compliance purposes", it added. The amendments also remove the requirement for companies to notify the FTA of a system failure within two business days of it happening. The ministry said the amendments are aimed at improving the ease of doing business in the UAE "by reducing operational burdens on businesses, providing greater flexibility during the implementation of the electronic invoicing system, and ensuring that regulatory requirements support an efficient and business-friendly environment". The latest decision comes as the first major compliance requirement in the phased transition to e-invoicing approaches on October 30. The ministry extended the deadline for appointing an accredited service provider (ASP) for businesses in the UAE with annual revenue of Dh50 million ($13.6 million) or more to October 30, from July 1, under the first phase of the programme. Under the UAE's unified e-invoicing model, all qualifying transactions must be validated and sent through an ASP.

events.title: Australia could be without structural and rail steelmaking for up to five years
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Whyalla blast furnace closure could leave Australia without major steel production for years The coal-fired blast furnace at Whyalla's steelworks closed last month after being offline since April. ( ABC News ) Unions predict Australia could be without domestic structural and rail steelmaking for up to five years, as about 500 employees are made redundant at the Whyalla Steelworks. About 250 employees are expected to take voluntary packages, but there will be forced redundancies . About 100 contractors will also go, after attempts to repair the plant's 60-year-old blast furnace failed. "Steel production is not possible without a blast furnace," Australian Workers Union branch organiser Shane Karger told 7.30. Shane Karger from the Australian Workers Union says the future of the Whyalla steel plant is uncertain. ( ABC News: Carl Saville ) Seventy-five per cent of the nation's structural steel comes from the Whyalla plant, and has been used in construction of the Western Sydney Airport and Optus Stadium in Perth. The steelworks is also the sole domestic manufacturer of rail steel. The plant will keep operating using stockpiled as well as locally and internationally sourced semi-finished steel product. "The iron ore mines will obviously still operate and export any product that they produce but for this period of time, Australia is reliant on the rest of the world for its structural and rail steel," Mr Karger said. Australian Industry Group CEO Innes Willox said it would become increasingly difficult to bring back structural and rail steelmaking capacity in Whyalla as time went on. "A clear, transparent path back to production is essential to give both the people of Whyalla, South Australia and industry more generally, confidence that there is a path forward. Right now, it's not so clear that there is one." Innes Willox says it will be harder for steelmaking to resume at Whyalla the longer production is paused. ( ABC News: Dan Fermer ) The South Australian and federal governments have publicly pledged almost $2 billion to help a new owner invest in a less emissions intensive electric arc furnace. Federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres didn't rule out putting more money on the table and told 7.30 his government was committed to the "fastest possible resumption" of steelmaking capacity. "The commitment from the two governments here ... is to deliver a pit to port mining facility, iron and steel making and of course, finished steel products," Mr Ayres said. "We're working closely with the final two bidders in the process to deliver the best outcome." Tim Ayres says the federal government is working to resume production at Whyalla as soon as possible. ( ABC News: Shaun Kingma ) The shortlisted bidders are Indian industrial company Jindal and Australian business M Resources, while Australia's largest steelmaker Bluescope holds a right of last offer. It had been hoped the coal-fired blast furnace would last a few more years, which would smooth the transition to that proposed electric arc furnace but Mr Karger believes cost cutting under previous owner Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance shortened its life span. "A decision was made … to throttle back the furnace," Mr Karger said. "A typical blast furnace of that type likes to run at near capacity, keep the temperature up and the iron flowing. Whyalla Steelworks is the only producer of structural and rail steel in Australia. ( ABC News: Lincoln Rothall ) A spokesman for GFG told 7.30 in a statement that Whyalla's problems did not begin with GFG and they have not ended since the company's removal. "Despite significant losses, over six years GFG preserved jobs and Australia's sovereign steelmaking capability while battling an aging plant and grossly inadequate protection against unprecedented levels of steel dumping," it said. "The blast furnace did not fail under GFG's watch … those now seeking to place all responsibility on GFG should also acknowledge Whyalla's long decline across successive owners, governments and policy regimes." GFG Alliance has been struggling to stay afloat globally since the collapse of key financier Greensill Capital in 2021. When the steelworks was placed into administration by the South Australian government in February last year, it was losing $1.5 million a day. The town of Whyalla depends on the local steel industry. ( ABC News/Carl Saville ) Administrators said they took control of a plant that had sustained a "long period of underinvestment, inadequate or no maintenance" and "poor health and safety practices".

events.title: Why Physical AI Is So Hard To Engineer
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Physical AI is the deployment of machines with autonomy, acting within the real world. It is not a single product, but a philosophy built on modular architectures. These systems can only be developed with a full systems approach, integrating sensors, actuators, and distributed compute systems, in a multi-physics methodology. Real-time constraints become much more important than in the past, and at the same time much more complex. Physical AI is changing how chips are designed and used, integrating sensing, AI inference, and real-time control into machines that can safely and predictably interact with the physical world. The challenges extend well beyond just performance. Engineers need to account for corner cases stemming from unpredictable environments, ensure these systems are safe and reliable, and they need to future-proof these systems by ensuring they are serviceable and upgradable. This will require new tools and methodologies, as well as some new design approaches. “AI is leaving the screen,” says Anthony Matarazzo, head of physical AI, digital twins, simulation-driven AI, and accelerated computing at Synopsys . “It is no longer about generating text or code. It is entering the physical world. It needs to understand, interact, sense, make decisions in a physical environment. We are moving from generative AI to agentic workflow orchestration to physical AI (see figure 1.) That is literally making intelligence actionable. But the consequences of being wrong fundamentally change. Life or death, plus or minus 1%.” Fig. 1: Three Eras of AI. Source: Synopsys Physical AI must see and interact with the real world. “It is challenging to make artificial intelligence see the world correctly,” says Chun-Ting “Tim” Wang-Lee, signal integrity application scientist at Keysight EDA . “Real-world information comes from the sensors, and the data has to be moved somewhere and processed so that the AI can decide and then act. There are decisions that need to be made.” This changes the design priorities. “Physical AI usually gets framed as a compute story,” says Justin Endo, director for marketing and sales at Mixel , A Silvaco Company. “But from our perspective it has really been an imaging story. Every robot, drone, and autonomous system comes down to cameras feeding an inference engine.” Physical AI builds on some of the connectivity and sensing technologies developed for the Internet of Things. “IoT was largely about connecting and monitoring things,” says Brad Rex, head of physical AI, UX at Renesas Electronics. “Physical AI is about giving machines the ability to perceive and act autonomously in unstructured environments. This is a completely orthogonal engineering problem, and it requires a step-change in system-level content — more sensing, more real-time compute, more sophisticated power management, and more safety considerations per device.” Within physical AI, there are two distinct classes of devices: “Those that can rely on a cloud connection and those that must operate fully locally without relying on connectivity,” says Ashley Stevens, director of product management and marketing at Arteris . “For example, vehicles cannot rely on continuous connectivity, as there are many locations where cellular coverage is inadequate. In contrast, an industrial robotic arm moves but is constrained to a particular location within a factory setting, and therefore can be connected to the cloud.” Others agree. “Unlike traditional AI applications that primarily generate information, physical AI systems influence real-world outcomes through continuous interaction with their environment,” says William Chen, product marketing group director for design IP at Cadence . “Traditional IoT often focused on collecting and transmitting data. Physical AI adds real-time interpretation and action. The result is a shift from connected devices to intelligent systems operating within sensing and control loops.” This requires new architectures and new methodologies. “The entire architecture is very different,” says Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics at Vinci . “Time-to-market is going to be much slower because people are still learning. Physical AI is the next step that they want, but the switch to it is not going to be easy. The easiest entry point will be a repetitive action, but people are not willing to pay much for that. They want it to do a lot more. That’s why it is going to take a more complex architecture to build, make reliable, and make it work for at least a day on a single charge.” It also requires significant processing power. “Robotics and drones require powerful, efficient compute capable of multimodal processing and accurate, real-time responsiveness in dynamic settings,” says Sameer Sharma, associate vice president for MediaTek’s IoT business. “Because of latency and bandwidth constraints, these devices require silicon capable of handling AI workloads at the edge, including AI acceleration for machine vision and object classification.” As systems get larger or more capable, additional challenges emerge. “You need longer reach through moving joints, aggregation of many cameras into few ports, and the functional safety expectations coming over from automotive,” says Mixel’s Endo. “But the standard is already moving in that direction. The mobile camera interface is becoming the robot’s optic nerve, and that mobile-proven maturity is hard for any alternative to match.” How quickly physical AI is adopted by different markets will vary, but the overall projections are noteworthy. At a high level, PwC estimates the global physical AI market will reach ~€430 billion by 2030, with “significant upside potential as systems scale and mature.” Deloitte, meanwhile, found that 58% of companies report at least limited use of physical AI today, with that number projected to rise to 80% within two years. Not all sectors will adopt this technology at the same time. “Physical AI is not just AI at the edge,” says Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategic programs for system solutions at Synopsys. “It is broader than just robotics, but it will be uneven. The question is how quickly each industry will adopt physical AI. It requires you to go beyond the chip to the full physics. The growth inflection comes when you have this full loop of sensing, reasoning, physical action, and then autonomy. It’s really a platform transition where everything is being elevated up to the system level.” New markets have repeatedly driven changes in the semiconductor ecosystem. “We believe physical AI is one of the most disruptive AI opportunities of the next several years,” say

events.title: Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools
events.summary: U.S. consumers are uneasy about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting prices U.S. consumers aren't just frustrated with high prices . They're angry and confused about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting those prices. Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like “dynamic pricing” and “surveillance pricing” are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product. Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they don’t understand and personal data they may not realize they’re sharing has touched a nerve. “There are major tensions happening right now between who’s really going to have the power with some of these algorithms and usage of bots and AI: the companies or the shopper,” said Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney. Companies using the technology say some concerns stem from misconceptions about how their pricing tools work. Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers’ time and keep prices up to date. He said the labels aren’t used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper. “We price the product, not the person,” Furner wrote. But companies aren't always transparent about the customer data they collect and how it's used, which has made consumers suspicious and led to speculation. For example, social media posts falsely imply that electronic shelf labels Walmart plans to put in all its U.S. stores scan shoppers’ faces or cellphones to set individualized prices, Thomas said. Lawmakers and regulators are taking action. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law. Here are some of the pricing practices and technologies drawing scrutiny. What it is: Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand . An airline that adjusts ticket prices as departures approach is using dynamic pricing. Uber's practice of lifting fares when demand outstrips the supply of available drivers, such as during rush hour, is a type of dynamic pricing known as surge pricing. Why it matters: Frequent price changes extend well beyond food. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies. About half the U.S. changes it recorded were decreases, contrary to consumers’ assumptions that dynamic pricing only raises prices, said Gabriele Vitke, a senior product marketing manager. What they are: Digital displays that let stores update shelf prices electronically instead of replacing paper tags. Why it matters: Digital price labels, long used in Europe and Asia, are drawing more attention as they spread to major U.S. retailers like Walmart and Whole Foods. Consumer advocates have argued that digital labels could eventually be used for surge pricing or personalized pricing. Labor unions also have opposed the technology. The electronic shelf labels make frequent changes easier but don’t necessarily lead to higher prices during periods of strong demand. Retailers typically update electronic shelf prices on a regular schedule, often weekly, because shoppers value consistency, said Asa Farquhar of Relex Solutions, a retail technology company. Researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found “virtually no surge pricing” after the labels were introduced. “Changing prices throughout the day, the way airlines or rideshare apps do, is exceedingly rare in grocery and general merchandise today,” Farquhar said. 2 dead, 11 injured after Kansas mother drives onto soccer field during game: Police Airman killed rappelling from Alamodome's ceiling in Salute to Armed Forces ceremony Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say What it is: Personalized pricing means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information about individuals or groups of shoppers. Some advocacy groups and regulators use the term “surveillance pricing" for the same practice. Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely businesses use personal information to customize prices.

events.title: Engineer was so sick of office pranks, he 'wiped' his antagonist's disk
events.summary: Monday mornings are no joke, so The Register always tries to lighten them up with a new installment of "Who, Me?" – our reader-contributed column that shares your stories of workplace japes, mistakes, and escapes. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Joe" who told us that while studying for an electrical engineering degree in the late 1990s, he scored a gig in the messaging lab at an Australian mobile carrier. "The office there was full of practical jokers," he wrote. "Boxes of confetti balanced on a door, a bag of prawn heads left under the carpet in one of the senior engineer's cars, hand cream on the phone earpieces... all the usual stuff." Joe told us that one colleague, whom he suggested we call "TF," took the pranks a little too far. "TF liked to sneak up behind me and ROAR in my ear to scare me in the hope I would jump," Joe wrote. "As this was not an especially clever tactic, I resolved to make my revenge a legendary once-and-for-all-time affair." Joe couldn't find an opportunity until his last week in the job, which helpfully coincided with TF attending a conference. "All the PCs had Borland C compilers installed," Joe explained. "I used it to write a completely harmless program that looked exactly like MS-DOS formatting a disk." The program even wrote junk data to a temporary file so the PC's disk activity light would flash, making the fake formatting operation more convincing. After a few minutes of blinkenlights faking the formatting, the program displayed a message revealing the prank. Joe added the program to autoexec.bat so it would run whenever the PC booted, but set it to terminate immediately until a month after his departure. "About five or six weeks later I got a phone call from one of the other guys," Joe recalled. "You're a bloody genius, TF just about shat himself this morning." "Mission accomplished!" Joe declared. By then, he was safely out of the job. Have you pranked your way to revenge? Email Who, Me? and tell us how it went. ®
