events.title: Dubai Investments to list DIP Holding shares in first DFM IPO this year
events.summary: Dubai Investments , a Dubai-listed conglomerate, is selling a 20 per cent stake in its subsidiary DIP Holding in the first initial public offering in the UAE this year. The deal will comprise the sale of 1.74 billion shares by existing shareholders in DIP Holding, which owns the mixed-use development Dubai Investments Park, the company said on Monday. Parent Dubai Investments will continue to control the remaining 80 per cent shareholding in DIP Holding, contingent on the offering size remaining unchanged and all shares on sale being allocated to investors, it said. Subscriptions for the sale are set to open on October 27 and will run until November 3. Final pricing for the deal will be announced on November 4. DIP Holding shares are expected to start trading on the Dubai Financial Market on November 11, according to the offer document. "Our IPO marks an important milestone in DIP Holding’s journey and reflects the strength and resilience of our differentiated, infrastructure-like business model, said Omar Al Mesmar, chief executive of DIP Holding. "Looking ahead, we see clear opportunities to build on this foundation." The deal breaks the lull in the IPO market in the UAE. The Arab world’s second-largest economy was a hotbed for public floats, with the DFM and the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange both attracting a steady stream of IPOs over the past few years. The Middle East IPO market last year slowed after it was hit by lower oil prices , geopolitical unrest and weaker post-listing performances. Companies in the region raised $7.1 billion from 61 listings, down from $13 billion a year earlier. UAE companies raised a total of $1.1 billion through three IPOs in 2025, Dealogic data shows. The US-Iran war, now in its eighth month, has further disrupted the already slowing momentum as companies put their plans of tapping equities markets to raise capital on hold. Dubai Investments , in which the sovereign investment fund Investment Corporation of Dubai holds a stake, was among the UAE companies that expressed intentions to list shares in its units before war-driven volatility sapped deal volumes. The company in September last year said that it was in talks with banks and planned to list up to 25 per cent of Dubai Investments Park. Dividend policy Situated near Al Maktoum International Airport and Jebel Ali Port, Dubai Investments Park is home to 1,000 tenants, 5,700 subtenants and more than 150,000 residents. The district was established in 1997 and hosts warehouses, hotels, retail outlets, schools and medical centres, making it one of the largest mixed-use developments in the emirate. DIP Holding intends to adopt a semi-annual cash dividend distribution policy. The company expects to pay annualised dividends of Dh700 million, Dh725 million and Dh750 million for 2026, 2027 and 2028 financial years, respectively. In 2029, the company expects to pay dividends in line with, or above the 2028 payout, it said in the offer document. "Our intention to list DIP Holding on the Dubai Financial Market represents a natural next step in a journey that began more than 25 years ago," said DIP Holding chairman Khalid bin Kalban. "What began as an ambitious vision for an integrated mixed-use destination has developed into a fully established and highly sought-after platform supporting businesses and communities across the logistics, industrial, commercial and residential sectors."

events.title: ConnectWise turns off its SaaS-y backup, security, and management services to probe security SNAFU
events.summary: SaaS-for-managed services providers ConnectWise has initiated a “service interruption” for its some of its offerings after detecting unauthorized access. ConnectWise offers ERP tailored to the needs of managed services providers (MSPs), plus tools they can use to manage their customers’ environments. Cloud Backup is one of those tools and does what it says on the tin for data stored on-prem, in the cloud, or in SaaS services like M365 and Google Workspace. On October 16, the company published an advisory revealing that on the 15 th it “identified unauthorized access to application identities within the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment.” “The service interruption affects partners and customers using Cloud Backup, formerly known as SkyKick. Because SaaS Security and Cloud Management are integrated with Cloud Backup, those services have also been suspended out of an abundance of caution while our investigation and remediation continue,” the company advised. The suspension does not mean MSPs, or their customers, should assume that their environments were compromised, just that ConnectWise isn’t confident it can operate its services safely at this time. As of 16:00 UTC on October 18, the services remain unavailable, which means end-users can’t back up data, access their archives, or restore data. “Existing archives remain encrypted, isolated, and preserved, with no evidence of unauthorized access. Our teams continue monitoring affected environments, conducting forensic analysis and threat hunting, and carrying out remediation activities,” the company’s veep of security operations, Jason Ferguson, wrote on Reddit . ConnectWise has not offered much detail on the incident, other than to publish some indicators of compromise it thinks are tied to a handful of IP addresses and integrations with third-party apps. It has also disabled some integrations between Cloud Backup and Exchange, Teams, SharePoint Online, and its own products. Security outfit Huntress offered a starker view and wrote “A Microsoft 365 credential (API secret) belonging to ConnectWise Cloud Backup has been compromised, and Huntress has confirmed it is being used to gain unauthorized access to customers' M365 environments.” “In one Huntress partner tenant, a second ConnectWise application, ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams (Application ID 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640), gave itself Global Administrator and then added new credentials to two other applications in that tenant, one of them being a single-tenant Huntress application unique to this partner.” “Disabling M365 apps, including the abused ConnectWise apps will not remove credentials that were already added,” the firm warns. “You must review the credentials on all of your M365 applications.” ConnectWise says it “cannot discuss threat actor attribution at this time” because it is focused on “investigation, remediation, and supporting affected partners and their customers.” It has, however, called on its customers to probe any M365 environments they manage for signs of compromise. This is where things get tricky, because ConnectWise has no knowledge of those setups – as is proper because it is a platform provider and its MSP clients manage end-user relationships. It’s therefore relying on MSPs to do the right thing. MSPs are under no obligation to disclose the platforms they use to deliver their services. Indeed, for some organizations the allure of working with an MSP is to access packaged services they never need to learn or worry about. End-user organizations that may be happily oblivious about ConnectWise’s contribution to their business are therefore in an awkward position. Businesses that serve MSPs are a frequent target for attackers, who see the chance to compromise the likes of ConnectWise as a possible route to crack all of their partners and those service providers' end-users. The 2021 attack on Kaseya is the most notorious example of such an incident. ConnectWise will be hoping it doesn't take the crown. ®

events.title: ICANN vows to work faster, improve transparency
events.summary: Internet governance organization the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) has come to the realization it needs to move faster. The org today opened its annual conference in Bali, Indonesia, with an opening ceremony during which chair Tripti Sinha noted that it’s now just over ten years since the US government effectively handed over internet governance responsibilities from the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) to ICANN. Sinha observed that much has changed online in the last decade, but that despite predictions to the contrary at the time of the handover, ICANN has kept multi-stakeholder internet governance alive and well. “A decade later, the strongest sign of success is what did not happen,” she said. “DNS did not fragment. The coordination of unique identifiers was not destabilized. The internet continues to work.” The chair said ICANN aims to ensure that success continues and said the org must therefore evolve. “If the multi-stakeholder model is to remain credible, we must have the resolve to examine and where necessary enhance the mechanisms through which we hold ourselves accountable,” she said. ICANN last year commenced a “review of reviews” that Sinha said reflects the organization’s willingness to examine its own operations. She thinks that work is necessary in part due to the advent of artificial intelligence, which she predicted will likely create new challenges for management of the resources ICANN tends to. “Agents could reshape DNS traffic patterns and intensify demand on the systems that enable discovery, authentication, and trust online,” she said, adding that AI could both create more malicious DNS registrations and help to defend against them. “ICANN must anticipate change without rushing ahead of evidence, innovating without compromising trust,” she said, calling for the body to deliver “Governance capable of adapting to the speed of emerging risk.” ICANN CEO Kurt Erik Lindqvist touched on similar themes in his speech, calling for the body to improve its ability to support and action community priorities. “Policy development is at the heart of this community,” he said. “Different interests and perspectives have to be heard, tested, and reconsidered. Once the community has done that work ,and recommendations become policy, ICANN has a responsibility to understand what the implementation requires, to make the necessary resources available to sequence the work sensitively, and to be clear about our progress and the choices we are making along the way.” Citing recent successful work on DNS abuse mitigation, Lindqvist said ICANN knows it can nail this process. “That experience showed that we are responding with pace when the objective is clear, responsibilities are understood, and there is alignment around what needs to happen next,” he said. “I would like us to bring that same discipline and rigor to more of our work.” He therefore called for ICANN to be at its best, more often. “There will always be more work than there is time, people, and resources allow us to pursue simultaneously,” he said. “I want to work with the community on how to strengthen the connection between strategy, prioritization, budgeting, and implementation, and how to make that process more clear and transparent.” ® Bootnote : The Reg is attending ICANN's conference. Feel free to get in touch if you want to catch up here.

events.title: Oman could become a cornerstone of Gulf energy security, but risks remain
events.summary: In its heyday, Oman’s maritime empire stretched from Mozambique and Zanzibar to Gwadar in Pakistan. The modern sultanate does not extend so far, but it still holds an important position overlooking the Strait of Hormuz. Oman has gained economically from the conflict, while seeking to mediate peace. Now it could make itself a foundation stone of Gulf security. The war has forced the IMF to downgrade economic growth forecasts across the region. But Oman is expected to expand by 4.1 per cent. It has managed to bring down its debt burden from a worrying 68 per cent of GDP in 2020 to a much more comfortable 35 to 36 per cent of GDP. The sultanate benefits from record oil and gas exports at a time of high prices, as well as from the rest of its heavy industrial base in refined petroleum, fertilisers and aluminium. The endless queues of lorries to and from the UAE border tell eloquently of Oman’s essential role as a transit route for goods . In May 2024, in a fortunate piece of advance planning, construction began on Hafeet Rail, which will link the industrial city of Sohar with Al Ain and Abu Dhabi . This is intended to be finished by the final quarter of 2027 and will be an invaluable route for industrial inputs to the UAE and for the export of finished products such as steel and aluminium. By late next year, Oman should also finish a direct connection to the GCC electricity grid, allowing it to exchange more power. This will benefit its fast-growing renewable sector. Oman has not stayed entirely out of the front line during the war. The oil terminals of Mina Al Fahal, Duqm and Salalah, and Sohar were attacked by drones, and several ships have been struck in its mainland waters, not to mention all those hit while crossing the Omani lane of the Strait of Hormuz. But the sultanate has suffered much less physical damage and disruption than its Gulf neighbours. New energy routes In 2016, the oil minister at the time, Mohammed Al Rumhi announced plans for an enormous 200-million barrel petroleum storage terminal at Duqm on its south-east coast. By comparison, Fujairah, which has also emerged as a strategic node during the war and is a central global refuelling point, has about 120 million barrels of capacity. Muscat’s intention was to reorient its crude oil exports from the crowded northern coast to a new terminal, which would also have the happy effect of shifting them further from Iran. It also had in mind that other GCC nations might connect to Duqm, to give themselves an option in case of a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait, which has no alternative outlet, was said to be interested. Kuwait Petroleum Corporation eventually invested in the major new refinery there. But it seemed far-fetched that a new pipeline route would be needed. Eventually only 5.2 million barrels of crude storage were built, mostly to serve the refinery. Drones, missiles, and Washington’s decision to confront Tehran on the battlefield changed that. Now Saudi Aramco is studying a pipeline to Duqm, estimated to span 1,000 to 1,200 kilometres through the dunes of the Empty Quarter, and expected to cost $7 billion. This new node has the advantage of bypassing not just Hormuz, but also the Bab Al Mandeb strait. Saudi exports through the kingdom's East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu have been hampered by attacks from the Houthis in Yemen and Iranian allies in Iraq. A Kuwait Oil Company representative told the World Energy Congress in Riyadh last week that his country was evaluating a possible route to Duqm, as well as through the UAE or Saudi Arabia. This would most probably involve delivering oil by tanker to a Saudi or UAE port for onward transport, rather than transporting it all the way overland. State energy investor OQ has announced plans to expand Duqm’s storage to 10 million barrels within three years, and eventually 40 million barrels. It is also considering buying two tankers to hold 4 million barrels in floating storage. In September, it signed an agreement with a German company to design a new marine bunkering site at the port of Shinas, just south of the UAE border. This would be about a third the size of Fujairah, which ranks as the world’s second or third-largest ship refuelling hub. Strategic risks Nevertheless, Oman’s centrality to the Gulf’s new infrastructure carries three risks. First, its sites are not much further from Iran than the rest of the Gulf is, and can still be attacked if hostilities escalate. Indeed, Muscat might even put itself in the line of fire if Tehran decides it cannot tolerate too much by-passing of the totemic Strait of Hormuz. The second is almost the opposite: if peace breaks out, much of this infrastructure might seem unnecessary. New pipelines will take from three to five years to build. By then, regional politics and security may look very different. Projects may be terminated halfway through, or left little-used. Oman does not have the deep pockets of its neighbours, who are able to invest heavily in strategic security. Third is that many of these projects are clearly competing with existing Gulf terminals. There is already some disquiet over Muscat’s apparent closeness to Tehran at times during its mediation. Most notably, this surfaced in the debate over tolls for use of the Strait, or essentially Iranian extortion. The other Gulf nations have suffered and spent heavily in the conflict. Of course, they want to leverage Oman’s strategic depth. But they do not want to make obsolete their own decades of massive investment in centres such as Fujairah, Jebel Ali and Yanbu, and new projects at sites such as Khor Fakkan, Al Rugaylat and Dibba. Past such ventures across Iraq, Syria, Turkey and Saudi Arabia have suffered from sabotage, nationalisation, or commercial breakdowns. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman wisely pointed out that successful multinational pipelines require stakeholders from all sides. Tying Gulf security to Oman needs not only sinews of steel, but political harmony.

events.summary: Investors are pivoting from volatile tech trades to high-yield equities as low bond yields, uneven economic growth persist Chinese investors have been flocking to dividend stocks, taking shelter from market turmoil spurred by sell-offs in technology companies and K-shaped economic growth in the Asian nation. Two key gauges of the mainland-listed companies with the highest dividend yield ratios outpaced the benchmark heading into October, when fears of financial tightening in the US and China’s flagging domestic demand weighed on investors’ risk appetite. The Shanghai Stock Exchange Dividend Index of the 50 selected stocks has risen 2 per cent this month, while the CSI Dividend Index, which tracks a broader pool of 100 such stocks on the Shanghai and Shenzhen bourses, has gained 1.6 per cent. In comparison, the CSI 300 Index has fallen 4.3 per cent and the chip-centric Star Market 50 gauge has tumbled 11 per cent. The two dividend indexes offer at least a 4 per cent dividend yield, trouncing the 1.65 per cent yield on China’s 10-year government bond.

events.title: Linux KVM guest-host escape rated critical, may represent a new way to attack penguin-powered networking
events.summary: Paulos Yibelo, the researcher who in early October claimed to have found a guest-host escape flaw in Linux KVM, the hypervisor used by most hyperscale clouds, has named the flaw PwnEscape and warned it might represent a new way to attack Linux – on top of being a 9.3-rated critical nasty in its own right. Yibelo’s work is now CVE-2026-99999 . It is a scary bug because it makes a guest-host escape possible with a few malformed IPv4 packets. Such attacks are a nightmare security scenario because the whole point of virtualization is carving up hardware into isolated “guest” virtual machines that share a “host” server’s resources – without ever being able to see what other guests or the host are doing. Public clouds rely on that isolation remaining impervious. So do private clouds, because if guest/host isolation is violated, an attacker could conceivably access all the VMs on a host or pool of virtualized hardware. Attacks on a host could give an evildoer access to thousands of VMs, plus containers because many developers now run those constructs in a micro-VM to keep them isolated. PwnEscape makes it possible for guests to access the host, by sending a guest malformed IPv4 packets. As explained in a message from Red Hatter Michael S. Tsirkin in the Linux kernel stable tree, ‘If a packet with bad checksum metadata gets into the ipv4 stack, skb_checksum_help can corrupt the network header and cause a bunch of mischief.” Analysis from threat-finding firm SOC Prime details the mischief. “Linux allows network packets to carry metadata indicating where a checksum operation should begin and where its result should be written. This optimization is legitimate and widely used for checksum offloading, but the security problem arises when less-trusted guest-controlled metadata can influence a write after the packet header has already passed earlier validation stages.” “Because the disclosure could be triggered repeatedly, an attacker controlling a guest workload could potentially collect information from a security domain that the virtual machine should not be able to inspect. This represents a direct failure of the guest-host isolation boundary.” Red Hat’s report says the impact can potentially include “arbitrary code execution on the host, a system crash resulting in Denial of Service, or information disclosure of sensitive memory.” A new class of threat Paulos Yibelo, the researcher who found the flaw, thinks he stumbled upon a novel attack. “As far as we know, PwnEscape exposes an entirely new class of attacks in Linux networking: untrusted checksum metadata can rewrite security-sensitive packet fields after the kernel has already validated and acted on them, undermining assumptions across the networking stack far beyond the original VM escape,” he wrote. “The popular mental model is that VM isolation lives in the virtual-machine monitor. Much of it does. But an attacker-controlled workload does not interact only with arch/x86/kvm/ . It interacts with a host OS full of optimized, highly composable interfaces.” “If the metadata crosses a trust boundary, every deferred consumer has to inherit the right invariants. And if the packet can be transformed after those invariants are checked, the invariants have to remain true in the new representation.” “That is why a bug that looks, at first, like a malformed checksum hint can become a memory disclosure and a guest-to-host escape primitive. The problem was not how difficult IPv4 is to parse. It was that different parts of Linux were allowed to trust different versions of the same packet.” That’s an important observation, because while Linux KVM is widely used, and free, it is part of Linux – a project comprised of over 40 million lines of code. A vendor named Edera, which offers a secure container runtime based on the Xen hypervisor, last week none-too-gently pointed out that’s a big attack surface and that researchers have found seven escape bugs this year alone including Januscape . AWS, which runs its cloud on KVM, says its elastic compute cloud is not at risk . Google Cloud’s method of using KVM means it is probably in the clear, too. Developers have created an upstream fix in the Linux kernel. It’s percolating into major distros like Debian, RHEL, and Ubuntu and hopefully into virtualization products that rely on KVM, such as Nutanix and Proxmox. In the age of AI, miscreants will doubtless quickly explore Yibelo’s discoveries, making PwnScape potentially quite a moment for Linux developers and users. ®

events.title: Time Lords kill leap seconds, before they become the new Y2K bug
events.summary: The Time Lords at the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) * have decided to stop introducing leap seconds, citing the likelihood they could cause problems with internet of things devices – and therefore a Y2K scale remediation effort – as a reason for the change. As The Register reported last week, the CGPM works to harmonize Universal Time – UT1, which boffins calculate using the changing speed of Earth’s rotation – and the Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) standard that humans use to set time. We big-brained hominids can set standards but can’t do much about the fact that the speed of Earth’s rotation is variable. When our planet’s spin slows, the CGPM adds leap seconds so that UT1 and UTC are in synch. In recent years, they have even pondered a negative leap second because Earth’s rotation has sped up a little. Like all good standards orgs, the CGPM conducts years-long debates about its work. The topic of leap seconds has very much been on the agenda in recent years, as they’re increasingly hard to implement now that humanity relies on billions of devices that can usefully share the same timing data but may not easily account for leap seconds. The matter came to a head at last week’s 28 th meeting of the CGPM, at which Time Lords voted to end use of leap seconds. The possibility of a negative leap second seems to have been a major factor. “A negative leap second has not previously been applied, and it is considered to pose a high risk of causing anomalies and disruption to critical infrastructures that are largely unprepared,” the Time Lords wrote in a resolution posted after their vote. “The preparation would create, for the industries that rely on time synchronization, a need for financial investment, whose amount is estimated to be similar to their preparations for the millennium bug.” Readers may recall that in the late 1990s, the world spent billions of dollars remediating software that, due to sensible-at-the-time memory-saving measures from the early years of business computing, couldn’t comfortably handle dates after December 31, 1999. Historians now cite the global cost of Y2K remediation at $300-$600 billion. It's widely thought that money was not well-spent. The CGPM also worries about connected devices. The growing influence of IoT (Internet of Things) technologies, dispersed multi-sensor systems, smart grids, and virtual services for contemporary society, creates an increasing risk of malfunction in operation of systems and services with the insertion of any leap second, especially with a negative one,” they wrote. Another concern raised in the resolution is: “The use of different mitigation methods for leap second introductions by global service providers in their server systems, in order to avoid time steps, leads to inconsistency in timing between different systems and in the disseminated time and frequency, which do not conform to the SI unit [the standard second].” The world is home to myriad manufacturers of IoT devices, but fewer standards on how they should behave. Some manufacturers therefore build shabbily insecure devices that ship with vulnerable software that allow them to be subverted with malware, or without facilities that allow easy updates. Billions of devices could therefore fail to implement a leap second. That would become a problem because digital certificates include a notbefore value – a time before which the cert won’t be accepted. Many systems that see a misbehaving cert would reject it. It’s therefore conceivable that if a major ISP’s modems could not accommodate a leap second, the extra sliver of time’s introduction could see the carrier’s network decide its own customers are not trustworthy enough to connect. Scenarios like that rather suggest Time Lords have taken a sensibly long view regarding the perhaps-inevitable fallibility of software developers. The CGPM's replacement for leap seconds is to allow UT1 and UTC to diverge by up to 3,600 seconds under a scheme called "Continuous UTC" that comes into force next year. Humanity has lots of practice adding and removing hours thanks to Daylight Saving time, which some want to sunset . ® * The organisation’s formal name is the Conférence générale des poids et mesures, which yields the initialism CGPM

events.title: A Composable Thermal Solver For Heterogeneous 2.5D/3D-IC Packages (Cadence, Notre Dame)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Cadence Design Systems and the University of Notre Dame published “A Composable AI-Accelerated Iterative Solver for 3D-IC Thermal Modeling.” Abstract : “Accurate thermal analysis of heterogeneous 2.5D/3D-IC packages is essential yet computationally prohibitive. A single full-package FEM simulation can take hours, while AI-based surrogates treat the entire stack as a monolithic prediction target and must be retrained whenever the die count or topology changes. To address this limitation, this work proposes Domain-Decomposed AI-Accelerated Iterative Solver for Thermal Analysis (DAIST), a composable thermal solver that decomposes the global package simulation into block-level subdomain problems, replaces subdomain solvers with neural operators, and couples them through iterative exchanges of interfacial temperature and heat flux. This local-to-global architecture eliminates the topology lock-in of monolithic models: block-level neural operators can be directly reused in unseen package assemblies without retraining. The iterative coupling strategy further provides a controllable accuracy-runtime tradeoff, where the iteration budget can be adjusted to trade accuracy for runtime. Evaluated on a multi-chiplet system and an advanced packaging system, DAIST achieves up to 178× speedup over traditional FEM solvers with mean temperature errors of 0.068% and 0.323%, respectively, while demonstrating cross-topology reuse of block-level models across structurally distinct package assemblies.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: Syria and World Bank to set up recovery and rebuilding fund
events.summary: Syria and the World Bank have agreed to set up a multi-donor trust fund for the country's recovery and reconstruction, the two sides announced in a joint statement on Sunday. Damascus is continuing to rebuild after a civil war that lasted for more than a decade and had destroyed the country's infrastructure. The Syria Recovery and Reconstruction Trust Fund – or “Start” – is a multi-donor fund that aims to provide concessional financing, investment guarantees and technical assistance, and build trust, the statement said. The agreement comes after Syria took part in the International and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. The gatherings were the latest to be attended by Syrian officials since the fall of president Bashar Al Assad's regime in December 2024. Syrian Finance Minister Yisr Barnieh said the agreement helps to set the foundation for a new phase of co-operation with Damascus's international partners. Partners in the US, Europe and Middle East expressed their support for the initiative, the statement said. “An important milestone in Syria’s recovery and reconstruction journey,” Mr Barnieh wrote in a post on X. The World Bank in 2025 estimated Syria's reconstruction would cost about $216 billion , making it one of the most expensive rebuilding efforts in history. The World Bank classified this as its best “conservative” estimate. The World Bank said infrastructure accounted for 48 per cent, or $52 billion, of total damage from the civil war, followed by residential buildings at $33 billion and non-residential buildings at $33 billion. Joint Press Release Between The Syrian Arab Republic and the World Bank Group pic.twitter.com/nsrs7Gdx6E — وزارة الخارجية والمغتربين السورية (@syrianmofaex) October 18, 2026 It said the multi-donor trust fund will help to support the delivery of basic services, strengthen institutional capacities and expand economic opportunities. “We look forward to working with all partners to support a comprehensive and sustainable recovery path,” said Ousmane Dione, World Bank vice president for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Syria's transitional government has been racing to secure investment commitments to help rebuild the country's infrastructure. Some of those pledges have recently gone to the implementation phase, including DP World's $800 million towards Tartus Port . The country has secured deals with its other Gulf partners, including a $2 billion Saudi Arabian investment package to develop two airports in Aleppo, as well as other projects involving energy, real estate and telecommunications. At this week's gatherings in Thailand, Mr Barnieh also held discussions with Qatari Finance Minister Ali Al Kuwari on supporting recovery and development work, the state-run news agency Sana reported. Norway also expressed interest in contributing to the trust fund, Sana reported. Qatar has also offered financing for projects to rehabilitate Syria's electricity grids, water networks, public services and the Damascus International Airport. Baker Hughes, Caterpillar and Visa were among a delegation of about 50 US companies that visited Syria last month to explore and deepen economic ties, which came weeks after the US delisted Syria as a state sponsor of terrorism. Syria will also return to the Arab group at the International Monetary Fund beginning on November 1, leaving the Russian-led group it joined in 2012, the Finance Ministry said in a post on Telegram. The IMF restarted communications with Syria in 2025. The fund said in August it had agreed on a technical assistance programme for the country after a staff-level visit in July. The IMF has not had an Article IV consultation with Syria since 2009.

events.title: Trump defends Russia sanctions waiver as Zelenskyy rift deepens
events.summary: US President Donald Trump on Sunday defended a recent decision to waive sanctions on Russian diesel , as relations between Washington and Ukraine soured further. Mr Trump on Friday waived key provisions of a recent package of sanctions against Russia , saying in an executive order that “such a waiver is in the national interests” of the US. The order waived a requirement by him to raise duties on Russian goods imported into the US by up to 500 per cent, and a separate requirement to place tariffs of up to 100 per cent on China, India and other top buyers of Russian energy. The order was signed two days before the law's implementation deadline and came a week after Mr Trump's surprising decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel, a move that drew opposition from Europe and his Republican party. Mr Trump said the decision rested on him refraining from doing "anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table", as a resolution to end the four-and-a-half year war remains out of reach. "Perhaps more importantly, Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way," he wrote in a post on Truth Social. Mr Trump also criticised President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as Ukrainian drones struck a major oil terminal and other targets in St Petersburg after a so-called energy ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow collapsed last week. Mr Zelenskyy said Russia has continued attacks on his country's energy infrastructure despite Mr Trump's energy ceasefire announcement last week. The US leader said Mr Zelenskyy is continuing the attacks on Russian diesel refineries "knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets". He also said Mr Zelenskyy "doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did". Earlier, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the administration invoked the law's 60-day pause “so we can see what's going on”. “The only thing that has been lifted is the diesel embargo,” he said. As part of the diesel deal , Mr Trump last week said Russia would immediately send 300,000 tonnes of diesel to US and global markets, with another 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. The move was quickly condemned by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said it would help to support Russia's war machine. The Kremlin on Thursday said Russian diesel had begun to reach global markets after its agreement with Mr Trump. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told ABC the waiver does not hand Russia an “economic lifeline”. He also dismissed the backlash. “They are all wrong,” Mr Wright said. “They don’t understand what President Trump’s doing.” “This is an incentive to Russia that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine , they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export will allow it to flow to world markets. This is a carrot to try to end a war.” The Trump administration is seeking to lower US diesel prices – which have surged past $6 a gallon ($1.59 a litre) in recent weeks – before the country's midterm elections on November 3. “Does it come with some short-term political pain? It does. But that's called leadership. President Trump wants to bring peace to the world and drive energy prices down,” Mr Wright said. But Mr Zelenskyy called the diesel deals “dangerous”, adding it does not have any meaningful influence on US energy prices. He said the Strait of Hormuz's prolonged closure was the driver behind this year's energy price shock. He also told NBC he believed the US government was responsible for a recent slowdown in US-provided Starlink internet. He said he believed the decision to limit the internet speed was “the message from [the] American government”. He said Ukraine was “blocked” from US intelligence “for some period of time, and then it was deblocked by the American side”. The Ukrainian leader said during this time his country did not see Russian attacks. The US has denied it has ordered restrictions on Starlink satellite internet services to Ukraine. “President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren't true,” Mr Bessent said. He also appeared to dodge the question of whether Ukraine was still a US ally. “President Trump has made it clear that he wants to end this war; that it must stop. And President Zelenskyy presented a false binary this morning that Ukraine must win,” Mr Bessent said. “The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement. And President Trump is working on that every day.” He also said the US supports Ukraine through providing intelligence, the Starlink service, and allowing Nato to buy US arms and resell them to Ukraine. “We're not providing those to Russia,” he said. When asked a third time if Ukraine is still a US ally, Mr Bessent said: “I'm not the Secretary of State. I'm not the President.”

events.title: UAE signs agreement to hold 2029 World Bank and IMF meetings in Abu Dhabi
events.summary: The UAE has formally signed the agreement to host the 2029 annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Abu Dhabi. The deal, signed at the conclusion of the IMF and the World Bank 2026 annual meetings in Thailand, is a mark of growing international confidence in the UAE’s economic and financial ecosystem, the UAE Ministry of Finance said in a statement on Sunday. The formal pact to host the meetings also reinforces the status of the UAE – the Arab world’s second-largest economy – as a global financial hub that is helping to shape the stability and future of the global economic system. Mohamed bin Hadi Al Hussaini, Minister of State for Financial Affairs, and Khaled Balama, governor of the Central Bank of the UAE, signed the agreement in the Thai capital, Bangkok, with the World Bank president Ajay Banga and the IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva. “The signing of the agreement marks a significant milestone, reflecting … confidence in the UAE’s readiness, the efficiency of its infrastructure and financial system, and its ability to host major international events of strategic importance,” Mr Al Hussaini said. The hosting of the event in the UAE will provide global financial leaders and decision-makers with a platform to explore how to advance the financial and monetary stability agenda as well as build development finance, the minister added. The UAE’s selection to host the event builds on the country’s track record in hosting major economic events. Scheduled to be held in October 2029, the summit will return to the Emirates for the first time in more than a quarter of a century. Dubai hosted the meetings in 2003. Participation in the annual meetings has continued to grow over the years, with more than 10,000 in-person and virtual attendees welcomed at each event. Country group meetings, civil society forums and press conferences with the World Bank president and IMF managing director are also held. They are closely watched by financial experts and policymakers from around the world. The World Bank-IMF annual meetings are traditionally held at their headquarters in Washington DC, and every third year a member country is selected to host them. London was the first city outside the US to host the meetings in 1947, while the UAE and Turkey remain the only countries in the Middle East to have hosted them. “The UAE has built institutions and infrastructure with a spirit of bold ambition and partnership, cementing its role as a global hub for economic dialogue,” Mr Banga of the World Bank Group, said. “Abu Dhabi is a fitting host for the annual meetings where our focus is on development impact, and delivering jobs, growth, and financing at scale.” The meetings usually bring together finance ministers, central bank governors, policymakers and economic experts, private sector representatives, civil society, media, and academics from more than 190 countries to examine the challenges and opportunities facing the global economy. The IMF and World Bank also release their outlook for growth and financial stability, and discuss future policy direction that supports inclusive and sustainable development. “The UAE has become an important hub for ideas, finance, innovation and international co-operation,” Ms Georgieva said. The 2029 meeting in Abu Dhabi will provide an opportunity to discuss the “challenges and opportunities ahead and help shape a better future”, the IMF managing director added.

events.title: Oh no, what happened to my OOHPod? Windows command prompt puts in a surprise appearance
events.summary: The Windows command line is a marvelous thing, beloved by administrators, but not quite so welcome when you're trying to get a parcel out of a locker. Today's example of Windows behaving badly comes from Ireland and one of the nation's OOHPod postal lockers. An eagle-eyed Register reader, trying to retrieve a parcel, found the locker screen instead teasing a command prompt. For the uninitiated, OOHPod is a service where people retrieve and deposit goods in lockers. Scan your ID (or enter it on a touch screen) and the appropriate locker door springs open and the item (or items) can be retrieved. This all works, assuming whatever is running behind the scenes isn't having a bit of a moment, as our reader experienced. Instead of a welcoming display on the locker's screen, our reader found a blank screen and what looked suspiciously like a minimized command-line window. "I tapped to maximize the window," they told us, "and a sudden command prompt appeared immediately afterward." A command prompt? More like an open invitation for mischief for the average Register reader. After all, while ordinary customers might have been flustered, this was surely an opportunity to teach the engineers who allowed it a lesson. Perhaps a cheeky FORMAT , or possibly the creation of a truly cursed batch file? Or something worse? This is surely what the comment section is made for. Unfortunately (or fortunately, depending on your perspective), no pop-up keyboard appeared for our reader to unleash havoc (not that they would dream of such a thing), and there was no handy socket to plug in a peripheral. The touchscreen accepted another finger jab, and the command window went away, replaced by the usual OOHPod interface, allowing packages to be collected as normal. It was the responsible thing to do, and the bank of lockers was left in a state where the next customer would not have to worry about what this odd cmd.exe thing was all about. However, the question remains. Would you have been so responsible? Or, if there was some way to enter commands, would you have tried to turn a minor bork into a life lesson for the engineer who let Windows give passersby a glimpse of its undercrackers? ®

events.title: Dubai's economy reaches Dh473 billion in first half of 2026 as key sectors expand
events.summary: Dubai's economy reached Dh473 billion in the first half of 2026, down 2.3 per cent from a year earlier, as growth in financial services, healthcare and construction helped offset weakness in other sectors. The emirate's real gross domestic product declined from Dh484 billion in the same period last year, according to figures released on Sunday by the Dubai Data and Statistics Establishment at Digital Dubai. The slowdown came as the Iran war, which began on February 28, disrupted regional travel and trade, weighing on Dubai's tourism and transport sectors and dampening economic activity during the first half of the year. GDP at current prices, however, increased by 0.2 per cent to Dh505 billion, reflecting growth across several key sectors. Helal Almarri, director general of the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, said the figures demonstrated the emirate's ability to navigate global uncertainty. "Dubai’s H1 2026 GDP performance reflects the strength and adaptability of an economy built to navigate periods of significant global uncertainty," he said. The first-half numbers, however, mark a reversal from the 2.4 per cent annual growth recorded in the first quarter , when Dubai's economy reached Dh232 billion despite regional economic challenges. Financial and insurance activities were among the strongest performers in the first half, expanding 8.8 per cent in real terms to Dh65.9 billion, compared with Dh60.6 billion a year earlier. The sector's contribution to GDP increased to 14 per cent from 12.5 per cent, highlighting its growing importance to the emirate's economy. The expansion comes as the Dubai International Financial Centre continues to attract international financial institutions , with the number of companies operating at the financial hub exceeding 10,000 in the first half of the year. Healthcare and social work activities recorded the fastest growth, expanding 14.3 per cent, while information and communication activities increased 2.7 per cent. Construction grew 2.4 per cent in real terms, generating Dh33.2 billion in value added, while government services expanded 2.9 per cent. However, several major sectors contracted during the period. Dubai's GDP reaches AED473 billion in H1 2026 #WamNews https://t.co/x6Y1agL9wD https://t.co/G8rxQVRfZ9 — WAM English (@WAMNEWS_ENG) October 17, 2026 Wholesale and retail trade, Dubai's largest economic activity, declined 6 per cent in real terms, although it continued to account for 20.5 per cent of GDP. Transport and storage fell 7.4 per cent, while real estate activity contracted 2.5 per cent in constant prices, despite growing 5.4 per cent at current prices. Manufacturing also declined 0.9 per cent in real terms. The slowdown reflects wider economic challenges across the region, with the UAE's economy expanding just 0.4 per cent in the first half amid disruption caused by the Iran war. Free zone boost However, despite the geopolitical headwinds, trade in the first six months of this year through Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (Diez) free zones achieved another record. The total value of trade across its three economic zones climbed 17 per cent annually to Dh246 billion, Dubai Media Office said on Sunday. The results marked Diez's sixth consecutive year of record first-half trade performance, reflecting the confidence of investors and international trade stakeholders in Dubai's and the UAE's position at the heart of global trade. The value of imports during the first half rose to Dh134.8 billion, a 14 per cent increase compared to the same period last year. Re-exports grew by 22 per cent to about Dh109 billion. Trade volumes reached approximately 270,000 tonnes during the first half of the year, compared to approximately 298,000 tonnes during the same period in 2025, the media office said. Projects continue Dubai is moving ahead with Dh2.1 trillion in projects covering housing, aviation and transport, including the expansion of Al Maktoum International Airport, as part of efforts to support long-term economic growth. Meanwhile, Dubai CommerCity announced a Dh1.8 billion expansion this month to boost its digital commerce sector and attract more technology investment. Mr Almarri said that continued growth across strategic sectors highlighted the strength of Dubai's economic fundamentals and its focus on long-term development. Dubai is pressing ahead with its D33 economic agenda, which aims to strengthen its position as a global business and investment centre. The emirate has also introduced measures to support businesses, including a Dh1.5 billion economic relief package announced in May to help sectors affected by regional uncertainty.

A New Generation of Windows PCs Has Arrived RTX Spark brings decades of NVIDIA accelerated computing innovation into a single superchip, combining an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and NVIDIA Grace CPU with up to 1 petaflop of AI compute and up to 128GB of unified memory. Read more in the press release . RTX Spark Launch Celebrations Light Up Berlin The arrival of RTX Spark brought fans, creators and PC enthusiasts together in Berlin during the Festival of Lights, an annual autumn art festival that transforms the German capital’s most famous landmarks, streets and squares into glowing canvases. This year, the festival featured RTX Spark-themed lighting on the Berlin TV Tower. Fans gathered hours ahead in anticipation for the launch celebration at XPERION, the gaming venue inside Saturn at Alexanderplatz, where attendees got hands-on with RTX Spark laptops from leading PC makers, exploring the latest gaming experiences, content-creation workflows and local AI capabilities. The celebration included a special appearance by Huang, who greeted an enthusiastic crowd, passed out popcorn and posed for selfies. He also gave out five personally signed RTX Spark laptops. Berlin held one of six RTX Spark retail launch celebrations worldwide. From San Francisco to Seoul: How the World Welcomed RTX Spark A massive crowd gathered at the JD MALL Shuangjing Store in Beijing to celebrate the highly anticipated launch, enjoying a night of innovation and community connection. Attendees at Vatan Bilgisayar Topkapı in Istanbul experienced a lively event filled with interactive demonstrations and specialized programming led by local creators. Seoul’s COEX East Lobby transformed into a bustling hub of creativity, hosting an eager crowd for engaging hands-on demos and captivating evening sessions dedicated to gaming and AI. Tech enthusiasts in San Francisco visited the local Best Buy store for an unforgettable morning of hands-on RTX Spark demos, fireside chats with local founders and a special appearance by tech influencer iJustine. The energy at Muse Garden in Taipei was electric as the local AI community came together for a vibrant evening of music, engaging discussions and incredible product showcases. Developers and AI enthusiasts can explore NVIDIA-tested recipes, playbooks and resources for running local AI on RTX Spark .
